rows.title: Meloni presses ahead with Italian election law that boosts far-right rival
rows.content:
Giorgia Meloni presses ahead with Italian election law that boosts far-right rival
Giorgia Meloni is pushing ahead with a contentious voting system redesign that analysts say will boost the influence of her far-right rival Roberto Vannacci in next year’s general elections.
The Senate on Tuesday approved the new law, which is designed to give a “majority bonus” to the coalition that wins the most votes, provided they reach a threshold of at least 42 per cent of the votes. It still needs final approval from the lower house.
Meloni’s Brothers of Italy has argued the new rules will guarantee political stability by delivering a clear winner — with an obvious ruling majority — immediately after an election, instead of protracted coalition building following the vote.
But the surging popularity of Vannacci’s Futuro Nazionale, which accuses Meloni’s ruling coalition of selling out its rightwing ideals, is drawing support away from her and her allies, Forza Italia and the League. Analysts say Meloni’s re-election prospects may now hinge on her willingness to ally with Vannacci, who opposes her support for Ukraine.
“This reform was conceived in a moment when Vannacci was not part of the picture,” said Lorenzo Pregliasco, co-founder of YouTrend, a political pollster. “It was designed . . . when Meloni did not expect to have an opposition to her right, which could erode support and prove decisive in the national election.”
Vannacci, Italy’s former military attaché to Moscow, has voiced admiration for Vladimir Putin’s Russia and has called for a normalisation of ties with Moscow while blaming Ukraine for rising petrol prices.
So far, Meloni has publicly ruled out any tie-up with any party that refuses to support Ukraine, and has accused Vannacci of acting in the interests of the leftwing opposition. But analysts suggest her views may change as elections draw closer.
“We should not exclude the possibility that in the end, Meloni will ally with Vannacci,” said Lorenzo Castellani, a political historian at Rome’s Luiss University. “The new system is designed to enlarge the coalition as much as possible.”
Surveys indicate Futuro Nazionale, which was founded earlier this year after Vannacci split from the League, polls at about 8 per cent, ahead of Forza Italia or the League. Analysts say if Vannacci’s popularity continues to rise, Meloni could be compelled to seek an alliance.
“If Vannacci keeps growing, it becomes more and more difficult to keep him out,” Pregliasco said. “You can get to a point where keeping Vannacci out somewhat means you’re not competitive.”
In Italy’s 2022 general elections, Meloni’s three-party alliance trounced a divided opposition, especially in the first-past-the-post constituencies that at present account for a third of parliamentary seats.
But with opposition parties now aiming to run as a bloc, Meloni sought to change the electoral system to reduce the likelihood of a hung parliament.
Under the new law, first-past-the-post constituencies will be eliminated in favour of full proportional representation. The pre-election alliance that wins the most votes will receive a “bonus” of up to 17.5 per cent of seats in parliament to ensure a stable ruling majority.
To claim that majority bonus, the winners must secure at least 42 per cent of the vote, creating strong incentives for both the centre-right and centre-left to form broad-based alliances ahead of the vote to ensure they come out on top.
YouTrend on Tuesday projected that under the new law, and with the current levels of support for Italy’s many different political parties, Meloni’s centre-right coalition would lose to a unified centre-left coalition unless she brought Futuro Nazionale into her fold.
YouTrend projected that under the existing law — used in the last general election — Italy would end up with a hung parliament, though with elections up to a year away, much could still change.
“The new electoral law makes it very visible that if you don’t form a clear-cut alliance before the election with Vannacci as a member of the coalition, you might lose the election,” said political analyst Roberto D’Alimonte.
Lawmakers within the ruling coalition — especially in Forza Italia and the League — were still unhappy, D’Alimonte said, believing that the new system was “backfiring” and that they would fare better if the next election took place under the existing law.
However, Meloni has reportedly threatened to ask President Sergio Mattarella to call snap elections if the election reform fails. That, D’Alimonte said, gave members of her alliance strong incentive to vote yes. “They will vote for it grudgingly,” he said.
After the open vote in the Senate, the reform will return to the lower house of parliament for final approval by secret ballot. Speculation is rife that the law could yet be rejected once MPs are protected by anonymity.
“If they feel that the previous law was better than this one, they could play some tricks . . . like people not turning up in parliament,” said Daniele Albertazzi, an Italian politics specialist at the University of Surrey. “They could still find a way to shoot it down if they wanted to.”

rows.title: Lib Dem leader Ed Davey urged to ditch the stunts and get serious
rows.content:
Lib Dem leader Ed Davey urged to ditch the stunts and get serious
Two years ago, Sir Ed Davey rode into his party’s annual conference in Brighton on a jet ski. In 2025, he headed up a marching band with confetti cannons.
But on Saturday, in the wake of calls from within the party to dial back the stunts and get serious, the Liberal Democrat leader’s conference opener was tamer: cooking fish and chips on the seaside resort’s pier.
“I think what you’ll see at this conference from Ed is a slightly different side,” deputy leader Daisy Cooper told the FT, emphasising the focus on outlining the party’s policies on the economy, immigration and defence.
Davey was not just a “playful centrist dad”, she said, but an economist, carer and a former cabinet minister in David Cameron’s coalition government, all crucial experience “given where we’re at in our politics”.
On Saturday, Davey promised to “take the brakes off the British economy” and “defend the traditional values that make our country great” — including fighting for “the intrinsic worth of every single human being”.
During the 2024 general election campaign, Davey bungee jumped to ask Conservative voters to take a “leap of faith” by voting Lib Dem, fell off a paddle board to raise awareness of sewage pollution and launched himself down a waterslide to raise awareness about children’s mental health.
These photo opportunities gained attention and helped propel the party to its best general election result in more than a century in 2024, with 72 seats.
But the approach was not without hiccups. One ill-conceived event involving Davey doing archery to promote the party’s new bereavement policy had to be cancelled at short notice because of concerns it was in poor taste, two people familiar with the matter said.
And in recent months, MPs’ simmering frustration at their party’s lack of progress in opinion polls has centred on what they see as a failure to convey what the Lib Dems care about.
“You can go back to the well too many times,” one senior MP said of Davey’s stunts, adding that the leader had “an opportunity . . . to define himself better to the public”.
There are “more parties competing in politics than ever, but the political centre ground has never been so unoccupied”, they said, pointing to the Tories’ rightward shift.
They added it was frustrating that the party had allowed Nigel Farage’s Reform UK to “steal our clothes” on its promise to raise the tax-free personal allowance threshold — part of the Lib Dems’ 2024 manifesto and a move it pushed for in the coalition government.
Despite its record haul of MPs at the last election, the Lib Dems are flatlining in fifth place in the polls. When pollster YouGov asked respondents to describe Davey last month, the two most frequent responses were “don’t know” and “who?”.
MPs raised concerns with Davey earlier this year that the party was “irrelevant in the national conversation”, one of the group said. One of the main messages was “stop these stupid stunts”, they said.
“If that’s all you’re putting out, you’re just chucking spaghetti at the wall and seeing what sticks,” they said, adding that they were now happier with what they viewed as a change in direction.
A senior strategist denied a shift in tactics, saying “very nice visuals” remained an important part of the party’s communications strategy. The focus was now on “preparations for the next elections”, they added.
In recent weeks, the party has hired a new political director, a new chief of staff for Davey, a new deputy communications director and a new head of comms. It has also expanded its social media team with hires including a TikTok influencer.
But structural barriers to the Lib Dems’ ability to connect with the public remain, including their position as the third-largest group in a parliament structured for a two-party system.
Frustrations were laid bare this week when the Commons Speaker denied the party’s request for an urgent question on artificial intelligence.
“We’re a huge chunk of the opposition, and that is not really reflected in speaking time, amendments . . . debates” or share of Prime Minister’s Questions, said MP Danny Chambers. “That’s why it’s even more important for us to ensure we improve our media and social media output.”
Asked about the party’s polling, Davey told Sky News on Sunday: “It’s elections that ultimately matter in politics. There are exciting politicians around. Donald Trump’s terribly exciting, he’s damaging America and he’s damaging the world. Nigel Farage is terribly exciting, he wants to bring Trump’s America to the UK and damage our country . . . I want to put forward practical, well-thought-through policies that will help people’s lives.”
He pointed to the party’s new “cost of living” announcements: a fuel duty cut and a £1 cap on bus fares. He also told the BBC that despite MPs’ frustrations, “I think we’re the most united party, actually,” blaming the party’s slow progress on the set-up of parliament.
A former senior party figure said it was time “for the party to shift into the new era of British politics” and “position itself as the answer . . . to a lot of anxiety and fears in the country” in response to the rise of Reform. “The stakes have got significantly higher,” they said.
Cooper said she agreed on the need for seriousness, but with a caveat: “I genuinely hope that it’s not the end of seeing [Davey’s] more playful side.”
Additional reporting by George Parker in London

rows.title: AI debt vs Treasuries
rows.content:
Good morning. Happy Fed day to all who observe, and good luck to Kevin Warsh. As Rob wrote the other day, we think a US rate increase makes sense, even leaving questions of central bank credibility. The big question is whether the Fed can, with rates or rhetoric, help pull Treasury yields down. The 10-year yield closed at a 19-year high yesterday. The latest fund manager survey from Bank of America, released yesterday, asked respondents to name the biggest tail risk for the market. The most popular response: a disorderly rise in bond yields, just a bit ahead of a bursting AI bubble. But why pick one when you could have both? Send us happier thoughts: [email protected]
Crowded house
Are the hyperscalers eating Scott Bessent’s lunch? More prosaically: are Big Tech companies issuing so much debt that they are leaving investors with less room in their portfolios for Treasuries? The idea often features prominently on the laundry list of reasons why Treasury yields are flying higher.
There’s something to this; bond investors and bankers have told us so. The question is the size of the effect. Lotfi Karoui of Pimco thinks it’s small:
If you go back to the last 12 months and you look at the largest hyperscaler deals, and look at the performance of Treasuries around those deal announcements, you don’t really see any abnormal returns around those days . . . Of course, that may change a year from now as you bring more debt, more variety. But for now, the market narrative has kind of got ahead of itself a little bit.
If hyperscaler debt was really crowding out Treasuries then we would have seen a big rise in the term premium for sovereign debt, Karoui argues. And when you look at the data, there has been a bit of a pick-up in the term premium since late June — but a more noticeable uptick in the inflation expectations:
The hyperscaler crowding-out argument relies on the notion that tech bonds are a substitute for Treasuries. Are they? Meghan Robson at BNP Paribas thinks the substitution is highly imperfect, for the simple reason that the tech bonds contain spread risk and Treasuries do not. And as hyperscalers issue more debt, the risk of widening credit spreads becomes more acute:
A lot of the debt issuance we’ve seen this year and that we forecast has been from the hyperscalers issuing long-duration debt. Ten years and beyond represents over two-thirds of the debt they’ve sold. It is in the same wheelhouse of maturity or duration to some of the Treasury yields in terms of competition.
But looking forward, our forecast for corporate supply for the first time and looking into 2027 actually exceeds Treasury supply; that’s excluding T-bills on the Treasury side, just looking at coupon [ie longer duration] issuance. Our forecast for hyperscaler issuance this year is $250bn. Next year we see a number closer to $400bn, and we don’t see demand necessarily keeping pace with that growth. So we see the floor on credit spreads as a bit higher.
Karoui at Pimco also points out that corporate debt in general, and hyperscaler debt in particular, is not as easy to trade as Treasuries. Even with improvements in secondary market corporate liquidity over the past decade, and loads of recent hyperscaler issuance, the corporate market is much shallower than the world’s largest debt market. “You could take the most liquid investment-grade corporate bond and calculate the turnover on that, and it will be a fraction of what you can get in Treasuries,” he says.
Ed Al-Hussainy of Columbia Threadneedle argues that crowding-out should show up in the relative performance of Treasuries and interest rate swaps, but it doesn’t:
If crowding out and fiscal factors were significant, we would see cash long-end Treasury bonds (which have a term premium) perform poorly relative to interest rate swaps (which just price the Fed). But this hasn’t happened. So I’m left with more evidence for a Fed repricing driving rates more than anything else.
There are enough big, unconstrained bond managers with a mandate to buy across sovereign and corporate bonds that there is probably some crowding-out of Treasuries at the margin. But there are much bigger forces at work on yields.
One good read
FT Unhedged podcast
Can’t get enough of Unhedged? Keep following Rob Armstrong and Katie Martin’s incisive and unfiltered analysis on the Unhedged podcast, a twice-weekly, 15-minute lively dive into the latest markets news and financial headlines. New episodes every Tuesday and Thursday.

rows.title: ECB staff demand clarity over Lagarde’s potential early exit
rows.content:
ECB staff demand clarity over Christine Lagarde’s potential early exit
The European Central Bank’s staff committee has urged its leadership to clarify whether president Christine Lagarde will leave before the end of her term, warning that “prolonged uncertainty” risks damaging trust in the institution.
In a letter to the ECB’s executive board, staff representatives warned that instability could “affect trust in the ECB’s communications, create concern among staff and stakeholders, and complicate the orderly planning of leadership succession and strategic priorities”.
The intervention reflects tensions between staff and the ECB’s leadership over internal governance. Lagarde has publicly stated that she will stay until 2027 but repeatedly avoided any commitment to finish her eight-year term, which expires in October 2027. She told journalists last week that there was “nothing to report” about her future.
An ECB spokesperson said it had ‘‘long-established institutional governance arrangements and great depth of expertise to ensure that it operates smoothly during periods of transition, and past changes have demonstrated that’’. Lagarde and the WEF declined to comment via their spokespeople.
The committee also asked the board to make clear whether executive board member Isabel Schnabel could leave before her term ends in December 2027. She is among several candidates in talks with the IMF to succeed Tobias Adrian as head of its monetary and capital markets department.
The staff representatives called on the institution’s leadership “to provide appropriate clarity regarding potential leadership transitions”, warning that the senior departures could “delay or dilute” reforms addressing its “speak-up culture, career incentives and confidence in internal processes”.
The committee pointed to the ECB’s 2025 staff survey, in which only 40 per cent of respondents said they felt able to express their views freely without fear of negative consequences.
New executive board members needed time to understand the issues at the central bank, the letter said.
Lagarde has been facing questions about a potential early exit since May last year, when the former chair of the World Economic Forum Klaus Schwab told the FT that he and Lagarde discussed the possibility of her moving to the WEF before the end of her term.
The WEF is expected to take a decision about its permanent next chair by November, with Lagarde being the preferred candidate, people familiar with the matter told the FT.
The FT reported earlier on Monday that Eurozone governments were gearing up for one of the biggest leadership reshuffles in the ECB’s 28-year history, with a deal over its three top roles expected to be agreed by the end of December.
A recent announcement that Lagarde’s autobiography Lady First would be published in January further fuelled speculation among ECB watchers that she might leave before the end of her term.
Asked last week how she would ensure that her public role as ECB president and commercial promotion of her book would be kept separate, Lagarde told journalists that “any marketing” would happen either on weekends or during her holidays.

rows.title: Oil price surge revives prospect of Bank of England rate rise this year
rows.content:
Oil price surge revives prospect of Bank of England rate rise this year
Surging oil prices are set to reopen debate at the Bank of England over whether it needs to increase interest rates before the end of the year, as policymakers prepare to meet later this week.
The Monetary Policy Committee will convene to discuss both its key rate and the pace at which it shrinks its balance sheet under the shadow of a bond-market sell-off that is putting mounting pressure on the government of Prime Minister Andy Burnham ahead of the October 28 Budget.
Markets are pricing in a less than one-in-three chance of a rise in borrowing costs on Thursday at the MPC’s September policy meeting. But rising energy prices driven by a renewed escalation of the war in the Middle East, accelerating inflation, and relatively robust UK GDP growth are set to prompt an intensifying debate within the BoE over how long it can keep its key rate at 3.75 per cent.
“The MPC’s patience may be running thin and the case for staying on hold is weakening slowly,” said Sanjay Raja, an economist at Deutsche Bank.
The European Central Bank on Thursday raised its own key interest rate — albeit from lower levels — and the US Federal Reserve is viewed by investors as likely to follow suit this week.
Traders will be laser-focused on the voting split among BoE rate setters, with the market consensus expecting six votes for holding rates, and three for a rise, according to LSEG data.
Some think that the surge in oil prices above $100 is testing the assumptions of the doves that broader effects of the Iran inflation shock will be contained and could lead to a more hawkish outcome.
Official data on unemployment and inflation is also due to be published in the days before the rates announcement on Thursday.
“With [the GDP] figures, with oil and the energy shock being far more persistent than the expectation . . . I think there is a real risk of getting to 5-4, but even potentially having a surprise hike,” said Akshay Singal, global head of short-term interest rate trading at Citi.
The market is currently pricing in four quarter-point rate rises by this time next year, compared with the two or three earlier this month, according to levels implied by swaps contracts.
A move at the BoE’s November meeting is now fully priced in. Andrew Bailey, the BoE governor, signalled increased concern about inflation in a hearing at the Treasury select committee on Tuesday, saying the “upside risks” were rising given the ongoing Gulf war.
Some investors believe the BoE’s inflation-fighting credentials could be at risk if it fails to keep up with other central banks as they lift borrowing costs, potentially weakening the pound.
Ales Koutny, head of international rates at asset management giant Vanguard, said there was “an element of credibility now” if the BoE did not follow suit in the coming months.
Allan Monks, UK economist at JPMorgan, said he expects inflation to hit 4 per cent or higher by early next year — double the BoE’s official target.
Investors are also awaiting a decision on the future of the BoE’s so-called quantitative tightening programme of reducing the government bond holdings that it built up through widescale purchases in past crises, and which has added upward pressure to UK borrowing costs.
Gilt market participants expect the BoE to slow its balance sheet shrinkage from £70bn to £50bn in the year to September 2027, which would imply about £20bn of active sales of gilts, including some long-dated debt.
Some think the BoE could further reduce or pause long-dated sales to the market following a brutal global sell-off driven by rising energy prices and inflation worries, as well as mounting concerns over a borrowing glut. The selling drove 30-year gilt yields this week close to 6 per cent, a level they have not crossed since 1998.
“Clearly there is space for them to send a message of support to the long end,” said Vanguard’s Koutny.

rows.title: Houthis launch missile at Saudi capital in escalation of hostilities
rows.content:
Houthis launch missile at Saudi capital in escalation of hostilities
Houthi rebels launched a missile attack on Riyadh, the first time the Iran-backed rebels have targeted the Saudi capital since reigniting the more than a decade-long war.
A Saudi military spokesperson said the kingdom’s air defences intercepted a ballistic missile in the early hours of Saturday.
Residents in Riyadh said they heard a loud boom around the time of the attack and smoke was seen rising from near the capital’s airport. Authorities did not report any damage, but the attack on Riyadh and other cities in the kingdom underscored the threat posed by the Houthis.
The Houthis said in a statement that their forces targeted Riyadh and Yanbu, a port on the Red Sea that is home to vital oil infrastructure, claiming the attacks “resulted in large fires at the targeted sites”.
The Saudi authorities had also issued air alert warnings late on Friday for Jeddah, Saudi Arabia’s second city, and half a dozen other cities. The Saudi military spokesperson said the rebels targeted Taif, Baish and the Red Sea island of Farasan.
After the latest attacks, the US issued a fresh travel warning advising Americans to “exercise heightened vigilance and be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions”.
Over the past 10 days the Houthis have escalated their attacks on Saudi Arabia, while mounting a lightning advance southwards along Yemen’s Red Sea coast to tighten their grip on the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a critical international waterway.
Saudi authorities said dozens of people have been wounded in the Houthis’ missile and drone attacks on the kingdom this month and that some oil operations in the south have been halted.
Separately, a drone attack this month from Iraq, where Iran-aligned Shia militias and Tehran’s Revolutionary Guards are active, forced the state oil company Saudi Aramco to close a pipeline it uses to ship crude from the east to Yanbu.
The attacks have pushed oil prices to their highest levels since mid-May.
Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen’s civil war in 2015 to lead an Arab coalition against the Houthis after the rebels seized Sana’a, the Yemeni capital, and ousted the internationally recognised government.
The warring parties agreed a truce in 2022 that had largely held until the Houthis declared in July that they were imposing a blockade on the kingdom’s ports and attacked Saudi tankers.
They then launched an offensive against Saudi-backed factions aligned with the Yemeni government to advance on Bab al-Mandeb. It has become a vital route for Saudi Arabia to export oil after Iran blocked shipping through the Strait of Hormuz in retaliation for the US-Israel war against the Islamic republic.
Analysts said the Houthis, who receive arms and technology from Iran, have developed more advanced weaponry in recent years.
The rebels want Riyadh to make concessions, including paying salaries in areas under Houthi control, allowing the militants access to Yemen’s oil revenues and enabling free movement at ports and airports controlled by the rebels.
But their escalation also bolsters Iran’s efforts to maintain pressure on global energy prices in its battle with the US.
The Houthis have accused Saudi Arabia of launching more than 300 air strikes in Yemen over the past week, as the Saudi-backed Yemeni factions seek to reverse the rebels’ offensive along the Red Sea coast.

rows.title: Inflation and interest rates tracker: see how your country compares
rows.content:
Inflation and interest rates tracker: see how your country compares
The FT global inflation and interest rates tracker provides a regularly updated picture of consumer price inflation and central bank policy rates around the world.
Our tracker features the latest inflation and policy rate data for most countries, historical figures, as well as key factors affecting policymakers’ decisions on borrowing costs. Bookmark this page to keep up to date as the global inflation story evolves.
Country-by-country overview
Many central banks have been lowering borrowing costs as global inflation gradually eases from the multi-decade highs recently recorded in many countries.
While inflation in most nations has come down from its peak, many policymakers have warned that the last leg of the journey to central banks’ target — which in most advanced economies is 2 per cent — will be the hardest.
Policy rate decisions
This chart shows the outcome of central bank decisions since the pandemic, when many policymakers moved to lower borrowing costs.
Higher borrowing costs helped ease the fast pace of price growth that swept the world during the pandemic, but many countries have now entered a fresh cycle of lowering rates.
How inflation swept the world
Entering the pandemic, inflation rates in many advanced economies were at or near the two per cent target level. But that changed, as this global animation shows.
Post-pandemic supply chain disruptions and rising energy prices resulting from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine triggered a wave of inflation that left few countries untouched.
Latest CPI figures
This chart allows you to compare consumer price index figures for any three countries.
Data in this chart is updated regularly following key releases from national statistics offices.
Central bank policy rates
This chart allows you to compare borrowing costs for up to three countries.
Data in this chart is updated regularly following central bank policy decisions.
CPI by component
The latest figures for the world’s largest economies show that core inflation, a key measure of underlying price pressures that excludes food and energy, remains elevated in many G7 countries.
Energy costs
A rise in energy prices was the main driver of inflation in many countries in recent years, but gas and electricity costs have retreated from their peaks during the energy crisis that followed Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Interest rate expectations
The yields on 2-year government bonds are strongly affected by market expectations of interest rates over that time.
House prices
The cost of homes soared in many countries during the pandemic, but high mortgage rates have led to a slowdown in house price growth in a number of countries.

rows.title: Saudi leader visits Egypt as war with Houthis intensifies
rows.content:
Saudi leader visits Egypt as war with Houthis intensifies
Houthi missile and drone attacks have targeted several Saudi Arabian towns this week, injuring more than a dozen people in the south as the Iranian-backed movement keeps up a days-long assault on the kingdom that has jolted oil markets and opened a new front in the Middle East conflict.
In a sign of Riyadh attempting to demonstrate “business as usual”, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman went ahead on Tuesday with a long-planned state visit to Egypt to meet President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi.
The two leaders committed to ensuring freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and the Red Sea, Egyptian state media said. Sisi also stressed Egypt’s support for measures taken by Saudi Arabia to protect its security and stability and “to reach a comprehensive and sustainable political solution to the Yemen crisis”.
But Riyadh is facing a deepening crisis as the Houthis have dragged the kingdom back into conflict, while an attack by Iranian-aligned militants in Iraq last week forced Saudi Arabia to shut its East-West oil pipeline, vital for its export crude since Iran throttled shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
The Houthis said they had fired dozens of drones and missiles at King Khalid air base in Khamis Mushait on Monday, in response to more than 300 air strikes against the rebels in Yemen over the past five days.
According to Saudi military spokesman Major General Turki al-Malki, the Houthi attacks targeted the Saudi towns of Abha and Taif as well as Khamis Mushait, wounded 13 civilians and damaged seven houses. The wounded, he said, suffered “minor to moderate injuries”.
In the early hours of Tuesday, residents of Jeddah, Saudi Arabia’s second city, Yanbu, where vital oil facilities are based, Taif and Al-Ulah were woken by a shrill alert on their phones warning them of a threat in their area and urging them to follow safety instructions. A second phone message later told them the threat had passed.
There were no reports of attacks on those cities. Similar phone alerts went off later on Tuesday, at about 1pm, in Jeddah and Mecca, home to Islam’s holiest site. While the warnings caused some nervousness, Jeddah residents said life was going on as normal.
Since reigniting a more than decade-long war with Saudi Arabia in July, the Houthis have targeted energy facilities in the kingdom and attacked Saudi tankers. Last week, they launched a lightning offensive southwards along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, pushing back Saudi-backed forces aligned to the Yemeni government and tightening their grip over the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
The strategic waterway has become crucial to Riyadh’s ability to avoid the Strait of Hormuz and export oil to Asia, and is also vital for global shipping between east and west through the Suez Canal.
The multiple attacks on Saudi Arabia, the world’s top oil exporter, and the Houthis’ advance along the Red Sea coast have pushed up crude prices to their highest levels since mid-May.
They have also shattered a four-year ceasefire between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis that had brought relative calm to Yemen’s civil war.
Riyadh had intervened in the conflict in 2015 to lead an Arab coalition against the Houthis after the rebels seized Sana’a, the capital, and ousted the internationally recognised government.
Before the truce took hold in 2022, the Houthis fired regular missile and drone barrages into the kingdom, most of which were intercepted by Saudi air defences.
But the Houthis’ latest escalation comes as stocks of interceptor missiles across the region have been depleted because of Iran’s retaliatory attacks since the US and Israel launched their war against the Islamic republic.

rows.title: The Iran energy shock is wrongfooting the world
rows.content:
Five ways the Iran energy shock is wrongfooting the world
Just as the global economy seemed to be shaking off its fever from this year’s energy crisis, the temperature is rising again and the prognosis is worsening.
The price of crude oil has pushed past $100 this month and inflationary pressures are mounting in the US, the EU and the UK. Fuel price protests have broken out from Syria to Guatemala, while India and the Philippines have introduced emergency energy-saving measures.
The summer was characterised by what many see in retrospect as a false sense of security. In June the US and Iran signed a deal to extend their fragile truce and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the world’s main oil chokepoint, allowing over 130 tankers to escape the Gulf and deliver their cargoes to the world.
The deal soon collapsed, and there now seems little prospect of a speedy end to the conflict, even as the Russia-Ukraine war puts further pressure on energy prices.
Many experts warn that the oil and gas market may be dangerously tight in the autumn and winter, with serious consequences for inflation and growth. Joe Brusuelas, chief economist at accounting firm RSM US, warns the world has entered “oil shock 2.0”.
He adds that central banks will need to “slow down the global economy if they want to push the inflation genie back into the bottle”.
But the energy price shock is not what many people think it is. Here are five ways in which it is wrongfooting the world.
Economists were too pessimistic. Now they face the opposite problem
To date, global growth has defied many economists’ forecasts, partly because the oil and gas trade turned out to be unexpectedly resilient after the US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28.
Fatih Birol, the head of the International Energy Agency, warned in March that the world was facing “the greatest global energy security threat in history”, referring to the scale of oil and gas cut off from global markets.
But although countries began preparing for shortages of key fuels, prices never broke through previous records because of a co-ordinated release of 400mn barrels of strategic reserves, the withdrawal of China from buying crude and the robustness of the global trading system.
The world economy grew at the same annualised pace in the second quarter of the year as in the first, according to calculations by Capital Economics, a research firm. Those numbers omit the six Gulf Cooperation Council nations, which include Saudi Arabia, the world’s top oil exporter, the United Arab Emirates, and Qatar, the second-largest producer of liquefied natural gas.
Isabelle Mateos y Lago, group chief economist at BNP Paribas, sees such economic resilience as the result of a “tug of war” between the AI boom, which has stoked growth, and the energy crisis. She thinks the trend can continue, noting the scale of capital expenditures on data centres and AI.
But the price pressures are making themselves felt. On Wednesday, the US Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time since 2023; it is far from the only central bank applying the brakes in response to the inflationary pressures caused by the war.
Last week the European Central Bank warned of “risks to the upside” for inflation and to the “downside” for economic growth, as it increased rates for the second time since the seven-month-old war began. On Friday, the Bank of Japan took its rate to a 31-year-high.
Neil Shearing at Capital Economics warns that if crude oil prices hover between $110 and $120 a barrel for the next six months, global growth would fall towards 2 per cent — markedly slower than last year’s rate of 3.5 per cent.
“It would start to feel pretty recessionary,” he says.
Fears of slower growth as central banks increase borrowing costs are also feeding back into the oil market, potentially putting a ceiling on how high crude prices will go.
This is a fuel crisis, not an oil crisis
The price of crude oil has traditionally been the warning signal for the global economy.
But consumers do not buy crude oil, they buy petrol, diesel and jet fuel, and it is the price of these fuels that ultimately feeds through into inflation.
Over the course of the Iran war, fuel markets have been far tighter than crude markets because of a shortage of capacity to refine oil into fuel and the high cost of shipping it to the right places.
As early as June, even as crude oil prices were coming down, Tom Baker, the head of oil trader Vitol in the Middle East, was warning about a gloomy outlook for refined fuels for the rest of this year.
That month, China’s independent refineries cut production to a nine-year low after a government ban on exports left them unable to sell fuel overseas.
In Russia, the world’s third-largest refiner after the US and China, a sustained campaign of drone attacks by Ukraine has reduced production by 30 per cent in the past year to its lowest level in over two decades. Ukraine has now hit all but four of Russia’s 32 largest refineries — the only four to escape are all in eastern Siberia.
By August, exports of diesel from the huge refineries in the Middle East had fallen to a quarter of their prewar level according to the IEA, which has been co-ordinating the response to the crisis.
The world’s refineries have been running at full speed. But they have been unable to catch up with the losses. Global output of refined fuels was over 4mn barrels a day lower in August than a year earlier, according to the IEA.
This month, the price of diesel in the US and Europe passed $200 a barrel and US diesel prices passed $6 a gallon for the first time ever, almost double their prewar level. Diesel, which is essential for trucking, as well as for heating in the winter, accounts for almost a third of global oil demand.
Things could get worse. China, which allowed its refineries to start exporting fuel again over the summer, is widely thought to be considering a fresh ban after seeing its domestic fuel stocks fall. If Beijing halts exports a second time, fuel prices will be under severe pressure.
This is not an old-fashioned oil shock
Even at $110 a barrel, oil is not as expensive as it used to be.
The record price for a barrel of Brent crude was $147.50 in 2008, the equivalent of $230 a barrel today when adjusted for inflation. Oil averaged more than $110 a barrel in 2011 and 2012, or $165 in today’s money.
Nor has the price rise been as steep as in the past: between 1973 and 1974, after Arab producers imposed an embargo in response to western support for Israel in the Yom Kippur war, prices quadrupled to $12 a barrel (worth $82 today).
Oil production is also less concentrated in the Middle East. The US is now the world’s largest producer, ensuring it will not have a supply shortage, and Canada, Brazil, Guyana, Venezuela have all increased production during the Iran crisis.
More importantly, a barrel of oil matters less to the global economy than it used to. Oil’s share of global energy demand has fallen below 30 per cent from a peak of 46 per cent half a century ago. At the same time, the amount of energy needed to produce a unit of GDP has fallen by more than a third since 1990.
Ben May, head of global macroeconomic research at Oxford Economics, says the inflationary impact of the Iran war has been dulled because “we went into the crisis with favourable oil supply” at a time when overall economic demand was “steady rather than spectacular”.
When the war began, by contrast with the 1970s energy shock, the world had strategic reserves, an oil glut and growing supplies of liquefied natural gas, and a sophisticated trading system in which thousands of tankers criss-crossed the globe.
Still, higher hydrocarbon prices have already led to changes in behaviour, such as a faster pace of electric vehicle sales in Europe and Asia. Over the past seven months, Chinese petrochemical plants have cut production, airlines have trimmed marginal routes and Asian countries have switched from gas to other fuels, including coal.
Gas prices have also risen 160 per cent since the war started and have been rising further in recent weeks. The continent is approaching winter without its usual backup stores.
Poor countries get hit the hardest
Protests broke out in Syria this week after the government raised diesel prices by 40 per cent and petrol by nearly 30 per cent, due to what it called “an exceptional increase in the global cost of procurement”.
Bangladesh and Pakistan have both struggled to import gas. Restaurants across India were forced to close because they had run out of liquefied petroleum gas. The Philippines declared a national emergency and mandated working from home.
By far the most common response to the crisis, according to the IEA, has been to shield consumers, with 94 countries cutting taxes, capping prices or subsidising fuel. So far, most countries have avoided unrest but at vast expense.
Smaller countries, and particularly those at the end of long and complicated supply chains, also face the threat of losing shipments of oil, fuel or gas altogether.
“There is a bit of a first-world, third-world problem in this,” says one energy trader. “The first world is better at planning and looking for solutions and the third world cannot afford it and does not have the capability to do some of that.”
The IMF has trimmed its forecasts for several oil importers because of the energy crisis, including Zambia, Morocco, Egypt and Tunisia, while raising its predicted growth for major exporters such as Nigeria, Angola and Algeria.
By contrast, the west has been relatively untroubled — so far. Europe had one of its busiest summers of air travel on record, with an average of almost 36,000 flights a day between June and August, up 2.4 per cent on last year, according to Eurocontrol. Despite high pump prices, Americans drove more road miles in June and July — figures for August are not yet available — than in the same months last year.
But while the price of petrol in the US remains far below Europe and elsewhere — due to lower taxes — the $5 a gallon now charged in some states is around the national peak reached in the Biden administration and far above the average during the former president’s term.
It is not the economic backdrop President Donald Trump wanted for the midterm elections on November 3 that will set the tone for the remainder of his time in power.
The oil industry is also in the dark
Oil and gas executives have warned about the looming crisis but have so far resisted making predictions about what it means for energy prices.
In part, that is because they do not know, one energy executive privately acknowledges. Many companies in the sector expected prices to soar after one-fifth of the world’s oil and gas supplies were cut off.
Instead, traders have regularly sold down their positions during the seven-month war, often reacting to claims from the White House that a peace deal was imminent.
The market has swung wildly because it has been flying blind, with no accurate and timely data on how much oil the world has in reserve, or on consumer demand. “Those are the two most important things to know and we do not know either of them,” says the executive.
The US publishes weekly data on its oil stocks. But many countries only release such information monthly, and China, the world’s largest importer of oil, does not release regular figures at all.
“The biggest black box is what is happening in China,” says Tommy Inglesby, an energy partner at consultancy Oliver Wyman in Houston, referring to the sudden drop this year in oil imports by the country, which previously had been building up its reserves.
Traders and analysts try to fill the gaps in knowledge by tracking tankers, watching the operations of refineries and using satellite data to estimate how full above-ground storage tanks are.
The IEA estimates that “observed” global oil stocks have fallen by 507mn barrels since the war began, an average of nearly 3mn barrels a day. But not all oil is observable: much of it is stored underground and is unmeasurable.
Without a clear picture, it is impossible to know how much oil is being moved out of storage to keep refineries running and how much longer the market can withstand the disruption before desperation pushes prices higher.
“How soon will reserves near tank bottom?” asked HSBC this week. “The answer has been, and still is, highly uncertain.”
Outside of his own network of petrol stations, the oil executive says he also cannot see how consumers are responding. Most countries publish fuel consumption data with a lag, leaving the market to work out demand from refinery activity, imports and sometimes traffic data.
Seth Carpenter, chief economist at Morgan Stanley, says that while crude prices are still shy of their 2022 peaks of more than $120 a barrel, analysts may have to revise their economic forecasts due to the lengthening shock. “Will it start to bite?” he adds. “Almost surely.”
Data visualisation by Ray Douglas and Keith Fray

rows.title: Salary stand-off delays abolition of NHS quango
rows.content:
Salary stand-off delays abolition of NHS quango
Ministers trying to abolish “the world’s biggest quango” may have no choice but to set up an entirely new public body to employ NHS England’s highly paid regional staff.
A year and a half after former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer promised to scrap the £200bn-a-year arm’s-length body to restore “democratic control” over the health service, ministers are still struggling to wind up NHS England because regional managers are paid well above civil service pay scales.
Health service leaders have warned that the uncertainty is harming efforts to improve patient care and are urging ministers to set up a new temporary quango.
Starmer’s surprise announcement in March last year that he would abolish NHS England and cut about half its 16,000 staff was initially delayed by a Whitehall tussle over the need to find about £1bn for redundancy payouts.
Remaining staff were meant to move into the Department of Health and Social Care, but this was complicated by the significantly higher pay rates offered to NHS staff compared with civil servants of similar rank.
While this has largely been resolved for NHS England’s central leadership team, a stand-off continues over regional staff who are paid too much to fit into civil service pay scales. Director and similar-level roles in the NHS can be paid about 25 per cent more than their civil service equivalent.
Ministers have proposed amendments to the Health Bill currently going through parliament that would make it easier to set up a “special health authority” to employ NHS regional staff until a permanent solution is found.
Two people with knowledge of the matter said no alternative had yet been found to setting up this new quango, other than delaying the abolition of NHS England beyond the April 2027 deadline.
Either outcome would prove politically embarrassing for Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who has pledged to reduce the power of arm’s-length bodies. During his time as health secretary he was the first to describe NHS England as “the world’s biggest quango”.
Sir Ciarán Devane, chief executive of the NHS Alliance, which represents health service leaders, said the deadlock was “starting to cause problems on the front line”.
“The longer this lack of clarity persists, the worse that will become,” he added.
Devane warned that the delays were hampering efforts to plan for the future, retain staff and implement government reforms designed to move care closer to home.
“We think there is merit in moving to a new leadership structure in shadow form — possibly via an NHS Executive created through special health authority status,” he said, adding this “would unlock the current impasse [and] allow transitionary arrangements to be put in place”.
One government figure insisted that Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, was determined not to delay the abolition of NHS England any further and was still trying to find other options.
“By stripping out the duplication and bureaucracy of two organisations doing the same job, the frontline will get more resources to deliver better services for patients,” the Department of Health and Social Care said.
“This will mean a leaner, more agile centre, and we are working through the detail of those changes with affected staff.”

rows.title: Memories of ‘friendly’ Russians fuel AfD’s rise in east Germany
rows.content:
In Germany’s east, old ties to Moscow fuel AfD rise
Martina Mielke, a former crane driver at Rostock’s old Neptun shipyard, recalls partying with the Russian crew of a newly delivered ship during East Germany’s heyday.
“It was just like in a movie! ‘Sto gramm!’” said Mielke, invoking the Russian expression for a 100ml serving of vodka. “You weren’t allowed to chicken out. There was bread, bacon, black tea. They were so friendly.”
Her experience, and that of many others in the eastern German state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, points to a view of Russia that has helped the far-right Alternative for Germany top opinion polls in this part of the country.
The party, founded in western Germany in 2013, recently secured a historic victory in Saxony-Anhalt, another former state in the German Democratic Republic, as East Germany was known, and is on track to come first in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern’s regional election on Sunday, polling at about 37 per cent.
Nearly five years after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, many here still oppose cutting trade and diplomatic ties with Russia, as well as the massive rearmament drive the war has unleashed in Europe’s largest country.
Even as Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government warns of Moscow’s escalating “hybrid war”, after an explosives-laden drone was found at Leipzig airport last month, nearly two-thirds of voters in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern see Vladimir Putin’s nation as posing “little or no threat”, according to a poll published last week by local newspaper Ostsee-Zeitung.
By contrast, 59 per cent of voters in western Germany regard Russia as a strong or very strong threat, according to an ARD survey published this month.
“There are differences between east and west, on arms deliveries to Ukraine, on the perception of Putin and Russia, and that’s to do with history,” said Steffen Mau, sociologist at Humboldt University in Berlin.
People in the communist GDR were more accepting of Soviet soldiers than those in other occupied European countries, given the crimes perpetrated by the Nazi regime, including against the Red Army. After reunification, eastern Germans became citizens of a Nato member state, but scepticism towards the US-led alliance endured.
“East Germans were very cautious about the expansion of Nato towards central and eastern Europe,” Mau said.
That enduring affinity for Russia has been reinforced by the economic pain of Germany’s break from cheap Russian energy and lingering resentment over the upheavals that followed reunification.
Together, those forces have created fertile ground for the Russia-friendly, Eurosceptic AfD, just as Germany has become Ukraine’s biggest military donor under Merz.
An AfD win in the state of just over 1.5mn people could have national repercussions for Merz and his coalition of Christian Democrats and Social Democrats.
The chancellor’s CDU has slumped below 7 per cent in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and risks missing the 5 per cent threshold to enter the regional assembly. Ejection from the legislature in the home state of Angela Merkel, the former CDU chancellor, would be a serious blow to Merz, who is battling record-low polls and an internal rebellion in his party.
During his only campaign appearance last month in Kühlungsborn, a Baltic Sea resort, Merz was booed and heckled as a “warmonger”. Last week, Tino Schomann, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern’s CDU deputy leader, called on the chancellor to quit.
In the final days of the campaign, anti-AfD mobilisation appears to be benefiting the ruling SPD, which has led successive state coalitions since 1998.
Once an advocate of close ties with Moscow, state premier Manuela Schwesig has recast herself as a bulwark against the far right. In the SPD’s red, her campaign posters declare: “Die Frau gegen Blau” — “the woman against blue”, a reference to the AfD’s signature colour.
Schwesig has also faced growing pressure to explain her U-turn on Moscow. For years she championed the Nord Stream 2 gas pipeline linking Russia and Germany, which comes ashore in the state. The pipelines were blown up in a sabotage operation in September 2022, which German authorities suspect was carried out by a Ukrainian commando.
Russia had become a “very controversial” issue and the AfD was exploiting it to “polarise” the campaign, Schwesig said in Rostock on Monday.
She warned against labelling people with a pacifist or religious background as Putin apologists — or Putinversteher. Equally, she said, “I don’t think it’s good when those who say Ukraine must be supported, including militarily, are insulted as warmongers.”
Leif-Erik Holm, the AfD’s candidate for state premier, said his party wanted to “make sure that we don’t end up in a war”. Born behind the Iron Curtain, he warned it would be wrong to “slide back into a cold war — hopefully only a cold war — lasting for decades”.
At a town-hall meeting Schwesig hosted in Rostock, Hannelore, a 73-year-old scientist born in East Berlin, said she would not vote for the AfD because it wants Germany to leave the Eurozone. But she said “this nonsensical war” in Ukraine, which “costs so much money and so many lives”, was the main driver of the party’s support alongside immigration.
She vented at what she saw as the German government’s portrayal of Russia as “our eternal enemy”, and Berlin’s readiness to blame Moscow for recent hybrid attacks.
“It’s the Russians before anything’s even been investigated . . . This anti-Russian rhetoric makes me sick,” she said.
Mau said the resurgence of Russia-friendly sentiment in the East was partly because of the economic disruptions caused by the war.
Mecklenburg-Vorpommern has become a tourist draw, bringing families to its Baltic beaches. But its economy and society remain scarred by the shock of reunification. The state has lost about 15 per cent of its population since 1990 as young people moved west, among them Mielke’s daughter.
Neptun, once an industrial giant that employed 6,500 people and built large merchant vessels for the Soviet bloc, shed more than three-quarters of its workforce within two years. Its surviving business, focused on river cruise ships, employs about 650 people.
After losing her job at the shipyard, which she had joined at 18, Mielke took whatever work she could find, including as a saleswoman for a painting company, until retirement.
“People were upset,” she said of being laid off. “You got your notice — just a piece of paper, and then you would go to one of those transitional agencies to get a bit of money.”
“I’d never experienced anything like that before. I felt stupid, angry and disappointed — and there wasn’t even a little farewell party. Nothing at all.”
Additional reporting by Laura Pitel in Berlin

rows.title: Burnham considers plan to give mayors greater oversight of water companies
rows.content:
Andy Burnham considers plan to give mayors greater oversight of water companies
Andy Burnham is considering a new system of oversight for England’s water industry that would give mayors and other local political leaders greater responsibility for companies in their regions.
The UK prime minister said in a speech in June that he wanted to “ensure all parts of the UK are able to take greater public control of essential services like water, housing, energy and transport”, without giving further details.
Now he is looking at creating nine new regional bodies that would be responsible for setting objectives for the water companies and holding them to account.
The bodies could meet Burnham’s desire to have greater public control of water companies. But it is unlikely to satisfy many MPs and campaigners who are calling for renationalisation after years of poor performance as well as rising debt and bills in the industry.
The idea of nine new regional bodies overseeing the water industry was proposed by Sir Jon Cunliffe in the “Independent Water Commission” published in July last year, although it was not taken forward by the last administration under Sir Keir Starmer.
The Daily Telegraph first reported the idea that ministers were considering reviving Cunliffe’s plan for nine regional systems planners to oversee water companies. One official said this was an “option” although other officials said it was “speculative” given the plans had not been finalised.
Cunliffe, who did not consider renationalisation as an option, suggested these regional water authorities should be responsible for planning, funding, setting water body objectives and monitoring delivery of plans.
The authorities would consist of mayors or local council leaders as well as experts from areas such as transport and agriculture.
Under Cunliffe’s plans the new regional water authorities would not displace the main water industry regulator, currently Ofwat.
The main recommendation in Cunliffe’s report — which has already been accepted by ministers — was for Ofwat to be dismantled and replaced with a more powerful regulator for the sector.
Its economic functions would merge with the water-related responsibilities of the Environment Agency, Natural England and the Drinking Water Inspectorate under the proposals.
Ofwat plays a major role in the industry by setting limits on what water companies can charge customers over five-year periods while adjudicating on whether they are investing enough in their infrastructure.
One water industry adviser said that he believed water companies would be “pretty relaxed” about the proposals for regional boards as they did not equate to state control and there had already been signalling about having local government leaders on boards.
Burnham promised to “end 40 years of neoliberalism” when he stood in the Makerfield by-election this summer, which paved the way for his seizing the premiership.
He called the water industry a “leaking monument to that approach — a country run in the private rather than public interest”.
On Monday a debate on public ownership of the water companies was held in parliament, with more than 60 MPs speaking in favour of ending privatisation.
Ash Smith, founder of Windrush Against Sewage Pollution, who organised the debate, said that “the idea that the public could exert control over something they didn’t own was an insult to the intelligence of the people who have been studying this industry for so long”.
“Only full public ownership will drive the radical changes this country needs,” he added.

rows.title: FirstFT: US equities eclipse Treasuries in rare foreign capital shift
rows.content:
FirstFT: US equities eclipse Treasuries in rare foreign capital shift
This article is an on-site version of our FirstFT newsletter. Subscribers can sign up to our Asia, Europe/Africa or Americas edition to get the newsletter delivered every weekday morning. Explore all of our newsletters here
Good morning and welcome to FirstFT. In today’s newsletter:
- Foreign investors prefer US stocks to Treasuries as debt worries grow
- Supreme Court blocks Trump’s plan to restrict postal voting for midterms
- China tightens control of overseas travel
- Putin moves summit over Ukrainian drone threat
You can listen to today’s top news stories in the FT News Briefing podcast.
Foreign investors are now buying more US stocks than government bonds in a rare move that comes amid fears that inflation and America’s fast-growing debt pile are undermining the “risk-free” status of Treasuries.
International flows into US stocks reached 2.8 per cent of US GDP on average in the year to June, overtaking Treasuries — at 2 per cent of GDP — for the first time this century outside brief episodes during the Covid-19 pandemic and in the aftermath of the global financial crisis, according to analysis of US Treasury data by Deutsche Bank.
The change reflects the ever-growing lure of the US stock market, with the S&P 500 on track for a fourth straight year of double-digit gains. The blue-chip S&P 500 is up about 12 per cent this year. Powering the rally has been vast AI investment, which is driving profit margins to new highs, according to FactSet data stretching back to 2009.
Booming corporate profits have allowed traders to shrug off warnings about the fallout from the near closure of the Strait of Hormuz and surging energy prices.
At the same time, Treasuries’ traditional role as the global risk-free asset is coming under increasing pressure as investors grow wary of lending money to heavily indebted governments and question the independence of the Federal Reserve in a move that could transform the way the US dollar trades. Today the 10-year Treasury yield reached its highest level since 2007.
The rise in yields comes despite US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent’s plan to buy back long-term government debt, with the announcement last week of a $6bn purchase disappointing investors.
Here’s what else we’re keeping tabs on today:
- Switzerland: The World Trade Organization publishes its latest World Trade Report on trends and policy challenges.
Join Ashley Armstrong, Philip Stafford and guests at an exclusive webinar for FT subscribers on Wednesday September 23 at 1pm UK time on the City of London: can it retain its edge as a leading financial centre? Register now.
Join senior leaders from across the global entertainment industry at the Business of Entertainment Summit on September 24. Explore the trends shaping the future of film, television, gaming and music. As an FT newsletter subscriber, you can get 10 per cent off your pass with code FTsub10 or get it automatically applied at the checkout.
Five more top stories
1. Exclusive: Russian President Vladimir Putin has moved this year’s annual meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club, his flagship foreign policy conference, from Sochi to Moscow due to concerns about Ukraine’s intensifying drone strike campaign, according to four people familiar with the matter.
2. The Supreme Court has rejected Donald Trump’s restrictions on mail-in ballots ahead of November’s midterm elections in a major blow to the US president.
3. China has implemented sweeping new controls on overseas travel for Chinese citizens as President Xi Jinping steps up efforts to secure state secrets, advanced technology and highly skilled workers.
4. Industrial America is contending with a fresh wave of supply-chain inflation as Trump’s Iran war pushes up energy costs, tariffs raise import prices and the AI boom strains supplies of crucial electronics.
5. Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney has urged the EU to deepen its economic alliance with his country as Ottawa tries to break its dependence on the US following the collapse of trade talks.
The secretive German ‘guerrilla unit’ buying up arms for Ukraine
In an extra-high-security wing of the German defence ministry lurks a team so secretive that some call it a guerrilla unit. The Sonderstab Ukraine is the engine behind Germany’s €11.5bn-a-year military support for Kyiv. Unlike the sprawling bureaucracy behind procurement for the German armed forces, this unit strikes deals to buy weapons for Ukraine in as little as two weeks. Laura Pitel takes a look at how the elite group gained a reputation for speed and efficiency.
We’re also reading . . .
- Saudi Arabia in a bind: The assault by Iran’s allies has spawned what may be the biggest test for Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman since the backlash against Jamal Khashoggi’s murder in 2018.
- ECB exclusive: European Central Bank staff are demanding clarity over president Christine Lagarde’s potential early exit.
- Nigerian IPO excitement: The flotation of Dangote Petroleum Refinery, owned by Aliko Dangote, Africa’s richest man, is sparking the interest of millions of Nigerians in the stock market.
- AI thrills: The technology has brought some excitement to auditing firms. But John Gapper warns they should not get carried away.
Graphic of the day
My colleague Paul Caruana Galizia uncovers the story of how Poland lost $230mn trying to buy Venezuelan oil with cryptocurrency swapped on USB sticks in Caracas restaurants.
Take a break from the news . . .
Returning to the office after the summer break may require a refresh of your shoewear. HTSI is here to help with a guide to the best places to go for perfectly fitted footwear.
Additional reporting by Irwin Cruz and Benjamin Wilhelm.
Thank you for reading and remember you can add FirstFT to myFT. You can also elect to receive a FirstFT push notification every morning on the app. Send your recommendations and feedback to [email protected]

rows.title: Carney urges EU to cement trade deal as Ottawa seeks pivot from US
rows.content:
Mark Carney urges EU to cement trade deal as Ottawa seeks pivot from US
Mark Carney has urged Europe to deepen its economic alliance with Canada as Ottawa tries to break its dependence on the US following the collapse of trade talks with Donald Trump.
In an interview with the FT, Canada’s prime minister called on the 10 EU member states that have not yet ratified the bloc’s nine-year-old trade deal with Canada to do so, saying closer ties would make all sides “more resilient, more independent” and more prosperous.
Carney will travel to Strasbourg to address the European parliament on Thursday.
He spoke to the FT on the eve of an investor summit in Toronto, where he will host Wall Street firms and Chinese companies and pitch Canada as a safe bet against global volatility while the US president threatens allies with more tariffs and upends long-term alliances.
“It doesn’t matter whether it’s the US, Canada, any country around the world, risk is increasingly being priced [in],” Carney told the FT on Monday.
The Europe trip and Toronto summit come as trade relations between Washington and Ottawa worsen with tit-for-tat tariffs imposed in recent weeks. Trump has mocked Carney and labelled Canada a “51st state”, prompting popular anger across the US’s second-largest trading partner.
“You’re at war when you’re attacked, and we got attacked,” the prime minister said last month after trade talks with the US collapsed.
Carney has courted investment from China and India and used a Davos speech this year to rally the world’s “middle powers” against a US-dominated world order that he said was undergoing “rupture, not transition”.
But he appeared to offer an olive branch to the US in his interview with the FT, saying his overtures to investors in China and allies in Europe were not a deliberate stance against the US, Canada’s largest trading partner.
“We are about what we’re for, not what we’re against,” Carney said. “It’s not a reaction in any way, shape or form to what’s going on in the US.”
The Liberal leader also brushed aside Washington’s criticism of Ottawa’s courting of Beijing, which is sending senior officials to the Toronto summit.
“I take note that the president of the United States is welcoming President Xi [Jinping] for a state visit,” he said, referring to the Chinese leader’s summit in Washington this month.
“The US has deeper co-operation with China, far deeper co-operation with China than Canada does,” Carney said.
Ottawa hopes the Toronto summit, akin to Saudi Arabia’s Future Investment Initiative, will kick-start $1tn in foreign investment over the next five years. Carney will tout more than 150 projects in mining, energy and AI to investors ranging from Wall St titans to the China Investment Corporation and Africa’s Dangote Group — and pitch Canada’s stability as a commercial partner.
“We’re a country that honours its commitments,” he said. “We have the most precious commodity, which is trust.”
The prime minister said a closer alliance with Europe was the best approach for a world of increasing uncertainty.
The trade agreement struck in 2017 has not been ratified by 10 of the EU’s 27 member states amid concerns over Canadian agricultural exports hurting European farmers.
Carney said the deal was “de facto in operation, even in those jurisdictions where they’re not ratified”, but the ties could go far deeper if the holdouts signed up.
“I would like to use this opportunity to encourage them to do so,” he said.
“It is a positive initiative because it’s good for Europe, it’s good for Canada, it will make us more sovereign, make us more resilient, more independent, as well as more prosperous,” he said.
Canada and the EU have agreed to work on agreements covering trade, security and regulations, critical raw materials, energy and clean technologies, visa liberalisation and financial systems.
A meeting next month in Montreal aims to advance the talks.
During his trip to Europe, Carney will also travel to Britain to meet his UK counterpart Andy Burnham, who he said was “off to a very strong start”.
Carney also said he was confident that US talks could restart, despite last month calling on American officials to “stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough” to allow for proper trade diplomacy.
“When the right opportunity comes, we’ll sit down and negotiate,” he told the FT.

rows.title: FT Weekend Fest: Is the AI boom a bubble?
rows.content:
FT Weekend Fest: Is the AI boom a bubble?
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
AI-related investments are now worth up to half of the entire value of the S&P 500. But is the AI investment boom a bubble waiting to burst? Tim Bradshaw, the FT’s global technology correspondent, speaks to Richard Kramer, founder of Arete Research, and Ophelia Brown, founder of Blossom Capital. Recorded live at the FT Weekend Festival on 5th September 2026.

rows.title: Von der Leyen to paint EU as the only port in a global geopolitical storm
rows.content:
Von der Leyen to paint EU as the only port in a global geopolitical storm
Good morning. A scoop to start: EU capitals have rebuffed Canada’s pitch for a “unique alliance” with the bloc, deflating Prime Minister Mark Carney’s attempt to forge a coalition of “middle powers” to stand up to the US and China.
Today, our man in Strasbourg explains what to expect from Ursula von der Leyen’s annual tour de table speech this morning, and our climate correspondent reports on the implementation of the EU’s long-awaited deforestation powers.
Full of terrors
Ursula von der Leyen will pitch the EU as the answer to the multitude of questions of how to deal with the interlocking crises destabilising the world in her State of the Union speech today, writes Andy Bounds.
Context: The European Commission president gives her annual address to the European parliament with the continent facing myriad geoeconomic, geopolitical and security threats, with the slow collapse of the transatlantic relationship exacerbating them all.
Von der Leyen believes the bloc’s 27 member states are too small to deal with the three big challenges of climate change, the disruption of AI and the looming collapse of industrial output, according to officials involved in discussions on the speech.
The German two-time president will throw out ideas to tackle them all in the address this morning in Strasbourg. Carney will be present in the chamber to illustrate that the EU has allies in a world rocked by US President Donald Trump, Russia’s Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jinping.
There will be an emphasis on adapting to climate change after a summer of wildfires and droughts, and she will repeat a tough message that China must reduce its €1bn-a-day trade surplus with the bloc or face tariffs.
AI is evolving faster than expected, von der Leyen will say, and she will back calls for better guardrails on the most advanced frontier models. She will also push for self-regulation and verification while emphasising that Europe must not allow itself to be left behind.
Von der Leyen will also reference the bloc’s new Kids Act, which will be formally presented tomorrow. The new act will propose a minimum age of 15 to set up a social media account, according to a draft seen by the FT.
The new rules apply not only to social networks but also to video-sharing platforms, online games, AI companions and AI chatbots. If the companies do not comply with the rules, they can face fines of up to 6 per cent of their annual sales.
Chart du jour: Tax race
As countries across Europe compete to lure the world’s wealthy with tax discounts, Switzerland has a peculiar advantage: its internal cantons have spent decades competing against each other.
Out of the woods
EU bans on imports linked to deforestation are finally set to bite following a two-year delay, after Commission tweaks to the regulation were waved through by the European parliament and member states, writes Ian Johnston.
Context: The EU’s deforestation regulation is a landmark environmental law designed to ban imports such as coffee, cocoa, rubber, wood and palm oil if producers cannot prove they are not grown in deforested areas.
In May, the Commission proposed a delegated act that required a yes-no vote from parliamentarians and member states. Multiple officials told the FT there had not been opposition from the parliament or EU capitals to prevent the law from entering into force.
The act will apply to large and medium-sized companies from December 30 and to smaller companies from June 30 2027.
The Commission has said the law will cut carbon emissions linked to the commodities and help protect biodiversity across the world, but trade partners including Indonesia (the EU’s biggest supplier of palm oil), India and the US have fiercely opposed the legislation.
It was twice delayed. Fierce opposition from trade partners forced a delay in 2024, while in 2025 there was another pause because of problems with an IT system tracking reporting by companies.
The tweaks put forward included proposals to exclude leather and retreaded tyres — made by applying new rubber to worn tyres — from the legislation’s scope.
Meanwhile, the Commission’s technological hiccups have also been dealt with, with one official adding that the IT system is working smoothly.
What to watch today
- European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen delivers her annual State of the Union speech.
- Nato secretary-general Mark Rutte travels to the UK.
Now read these
- Mecklenburg-Vorpommern: How enduring affinity for Russia underpins support for far-right AfD in Germany’s next state to go to the polls this weekend.
- Painful truth: Europe cannot afford to close itself off from Chinese supply chains, said the boss of Danish wind farm developer Ørsted.
- Fusion boom: Nuclear fusion start-ups are attracting billions in funding. Some experts doubt whether the technology will ever produce cheap electricity.
