rows.title: Will the Fed defy Trump and raise rates?
rows.content:
Will the Fed defy Trump and raise rates?
The US Federal Reserve looks likely to raise interest rates at its meeting next week, despite President Donald Trump’s repeated calls for cuts, as the world’s largest economy faces persistent inflation tied to energy and housing.
Traders in futures markets put the probability of a rate rise at more than 85 per cent after inflation data on Friday showed price pressures were stubbornly elevated in August, with the headline annual inflation rate unchanged from July at 3.4 per cent. Core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, was 2.4 per cent, down slightly from 2.5 per cent in July.
Oil prices have surged to more than $100 a barrel on renewed conflict in the Middle East while investors have sent yields on Treasury bonds to multiyear highs. US government debt rose above $40tn last month, driving new anxieties among global investors about the state of US public finances.
Still, policymakers will be mostly concerned with prices in the economy. “Investors should be prepared for a Fed that is more willing to tighten [rates] and should recognise that inflation . . . is the Fed’s central concern right now,” said Jason Pride, chief of investment strategy and research at wealth management firm Glenmede.
Fed governor Christopher Waller has already left the door open to a rate rise. “If the incoming data for August show . . . improvement [in inflation] has been fleeting, then it may be appropriate to raise the policy rate,” he said in a speech last week. Jill R Shah
Will the Bank of Japan bow to pressure for rate rises?
Traders are ascribing a 75 per cent chance to the Bank of Japan raising its benchmark interest rate by a quarter point at next week’s policy meeting, from the current level of 1 per cent.
The meeting has been hotly anticipated by investors given its likely impact on broader financial markets, not just from the decision itself but from any signals of what is to follow.
Bets that the BoJ would speed up its pace of interest rate rises have been a vital factor that, along with a historic US-Japan intervention in July and August, has helped the yen recover from a four-decade low of around ¥164 to the dollar before the operation to about ¥154.
If the BoJ’s signalling disappoints the market, which is expecting the benchmark rate to rise by 0.5 percentage points by January, it could pile pressure back on the currency.
“While avoiding the impression of a preset path, the BoJ may seek to steer markets towards viewing every meeting as live depending on incoming data, partly to prevent renewed depreciation pressure,” said Barclays analysts.
The BoJ’s more dovish members are caught, say the analysts, between Japanese leader Sanae Takaichi’s caution on rate rises and pressure from US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent for policy tightening. Ian Smith
How will the BoE respond to surging oil prices?
Investors will watch for signs of a widening divide between Bank of England policymakers who favour taking action and those who prefer to “wait and see”, when its nine-member Monetary Policy Committee meets on Thursday. Rate setters are widely expected to leave the policy rate unchanged at 3.75 per cent.
The meeting will include the MPC’s annual decision on the pace of bond sales under the BoE’s quantitative tightening programme — the process of shrinking the stock of government bonds accumulated under previous quantitative easing programmes. The decision will be closely watched at a time when gilt yields and government borrowing costs are under pressure.
Many economists expect the BoE to slow the annual pace of QT from £70bn to £50bn. With fewer gilts maturing over the coming year, this would allow the central bank to keep the volume of active bond sales broadly in line with last year’s.
On interest rates, Jack Meaning, economist at Barclays, expects six MPC members to vote for no change, with Huw Pill, Catherine Mann and Megan Greene backing a quarter-point increase, repeating July’s 6-3 split.
But Meaning sees a risk of additional hawkish votes, with deputy governors Clare Lombardelli and Sir Dave Ramsden potentially joining those seeking higher rates.
“At the least we would expect Lombardelli and Ramsden to highlight in their individual paragraphs that the inflation risks had become skewed to the upside and perhaps even that the decision was becoming more finely balanced,” he said.
The recent sharp rise in energy prices and borrowing costs has prompted traders in swaps markets to bet on four quarter-point rate increases over the next year, up from two expected a week ago.
The UK’s faster than expected 0.4 per cent GDP growth in July also suggested that current interest rates might not be as restrictive as some BoE rate setters thought.
Thomas Pugh, chief economist at audit, tax and consulting firm RSM UK, said: “The Bank of England will not follow the [European Central Bank] in raising rates . . . but the prospect of a synchronised global tightening cycle is growing.” Valentina Romei

rows.title: India rethinks newly implemented stock market pricing mechanism
rows.content:
India rethinks newly implemented stock market pricing mechanism
Good morning. India hosted a successful Brics summit, with the bloc uniting against the trade and geopolitical policies of the Trump administration. It was a busy weekend for Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who held 15 bilateral meetings with visiting heads of government over the three days of the summit.
It was also a busy weekend for corporate news. The Reserve Bank of India on Saturday rejected Tata Sons’ bid to avoid having to go public, a move that will force the vast conglomerate to undertake a radical transformation of its structure and operations. The company is expected to hold a board meeting on Thursday.
The country’s largest private sector lender, HDFC Bank, has submitted the names of two candidates who could take over when incumbent chief Sashidhar Jagdishan retires later this year. Big changes are afoot at some of India’s biggest corporations.
Note — regular readers might spot something new this week: the newsletter has an updated look. What hasn’t changed is what comes below. Every week, I’ll continue bringing you my take on the companies, people and trends shaping Indian business, and what they tell us about where the economy is heading. If you’re not already a subscriber, now is a good time to join us. Sign up here.
Sebi rethinks chaotic new closing-price mechanism
After a chaotic six weeks, India’s market regulator, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi), appears to be having a major rethink of the auction mechanism it introduced to determine end-of-day prices in stock and index derivatives. In a paper published over the weekend, Sebi has proposed two options: one that would limit the time the auction window is open, and a second that essentially scraps the entire thing to go back to the earlier model.
On August 3, Indian exchanges rolled out a closing auction system (CAS), which calculates the closing price of eligible stock and index derivatives based on a 20-minute auction at the end of trade, rather than the average price during the last 30 minutes of trading. The new system resulted in severe volatility in the last few minutes of trade, which operators struggled to handle. On expiry days of derivative contracts, price chaos was even more acute.
A couple of weeks into the experiment, Sebi said it had found evidence of manipulative trading during CAS on the BSE Sensex index’s weekly expiry and had temporarily barred Copthall Mauritius Investment Limited, a JPMorgan Chase unit, and Mansi Share & Stock Broking from the markets. It has since restored their access to the broader markets, although they remain barred from participating in the auction until further orders.
In its paper, Sebi’s data shows why the closing window has become such a flashpoint. Comparing expiries before and after the new system’s implementation, Sebi found that a larger share of trading activity is now squeezed into a much narrower window, leaving the closing price more exposed to manipulation. Compounding this is the fact that the Indian market is not sufficiently liquid to absorb the shocks of the auction system.
The regulator is inviting public comments on the proposals until October 3. Just last week, at the Global Fintech Fest, Sebi chair Tuhin Kanta Pandey said CAS “is not going anywhere”, pointing out that other markets had faced similar liquidity teething problems when they first introduced closing auctions. Still, it’s hard not to see Sebi’s second option as something close to a rollback, even though the regulator frames it as a temporary arrangement it will revisit in a year, once market participants have had more time to adjust.
This episode adds to a pattern of hastily implemented policy changes that have sown confusion in India in recent years. This is compounded by a communication problem, where regulators say one thing and then do the opposite. Just last month, the Reserve Bank of India closed its special deposit scheme for the diaspora a month ahead of schedule, even though governor Sanjay Malhotra had told reporters barely a week earlier that no such move was “under consideration”.
Stable policymaking is meant to be a foundation of economic growth. In India lately, it has started to feel more like a video game — a series of surprises and sudden challenges that markets have to constantly negotiate.
Do you think Indian markets are better off going back to the old system? Hit reply or email me at [email protected]
Recommended stories
- Oil hits $108 after Gulf states postpone talks with Iran over the Strait of Hormuz.
- US Federal Reserve chief Kevin Warsh and Donald Trump are on a collision course as investors expect the central bank to raise rates.
- Global AI stocks slip over concerns about safety risks. But Trump has rejected calls from tech bosses for an AI slowdown.
- The Middle East war tests Dubai’s island dreams.
- Pokémon cards are selling for more than $1mn.
PwC consolidates Indian operations in JV with US business
PwC, the Big Four accounting firm, is consolidating its India operations into a joint venture that will house its India consulting business as well as the offshore centres supporting its US operations. The new structure will help the firm optimise resources as competition intensifies in consulting and as AI disruption begins to bite.
Previously, the firm’s US advisory business — which ran business “acceleration centres” in India — sometimes competed for work with its own India consulting arm, a duplication this consolidation resolves. Unlike traditional multinationals, PwC and its Big Four peers operate as a network of locally owned partnerships, which can create complexity when serving international clients and occasionally creates tension between member firms over how to split lucrative cross-border work. The new structure will house roughly 40,000 employees, accounting for more than 10 per cent of PwC’s global workforce.
Consolidation is fast becoming the default strategy across consulting. Capgemini’s $3.3bn all-cash acquisition of WNS, announced in July last year and closed in October, was framed explicitly around building scale in AI-driven business process services, which is the same offshore, labour-intensive layer PwC is now restructuring.
Consulting firms and Indian IT services majors began building these acceleration and delivery arms roughly three decades ago to help them reduce costs by moving routine, process-heavy work to India on behalf of western clients. That is also the layer where AI is improving fastest, and firms are racing to retrain staff for higher-value, less commoditised work before the arbitrage advantage erodes further.
For PwC, this is the second leg of a broader consolidation push. In April, it merged its UK risk and consulting divisions, which was part of a wider effort to standardise service delivery across its network and optimise shared staffing at its India acceleration centres.
Consolidating fragmented centres into unified JVs gives PwC — and rivals following similar playbooks — cleaner books, less internal competition for client mandates and fewer but better-utilised delivery hubs to retrain for higher-margin, judgment-heavy work. For India’s services economy, the question is whether “higher value” retraining will happen fast enough, or whether headcount growth at these centres will plateau first.
Go figure
This week, Singapore’s Prime Minister Lawrence Wong was awarded a $1mn pay rise, following the city-state’s peculiar and controversial policy of paying its political leaders on par with business executives. The policy, perceived as a bulwark against corruption, has largely been popular, although it faces criticism when costs are rising.
Quick question
We seem to have arrived at the “Could AI wipe out humanity?” stage of the proceedings. Do you think the technology should be tightly regulated? Tell us here.
Buzzer round
On Friday, we asked: which Chinese technology company, whose chief financial officer became a central figure in the US-China technology conflict, is facing a major US criminal trial?
The answer is Huawei, which is poised for a trial in New York.
Asuwath Kumar was first with the correct answer, followed by Aniruddha Dutta, Srinath V and Ranjan Kumar Sinha. Congratulations!
Thank you for reading. India Business Briefing was edited by Stephen Harris today. Please send feedback, suggestions (and gossip) to [email protected].

rows.title: Trump’s Venezuela oil deal: deeply flawed or too big to fail?
rows.content:
Trump’s Venezuela oil deal: deeply flawed or too big to fail?
Hello and welcome to Energy Source, coming to you from Bogotá, Caracas and New York today as we try to piece together what is going on in an energy sector caught in the grip of geopolitical uncertainty.
Brent crude prices jumped as much as 5 per cent to $109.80 a barrel after Saudi Arabia closed a vital oil pipeline following a drone attack, before easing back somewhat to above $107 in trading on Tuesday morning.
The attack from Iraq, where Iran-backed Shia militias and Iran’s Revolutionary Guards are active, cut 4mn barrels a day from the market, showing how Tehran is tightening its grip on Middle Eastern oil to pressure Washington.
US diesel prices are trading at record levels above $6 a gallon and petrol prices are threatening to eclipse the highs seen following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Europe is also feeling the strain with gas prices surging to four-year highs as traders start to fret about low storage levels ahead of winter.
The energy crisis is feeding global inflation and pushing yields on 10-year US Treasury bonds above 5 per cent — a worrisome level for a financial product that acts as a benchmark for trillions of dollars in assets worldwide.
It is no wonder that the Trump administration has tried for several months to pull certain policy levers. It has released crude stocks from the strategic reserve, amended restrictive shipping rules in the US, tinkered with environmental rules on petrol and encouraged producers to boost output.
These efforts have had some limited impact but nowhere near enough to insulate the global market from the loss of 2.6bn barrels from the Middle East between the start of March and the start of August. Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have further stressed the market, particularly for refined products such as diesel.
S&P Global Energy research published today warns “winter is coming for diesel” due to low inventories, scarce refining capacity and seasonal demand set to increase at just the wrong moment. The fuel is critical for agriculture, transport and home heating and has in recent days caught the attention of US President Donald Trump, who said on Monday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop targeting energy infrastructure.
Analysts doubt that any bilateral deal (if there is any agreement given the initial reaction of Kyiv and Moscow) will stand the test of time. And this leaves policymakers with tough choices and uncomfortable trade-offs, according to Karim Fawaz, executive director at S&P Global Energy.
“Protecting consumers from higher fuel costs, preserving energy security and maintaining open trade flows becomes increasingly difficult when the world is short of available refining capacity. The longer this disruption lasts, the harder those choices become,” he said.
Our main item today is about another of the Trump administration’s efforts to boost US energy dominance: agreeing a massive oil deal with Venezuela.
Thanks for reading, Jamie
Trump’s Venezuela oil play
Oil executives in Venezuela are frantically trying to understand the implications of the highly unusual deal announced by US President Donald Trump late last month, in which Washington will participate directly in the South American country’s oil industry for a century.
Venezuela’s local oil industry was largely sidelined on August 28, when Trump took to Truth Social to announce “THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY!” That deal will see the US take control of 65bn barrels of Venezuelan crude, while taking a 35 per cent stake in North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), a company controlled by divisive Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt.
That stake would give the US the right to buy a guaranteed 20 per cent of output from all the company’s current and future fields at production cost, plus first refusal on the remaining 80 per cent to ensure guaranteed supply in emergencies.
In the weeks since then, international majors including Chevron and Eni have signed a flurry of deals aimed at revitalising the country’s dilapidated oil industry while lowering fuel prices at the pump in the US. BP and Shell have also signed recent deals.
“What was announced at the end of August isn’t a single agreement, and that’s the point a lot of people are missing,” said Carlos Borges, a business development specialist in oil services. “It’s an ecosystem.”
According to a White House factsheet, NABEP plans to award licences or establish joint ventures with energy groups to develop 17 Venezuelan oilfields via 100-year concessions. The White House said that “the majority of the incremental oilfields to be operated by NABEP” had previously been controlled or operated by Russian and Chinese groups.
Last week, Borges and a host of the country’s oilmen met in Caracas to grapple with the ramifications of the deal and what its chances of success are in a country that saw oil production fall from about 3mn barrels per day at the turn of the century to about 400,000 b/d in 2020, as part of a wider economic collapse that saw millions of Venezuelans flee abroad. Following a slight recovery, production currently hovers around 1.1mn b/d.
The political upheaval in Venezuela, which boasts the world’s largest proven oil reserves, began in 1999 following the election of revolutionary socialist Hugo Chávez, who swiftly redrafted the country’s constitution and overhauled the oil industry.
Under Chávez’s tenure, Petróleos de Venezuela (PDVSA), the state-owned but once technocratic firm, was brought under political control while assets belonging to Exxon and ConocoPhillips were expropriated and nationalised. In response to an oil strike in 2002-03, Chávez fired more than 18,000 workers at PDVSA, accusing them of disloyalty. In the following years, thousands of engineers, administrators and technicians sought better lives abroad.
The situation worsened under Nicolás Maduro, who assumed the presidency after Chávez died from cancer in 2013 and ruled until January this year, when US forces arrested him in a daring night-time raid on Caracas.
Maduro’s vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, received the Trump administration’s backing to lead Venezuela and has since passed a hydrocarbon law reform that dramatically weakens PDVSA’s grip on the sector, allowing private companies to operate wells directly.
“The big bottleneck now isn’t even power, it’s human resources,” Borges said at the conference last week. “There’s no workforce because they left, with Venezuelans now boosting oil production around the world. These people need to come back.”
Roy Biagioni, who heads an oil industry association in the country’s western oil heartland of Zulia, echoed the need for skilled personnel to return. “We have agreements with universities to train technical staff, because we need welders,” said Biagioni, who added that the private sector would be crucial to resolving ongoing electricity bottlenecks in Venezuela, which have affected industry and residents alike.
“Repsol has its own self-generation projects, and NABEP is generating power in certain parts of Zulia,” said Biagioni, who plans to reach 1mn b/d of production in Zulia state — a boost of about 350,000 additional daily barrels — something he said would entail bringing at least 5,900 wells back online.
The deal is hardly without its critics.
Rafael Ramírez, who served under Chávez as president of PDVSA and as oil minister before breaking with Maduro, said the agreement was unconstitutional as it surrenders sovereignty over Venezuela’s natural resources.
“Everything about it is deeply flawed and badly executed,” Ramírez told Energy Source. “You can tell it stems from a political situation that looks like a desperate attempt to cling to power, but it’s committing an entire country for the next hundred years.”
Opposition politicians have also questioned the deal, with lawmaker Henrique Capriles last week saying there were a host of “legal and constitutional problems” with it.
Schreiner Parker, an analyst at Houston-based research group Rystad Energy, was more bullish.
“The challenges are myriad but the likes of Chevron, BP, Shell and others feel as if they’re manageable,” Parker said. “Long-term durability is still in question from an aboveground perspective but the resource base, coupled with geographic location, makes Venezuela a compelling case for future western hemisphere supply. In the end it may be too big to fail.” (Joe Daniels and Ana Rodríguez Brazón)
Power Points
- Two US companies are seeking to advance Trump’s vision of Alaska as a major gas exporter — but face long odds in developing projects to profit from some of the world’s most abundant untapped gasfields.
- Donald Trump’s administration said it would axe climate rules limiting greenhouse gas emissions from power plants.
- “Offensively cheap” solar power is looking up: Chinese-made panels on rooftops across the world are changing the facts of life for big utilities.
Energy Source is written by Jamie Smyth, Martha Muir, Alexandra White, Rachel Millard, Malcolm Moore, Ryohtaroh Satoh and Stephanie Findlay with support from the FT’s global team of reporters. It is edited by Benjamin Wilhelm. Reach us at [email protected] and follow us on X at @FTEnergy. Catch up on past editions of the newsletter here.
