rows.title: Scrapping triple lock on pensions need not wreak political damage
rows.content:
Scrapping triple lock on pensions need not wreak political damage
This article is an on-site version of our Inside Politics newsletter. Subscribers can sign up here to get the newsletter delivered every weekday. If you’re not a subscriber, you can still receive the newsletter free for 30 days
Good morning. The state pension is on course to rise above the tax-free income threshold for the first time. That creates a problem for John Healey — and puts the “triple lock” back in the political spotlight. Some thoughts on how he could finesse the government’s way out of the triple lock and avoid the politically explosive issue of taxing the state pension.
Inside Politics is edited by Georgina Quach. Follow Stephen on Bluesky and Georgina on Bluesky. Read the previous edition of the newsletter here. Please send gossip, thoughts and feedback to [email protected]
The way to welfare savings
The purpose of the triple lock is — or rather, was — to increase the value of the UK’s state pension relative to our peers in the OECD in a gradual, and therefore lower cost, way by raising it by whichever is the highest out of average wage growth, CPI inflation or 2.5 per cent.
The political question has always been: does what was a gradual option in 2010, which was cheaper than a once-and-for-all uplift, become an ever more expensive liability because no government feels able to discontinue it?
That question is increasingly important because of the UK’s difficult fiscal position, ailing public services and elevated debt costs. There is a policy dividend to be had for the government if it can use this Budget to, in no particular order, speed up the pace at which the UK reduces its debt, put more money into public services and get the cost of borrowing back down to its historic norm relative to its peers.
I use the term “relative to its peers” quite deliberately. The UK’s big problem when it comes to government debt is that global debt costs are rising at a time when our own debt is no longer as attractive to our peers as it was before Liz Truss’s “mini” Budget back in 2022. As Martin Wolf set out in his column this week (emphasis mine):
The chancellor should dare to go for more ambitious fiscal targets than those now being followed. This will surely mean higher taxes. The question is how to raise taxation without badly damaging the economy. In my view, this means reconsidering the manifesto tax pledges. Some increases in income tax, removal of the ridiculous number of exemptions under VAT and other important tax reforms must be on the table. So, too, must cuts in spending.
As I’ve written before, I don’t really buy that there are short-term savings to be had in the working-age welfare budget. Every attempt to do so has only resulted in essentially the same amount being spent to ever-decreasing effectiveness: there is a lot that you can do to “reform welfare”, much of which I think would result in lower costs, but I don’t think you can meaningfully reduce expenditure via this route.
I think the route to reducing the number of people in the UK who are neither in employment, education or training (Neet) runs through greater incentives for businesses to hire employees who are far from workplace-ready, lowering costs to hire people, particularly the youngest workers, and better and more freely available further education and training.
You can flatter the forecast by tweaking thresholds and declaring that you will cap costs in the welfare system, but the UK needs to stop doing things that flatter the forecast and actually start getting real savings in.
All of this costs the government money in the short term. For that reason, I think the government should look at the triple lock: the policy is at or near the point it has achieved its purpose, and by exiting from it, the government can actually make a genuine dent in the “welfare bill”.
The earnings link will see the state pension rise to £13,060.23: very, very close indeed to the amount that Pensions UK estimates a British pensioner needs to have the minimum decent standard of living, which is £13,900. But crucially this will take it above the current taxable threshold of £12,570, meaning that a pensioner who only receives the state pension would have to pay tax on it, something that both Rachel Reeves and her successor, John Healey, have said they will avoid.
One way for Healey to solve a number of the government’s problems at once would be to announce that
a) the state pension is from now on a non-taxable benefit, and that no one who is in receipt of it alone need fill out a tax return or pay tax on it, regardless of where the taxable threshold might fall in the future
b) the new state pension will have a one-off slightly larger increase, not to £13,060.23 but to that £13,900 figure
c) having reached that £13,900 figure, the UK will instead have either a double lock or, in my view, a single lock designed to protect the state pension’s value relative to household earnings.
I think this package, taken together, could manage the politics of declaring “mission accomplished” on the triple lock in a way that the government could both weather and get a policy dividend from.
Now try this
I saw the first part of the new Charles de Gaulle biopic (Resistance) in cinemas and I was absolutely blown away by it. It’s the best film I’ve seen this year. It is an adaptation of Julian Jackson’s brilliant biography, A Certain Idea of France, which I hope will get a second rush of interest as a result.
Top stories today
- End of Wandsworth’s ultra-low tax era | Wandsworth currently charges the lowest council tax in England, at £509.84 for Band D, plus a £510.51 precept set by the Greater London Authority. But the borough’s Conservative administration has announced plans for a 94 per cent rise, Britain’s biggest ever annual increase (from a total of £1,020 to £1,978). The borough says it was forced by a change in local government funding.
- Reform leader in Wales exits | The leader of Reform UK in Wales has stepped down from his position after being arrested and bailed on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour.
- The self-sufficiency trap | The UK’s call to “buy British by default” has a sort of wartime air to it. But it is hard to do in practice, argues Lex writer Louise Lucas (requires premium FT sub). UK defence companies rely on hundreds of small and medium-sized suppliers, spread across the world. If governments really want to keep their defence procurement close — which isn’t irrational in an increasingly belligerent world — one solution is to team up with allies.
- Armoured vehicle boost | Speaking of teaming up . . . A US defence giant and a German military start-up are joining forces to deploy autonomous “land drones” aimed at transforming the British Army’s Ajax armoured fighting vehicles, which have been beset by cost overruns and noise problems.

rows.title: US billionaires line up to bankroll Republicans’ election push
rows.content:
US billionaires line up to bankroll Republicans’ election push
America’s mega-donors are overwhelmingly backing Donald Trump’s Republicans in this year’s race for Congress, as billionaires from Silicon Valley to Wall Street bankroll the party’s midterm push.
Sixteen of the country’s 20 largest donors have ploughed money into the Republican campaign, according to the FT’s analysis. George Soros is the standout Democratic backer. Other mega-donors have funnelled cash to candidates pushing deregulation of cryptocurrency and gambling or to promote AI. 
The findings reveal another US election drawing colossal sums to shape the outcome — and also show how the wealthiest donors are tilting Republican, even as the party trails Democrats in the polls. It also marks a reversal from the 2024 presidential race, when Kamala Harris raised and spent significantly more money than Trump but lost.
“What you’re seeing is a mild break from expectations,” said Stanford political scientist Adam Bonica, who has studied donations from America’s wealthy since 1980. It is not unusual for top donors to lean Republican, but the balance in this election is “especially skewed”.
The money is flowing through several channels. Some of the largest donors are financing candidates directly. Some are building huge war chests around industries such as crypto. A smaller group of billionaires are using networks of Super Pacs to funnel funds into House and Senate races, and intervened in primaries first — where the money had extra influence.
At a time of populist revolt against perceived elites, political money has become more concentrated among the ultra-rich. More than a third of the $2.8bn raised for the current 2025-26 election cycle comes from the 20 biggest mega-donors, according to an FT analysis of the most recent filings.
In more than 30 House and Senate contests, more than a third of outside spending came from groups that received at least 80 per cent of their money from mega-donors, defined as people who each gave at least $5mn.
“We now have a system that is geared towards and depends on these ultra-wealthy mega-donors,” said Brendan Glavin, research director at OpenSecrets, a non-profit that tracks campaign spending.
These wealthy elites “pour hundreds of millions of dollars into the system and really have an outsized effect”, he said.
Top Republican donors have also donated millions of dollars to Maga Inc, the Super Pac that backed Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign. It now boasts a $400mn electoral war chest.
Special interest groups have also contributed. Crypto entrepreneurs Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss donated about $11mn. Silicon Valley tycoons Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz and their spouses have given $18mn, while OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman and his spouse donated $25mn.
Maga Inc has so far spent just $10.8mn, backing Trump-allied Republicans in Texas, Tennessee and South Carolina. A new group, No Going Back Pac Inc, has booked more than $89mn in advertising across two dozen House and Senate races since it was formed on September 1, including at least $10mn deployed since Monday. Although Maga Inc has not confirmed its ties to the group, the two share a treasurer, address and depository bank.
Elon Musk, who spent more than $250mn on Trump’s 2024 election campaign, is also stepping up his support for Republicans in the midterms.
The world’s wealthiest man gave about $50mn to America Pac, mostly last year, and the group spent almost all of it by the end of June. The Super Pac launched an $8mn-plus ad campaign in early September. US media has reported that the Tesla and SpaceX boss could spend $100mn on the 2026 race.
The crypto industry has amassed one of the election’s largest political war chests, using its growing clout under Trump to back candidates who support the sector.
Fairshake, a crypto Super Pac, has raised more than $99mn in individual contributions — nearly all from a handful of companies and investors, including Coinbase, Ripple, and Andreessen and Horowitz.
The political spending comes as Washington makes crucial decisions on AI, Big Tech and digital currencies, said Columbia law professor Richard Briffault. “There’s just a huge amount that’s financially at stake.”
Fairshake has transferred $65mn to Super Pacs supporting candidates from both parties — all designed to promote and defend crypto — in races from Illinois to Alabama and Texas. 
Some billionaires have also financed multiple Super Pacs, adding another layer between themselves and the candidate they are trying to elect.
The Uihlein family, shipping magnates from the Upper Midwest, almost entirely funded two campaign groups focused on Republican primaries in Wisconsin and Kentucky.
JB Pritzker, Illinois’ billionaire Democratic governor and a potential 2028 presidential candidate, provided nearly 80 per cent of the money raised by a Super Pac that spent close to $9mn supporting Democrat Juliana Stratton’s US Senate bid.
Citadel chief executive Ken Griffin, another Republican billionaire backer, has used several vehicles to intervene in races around the country. He is the sole backer of Fighting for Wyoming and American Patriots, which supported candidates in Wyoming and Tennessee, and also accounted for about one-third of the funds raised by a group that spent about $2.8mn opposing the Democratic challenger to Republican senator Dan Sullivan in Alaska.
The concentration of wealthy donors’ money is stark in primaries in safely Democratic or Republican districts, where the party contest can in effect decide who goes to Congress.
Donors might have realised that early spending in those primaries could be more efficient than during a general election, said Stanford’s Bonica.
“In primaries, you can have a pretty sizeable effect,” he said.
Pritzker’s money helped propel Stratton to victory in Illinois. In Texas, Lone Star Rising Pac, funded mostly by tech billionaire Reid Hoffman, had deployed $15mn to support Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, including $1.5mn from Hoffman in support of his primary campaign.

rows.title: Chinese restaurant chains put AI on the menu
rows.content:
Chinese restaurant chains put AI on the menu
Asia’s love of hotpot, a cuisine that involves diners dropping raw meat and vegetables into boiling broth at their table, may look like a way for restaurants to cleverly outsource cooking to their customers. It is also the kind of business that seems far removed from the artificial intelligence boom. But Chinese restaurant operators, whose business models rely heavily on controlling labour and food costs, could be among AI’s early beneficiaries.
Take Hong Kong-listed Haidilao, which runs China’s biggest chain of hotpot restaurants. It uses AI to increase table turnover, analysing video footage to track how far along diners are in their meal across more than 1,200 restaurants. On top of that, robots help deliver dishes from the kitchen to tables, automated kitchen equipment handles repetitive food preparation tasks and intelligent systems assist in managing inventory. Restaurants can generate more revenue from the same real estate and labour, while reducing food waste.
Similarly, Yum China, which owns KFC and Pizza Hut in China and is the country’s largest restaurant operator with more than 19,000 restaurants, is already pushing AI into its daily operations. AI digital assistants help managers with scheduling, inventory and food safety tasks. AI is also being used for new restaurant site selection, forecasting sales to determine when stores need restocking as well as optimising food supply deliveries based on traffic conditions.
The pay-off is starting to show. In the first half of this year, the restaurant-level operating margin at Haidilao’s overseas business, separately listed as Super Hi International, grew to 10.7 per cent from 6.4 per cent. The leap suggests that, as well as benefiting from scale as the number of restaurants increases, the group’s AI investments are starting to improve productivity. For Yum China, too, operating margin in the second quarter reached 11.1 per cent, the ninth consecutive quarter of expansion.
Of course, AI alone cannot take credit for these improvements. Conventional cost control still matters. But across thousands of locations, AI-driven reductions in food waste and labour costs can make the economics of restaurant chains that much more juicy.
For Chinese restaurant stocks that are battling weak consumer sentiment, this provides a helpful buffer. And, more broadly, it points to the next iteration of the AI trade. Investors have spent much of the past year betting on the companies that build the chips and infrastructure powering the technology. The next beneficiaries will be traditional businesses using AI to make existing assets more productive.

rows.title: McLaren to compete against Lamborghini and Ferrari with its first SUV
rows.content:
McLaren to compete against Lamborghini and Ferrari with its first SUV
McLaren is to launch its first SUV in a move the British sports-car maker hopes will boost enough sales to build a second plant in the UK.
The plan for the new vehicle, which will run on a hybrid engine, comes as the carmaker, freshly armed with a £500mn investment from its Abu Dhabi owner and a debt-cleared balance sheet, seeks to end years of losses.
Ferrari, Lamborghini, Bentley and Aston Martin have all expanded outside their traditional supercar range, launching SUV-sized models that have helped increase sales and profits.
“There’s not a region that I can think of where the SUV hasn’t taken . . . very significant market share, particularly in the luxury segments,” said chief executive Nick Collins.
Collins declined to share details of its first four-door “performance SUV” but the product is expected to be launched in the next few years.
As part of the investment, McLaren said it also planned to build a new assembly plant in the UK, although the exact location had not been decided.
McLaren sells more than 2,000 cars a year, less than half of a record 4,800 vehicles it sold in 2018. The group produces all of its cars in the UK from a plant in Woking, which has a targeted production capacity of roughly 3,000 vehicles.
Michael Straughan, its chief operating officer, said other luxury brands all generated sales volumes of between 2,000 and 6,000 from their SUV models. Combined with its current supercars, he said “the capacity isn’t there now”.
“I think this management team is very keen to make sure that . . . we don’t overstretch ourselves financially but we still have to meet the growth targets that we’ve set ourselves,” said Straughan, who was previously the chief operating officer at Aston Martin.
Its pivot to hybrid vehicles comes despite last year’s merger with premium UK electric-vehicle start-up Forseven Holdings.
“We’ll do an EV when our customers ask us to do one, and they’re not asking right now,” Collins said. “We know how we would do it, but we have no imminent plans to execute an EV.”
For the first time, McLaren will also design and build its engines and transmissions in-house, while the new investment will also be used to boost its carbon fibre capabilities and upgrade its paint shop to meet increasing personalisation needs.
The company had come to realise that owning critical parts of the supply chain “allows you not only to drive higher levels of technology . . . but it also allows you to drive the pace of execution in the company”, Collins said. 
CYVN Holdings, the Abu Dhabi government-owned investment company now called L’imad, last year acquired McLaren’s automotive business from Bahraini sovereign wealth fund Mumtalakat and laid out plans to invest $2bn over the next five years to revive the lossmaking group. 
The £500mn programme is expected to create at least 1,000 jobs in the UK by 2032. The group, which currently employs more than 2,500 people, said up to 3,000 additional jobs were likely to be created across its supply chain.
“McLaren Automotive is doubling down on Britain, keeping the design, the engineering and the building of every future car here,” Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in a statement on Wednesday.

rows.title: Ukraine hits Moscow with ‘largest ever’ drone attack
rows.content:
Ukraine hits Moscow with ‘largest ever’ drone attack
Ukraine has hit Moscow with what local authorities said was the largest ever drone attack on the capital, setting a major oil refinery ablaze and killing at least two people, as voting in Russia’s stage-managed parliamentary elections entered its final day.
Moscow’s mayor Sergei Sobyanin said air defences shot down 450 drones as they approached the capital on Saturday night, calling the attack “unprecedented”.
Sobyanin claimed the attack was “clearly planned to disrupt the elections”, adding that “the enemy did not succeed”.
Several drones hit the Moscow Refinery in the south of the capital, one of Russia’s largest.
Videos on social media showed a drone exploding into the refinery, with plumes of black smoke shrouding the sunrise, and several areas of the facility on fire. A nearby power station, warehouse and market were also hit.
Drones also hit residential buildings near the refinery and at least 11 suburban towns in the surrounding region, authorities said. Two people died in the attacks and a further 20 people were injured, including three children, according to Andrei Vorobyov, governor of the Moscow region.
Flights were grounded at all three of Moscow’s main airports. Russia’s defence ministry claimed to have shot down a total of 1,110 drones across the country overnight.
Kyiv and Moscow have continued striking each other’s energy infrastructure throughout the week despite Donald Trump’s claim on Monday that the warring sides had agreed to halt such attacks, which the US president blamed for the surge in global diesel prices. Trump has not commented on the attacks, which Russia and Ukraine continued within hours of his statement.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy posted on social media that Ukraine had used domestically produced drones and cruise missiles to target facilities he said earned “billions of dollars that support the war machine”.
Zelenskyy said a plan to de-escalate the strikes on energy and food export infrastructure was “on the table” but required “political will”.
Russia has rejected calls for a ceasefire of attacks on energy and other infrastructure ahead of what is expected to be a major campaign of air strikes against Ukraine this winter. Russian President Vladimir Putin expects the strikes to strengthen Moscow’s position and help extract concessions from Ukraine, according to people familiar with his thinking.
Polls in the three-day parliamentary elections, the first since Putin ordered the invasion of Ukraine in 2022, were set to close on Sunday evening. Turnout at noon local time on Sunday was 48 per cent, according to the central election commission.
The vote has proceeded without drama even by Russian standards as an array of Kremlin-run, pro-war parties compete for seats in parliament. Russia’s supreme court removed Yabloko, the only party that had expressed even mild opposition to the war, from the ballot last month.
A Russian air strike overnight on Kyiv killed a mother and two small children, while another mother and her child were injured in a separate attack, according to Ukrainian authorities.
Regional authorities said a drone destroyed a vehicle in the north-eastern region of Sumy, killing four people.
Ukraine’s air force said Russia had fired 138 drones overnight, half of them jet-powered models that pose a greater challenge for air defences.
On Saturday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s state security service, the SBU, had brought down jet-powered drones using a new interceptor drone.

rows.title: Nvidia and Meta bosses reject efforts to co-ordinate AI slowdown
rows.content:
Nvidia and Meta bosses reject efforts to co-ordinate AI slowdown
Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg have pushed back against efforts by “frontier” AI labs to co-ordinate a slowdown in research in the name of safety, arguing companies should address the risks individually.
The two chief executives in separate comments on Tuesday emphasised the responsibility of individual companies to tackle concerns that AI research risks spinning out of control and posing a threat to humanity.
Huang, who has been dismissive of such existential warnings, went further, saying there was no need for new US laws or regulations on AI safety, and urging AI labs not to fall into a “false choice” between the speed of innovation and the ability to develop safe products.
The pair of tech founders weighed in after Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Elon Musk on the weekend publicly called for a co-ordinated slowdown in research to properly tackle the risks AI poses.
The rare moment of unity among the three bitter rivals followed mounting public outcry and warnings from researchers that an all-out race to advance AI risked humans losing control of the technology with catastrophic consequences.
Zuckerberg, who has created a major AI lab inside Meta, and Huang, who leads the world’s biggest supplier of AI hardware which offers its own suite of AI models, have not signed up to those proposals for industry co-operation to “pace the frontier”, even as Google and Microsoft have signalled support.
Their split reflects deeper divisions in the AI industry between the leading developers of proprietary “closed” models, such as OpenAI and Anthropic, and those advocating for customisable “open” models.
Huang has pushed the importance of open models to encourage widespread AI adoption, while Meta has released some closed models but generally argued for open systems. Some open model advocates say regulations or controls on development would advantage big labs that sell closed systems.
Huang on Tuesday argued companies should individually focus on not releasing dangerous products.
“The market forces are already there, we don’t need any new laws, we don’t need new regulations,” he said at an event with Salesforce’s chief executive Marc Benioff in San Francisco on Tuesday.
“If you build a product or a service and you’re not confident in its functionality, capability or safety, then don’t release it,” said the Nvidia boss, whose company is a big investor in OpenAI, Anthropic and Musk’s SpaceX. “That’s a very obvious thing to do: You pace yourself until you are confident you’re releasing something that the market will appreciate.”
“You could definitely have both [innovation and safety] at the same time,” Huang added. “So run as fast as you can, but if you feel at any given point in time the company is out of control or products are not going to be safe, you know, take a pause and get it right.”
The head of the world’s most valuable company has aligned himself with Donald Trump against an AI slowdown. Huang took a phone call from the president while on stage at an event on Monday, where Trump again rejected existential concerns about the technology as a “hoax” and railed against moves to slow US research and data centre construction.
“You’re right. We’re not going to let that happen, sir,” Huang responded.
Zuckerberg outlined his views in a post on X later on Tuesday, echoing Huang’s argument that the responsibility to ensure safety lies with individual AI labs.
“Every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely, and the ability to take its own actions to ensure that happens,” Zuckerberg wrote. “Labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this as well.”
Zuckerberg said Meta delayed shipping its own Muse AI agent for several months but “didn’t call for everyone else to do this before we would”.
He added that a “larger and more diverse ecosystem of evaluators”, the independent experts used by labs to assess models, would be helpful. But he did not address proposals from Anthropic to give these evaluators greater access.

rows.title: EU capitals rebuff Carney’s ‘unique alliance’ with Canada
rows.content:
EU capitals rebuff Mark Carney’s ‘unique alliance’ with Canada
EU capitals have given a cool reception to Canada’s bid to be granted a “unique alliance” with the bloc, deflating Prime Minister Mark Carney’s pitch for “middle powers” to close ranks against the US and China.
Carney, who is visiting France and the UK this week, in an interview with the FT urged Europe to deepen its economic alliance with Canada after previously floating the idea of “associate membership” for his country.
But his charm offensive has failed to sway governments wary of giving Ottawa preferential trade access, according to five EU diplomats involved in the talks.
Instead, the sceptics have countered that Canada could instead be offered better implementation of existing agreements, the diplomats said. There is also consensus about the bloc intensifying its collaboration with Canadian arms makers and critical mineral mining companies.
“We love the Canadians but everyone is very realistic about what’s possible and what’s not,” said one EU diplomat. “Saying ‘everything but membership’ sounds good, but came across as not really thought through,” they added. “But I don’t fault [Carney] for trying.”
Another diplomat said concerns over how US President Donald Trump might react to a significantly enhanced relationship with Canada were also influencing some EU capitals. Countries that rely on Nato protection in the face of Russian threats, such as the Baltics, were especially concerned, said a third diplomat.
“Of all the third countries, Canada is one of the few that we all want to get closer to right now,” said a fourth diplomat. “But even with them, we all know we have to be careful when you start talking about trade access and preferential treatment.”
Carney has pitched himself as a geopolitical lightning rod for western liberal democratic collaboration to protect multilateral bodies threatened by the Trump administration’s aggressive foreign policy. Canada is one of just two countries — alongside China — to impose retaliatory tariffs on the US in response to Trump’s trade war.
As part of his campaign to woo the EU, the Canadian premier will attend the annual State of the Union speech by European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen in Strasbourg on Wednesday, and deliver his own address to the European parliament on Thursday.
Carney had coined the term “middle powers” in a speech to the Davos event this January and said they had to coalesce to withstand superpowers such as China and the US. Von der Leyen has broadly endorsed the same concept.
But at last week’s meeting of ambassadors from EU member states to prepare for Carney’s visit, one remarked that the bloc was “not a ‘middle power’” and the much smaller Canada should not expect any special treatment, according to people briefed on the exchange.
“Many capitals feel that there needs to be a bit of a sense of realism,” said a fifth diplomat. He pointed to the fact that 10 countries, including France and Italy, have yet to ratify Canada’s 2017 free trade deal with the EU (Ceta), which was held up over objections from several national assemblies to provisions that would give Canadian investors more rights to sue governments and to lower tariffs for agricultural goods.
In his interview with the FT, Carney notably moderated his aspirations, asking for the 10 EU countries to ratify Ceta.
The deal is in force provisionally, meaning most of its provisions — including tariff cuts, customs rules and market access for goods and services — already apply.
But full ratification is looking increasingly uncertain: France faces presidential elections, while Italy’s Giorgia Meloni may have to strike an alliance with a far-right nationalist ahead of next year’s general election, dimming the prospects for approval in two of the EU’s largest member states.
A gap in rules and standards has also dimmed prospects for closer Canada-EU alignment, particularly given the pull of the US market. The EU accounts for less than 6 per cent of Canadian goods exports, limiting the scope for deeper trade ties.
Beef is a case in point. Canada exports none to the EU despite a low-tariff quota under Ceta because its producers use growth hormones that are banned under the bloc’s rules.
Many trade irritants remain. The EU wants Canada to drop its tariffs on EU steel and some products such as nails. It also wants it to water down “Buy Canadian” rules that favour domestic production over imports.
Ottawa is similarly unhappy with the EU’s proposed “made in Europe” policy and its environmental regulations that will raise costs for critical exports such as lumber and aluminium.
The two sides hope to conclude a digital trade agreement before an October 29-30 summit in Montreal.
But EU countries are aware that many regulations are set at provincial level in Canada, making it hard for the federal government to deliver promised changes.

rows.title: US charges five people linked to Russian ‘assassination network’
rows.content:
US charges five people linked to Russian ‘assassination network’
The US has charged five individuals in connection with what it called a “global assassination network” controlled by the Kremlin in a sweeping indictment that includes claims of a murder-for-hire plot on American soil.
The Department of Justice said the group, composed of Russian, Cuban and Venezuelan nationals, was paid to conduct surveillance and plotted to kill dissidents in the US and Lithuania. It also targeted military and civilian infrastructure in European countries that are supportive of Ukraine.
Jamie McDonald, New York’s top federal prosecutor, on Tuesday said: “The defendants, working for the intelligence services of Russia, conspired to cause destruction and mayhem around the world, including right here in the United States.”
The defendants are at large, he added. The DoJ said the Russian intelligence network, known as RIS, had operated since at least 2024.
The indictment marks a rare public example of an alleged Russian-backed assassination plot in the US. British and European officials have accused the Kremlin’s intelligence services of being behind the murder and attempted assassination of dissidents, dating back to the mid-2000s.
Moscow has stepped up efforts to target its critics and disrupt European support for Ukraine since it launched its full-scale invasion of the country in 2022.
The US indictment charged Yuri Khrameev, Kirill Khrameev, Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, Yaidel Delgado Suarez and Angel Eduardo Castro with participating in a conspiracy to finance terrorism. Yuri Khrameev, Suarez and Castro were also charged with conspiracy to commit murder for hire.
Suarez, described by the DoJ as a “prolific recruiter” for RIS, allegedly sought to enlist US-based individuals for surveillance and targeted killings. He and Castro are accused of offering a US resident $40,000 to “eliminate” or “disappear” an unnamed prominent Russian dissident suspected of residing in the US.
Prosecutors said the US resident agreed to “take pics”, or surveil, the intended target but would not do “the other stuff”.
The US government also said Yuri Khrameev recruited an individual living in the US to assassinate an individual in Lithuania who he accused of “spreading dirt about my country”. Khrameev allegedly offered the US-based individual $25,000 to kill the dissident and suggested it could be carried out by “throwing a bottle of gasoline” or “sticking a knife” in the person.
The US-based individual declined to help kill the dissident because they believed there was no way to carry out the killing without being caught, according to charging papers.
US attorney-general Todd Blanche touted the administration’s efforts to crack down on terrorism earlier on Tuesday, saying FBI data showed a 38 per cent increase in arrests related to foreign terrorist organisations from the prior administration.
This year, Moscow has appeared to escalate its sabotage attempts against critical infrastructure and logistics hubs in Europe. German officials earlier this month blamed Moscow after an explosive-laden drone was discovered near a Ukrainian plane at Leipzig airport.

rows.title: Hormuz crisis threatens to undermine long-term LNG demand
rows.content:
Hormuz crisis threatens to undermine long-term LNG demand
This article is an on-site version of our Moral Money newsletter. Premium subscribers can sign up here to get the newsletter delivered twice a week. Standard subscribers can upgrade to Premium here, or explore all FT newsletters.
Visit our Moral Money hub for all the latest ESG news, opinion and analysis from around the FT
Welcome back.
Donald Trump’s administration has scrapped rules limiting greenhouse gas emissions from US power plants — its latest move to drive growth in the country’s fossil fuel sector.
But this year’s conflict with Iran is creating new threats to that “energy dominance” agenda, as I explain below.
Clouds gather over the LNG outlook
Trump returned to power last year promising a new age of international growth for US sales of liquefied natural gas. On his first day back in office, he signed an order reversing Joe Biden’s pause on approvals for new LNG export terminals — part of a drive to boost the uptake of US fossil fuel resources and “unleash energy dominance”.
But the conflict that Trump entered into this year has created new risks to the outlook for US LNG sales, as the developing markets that were meant to drive long-term growth recoil at soaring prices and turn increasingly towards low-cost renewables.
To be clear, the turmoil in gas markets since the Iran war began in February has meant a short-term windfall for US LNG exporters. The blockage of shipments through the Strait of Hormuz from Qatar — which previously accounted for a fifth of global LNG supplies — has created a shortage with inevitable price consequences.
The Japan-Korea Marker for LNG prices, a key benchmark, which started the year below $10 per million British thermal units (MMBtu), reached more than $22 per MMBtu in March. Having moderated somewhat over the summer, it has been surging again over the past month, reaching a new high for the year this week above $25 per MMBtu.
This has brought bumper revenues for US exporters, who have increased their LNG shipments to “near maximum output levels”, according to a recent update from the government’s Energy Information Administration. Helpfully for the sector, new terminal capacity approved before the Biden pause has now come into action, enabling a 23 per cent rise in US LNG exports in the first half of the year.
But while the price jump is boosting LNG profits for now, it is threatening the foundations of future growth — especially in the developing Asian economies that the sector has been counting on to drive increases in long-term demand. These countries have been cutting back their gas power generation in response to the higher prices — in India, for example, it fell 25 per cent in the second quarter of the year.
In India and other Asian economies such as Vietnam, that has brought a near-term bounce in coal-fired generation, the most carbon-intensive fossil fuel. But the gas squeeze has strengthened policy moves in the region to accelerate the shift to renewables.
This month, Thailand announced a goal of helping 1mn households install 5 gigawatts of rooftop solar panels in an effort to reduce reliance on gas, which at present fuels most of the country’s power generation. Recent government strategy documents envisioned a far smaller long-term role for gas-fired power than had been the case previously, said Christopher Doleman, Asia gas specialist at the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis.
Similar dynamics are emerging across much of Asia. Vietnam’s Vingroup has cancelled a $6.8bn plan for the country’s biggest gas-fired power station, instead moving to build a plant using solar and wind power backed by battery storage.
Prices for large-scale batteries have declined dramatically over the past three years, offering a newly cost-effective source of grid flexibility that threatens one of the key arguments for gas plants, which can be fired up more quickly than coal power stations.
This has enabled countries including Pakistan to significantly expand their plans for the deployment of renewable power. Last month, Pakistani power minister Awais Leghari announced a new national target of achieving 90 per cent clean generation in the national power mix by 2035, saying battery storage would be “a strategic asset for our energy sovereignty” by reducing reliance on imported gas.
Within the US, solar and wind plants now account for the vast majority of new generation capacity being added to the grid. Gas power is, however, getting a boost from the surge in data centre construction to serve the AI needs of US tech companies. Many developers are building on-site gas plants to power their new data centres rather than endure long waits for grid connections.
Yet the increased US demand for gas power is causing yet another barrier to international growth — by creating huge delivery backlogs for gas plant turbines and sending their prices surging. This was a major factor behind the strategic rethink on gas power in south-east Asian countries such as Thailand, said Doleman at the IEEFA.
In its recent annual report, the International Gas Union predicted that global gas demand would resume its strong upward trend after a decline this year. “The longer-term structural role of gas in meeting accelerating global energy demand will continue,” said the trade body’s president Andrea Stegher. But in many of the developing economies driving that energy demand growth, doubts about gas’s role appear to be rising.
“It is about the energy transition,” Thai energy minister Akanat Promphan said after this month’s rooftop solar announcement, “because otherwise we’ll be subjected to what’s happening in the Middle East forever.”
Smart reads
- US billionaires are lining up to fund Republican candidates ahead of this year’s midterm elections.
- Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg are opposing calls for AI companies to co-ordinate a research slowdown in the name of safety.

rows.title: Trump says 250ft arch will be ‘military complex’ with drones and snipers
rows.content:
Trump says 250ft arch will be ‘military complex’ with drones and snipers
Donald Trump said he plans to convert his proposed Triumphal Arch in Washington into a “top grade military complex” featuring snipers, drones and ammunition storage.
“There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World,” the US president posted on Truth Social on Sunday.
Trump wants to build a 250ft-high Triumphal Arch in the grassy middle of the busy Memorial Circle, which sits between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington Cemetery.
“At the strong request of the United States Military, and for National Security purposes, I have agreed to convert the magnificent Triumphal Arch . . . into a top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch, to house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage,” Trump said in the post.
Three Vietnam war veterans and an architectural historian have sued to block construction of the arch. They argue that it would ruin the view between the two memorials, which symbolise the unification of the country after the Civil War, and that Congress has not authorised spending for it.
Interior secretary Doug Burgum announced on September 3 that excavation work would begin. Public Citizen, which is representing the plaintiffs, filed a temporary restraining order. US District Judge Tanya Chutkan then ordered the government to provide the court with 48 hours’ notice before engaging further.
“The President’s belated efforts to manufacture a national security justification for this project do nothing to cure its fundamental illegality,” Nick Sansone, an attorney at Public Citizen, wrote to the FT. “Congress has not authorised the arch and unless and until Congress does so, the project should not be permitted to move forward.”
The Cultural Landscape Foundation said they had asked the National Park Service to explain how the revised design would affect traffic circulation and public access, and whether a security perimeter would need to be erected.
The White House and NPS did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Trump is planning more than $1bn worth of redevelopment projects in Washington, including the new White House ballroom, renovations to the Kennedy Center, National Garden of American Heroes and Reflecting Pool, and the new Triumphal Arch. The Trump administration has also relied on national security arguments to advance the construction of the ballroom.
Trump’s projects have led to a backlash in Washington. Thousands of people protested this weekend at the Kennedy Center after Trump threatened to rip it down.
Washington residents have also protested against the Triumphal Arch. On June 4, the National Capital Planning Commission, the federal design and construction review panel, held a meeting where the public could give their views. The vast majority of the 1,696 written comments were negative.
Dozens showed up to express their opposition in person and chant outside the nondescript office building with a cardboard cut-out of Trump with a cartoon bubble: “I’m stealing from YOU!”
The commission, which is stacked with Trump loyalists, has not yet given its final approval.

rows.title: The BoE’s three balance sheet problem
rows.content:
The BoE’s three balance sheet problem
September is usually when Alphaville starts speculating about the Bank of England’s quantitative tightening review, the annual decision on how fast and by how much it wants to reduce its balance sheet over the following 12 months. This year is no different, with the Monetary Policy Committee’s decision due alongside the interest rate decision on Thursday, September 17.
But rather than give you yet another piece calling for an end to gilt sales, we thought we’d turn to one of QE’s less-discussed distortions of the BoE balance sheet: the Issue Department.
Victorian plumbing
The Issue Department is the BoE’s unsexy and largely imaginary second balance sheet. It’s an accounting treatment created by the 1844 Bank Charter Act to split out the BoE’s role as issuer of the sovereign currency from its role as a bank. Under the terms of the legislation it’s allowed to hold only one liability — banknotes — and, on the asset side, it holds securities and other assets sufficient to match the note issue. Everything else — reserves, repo operations, etc — sits on the Banking Department.
Most of the time the legal separation of the balance sheets doesn’t really matter. It’s an accounting fiction that helps to clarify what claim HM Treasury has on the profits of the central bank. The income on the assets backing the note issue pays for the design, production and distribution of banknotes, with the remaining seigniorage — the profits generated by issuing currency — passed to HM Treasury.
At many central banks the policy and note issue functions take place on one consolidated balance sheet. That allows them to “back” the note issue with a mix of assets. (Technically speaking, no liability needs to be backed one-for-one by a specific asset as long as the balance sheet balances.) This is the mechanism that enables central banks such as the Federal Reserve, through accounting wizardry, to defer QE losses by booking them against future notes income. And they’re hardly the only ones doing this.
But it matters for the BoE now because, for the past 17 years, the note issue has, in effect, been backed by the APF loan which is being unwound through gilt maturities and sales. To explain this, here’s a stylised diagram:
Historically, the BoE used an Issue Department deposit with the Banking Department (electric raspberry pink boxes) as a balancing item to handle small fluctuations in the demand for banknotes. But before the global financial crisis, it had never been used to cover almost the entirety of the note issue. In 2006 and 2007 the deposit was about £50mn, matching 0.1 per cent of notes in circulation (the rest was backed by repos against high-quality collateral and what is known as the Ways and Means advance to the National Loans Fund). Between 2009 and 2026, it grew from around £29bn to almost £100bn, or 99 per cent of the note issue.
Although it’s not a “real” asset, it earns interest, which flows from the Banking Department to the Issue Department and ultimately a Treasury account at the BoE (the National Loans Fund). And as the deposit has grown, so has the interest it earns. Here is the BoE’s own description of the arrangement in its most recent annual report (our emphasis):
The Issue Department is funded by interest‑yielding assets which are held to back the notes in circulation. The interest earned on these assets is used to fund the costs of note production and supply. The net profits/losses of the Issue Department are referred to as seigniorage, and paid/claimed directly to/from HM Treasury via the National Loans Fund (NLF), an account held at the Bank by HM Treasury. The £3.8bn net seigniorage income is comprised of income and profits of £3.9bn, less £61mn expenses and a buffer withheld by the Bank of £8mn. The increase in income and profits is mainly driven by increased interest earned on the deposit with the Banking Department.
Gilts by association
Where this links to QE is that during the era of large-scale asset purchases the main asset on the BoE balance sheet became the loan to the asset purchase facility (blue boxes), which holds gilts purchased for QE. For QE to expand, the APF’s balance sheet expanded, and this meant that the loan from the Banking Department to the asset purchase facility had to grow. With the asset side of the Banking Department’s balance sheet expanding, so too grew the liability side — and this meant commercial banks’ reserve balances. But it also meant that the mix of assets backing banknotes was increasingly dominated by loans to the APF, and ultimately QE gilts in this weird daisy chain of intra-balance-sheet claims.
That was all fine until the BoE started to shrink its balance sheet in 2022 and replace reserves created by QE with reserves created by repo. This is where we are today:
This Thursday the MPC is widely expected to slow the pace of QT to around £50bn, which would reduce the size of the APF to around £438bn by September 2027. As the APF continues to shrink, the BoE will need to decide how to back the note issue, which has been growing at a rate of about 3 per cent per annum.
Repo is a poor match to play that role. Banknotes are a stable, quasi-permanent liability, while repo fluctuates with banks’ demand for liquidity, and it would charge commercial banks to provide a public good.
The cleanest answer would be to stop pretending there are three balance sheets. As Monetary Policy Radar’s Elettra Ardissino argued in a recent newsletter, merging the balance sheets would probably require amending the Bank Charter Act. That may be within the government’s gift, but it’s not the sort of thing a new government is likely to want to squeeze into an already tight legislative timetable.
So, what should the BoE do?
The once and future gilt portfolio
This summer, veteran APF watchers and friends of Alphaville Moyeen Islam at Barclays and Sanjay Raja at Deutsche Bank independently unearthed pre-Covid hints by the BoE that it would back the note issue with gilts. “There is … a strong case for holding some longer maturity assets, such as gilts, outright to back the stable portion of demand for banknotes,” Mark Carney said in 2018.
This is not just about giving the gilt market a new price-insensitive, structural buyer. A structural gilt portfolio would also give the BoE a clear way to manage autonomous factors — the balance sheet items that move independently of monetary policy but still affect the supply of reserves. If banknote demand is broadly stable, holding stable assets against them is less weird than funding the whole thing through repo or a rapidly diminishing APF loan.
For Islam and Raja, this provides support for the argument that the BoE could, if it wants to, declare victory on QT and turn to the design of a permanent bond portfolio. There are a variety of reasons to want this, not least of which is that it would reduce the volume of gilts the market will need to absorb over the coming years, albeit only marginally. Obviously, it would also be good for the portfolio of anyone who currently holds gilts. But the more interesting point is that the BoE may eventually need some kind of structural asset portfolio anyway, if only to give the note issue something less weird to sit on.
Put another way, the APF could already be about £100bn smaller than it is today. The slice of the APF balance sheet that matches the note issue through the chain of deposits and loans is ultimately funded by banknotes, a non-interest-bearing liability. Yes, the Banking Department pays interest on the Issue Department deposit, but that interest becomes Issue Department income, which flows to Treasury as seigniorage, which then pays it back out to cover the APF’s interest expenses to Banking Department. It’s money on a round trip through the government’s various debt and cash management accounts.
Indeed, the BoE had already started to back the note issue with gilts before the global financial crisis. Its motivation then was to provide a structural source of reserves:
The Bank’s objective in purchasing bonds is to provide longer-term financing for the banking system to ensure, as a necessary precondition for implementing monetary policy effectively, that it provides the right amount of central bank money for the banking system.
But to avoid the confusing optics of the central bank operating in the gilt market for two different purposes, it suspended the Issue Department gilt purchases when it started QE. The £5.4bn of gilts it purchased between 2008 and 2009 remained on the balance sheet, however. The rump of that portfolio that hasn’t matured yet is still there and worth just £732mn at the last valuation.
For the past two years the BoE has had to contend with dwindling demand for the APF’s long-dated gilts. In fact, on Tuesday the Telegraph reported that the BoE has been in discussion with HM Treasury and the DMO to stop selling long gilts altogether. But moving some of those unloved bonds from the APF to the Issue Department would offer a tidy accounting solution to the three-balance-sheet problem. Economically it changes very little. There is no one neat trick to avoiding the QE losses. It is just a matter of when and where they are recognised.
The QT decision this week will be interesting less for the pace of balance sheet reduction than for what it might say about QT’s terminal destination. The three balance sheet problem is not by itself a big enough reason to stop QT, but it is a useful reminder that the BoE cannot shrink its balance sheet forever without deciding what sort of balance sheet it actually wants.
Further reading:
— The UK Treasury can’t avoid the Bank of England’s losses (MainFT)
— What happens after the Bank of England has declared balance-sheet victory? (FTAV)
— The Bank of England gets with the programme on QT (FTAV)
— Could the DMO take the BoE’s long gilts off their hands? (FTAV)

rows.title: The EU should not increase resilience at the expense of trusted partners
rows.content:
The EU should not increase resilience at the expense of trusted partners
The writer is Japan’s ambassador to the EU
Remember the Inflation Reduction Act? The Biden administration’s objective then was clear: to accelerate the green transition and strengthen America’s industrial resilience. Yet some of its provisions caused an outcry among US allies, particularly in Europe, because they risked disrupting investment and supply chains involving trusted partners.
The EU’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act appears to go further down the same path. It intends to strengthen European competitiveness and reduce strategic vulnerabilities. However, there are elements of the legislation that similarly risk creating unintended consequences for Europe’s closest partners, including Japan.
Consider the proposed conditions in the IAA for financial support for corporate electric vehicles. Eligibility would depend on detailed EU content requirements, which are dubious in the light of WTO rules. Those overlook the reality of today’s integrated supply chain ecosystem, inadvertently penalising trusted partners that are already deeply integrated into Europe’s industrial base. Moreover, if EU-made components are sent outside the bloc and later return as finished products but are no longer treated as EU products, European companies themselves could also be affected.
An automobile is the product of years of research and development, which requires long-term capital investment and a network of suppliers across borders. A vehicle may be designed in one country, contain components and technologies developed and produced in several others, and the whole be assembled somewhere else.
Japanese automobile companies have long invested in Europe. In 2025, they produced approximately 614,000 vehicles within the EU. They currently operate 13 manufacturing bases and 19 R&D centres with 160,000 European workers. In effect, they are contributing to Europe’s industrial strength.
What is needed to enhance European competitiveness is to create a more reliable and secure supply-chain process encompassing trusted partners such as Japan — not simply focusing on the nationalities of car brands or where one part of the process, such as final assembly, takes place.
Today, competitiveness and economic security are increasingly two sides of the same coin. And Japan and the EU are showing how this works in practice.
Take critical minerals. France’s Caremag rare earth refining project is being supported by Japan’s Jogmec and Iwatani. Japan and France are investing up to €206mn together and have secured a long-term supply agreement for heavy rare earths, while the project will also process recycled materials. This is precisely what resilient supply chains should be: European industrial capacity combined with trusted international investment, technology and long-term commitments.
Europe has every right to promote domestic investment and strengthen its industrial base. It is also not unreasonable for governments to attach conditions to public support in accordance with international rules. The question, however, is whether those conditions recognise the realities of today’s cross-border supply chain ecosystem and the value of trusted international partnerships.
The IAA should not — even inadvertently — penalise the companies of close partners, which have invested deeply in Europe and become part of its industrial networks simply because their headquarters happen to be elsewhere. Trusted international partners are part of Europe’s industrial strength.
In today’s increasingly challenging geopolitical and geoeconomic environment, Japan and the EU will be stronger together. We have repeatedly proven that challenges can be overcome through collaboration and co-operation, and should do the same this time around.

rows.title: Wave of murders spreads fear in Johannesburg
rows.content:
Wave of murders spreads fear in Johannesburg
A wave of killings of women in South Africa’s largest city has caused fear and anger even in a country accustomed to high rates of violence and crime.
Two women were found murdered days apart this week, the latest in a series of grisly discoveries in Johannesburg’s east — close to its international airport — that have shone a spotlight on South Africa’s epidemic of violence against women.
Since July, the mutilated bodies of eight women have been found in fields, along highways and on pathways in the Ekurhuleni area, all of them half naked and showing signs of assault.
The first victim was identified in July, a 37-year-old woman who had been strangled with cable ties. Police said they were investigating the possibility that the eight deaths were linked.
The killings have brought renewed attention to South Africa’s longstanding crisis of violence against women and its femicide rate, one of the world’s highest. Women were killed in the country at a rate of 12.2 per 100,000 people in 2022, nearly six times the global rate, according to the UN Office on Drugs and Crime.
Images have circulated widely of a smiling Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo during a marathon. The 38-year-old mother disappeared on September 9 after leaving her Kempton Park home for her usual evening run. Her eight-year-old daughter raised the alarm when she failed to return.
“In this country we are prey,” Sakane Mokoena, her friend and fellow runner, posted on Instagram.
Rose Ncube, who lives in the same Kempton Park neighbourhood, said she had stopped allowing her two young daughters, aged 13 and eight, to walk to nearby shops or play in the park.
“I’m scared for them. It’s not good for them to stay inside, but they are safer this way,” said Ncube, a 41-year-old accountant.
“I can’t describe the fear. You try to put it out of your mind but in South Africa, something happens again and again to remind you. That fear is never far.”
President Cyril Ramaphosa on Tuesday said he had “directed that these cases be prioritised and that no stone be left unturned in bringing those responsible to justice”. But there has been widespread anger at what campaigners say is a lacklustre government response to the violence.
Kayan Leung — a deputy director of Lawyers for Human Rights and member of #NotFitForPurpose, an advocacy group campaigning for legal changes in the area — said: “This is not new . . . the gender-based violence and femicide in South Africa is a pandemic. The recent events simply draw attention to the issue when women face this fear and lived reality daily.”
Ramaphosa declared gender-based violence and femicide a national crisis in 2019, but the government has failed to properly fund or implement a national plan since then, campaigners said.
“We constantly have to protest and shout outrage. Women’s lives are at stake and this is not a political opportunity to campaign,” Leung said.
The violence cuts across class and race. In 2025, the killing of 30-year-old Olorato Mongale after a date with a man she had met at a mall sparked widespread anger, as did the murder of teacher Kirsten Kluyts, who was murdered while taking part in a run in upmarket Sandton in 2023. Kluyts’s killer was convicted this week.
The latest killings have prompted a backlash against police advice that women should take measures to protect themselves. “We are tired of being told to be vigilant when women are already doing everything possible to stay alive,” said Women For Change, an advocacy group.
“We are angry because we are watching the response suddenly ramp up. Police, search teams, K9 units, forensic specialists, tracking teams, even politicians, everyone is arriving now. Where was this urgency before?”

rows.title: Trump says he will not renovate Kennedy Center unless his name is on it
rows.content:
Donald Trump says he will not renovate Kennedy Center unless his name is on it
Donald Trump said the Kennedy Center would not be renovated unless the courts allowed Washington’s top performing arts facility to put the US president’s name on the building.
Trump announced that the centre’s board of trustees agreed on Tuesday to close the building “for safety reasons” but that its reconstruction would not proceed until courts greenlit the new name.
“If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is not overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court, the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place,” he wrote on Truth Social.
Trump’s vow came after a federal judge rejected the president’s latest effort to stick his name on the memorial to the late Democratic president John F Kennedy without congressional approval.
US District Judge Christopher Cooper said the board’s August vote to inscribe “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump” on the building’s facade violated federal law and his earlier ruling to strip the president’s name from the centre.
Cooper previously ruled that the board had unlawfully voted to rename the building as the “Trump Kennedy” centre.
“Simply put, Defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress’s blessing,” Cooper said.
The Kennedy Center did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The judge on Tuesday also barred the board from renaming the centre’s campus the “President Donald J. Trump Plaza”. The DoJ appealed against the ruling Tuesday evening, after Trump said the agency would seek “expedited” review.
The president fixed his sights on the Kennedy Center early in his second term. Trump placed some of his top aides on the centre’s board soon after returning to the White House and they later appointed him as chair, prompting swift backlash from artists and a wave of high-profile cancellations.
The renovation of the renowned performing arts centre is one of several construction projects that have been bogged down by legal challenges as Trump pursues a $1bn renovation of the nation’s capital. The projects include a new White House ballroom and so-called Triumphal Arch.
Leadership of the performing arts centre has long called for renovations.
On Monday evening, commerce secretary Howard Lutnick posted a video on social media showing plaster from the centre’s ceiling “crashing violently” to the ground. He claimed it dropped from 60 feet and weighed more than 150lbs.
“The entire building is in this kind of shape,” Lutnick said. “People cannot be allowed to go into this building any longer. It must be closed and reconstructed, and a major fundraising effort must take place to cover the Kennedy Center’s operating expenses.”
Joyce Beatty, the Democratic Congress member and ex officio board member who sued over Trump’s Kennedy Center takeover, said in a statement that the institution had long planned to undergo phased renovations, which would have allowed some performances to continue as upgrades were made.
“This is how major performing arts centres in the country operate,” she said. “But donors, patrons and artists all fled after the unlawful attempt to rename this sacred memorial after Donald Trump.”
“Donald Trump only cares about the Kennedy Center for his vanity,” she added.

rows.title: The capital city that’s one of Europe’s top birdwatching destinations
rows.content:
Postcard from Athens: the capital has history, culture — and some of Europe’s best birdwatching
It’s 8am and a long, fractious queue is already snaking up the steep, dusty path to the Acropolis. Yet just 600 metres away, shaded by Aleppo pines on neighbouring Philopappou Hill, I’m patiently waiting to observe another ancient sight in a peaceful and crowd-free park.
Thousands of white-bellied alpine swifts migrate through the city and it’s not long before I spot their forked tails and boomerang-shaped wings soaring through the cloudless sky, feeding on insects (these agile aerialists rarely land despite travelling over 4,000 miles a year).
“Alpine swifts have been spotted in Athens for centuries, settling in rocky outcrops to breed in summer — it’s wonderful to see them flying over the Parthenon,” says Spyros Skareas, founder of Greece Bird Tours and a professional bird guide for the past two decades.
The birds are on many twitchers’ “life lists” along with the Rüppell’s warbler, Cretzschmar’s bunting, sombre tit and rock nuthatch — all of which can be ticked off in Athens and its environs. “Athens is one of Europe’s top birdwatching destinations because it has such a surprisingly diverse mix of habitats so close to the city centre,” says Spyros. “It’s definitely the best European capital for a birding city break.”
Nature is not the first thing you think of when walking around this ancient city’s sun-baked and chaotic streets. Yet Greece’s capital is as rich in birdlife as it is in history, culture and feta-based dishes. Positioned on migratory routes between Europe, Asia and Africa, the landscape surrounding it includes a wide variety of bird-friendly habitats — wetlands, coastal lagoons, mountains, forests and Mediterranean scrub are all under an hour’s drive away.
Autumn and spring are the best times to visit, when the bird population explodes with migratory species. But Greece’s mild Mediterranean climate supports birdwatching all year round with water birds, including common kingfishers, herons, egrets, ducks and grebes, wintering in Athens’ nearby wetlands.
As we climb steps made of the same white Pentelic marble as the Parthenon, Spyros’s eyes dart constantly between sky, trees and bush. “Spotting birds is as much about noticing patterns and listening as it is about looking through binoculars,” he says. We hear (but don’t see) an elusive Sardinian warbler, its rapid high-pitched call identified by Spyros rather than Merlin, the birding app I usually rely on at home.
The distinctive black and white striped wings of a hoopoe disappear into a bush before I can lift my phone to capture it, and a handful of raptors circle menacingly overhead. Peregrine falcons, sparrowhawks, kestrels and buzzards congregate beside the Acropolis to hunt, while Eurasian magpies and hooded crows hop around the parched soil waiting to feast on leftovers. I start to feel the mindful benefits of slowing down on a city break rather than rushing around to see every museum, market or monument.
Unfortunately, there’s no sign of the sacred symbol of Athens itself: the little owl, usually especially active at dawn and dusk. According to myth, the little owl accompanied Athena, goddess of wisdom; ancient Greeks stamped it on silver tetradrachm coins (on display in the Archaeological Museum) and the same fifth-century BC image of it appears on modern Greek euro coins. I take one out of my purse to see what I’ve missed. Spyros explains that, unlike in central Europe, where their population is in decline, in Athens city centre they’re thriving. Like the alpine swift, little owls sometimes nest in its monuments, including the Parthenon.
Other species, such as the European goldfinch, griffon vulture and blue rock-thrush are not so lucky; rapid urban and coastal development in the 1990s, as well as the recent wildfires, have destroyed a significant part of their natural habitat. Greece’s famous stray cats don’t help either. But Spyros hopes that educational tours such as his, as well as local conservation measures, will gradually help numbers increase.
To supplement his own numbers, in terms of income rather than clients, Spyros works as a honey expert in the summer months. “I run honey-tasting experiences, keep hives on the east coast and judge international competitions,” he explains. I smile at the thought of this mild-mannered man quite literally making a living from the birds and the bees.
Reaching the top of Philopappou Hill, I lower my binoculars to take in the early morning view. There are four cruise ships docked in the port of Piraeus to the west and I imagine their passengers already packed into tour buses on their way to the Acropolis. If they only had the wisdom of the little owl, they’d skip the line, which has doubled since I arrived, and admire the ancient citadel, along with birdlife, from where I’m standing instead.
Details
Emma Justice was a guest of Spyros Skareas (greecebirdtours.com) and the Athens 1890 Hotel & Spa (ariahotels.gr; doubles from about €210), a restored 19th-century mansion just a short walk from the Acropolis. A two-hour private birdwatching tour with Spyros on Philopappou Hill or in the National Gardens costs from €50 per person
