Rob: “Few life swerves are so productive”

rows.title: Carney takes his investment pitch from ‘Maple Davos’ to Strasbourg
rows.content:
Mark Carney takes his investment pitch from ‘Maple Davos’ to Strasbourg
Mark Carney took his push to diversify Canada’s economy away from the US on to the global stage this week, risking a fresh rupture with Donald Trump.
It began on Monday with a pitch to bring foreign cash into the country by offering tax breaks and private investments in Canada’s airports at a kind of “Maple Davos”.
The government said it raised C$500bn (US$357bn) in new investment largely from Canadian institutions after the summit of about 200 financiers at Toronto’s Four Seasons Hotel, which included the chief executives of BlackRock, Barclays and Singapore’s Temasek. But there were few immediate announcements of new foreign investment.
Former finance minister John Manley told the FT: “While bringing global investors to Toronto is already a success in itself, the proof that Carney’s strategy is working will only be present when the investors open their cheque books and projects break ground.”
The prime minister hopes to attract C$1tn in new investment to Canada in the next five years, supercharging his plan to decouple from the US and put his country at the vanguard of a new alliance of “middle powers”. He has pitched his nation as a haven for investors amid escalating trade tensions fomented by the US president, who continues to refer to Canada as the “51st state” of the US.
Those tensions led some executives to think twice about attending Carney’s summit this week.
“I was waiting for the call from the White House,” said one attendee.
At a welcome dinner of salmon, beef and Canadian wine on Monday evening, Carney repeated his now famous line from Davos that the global order was undergoing a “rupture”. But he offered no clear roadmap for investment and growth for Canada, according to people familiar with the matter.
On Tuesday, the prime minister sweetened his pitch by announcing an expansion in tax deductions from 15 per cent to roughly two-thirds of capital investment. This, he claimed, would offer the lowest marginal effective tax rate in the G7 and “make Canada by far the most tax-competitive advanced economy for new investment”.
He also said the country would seek private investment through “long-term concessions” to operate Canada’s four largest airports. The government has hired Morgan Stanley and Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce to advise on the process, said people familiar with the matter. Morgan Stanley and CIBC declined to comment. Bloomberg first reported the mandate.
“Better than [Monday] night,” said one attendee after Carney’s remarks on Tuesday.
There was a full conference programme to make the case for Canadian investment but much of the action was in discreet meeting rooms a few floors up in the hotel.
CS Venkatakrishnan, chief executive of UK-based bank Barclays, described Carney’s efforts as “heroic”, while Christian Sewing, CEO at Deutsche Bank, said Canada “is now on the map, far more important than ever before”.
“Historically, we’ve always been challenged in finding deals within Canada itself,” said BlackRock chief executive Larry Fink. “And I do believe what has been announced the last two days is going to be opening up the opportunities to bring forth more capital to Canada.”
But investors need to overcome a morass of regulations, tax and interprovincial barriers in the country if they are to participate in Carney’s pitchbook of Canadian infrastructure projects, which range from natural gas processing hubs to oil pipelines and data centres.
That is a big ask for a country that has been dependent on selling oil, lumber and agricultural products to the US for more than a century.
Finance minister François-Philippe Champagne managed expectations by telling reporters that success was “the momentum in the room”.
One member of Carney’s administration said the benefits from the summit would not be known for another 12 months or more.
The stakes of the prime minister’s effort to diversify Canada’s economy away from the US were underscored just days before the summit, when Trump banned some Canadian imports such as dairy products and motorcycles. The two countries have also imposed tariffs on each other’s imports.
In the end, there was no public interference or heckling from Trump during Carney’s summit, or even much of a mention of the US president. His main cameo was in an anecdote the prime minister recounted about the time when Trump gave him a golden key to the White House as a gift.
“He’s like: ‘It’s a key to the White House. You just bring it, they’ll let you in,’” said Carney. “And then he says: ‘Maybe they’ll shoot you.’ And that sort of sums up the relationship.”
Former Conservative prime minister Stephen Harper, who Carney worked for during the global financial crisis when Bank of Canada’s governor, delivered a closing speech highlighting the bipartisan support in the country for Carney’s agenda.
“Canada should be an energy superpower. Whatever the energy mix of the future, Canada should be a major and a global supplier,” he said.
Immediately after the summit, Carney travelled to Strasbourg to broaden his pitch with an address to the European parliament on Thursday.
Pursuing closer ties with Europe has been central to Carney’s plan to lessen Canadian dependence on US trade, which is the buyer of more than 70 per cent of the nation’s exports.
That plan was given a boost when European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen endorsed Carney’s push for Canada to become an “associate member” of the EU.
This is when the risk of a further “rupture” to global trade inherent in Carney’s plan became apparent.
Trump warned that such a Canada-EU deal would be considered a “hostile act” and threatened to impose “very serious tariffs” on the bloc.
The risk of tariffs aside, sceptics have cautioned that trade with Europe is unlikely to be enough on its own to pick up the slack from lessening Canada’s dependence on the US.
Canada’s economy grew 1.7 per cent in 2025 while the EU’s expanded 1.5 per cent. Both lagged behind the US’s 2.1 per cent growth.
“Canada has low productivity, Canada is not in innovative sectors. Canada has the same problems that the European Union has,” Jeremy Carter, global analytical head at Fitch Ratings, told a Milken conference in Toronto.
“Canada needs to have productive trade relations with the US and I don’t think it’s going to replace that with Europe.”

rows.title: Japan’s central bank set for pivotal moment on rates
rows.content:
Japan’s central bank set for pivotal moment on rates
The Bank of Japan and governor Kazuo Ueda are poised to raise interest rates this week to the highest level in 31 years, a decision that must balance domestic economic risks, global market shockwaves and unprecedented pressure from Donald Trump’s administration.
While markets are convinced that Ueda will raise interest rates by 0.25 percentage points to 1.25 per cent, the run-up to the BoJ’s monetary policy meeting has been unusually fraught, according to traders, with Ueda’s signalling and the bank’s forward trajectory — a rapid schedule of further increases or a sudden pause — a subject of exceptional uncertainty.
At the same time, US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent’s repeated claims of “asymmetric information” about the BoJ’s next moves have put unprecedented strains on Ueda’s independence. While Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi favours reflationary policies and lower rates, Washington is willing Japanese rates higher and appears increasingly comfortable interfering in Tokyo’s monetary affairs.
“There’s a lot of pressure on Ueda because this is one of those times where big moves in the market have less to do with changes in economic fundamentals and policy and more to do with market sentiment about what those fundamentals mean,” said Richard Katz, an economist and longtime Japan watcher.
He added that Ueda, an academic before he became BoJ governor in 2023, had not shone as a communicator.
Markets will be scrutinising both the BoJ’s statement and Ueda’s comments for hints of how much the central bank’s decision is based on the need to stabilise inflation versus its perceived duty to maintain upward momentum for the yen.
Japanese authorities undertook a $96bn intervention with the co-operation of the US in July and August to support the currency, which had fallen to 40-year lows of almost ¥164 per dollar.
Ueda is also facing ructions within his policy board. In July, when the BoJ opted to keep rates on hold, one member, Hajime Takata, voted to raise. In a public appearance this month, Takata hinted that the bank should consider more aggressive measures to keep itself ahead of the curve, such as faster or larger rate increases.
The BoJ last raised rates in June to 1 per cent, putting Friday’s expected rate rise well ahead of the bank’s previous steady “normalisation” schedule of every six months.
On the other hand, analysts said, Ueda is likely to face significant pressure from Takaichi’s inner circle as the prime minister pushes her agenda of stimulating economic growth.
The key figure is Minoru Kiuchi, minister for economic and fiscal policy, who will attend the BoJ’s board meeting, and whose comments, which will appear later in the published minutes, could offer markets a signal about Takaichi’s thinking on monetary policy or express pressure to slow the pace of future increases.
“I don’t think market players or Bessent appreciate the dilemmas facing Ueda,” said Katz. He added that while headline inflation of 2.3 per cent remained above the bank’s 2 per cent target, demand-led inflation was still weak and real wage growth remained low.
“Japan faces stagflation,” he said. “That’s tough for any central bank. And I doubt the market would be happy with Ueda emphasising these dilemmas.”
The yen meanwhile has swung violently over the past six weeks while yields on closely watched 10-year Japanese government bonds have surged to the highest level in 30 years. Yields move inversely to prices.
Currency analysts warned that a perceived mis-step by the BoJ, or a poorly received message from the governor, risked rekindling a rapid unwinding of the “carry trade”, where speculative investment is fuelled by cheaply borrowed yen.
But the yen’s rapid rally over the past week — strengthening past ¥153, to levels not seen since February and beyond what earlier interventions achieved — has also given political cover to Ueda to be less hawkish, analysts said.
The BoJ and Ueda’s greatest fear is that by moving too aggressively, they risk pushing Japan’s economy back into deflation, a situation they have spent decades trying to escape.
“If the yen is one of [the government’s], and the BoJ’s, key variables, what’s the need for Ueda, who cares about the real economy data, to take a risk here?” said Shoki Omori, chief strategist at Deutsche Bank in Tokyo.
Goldman Sachs senior economist Tomohiro Ota said that while markets were beginning to price in the possibility of an accelerated pace of rate rises — such as consecutive moves in September and October — that outcome was unlikely unless inflation significantly overshot expectations.
The BoJ’s statement and Ueda’s press conference will be combed for any change in wording on increased inflation risks from the war in the Middle East, AI-related demand and a weaker yen, Ota said.
Critically, analysts will be looking for whether the phrase “financial conditions have been accommodative” survives even after the policy rate is raised.
With the stakes so high, Ueda’s best hope is to avoid breaking an extremely delicate equilibrium, Citi’s chief Japan foreign exchange strategist Osamu Takashima said. “Ueda will try not to surprise the market . . . the market is becoming fragile.”
Data visualisation by Haohsiang Ko in Hong Kong

rows.title: Indonesia’s Prabowo fires finance minister after just a year
rows.content:
Indonesia’s Prabowo Subianto fires finance minister after just a year
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has fired finance minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa after just one year in the role, in the latest shake-up in south-east Asia’s largest economy.
Suahasil Nazara, who had been serving as deputy finance minister since 2019, was sworn in as Purbaya’s replacement on Monday. The government did not say why Purbaya was removed.
Suahasil is seen as a technocrat and has extensive experience in fiscal policymaking, having previously led the country’s fiscal policy agency for more than three years.
Jakarta’s benchmark stock index pared losses after the announcement. Initially down by 2.5 per cent, the index closed down 0.1 per cent following the reshuffle.
After being sworn in, Suahasil said Prabowo had asked him to safeguard “the health and credibility” of the state budget. He said the country’s fiscal deficit would be kept under the legal cap of 3 per cent.
Asked if he had any message for the markets, Suahasil said: “This is just a continuation, not a change . . . We will continue to manage the state’s finances in a better way.”
The reshuffle at the finance ministry is the second such change under Prabowo. Purbaya was appointed to the post in September 2025 after the surprise ousting of Sri Mulyani Indrawati, who was widely respected, especially among the country’s foreign investors, for her fiscal discipline.
As minister, Purbaya did not inspire much confidence in the market, as he advocated for looser fiscal policy and criticised the central bank for the weakening of the rupiah currency. He strongly supported Prabowo’s ambitious goals to boost annual economic growth to 8 per cent, from the current level of about 5 per cent.
While Purbaya’s replacement prompted an immediate positive market reaction, investors could view the change as evidence of more policy uncertainty in Prabowo’s Indonesia.
Shares on the Jakarta exchange have stabilised in recent weeks, but they have lost about a quarter of their value so far this year, making it one of the world’s worst-performing equity markets.
Investors have been particularly concerned about Prabowo’s costly welfare policies and their impact on an already strained budget, growing state interventionism and the possibility of a downgrade by index provider MSCI.
In July another respected technocrat, Perry Warjiyo, resigned as the central bank governor amid pressure from the government to support Prabowo’s ambitious economic goals.
Dedi Dinarto, associate director at strategic advisory firm FGS Global, said Suahasil’s appointment should offer some reassurance to investors.
The new minister was “a more familiar and orthodox technocrat with deep roots in the finance ministry, in contrast to Purbaya, who came in with a stronger pro-growth mandate and a greater willingness to push the policy envelope”, Dedi said.
“But the real test is whether Suahasil has the flexibility to maintain fiscal discipline while delivering Prabowo’s ambitious growth and spending agenda,” he said.

rows.title: Kevin Warsh needs to walk the walk
rows.content:
In Jackson Hole last month, US Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh delivered an unexpectedly hawkish keynote speech, warning that monetary policymakers had “work to do” if inflationary pressures in the US did not ease clearly and quickly enough. Until then, investors had wondered whether Warsh would bow to President Donald Trump’s long-running demands for lower interest rates, or stand firm on the independence of the world’s most influential central bank. His words offered some reassurance. But as the Federal Open Market Committee begins its two-day rate-setting meeting today, Warsh must now walk the walk. It is time for the Fed to raise the cost of credit for the first time in more than three years.
There is a reasonable economic case to raise rates. Data released last week showed that annual growth in the consumer price index remained stubbornly elevated at 3.4 per cent in August. Worryingly, monthly growth in the core measure — which excludes volatile food and energy components — nudged higher. At the same time, bumper job creation last month and booming capital expenditure in AI point to robust demand.
Broader price pressures are in the pipeline. US manufacturers are contending with a fresh wave of supply chain inflation as the Iran war pushes up energy costs and tariffs raise import prices. Higher gasoline prices have also raised households’ one year-ahead inflation expectations, which raises the risk of higher prices becoming entrenched in the US economy. In turn, the Fed’s Cleveland branch now projects annual growth in the core personal consumption expenditure index, the FOMC’s preferred inflation gauge, to rise to 3.5 per cent this month — only a slight rise, but still well above the 2 per cent target.
Inflation may not be about to spiral out of control. But it is moving in the wrong direction. A rate rise of 25 basis points on Wednesday would at least reduce the risk that the Fed falls behind the curve. It would also reinforce the central bank’s credibility. After all, the inflationary concerns Warsh flagged last month have only grown. Back then he said financial conditions were not particularly restrictive and that any decision to raise rates in September would be data dependent. With Friday’s CPI release coming in firm, investors are now pricing in a 90 per cent chance of a small rate rise on Wednesday.
A failure to act risks undermining financial markets’ trust in Warsh’s communications. As it is, the Fed chair has committed to reducing how much the central bank publicly telegraphs its decisions. Given his recent pronouncements, a decision to continue holding rates also risks being interpreted by market participants as an attempt to appease Trump just weeks before the midterm elections, in which the Democrats could make notable gains.
A failure to raise rates could then muddy the Warsh Fed’s ongoing efforts to guide policy and raise the inflation risk premium investors require to hold US Treasuries, which would worsen the US fiscal calculus. Amid the ongoing global bond sell-off, the 10-year yield reached its highest level since 2007 on Tuesday. The Bank of Japan has a similar test on Friday. With markets expecting a rate rise, failing to deliver could likewise unsettle bond markets.
Central bankers should not blindly kowtow to investor expectations. But when inflation is well above target, price pressures are moving in the wrong direction and policymakers have already signalled that higher rates are on the table, failing to follow through carries risks, particularly in today’s volatile sovereign bond market. Warsh has spent his first months in the job trying to convince markets that the Fed will follow the data, not the president. Now he needs to show it.

rows.title: UK inflation rose to 3.1% in August
rows.content:
UK inflation rose to 3.1% in August
UK inflation accelerated to 3.1 per cent in August, worsening the squeeze on households and businesses and keeping open the prospect of a Bank of England rate increase this year.
Wednesday’s figure from the Office for National Statistics was above July’s 2.9 per cent reading and in line with the prediction of economists polled by Reuters.
Rising petrol prices were the major driver of August’s increase, with higher household energy bills also contributing, the ONS said.
The increase takes inflation further above the BoE’s 2 per cent target as the Monetary Policy Committee prepares to set its key interest rate on Thursday. Economists and traders expect the MPC to hold its rate at 3.75 per cent, but signal that an increase in borrowing costs could come as soon as its November meeting.
Despite the energy shock from the Iran war, the MPC has resisted lifting interest rates as officials await further evidence on whether higher inflation is becoming entrenched in the economy.
The MPC voted 6-3 to hold rates at its last meeting in July, exposing deep divisions on how to respond to surging oil and gas prices.
Yael Selfin, chief economist at KPMG, said rising energy prices were likely to test the BoE’s “wait-and-see approach” on rates.
“The MPC will be wary of a prolonged period of above-target inflation feeding into significant wage changes and price-setting behaviour,” she said. “There is little evidence of that occurring so far, but without a marked improvement in the outlook, the balance of risks could shift towards a rate rise before the end of the year.”
The steep rise in global energy costs has prompted the European Central Bank to raise borrowing costs twice since June, while traders are betting the Federal Reserve will later on Wednesday lift interest rates for the first time since 2023.
The blistering rally in oil prices poses a significant political challenge to Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who was swept into Downing Street by Labour MPs on the back of a promise to ease the cost of living for voters.
But a steep rise in government bond yields is estimated to have more than halved the government’s fiscal headroom, limiting the scope for giveaways in the October Budget.
Despite the pick-up in headline inflation, Wednesday’s data suggested that the spillover of energy prices into the wider economy remained limited — a key point for those MPC members who have voted to hold rates since the Middle East conflict began in February.
Services inflation, closely watched by rate-setters as a gauge of domestic price pressures, held steady at 3.4 per cent in August, below economists’ expectations of 3.5 per cent. Core inflation, which excludes energy and food, remained at 2.6 per cent during the month.
Francesco Pesole, strategist at ING, said there was “still no evidence that inflationary pressures are spreading beyond energy [prices]”, which “gives BoE doves something to cling on tomorrow”.
Official figures on Tuesday underlined the continued weakness of the jobs market and subdued wage growth.
Following the release of the August inflation data, traders continued to expect a string of rate increases over the coming year, but dialled back their expectations on the pace. They also cut bets on a move at this week’s meeting from 35 per cent to 20 per cent.
Two-year gilt yields, which are more sensitive to changing interest rate expectations, fell 0.11 percentage points to 4.79 per cent. The pound slipped 0.2 per cent against the dollar to $1.345.
Responding to August’s figures, chancellor John Healey said: “The war in the Middle East is impacting on inflation worldwide, not just here at home. In our bills, our weekly shop and at the petrol pumps. We have taken early action to help families and give businesses breathing space.”
Andrew Griffith, shadow chancellor, took aim at the government for August’s increase, saying: “Inflation is now at 3.1 per cent, meaning that every family is paying the price for Labour’s choices.”
Economists cautioned that the expected acceleration in headline inflation in coming months could prompt the MPC to raise rates later this year, even if officials resist making further increases.
CPI inflation is now expected to hit or exceed 4 per cent by early next year — double the BoE’s target.
Andrew Goodwin, UK economist at Oxford Economics, said August’s figures offered “no evidence that second-round effects are emerging”, but added that “the pick-up in external price pressures has been so great that it looks increasingly likely to force the MPC’s hand”.

rows.title: Freedom in adulthood isn’t what you think
rows.content:
Freedom in adulthood isn’t what you think
American folk hero turned vice-president JD Vance was to be found doing his best intellectual-man-of-the-people impression this week, combining searing sociocultural commentary with all the butter-wouldn’t-melt energy of a man who has never told the president of a country under heavy invasion by Russia to say thank you, publicly, to Donald Trump.
“Let me give you my meta-analysis of Emily in Paris and why it’s genius,” Vance said in a TikTok video posted on Tuesday. “It’s obvious to everyone watching the show that she should end up with the French chef and they should start a family . . . The fact that they keep on making atrocious decisions is kind of like the best bit of cultural commentary — I would say cultural criticism — of my generation.”
Fox News gushed that Vance was “using one of Netflix’s biggest pop culture hits to make a much broader point about modern adulthood”; about “a culture increasingly questioning marriage, having children and building a family”.
One might be forgiven for pointing out that adulthood is also about responsible decision-making in one’s professional life, particularly when it may have a profound impact on America and the rest of the world. It could be said, for instance, that sane-washing each mad Trump idea — take annexing Greenland (“we can’t just ignore the president’s desires”) — is irresponsible in the extreme.
But Vance was, nevertheless, touching on a point worth exploring: the prevalent modern notion that happiness in adulthood lies in keeping your options open, minimising your responsibilities, and being able to do whatever you want, wherever you want, whenever you want.
Many people would describe this as freedom, and indeed it would probably fit with the definition provided by the English political theorist and philosopher John Stuart Mill. “The only freedom which deserves the name is that of pursuing our own good in our own way, so long as we do not attempt to deprive others of theirs, or impede their efforts to obtain it,” Mill wrote in his 1859 essay On Liberty.
All very well, one might think. But there’s a problem. We don’t always know what it means to pursue our own good. We might think that it makes us happy to do as we please, but actually part of growing up is realising that some degree of discipline, commitment and narrowing down your options can lead to greater contentment. Furthermore, if pursuing our own good means impulsively following every urge, is that really freedom?
That question is explored by Patrick Deneen, the Catholic conservative political theorist (and intellectual influence on Vance) in his 2018 book Why Liberalism Failed. In it he argues that modern liberals wrongly equate liberty with absolute personal autonomy. This, Deneen argues, is a relatively new conception of freedom. Of the ancient world, he writes: “To be free, above all, was to be free from enslavement to one’s own basest desires, which could never be fulfilled, and the pursuit of which could only foster ceaseless craving and discontent . . . Liberty was thus the condition achieved by self-rule, over one’s own appetites and over the longing for political dominion.”
I don’t quite buy the book’s core argument: Deneen romanticises the premodern world while not fully acknowledging the huge leaps that liberalism has brought in science, human rights, social mobility and overall wellbeing. Further, I am grateful that I live in a world in which I largely get to decide how to live my life, rather than having it dictated to me by society.
But I do find the argument that freedom has been misunderstood persuasive. Surely the freedom from one’s own worst impulses, and therefore the capacity to live a considered life of virtue, contentment and purpose, is just as important as the freedom to follow one’s desires, if not more so. As children, we face all sorts of rules, which give us the courage to explore without fear. As adults, we have to find other ways to govern ourselves.
It is precisely the kinds of constraints that are often imagined to be the antithesis of freedom that can in fact give our lives meaning: not just the Maga obsession with babies and marriage, but things like being a member of a real-life community that entails shared burdens, committing to regular voluntary work, or even following a somewhat prescriptive moral framework.
“Everybody’s freeeee to feel good,” sang the Zambian-Zimbabwean singer Rozalla in 1991. But the lyrics to the rest of the song, with its nod to making it through life together, are worth reading. Feeling truly free, and good, requires showing up, shared problems and mutual responsibility — without them, we’re anchorless.

rows.title: Ten-year Treasury yield hits highest level since 2007
rows.content:
Ten-year Treasury yield hits highest level since 2007
US borrowing costs hit their highest level since 2007 on Tuesday, as a global bond sell-off deepened following a renewed surge in oil prices and expectations of an interest rate increase by the Federal Reserve this week.
The 10-year yield, a benchmark for debt markets worldwide, jumped as much as 0.08 percentage points to 5.04 per cent, its highest point since July 2007. It later fell back to around 5 per cent, a level it topped on Monday for the first time in almost three years, in a bond rout sparked by the Iran war energy shock.
The sell-off comes ahead of a crucial Fed meeting on Wednesday. Traders in futures markets are putting a roughly 90 per cent probability on the central bank raising rates by a quarter of a percentage point — a move that would put it on a collision course with US President Donald Trump’s desire for lower borrowing costs.
The bond sell-off has been “relentless”, said Matt Amis, an investment director at Aberdeen Investments.
“[It] feels like investors are throwing in the towel on long-held positions. Yields look elevated here, but until oil stops heading higher, it will be a struggle to add risk,” he continued.
Soaring energy prices as a result of the Iran war have fuelled concerns about persistent above-target inflation in the US and elsewhere, leading traders to price in higher interest rates and knocking bonds. Investors’ attention has also turned towards the US’s $40tn debt pile, amid concerns that Washington is on an unsustainable fiscal path.
Scott Bessent, the US Treasury secretary, told Congress on Tuesday that a “fiscal consolidation is coming” and the country had “to get our house in order”, but pointed to strong recent debt auctions as evidence of ongoing global investor confidence.
Some analysts argue that the Fed under new chair Kevin Warsh needs to raise rates to demonstrate its commitment to tackling inflation. The price of Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, was up 3.2 per cent on Tuesday at $109 a barrel.
“The Fed’s credibility is under scrutiny,” said Jenny Zeng, chief investment officer for fixed income at Allianz Global Investors. “Markets will be looking for chair Warsh to back recent rhetoric with action.”
Stock markets also weakened. The S&P 500 was down 0.4 per cent during afternoon trading in New York, while the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.7 per cent. The Stoxx Europe 600 closed 0.3 per cent lower.
Yields on Japan’s benchmark 10-year bonds also climbed on Tuesday to their highest level in 30 years, reaching as high as 3.04 per cent, ahead of a broadly expected interest rate increase by the Bank of Japan on Friday. Yields move inversely to prices.
Markets are pricing in a roughly 80 per cent chance that the BoJ will raise rates by 0.25 percentage points to 1.25 per cent this week, the highest level in 31 years.
“Markets are increasingly confident about a September BoJ hike and are pricing a higher terminal rate, which continues to put upward pressure on JGB yields,” said Masahiko Loo, senior fixed-income strategist at State Street in Tokyo.
In the UK, where the Bank of England is expected to hold rates this week, the 10-year gilt yield rose as much as 0.06 percentage points to 5.44 per cent before slipping back to 5.39 per cent.
Some expect the BoE to further pare back or halt sales of long-term debt through its so-called quantitative tightening programme at a scheduled decision on Thursday.
The multiyear highs in countries’ long-term borrowing costs, on top of record overall issuance across rich nations, are feeding anxiety over the world’s rising debt-servicing bill, which is already above $2tn, or 3 per cent of GDP, for OECD nations.
Strategists said borrowing costs in the US would need to rise higher for investors to pull significant money out of stocks. “We would need [a percentage point] more to really have some more negative implications for the S&P 500,” said Frank Benzimra, head of Asia equity strategy at Société Générale.
Bank of America’s closely watched survey of global fund managers showed on Tuesday that a “disorderly rise in bond yields” was now considered the biggest market risk for investors, with a third of respondents giving that response, overtaking an “AI bubble”.
In a sign that the bond move is dominating investor bets, the survey also found that “short US Treasuries” was named as the second most crowded trade in the market, after “long global semiconductors”.
Bessent attempted to steady the government bond market by launching a $6bn bond-buying programme last week. But the move did little to soothe investors’ nerves, with yields on the 10-year and 30-year bonds continuing to surge higher.

rows.title: How novelist Tracy Chevalier was bitten by the fossil-hunting bug
rows.content:
How novelist Tracy Chevalier was bitten by the fossil-hunting bug
Tracy Chevalier remembers the exact moment she first encountered Mary Anning. It was 2006. She and her husband, Jonathan Drori, were down from London at their village getaway in Dorset for half term. Their son Jacob was seven and it was raining. The only thing to do under such circumstances, she says, was to head for the Dinosaur Museum Dorchester, of course.
There, in a corner, was a tiny display about a 19th-century fossil hunter from Lyme Regis she’d never heard of. Three things immediately piqued Chevalier’s interest. “One was that she was a woman working in palaeontology at the time when it was all men from Oxbridge,” says Chevalier. “Two, that she was working class, and yet was working alongside educated middle-class men — so she had two strikes against her . . . yet, she did amazing things. And the third thing was that she was struck by lightning as a baby and survived.”
Chevalier resolved to write about Anning, and within a year began work on her 2010 novel Remarkable Creatures. The pair have been time-travel companions ever since. In late August, I went to Dorchester to meet Chevalier, who is curating an exhibition about Anning’s uncommon life opening at the Dorset Museum and Art Gallery in January.
In Remarkable Creatures, Anning jumps off the page as the kind of person you’d meet once and never forget. Chevalier starts with a first-person account of her miraculous survival as an infant, when a bolt of lightning struck and killed the woman holding her as they sheltered from a storm under a tree. The lightning becomes a metaphor for the discoveries that punctuate her childhood, spent digging out what she called “curies” (or curiosities) on beaches and cliffs with her father and her brother.
The novel remains the one Chevalier is happiest with, and the one people talk to her about the most, even after her 1999 bestseller, Girl with a Pearl Earring. “And it’s made people go to Lyme Regis,” she adds. “The museum there did a survey of the visitors and 20 per cent of the people who came to the museum came because they had read the book.”
As a longstanding member of the board at the Dorset Museum & Art Gallery, Chevalier is hoping this exhibition — which marks the 180th anniversary of Anning’s death — will yield similar results for Dorchester. She shows me a hand-drawn map in pencil of the exhibition layout, still a work in progress. The museum estimates there are 4mn objects in its stores, including 20,500 geological specimens, the vast majority of which (20,000) are fossils. For the exhibition it is also calling in loans from the Natural History Museum and the Wellcome Collection in London, the Oxford University Museum of Natural History, the Lyme Regis Museum, the University of Bristol Special Collections and the Dorset History Centre in Dorchester.
Anning’s major discoveries — coprolites, a brittle star, a pterosaur, along with a cast of the head of the first ichthyosaur she found with her brother, when she was 12 (the original is in the Natural History Museum in London; the body was lost a long time ago) will be bolstered by archival materials and interactive displays. A private collector is loaning a rare sketch by Anning, displayed alongside the geology and mineralogy book the curators have identified as the one Anning was drawing from (it has her signature on the title page). Children will get to dress up in 19th-century attire and touch a cast of that first ichthyosaur, subsequently renamed Temnodontosaurus platyodon. They can also uncover fossils on the beach being created in the exhibition room, and handle fossils in the recreated Anning shop.
Chevalier wants all visitors to be able to handle some fossils. She has put out a call to hunters in Lyme Regis, asking for donations. When researching the book, she took up hunting herself: a beach trip on a good day will yield at least a belemnite (one of those smooth, bullet-shaped fossils of a cephalopod).
In Anning’s time, local people had all kinds of folk names and beliefs about these strange rocks, of which Chevalier is compiling a chart for the show. Exhibitions manager Lucy Johnston fetches from the stores boxes of ammonites (“ammos”, Anning calls them in the book), which were thought to be serpents curled up and decapitated — you duly kept one in your pocket to ward off snakes. Having a fairy stone (a segment of fossilised crinoid or sea lily stem) was thought to guarantee a steady supply of bread, because, as Chevalier puts it, “they thought that they looked like the bread that fairies would eat”.
The last display the museum dedicated to Anning took place in 1999. When I googled it, the only clipping I could find was on page 30 of local paper The Downsman, about “the fossil lady of Lyme”. Since then, however, Anning’s star has risen. She featured in the overhauled history curriculum for primary schools in England devised in 2013 as a palaeontologist that Year 6 pupils should learn about, alongside Charles Darwin and Alfred Wallace. A few years later, in 2019, one outraged 11-year-old from Lyme Regis, Evie Swire, set up a campaign to have a statue of Anning erected in their joint hometown, after finding out there wasn’t one.
Quite why there wasn’t is as much about the entrenched gender biases that have shaped scientific progress as it is about class and money. In 1995, historian Hugh Torrens dubbed Anning the world’s greatest fossilist. In its permanent display, the Dorset Museum highlights her importance not just in contributing to palaeontology but in helping to create palaeontology as a discipline. Yet very few of her finds come with clear provenance leading back to her fossil shop in Lyme, now the site of the town’s museum. Anning didn’t sign or leave her mark on them and buyers omitted to reference her in their records. As Chevalier puts it, “she wasn’t considered important”. 
Women wouldn’t be granted membership of the Geological Society until 1919. That first ichthyosaur, which people thought to be a crocodile, was known not as Anning’s but Henley’s crocodile, for the Lord of the Manor of Colway, Henry Hoste Henley, who bought it from her. Geologists including Tom Sharpe are now studying markings on framed Victorian fossils to ascertain which Anning mounted and framed herself.
Further, despite her undeniable contributions to science, Anning died as she lived, in great poverty. Her father, a cabinet maker and sometime fossil hunter, succumbed to tuberculosis when she was 11, leaving her mother with debts of £120. For that croc, Henley forked out £23, the cost of a decent dairy cow, not a sum Anning could turn down. “Without the sea,” writes Chevalier in the voice of Anning as a child, “the bones stay locked up in their rock tombs forever, and we’d have no money for food and lodging.” 
These tensions between knowledge, access, collecting and cost are dividing the fossil world anew. Instagram is flooded with fossil-hunting content creators digging up bones and splitting rocks across the globe, from Gauteng in South Africa and Alaska’s Boneyard, to Utah’s Antelope Springs and Dorset’s Jurassic coast, to varying ethical standards.
Pundits note the 21st-century gold rush this represents. In July, a 10-minute auction battle at Sotheby’s New York resulted in a mounted T-Rex skeleton from South Dakota, known as Gus, going for $50.1mn, beating the previous record by over $5mn. In August, a 318-strong collection of British Jurassic fossils was bought for an undisclosed eight-figure sum by the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi. Neither London’s Natural History Museum nor Amgueddfa Cymru in Wales could compete. 
Editorials on the subject, one referencing Remarkable Creatures, highlight the need for these objects to be afforded national treasure status, so that all can enjoy them for centuries to come. To watch Chevalier examine a tiny fairy stone and point out how much it looks like a flower is to understand why. You feel like you’ve found it yourself. “It is quite something, being on the beach,” she says. “People stop looking at their phones and start looking, just looking.”
‘Mary Anning: Fossil Hunter’, January 30-May 2 2027, dorsetmuseum.org

rows.title: US retailer rations motor oil as prices quadruple and supplies run dry
rows.content:
US retailer rations motor oil as prices quadruple and supplies run dry
A worldwide shortage of motor oil is becoming more acute, with prices of the car engine lubricant reaching new highs, oil-change shops running dry and a US retail group rationing sales to do-it-yourself customers.
The surge in the cost of base oil used for the full synthetic motor oil required for many newer cars far outpaces steep price rises for crude oil, petrol and diesel. The US price of so-called Group III base oil has almost quadrupled since February to a record $12.45 a gallon on Friday, according to Argus Media.
Retail chain Costco Wholesale raised the price for 10 quarts of one type of full synthetic motor oil to $57.99 and is now capping purchases at one per customer, according to its website. The brand was selling for about $30 last year.
Walmart’s website this week reported low stocks for several brands. “We work closely with our suppliers to keep products available at the low prices our customers expect,” Walmart said.
“There will be some spot outages that we have to just deal with,” said Mauricio Quezada, chief executive of Jiffy Lube, a US oil-change and auto-repair chain. Jiffy Lube was part of Shell until its $1.3bn sale to a private equity firm in July and still received most motor oil from Shell’s Pennzoil business, Quezada said.
Motor oil sells in small volumes but serves a critical function greasing the insides of internal combustion engines. Global lubricant base oil exports are typically only about 350,000 barrels a day, a fraction of the more than 100mn b/d world oil market.
Base oil supplies were first disrupted after an Iranian strike in March damaged a huge Shell gas-to-liquids plant in Qatar in retaliation for the US and Israel’s war against the Islamic republic. The plant is a leading producer of Group III base oil.
The military stand-off in the Strait of Hormuz has also hindered tanker shipments of crude oil from the Gulf to the world’s other major producers of base oils in South Korea.
The price rise comes as consumers bemoan a cost of living crunch driven by energy, food and housing.
New York-listed retail oil-change chain Valvoline, whose principal motor oil supplier is Saudi Aramco, said there had been no shortages at its almost 2,500 stores, but it has raised the price of an oil change by $5 to $7 to offset a 60 per cent increase in lubricant costs since March.
Asked at a Goldman Sachs retail conference this week where prices were headed, Valvoline chief executive Lori Flees said “higher”.
“You’re looking at four to six months once the strait is fully open for Group III base oils to be back flowing in the way that they were pre-conflict,” she said.
The situation is more difficult for independent shops and blending companies that lack long-term supply agreements with major oil companies.
Mike Tailor, the owner of Rapid Lube in the US state of New Jersey, said customers shook their heads when they saw the higher oil-change prices he had taped to the wall of his waiting room.
“It’s never been like this before. Not even when gas went to $5,” he said, referring to when US petrol prices hit a record $5 a gallon in 2022. He said obtaining his bulk supplies of full synthetic motor oil was “hit or miss”.
Greg Schmidt, the owner of a garage in New Jersey, pointed to an oil specification called Dexos that is required for newer General Motors vehicles. “It’s very hard to get right now,” he said.
“We’re closely monitoring the situation and working with suppliers and dealers to help ensure continued supply,” GM said.
For the blenders that buy Group III base oil, “if they have a contract with a supplier, in a lot of cases they are being placed on allocation, which means they don’t get the full amount”, said Holly Alfano, chief executive of the Independent Lubricant Manufacturers Association.
“And for those who don’t have a contract, they are struggling to get supply. They are calling around trying to find Group III and they are having a hard time finding it,” she added.
Carmakers have been attempting to turn to new blends of motor oil and lubricants in an attempt to ease the supply shortage. The American Petroleum Institute, which sets standards for the oil industry, said it had invoked emergency provisional licensing for vendors seeking to pivot to other base oil supplies.
But motor oil blenders have been unable to make the switch because of strict formulation and testing requirements for full synthetic oils, said John Dietrich, head of US base oils pricing at Argus Media.
Quezada said that despite scattered shortages, the product was at present available at all of Jiffy Lube’s almost 2,100 locations, most of which are owned by franchisees. “Customers can’t wait. They need to get their car serviced,” he said.

rows.title: A UN gathering notable for its absences
rows.content:
A UN gathering notable for its absences
Hello and welcome to the working week.
If you are a world leader, New York is the place to be this week for the UN General Assembly. Unless, that is, you are Friedrich Merz.
The German chancellor will be staying at home trying to shore up his leadership. More on that in the coming hours given the loss of seats expected for Merz’s Christian Democrats in the regional elections held over the weekend just gone in Berlin and the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.
The main thing on the minds of those mingling in Manhattan (apart perhaps from what on earth US President Donald Trump will say) will be the UN secretary-general succession race. António Guterres steps down from the role at the end of the year, with eight official candidates in the running, three of whom have a viable chance. But there is speculation that there will be additional late entrants to the race. It is a big moment because whoever takes over will have to contend with slashed budgets and more limited ambitions, as Guterres told the FT’s foreign editor Alec Russell.
Chinese President Xi Jinping will also be skipping the UN General Assembly, chiefly because he has a better offer: the opulence of a state visit in Washington, including dinner and one-to-one conversation with Trump. The US president will be on hand to greet Xi when he arrives at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday. The pair will then spend Thursday at the White House, where the conversation is expected to include trade, AI and national security.
Andy Burnham is hoping for some face time with Trump too for the first time since becoming British prime minister. The rest of the Westminster political class has begun shifting out of London for the UK conference season. The Liberal Democrat party conference wraps up in Brighton on Tuesday with leader Ed Davey giving the closing address, while Labour Party members travel to Liverpool for their shindig among the Scousers beginning on Sunday. For intelligent insights from the conference floor, I recommend following Stephen Bush’s Inside Politics newsletter.
The corporate diary this week goes from Big Tech to little tech. Mark Zuckerberg will address the Meta Connect developer conference in Menlo Park, California, on Wednesday. Meanwhile, the corporate earnings run will bring quarterly figures from Cambridge-based budget computer designer Raspberry Pi (whose founder Eben Upton I interviewed two years ago and who went for lunch with the FT last week) and Canadian tech Lazarus BlackBerry.
After the rush of inflation and interest rate announcements, the next few days will feel light on economic data, the most significant release being the international purchasing managers’ index comparisons. But be warned: the central bankers are out in force. More details below.
One more thing . . .
This week marks another change in the seasons. For the Moules household, we’ve entered a non-meteorological one: the last of the season of father-son university open day visits.
I’ve been through this with the older two already, so I am well prepared for the next few weeks of criss-crossing the UK with my 17-year-old. Each has felt a special travel experience, but this week’s will be particularly thrilling as we head to Dundee on the Caledonian Sleeper, one of the great British rail journeys (at least in my book), which has been made even more enjoyable since the rolling stock was upgraded seven years ago.
I’m open to tips on making this trip — and ones in coming weeks to Belfast (by plane) and Cardiff (by train) — as memorable as possible. Email me at [email protected] or, if you are reading this from your inbox, hit reply. And have a good week.
Key economic and company reports
Here is a more complete list of what to expect in terms of company reports and economic data this week.
Monday
- IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva speaks at the IMF Legal Department 80th anniversary conference in Washington
- Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago president Austan Goolsbee answers audience questions at the Official Monetary and Financial Institutions Forum event in London
- Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem gives a speech to the Halifax Partnership in Halifax, Nova Scotia
- Israel: Yom Kippur. Financial markets closed
- Japan: Respect for the Aged Day. Financial markets closed
- UK: S&P Global consumer sentiment index
- Earnings calls: Abivax HY, Remgro FY
Tuesday
- China’s Ligent Technologies seeks to raise about HK$5.67bn (US$723mn) in a Hong Kong initial public offering
- Federal Reserve Bank of New York president John Williams speaks at the 2026 US Treasury Markets Conference in New York
- Reserve Bank of Australia governor Michele Bullock engages in a fireside chat at the Fullerton Hotel in Sydney
- France: July retail sales figures
- Japan: Bridge public holiday. Financial markets closed
- UK: August public sector finances
- Earnings calls: AutoZone Q4, Exor HY, Henry Boot HY, Kingfisher HY, Miller Knoll Q1, Origin Enterprises FY, PureTech HY, Smiths FY, Thor Industries Q4, Tui pre-close trading update
Wednesday
- Mark Zuckerberg speaks at the Meta Connect developer conference
- Eurozone, France, Germany, India, UK, US: flash S&P Global/HSBC manufacturing and services purchasing managers’ index (PMI) data
- Japan: Autumn Equinox Day. Financial markets closed
- Earnings calls: Cintas Q1, Elixirr International HY, JD Sports HY, Manchester United Q4, OVS HY, PayChex Q1, Renishaw FY, Soul Patts FY, Worthington Enterprises Q1
Thursday
- Bank of England deputy governor for monetary policy Clare Lombardelli speaks at the sixth biennial conference “Macroeconomic Policy in a Heterogeneous and Imperfectly Rational World” in Poland
- Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond president Thomas Barkin speaks at an Economic Club of Washington event
- Australia: August labour force survey
- Germany: Ifo business climate survey
- Japan: flash S&P global manufacturing and services PMI data
- UK: BRC September Consumer Sentiment Monitor
- Earnings calls: BlackBerry Q2, Costco Q4, CVS FY, Darden Restaurants Q1, H&M 9M, Raspberry Pi HY, Scholastic Q1, TD SYNNEX Q3, Vistry Group HY
Friday
- Pinewood.AI shareholders are due to vote on the recommended £545mn cash acquisition by Ridgeview Partners
- Federal Reserve Bank of New York president John Williams speaks at the Monetary Economics Conference, hosted by Oxford university
- China: Mid-Autumn Festival. Financial markets closed
- UK: GfK Consumer Confidence Survey
- US: University of Michigan Survey of Consumers
- Earnings calls: Selena HY
World events
Finally, here is a rundown of other events and milestones this week.
Monday
- Day of Atonement/Yom Kippur, the most sacred day in the Jewish calendar
- UK: Liberal Democrat party conference continues in Brighton, ending with leader Ed Davey’s speech tomorrow afternoon.
Tuesday
- UK: Booker Prize for Fiction shortlist announced in London.
- US: UN General Assembly begins with various heads of state and government giving addresses, continuing until September 28.
Wednesday
- France: OECD Interim Economic Outlook released in Paris
- Morocco: parliamentary elections
Thursday
- Isle of Man: parliamentary elections
- US: President Donald Trump hosts Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House
Friday
- France: Pope Leo XIV begins a four-day apostolic tour, meeting President Emmanuel Macron at Élysée Palace and visiting Unesco’s headquarters in Paris
- Hong Kong: Mid-Autumn Festival, or Mooncake Festival, takes place in parks, beaches and on the waterfront, featuring a mass lighting of lanterns
Saturday
- UK: 2026 Turner Prize exhibition opens to the public. Established in 1984, the £25,000 prize is awarded to a British-based artist for an outstanding exhibition or presentation of work in the preceding year
Sunday
- France: Senate elections
- UK: Labour Party conference begins in Liverpool

rows.title: End of an era as Thatcher’s favourite council backs 94% tax rise
rows.content:
End of an era as Thatcher’s favourite council backs 94% tax rise
For Margaret Thatcher, it was the exemplar local authority — “where Wandsworth has led, let other Conservative councils follow” she told the Tory party conference in 1982. This south London borough blazed the trail that came to be known as Thatcherism — privatisation of local services, right to buy for council tenants and, above all, low taxes.
But on Tuesday night, Wandsworth’s half-century era of ultra-low council tax came to an end as the borough’s Conservative administration announced plans for a 94 per cent rise, Britain’s biggest ever annual increase.
Andy Burnham has often cited the 1980s as the decade when Britain took a wrong turn. Wandsworth Tories have accused his government of serving its revenge very, very cold, with the end of the borough’s low-tax experiment marking a symbolic moment in his repudiation of Thatcher’s economic model.
Wandsworth, a prosperous residential area which is home to the US embassy, said its decision to raise tax was forced by a change in local government funding. The council’s central government grant has been cut by 40 per cent as cash is diverted to more deprived areas, mainly in the north and Midlands.
Angela Rayner, the local government secretary who began the changes before Burnham took office, is accused by the borough of “deliberately targeting” low-tax councils. “I don’t think it’s about the place for her. It’s about the nature of our low-tax offer, which they regard as simply wrong,” said Cllr Robert Morritt, Tory leader of the council.
“For decades, residents in our part of London have made a conscious choice to support efficient, well-run low-tax councils, and they’re now being penalised for that.”
Rayner, however, argues that the existing system is “unfair” and has seen deprived areas, which struggle to raise tax locally, hit doubly hard by reductions in council funding during the austerity years.
She is reallocating central government grants on a new formula based on assessment of local needs, including population age and deprivation. Crucially, this now deducts what local areas could raise if they all imposed council tax at the national average level, currently £1,940 per year for a band D property. This rises to £2,392 once precepts for combined authorities and others are included.
Wandsworth currently charges the lowest council tax in England, at £509.84 for Band D, plus a £510.51 precept set by the Greater London Authority. Wandsworth’s share of the Band D bill will rise to £1,468 from next April. The total Band D bill including the GLA precept will now almost double to £1,978.
Wandsworth is one of six councils, all in London and the South East, with “historically very low bills” where ministers gave the green light to significant increases.
Elizabeth Campbell, Conservative leader of Kensington and Chelsea — one of the six low-tax councils — accused ministers of a “totally political . . . attack on inner London”, coming at the same time as a “ridiculously badly thought-out” mansion tax on properties worth more than £2mn.
She said she would now have to impose “very large tax rises” as well as cutting services. “Our residents know what’s coming, but it’s just going to be very, very brutal, very difficult, very unpleasant and very fast,” she said.
In Wandsworth, Morritt acknowledges a rapid rise is “going to be a shock” for residents and “will be super difficult” for some. He accused ministers of “trying to kill off local choice” through the new formula, saying democracy “ultimately should mean that local people can vote for lower, more efficiently run councils.”
Allies of Rayner dismiss this, saying the changes are not a judgment on the low-tax model in Wandsworth, but a byproduct of a reformed system designed to help other areas.
One government figure pointed to Wandsworth’s £194mn of reserves. “For too long, an outdated council funding system, based on decades-old data, has entrenched inequality, leaving councils on a cliff edge and communities in deprived areas facing service cuts and rising bills, while some councils in less deprived areas have benefited disproportionately, building up their reserves.”
Labour has long argued that Wandsworth’s low rates were enabled by the decision of John Major’s Conservative government to bake in higher central government grants when it created council tax in 1993 to allow them to continue to hold it up as an exemplar.
The Tories spent much of the 1980s using Wandsworth’s low rates as a stick to attack Labour profligacy, after the Conservative council leadership elected in 1978 enacted the platform that became Thatcherism.
“It was absolutely totemic,” said Robert Colvile of the Centre for Policy Studies, the right-leaning think-tank which championed the Wandsworth model in the 1980s.
“It was hugely important as proof of concept — it was one of the first to do right to buy, one of the first to privatise services and to focus on cutting costs. One academic study called it the cradle of Thatcherism. At a time when Ken Livingstone was running the Greater London Authority from the hard left, it was an alternative vision of how you could run local government.”
Colvile called Rayner’s reform “a pretty high-handed act of national control from a government that claims to believe in devolution”.
However, Kate Ogden of the Institute for Fiscal Studies argued that the choice about tax levels remained with local residents. The reforms were “saying if you set higher council tax you can keep the money for better services, and if you want to have lower council tax bills that’s fine, but we are not going to give you higher grant funding to make up for that”.
She said that while assessments of need were always political, the previous funding formula was “arbitrary and quite hard to defend”. Residents in areas like Wandsworth would now have to accept that lower council tax “comes with consequences for public services”, she said.
Councils across England have been struggling with rising costs in areas such as social care and special educational needs. Although the majority of council spending is on such legally mandated services, Ogden said they can “still choose to set lower council tax bills” by reducing other services.
Her analysis previously suggested that Wandsworth’s share of council tax would have to reach about £900 by 2028-29 to hold funding flat in cash terms.
Simon Hogg, leader of the Labour group in Wandsworth, said the increase was “cruel and unnecessary”, accusing the Tories of imposing a higher rise than needed in order to cut taxes before the next local elections in 2030. “There’s no financial need for a vast increase this year. The decision is purely political,” he said.
Wandsworth’s low-tax era may be ending, but Labour’s response locally shows how it has changed the terms of debate. Hogg accused the Tories of having “made no effort to reform the council and make it more efficient”. Labour, he promised, would “keep any council tax increase below 5 per cent”.

rows.title: Sullivan & Cromwell discovers private equity
rows.content:
Sullivan & Cromwell discovers private equity
One scoop to start: OpenAI has held early conversations with investors about raising another private funding round at a $1.2tn valuation before its planned IPO, as it seeks to capitalise on the success of its latest AI model.
And another thing: A US House panel unanimously voted to hold Apollo Global Management’s co-founder Leon Black in contempt on Tuesday for defying subpoenas to testify on his relationship with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Welcome to Due Diligence, your briefing on dealmaking, private equity and corporate finance. This article is an on-site version of the newsletter. Premium subscribers can sign up here to get the newsletter delivered every Tuesday to Friday. Standard subscribers can upgrade to Premium here, or explore all FT newsletters. Get in touch with us anytime: [email protected]
In today’s newsletter:
- SullCrom catches the buyout train
- Zach Dell’s power business
- Vodafone’s missing €1.1bn
SullCrom realises private equity is quite big
Well over a decade ago, a lot of top law firms realised how working for private equity clients could transform their M&A practices — and by extension their entire businesses.
Unlike large corporate clients who might do one significant deal every few years or more, buyout groups strike deals on a regular basis and generate work in areas such as leveraged finance and fund finance. DD readers are well aware of how private equity’s boom fuelled the meteoric rise of firms such as Kirkland & Ellis and Latham & Watkins. (This vintage 2019 article is a must-read on the subject.)
In 2026, the implications of this enormous shift in the financial services industry are finally forcing a rethink at Sullivan & Cromwell, a law firm best known on Wall Street as a go-to adviser during banking crises such as the 2008 meltdown and the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023.
For the first time, it’s building a US private equity practice made up of partners that solely focus on private capital clients. “Private equity is now, in the US, a third of M&A activity,” Scott Miller, co-chair of S&C, told DD’s Kaye Wiggins and Sujeet Indap. “We simply have to participate in that part of the market.”
S&C is among a group of elite firms that have largely avoided working for buyout groups, choosing instead to focus on Fortune 500 clients. For years, that approach was tied to a view that acting for the barbarians at the gate might not be compatible with keeping blue-chip corporate clients happy.
“The image you might have had from the turn of the century of private equity, slash-and-burn, cut costs, lever companies up, and pick at the bones of the carcass, that’s not the way these firms operate . . . I don’t think they ever really did operate that way, but that was certainly the perception,” Miller said. He said that was seen as “inconsistent with how a firm like ours . . . would practise”.
S&C is hiring four Kirkland partners in its private equity push and expects to hire more laterals in the future. That, too, marks a shift at the firm, which has historically relied on homegrown lawyers.
In the past “we would have viewed it as a very big change to our culture” to hire a group of partners from a rival, he said. “We made a decision a couple of years ago that we could do that, and bring in people and integrate them into our way of thinking, without having to do it one partner at a time.”
But he isn’t trying to rival the scale of Kirkland and Latham’s private equity practices. “I think we’ll focus on more selective transactions,” Miller said. “What we offer to lawyers who join us . . . is the highest quality work.”
The scion disrupting American power
Many heirs to billion-dollar fortunes are tempted to take it easy and put their inheritances to work on vanity projects or acquiring trophy assets.
DD can’t fault someone such as David Ellison, son of Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, who’s pursuing his passion for the movies as he consolidates Hollywood businesses. Another growing interest among the children of billionaires is owning a professional sports team.
This is a satisfying venture for some, including James Dolan, who inherited the New York Knicks from his father and took home a National Basketball Association title this year. It’s less glorious for others, such as Woody Johnson, heir to the Johnson & Johnson fortune, who owns the worst team in American professional sports and regularly gets blamed for a “ready, fire, aim” strategy.
But Zach Dell, scion of PC billionaire Michael Dell, is not like the others in his set. He’s been busy trying to solve a complex policy problem, and business is booming.
Zach’s Base Power is installing thousands of batteries in households to supply the electricity grid as the US confronts an AI-driven energy crunch. The company, which Dell founded in 2023, just closed a $1bn funding round to value it at $13bn.
In addition to serving as energy storage for backup, the batteries are an active grid asset enabled by software that can tell them when to start delivering to the grid during peak demand.
Base Power retains control of the battery to profit through arbitrage, buying electricity to charge batteries when prices are low and discharging the batteries to sell when prices are high.
The 30-year-old Dell may simply be too ambitious to live off his father’s largesse. He previously started a dating app called Thread Dating and founded Sqwatt, a start-up providing “sanitation solutions” in the developing world.
“I think the biggest company in the world in a decade could very likely be a power company,” Dell told the FT. “And we think that we are pretty well positioned to become that company.”
Vodafone to take €1.1bn hit
How much of your potential future earnings would you be willing to give up in exchange for a more stable (business) partner?
For FTSE 100 telecoms group Vodafone, the answer is a stonking €1.1bn.
The UK group was in line to receive deferred payments of €487mn and a potential €595mn earnout from Patrick Drahi’s Geodesia Holding, provided their German broadband joint venture OXG achieved certain milestones and business performance objectives.
But then Société Générale agreed to acquire Drahi’s 50 per cent stake in OXG this month. The French bank will not be subject to the same commitments as Drahi was, the FT reveals.
The move means Vodafone will miss out on hundreds of millions of euros in potential earnings — something it did not deem worthy of informing investors.
When approached by the FT, Vodafone said its decision to partner with Drahi had provided “the best option between rollout funding certainty and strategic flexibility, and that was reflected in the terms that were agreed”.
“We’re supportive of their exit and replacing them with SG as a committed investor,” Vodafone added.
At the time that Vodafone partnered with Drahi’s telecoms business Altice to launch OXG in 2023, the French-Israeli billionaire was grappling with the impact of higher interest rates on his telecoms empire, which had been financed with billions of dollars of junk debt.
In the words of New Street Research analyst James Ratzer, Vodafone’s choice to partner with Drahi — who in June agreed a deal to sell his French telecoms business SFR for €20.35bn to alleviate debt problems — has proven “to be the wrong one”.
Job moves
- Wells Fargo has named Rob Biodrowski as head of commercial banking market coverage to succeed John Manning, who is retiring.
- Warburg Pincus has hired Philip Nolan as head of US wealth. He previously worked at Neuberger Berman.
- Proskauer has hired Stewart Ross as a fund finance partner in New York. He joins from Kirkland & Ellis.
- Houlihan Lokey has hired Emil Fajersson as a managing director in the firm’s capital solutions group. He joins from Northleaf Capital Partners.
- Citi has hired Sophia Wang as head of China financial institutional sales and senior relationship management in Shanghai. She joins from Bank of America Merrill Lynch.
Smart reads
Hard work Earlier this summer a former JPMorgan Chase banker was tapped for a tough turnaround job, the FT reports. Takis Georgakopoulos is now the CEO of troubled US fintech Fiserv and investors want to see speedy progress.
Stock moves Larry Ellison’s reversal on selling a large chunk of Oracle shares is a reminder that even for top executives, generating cash from their equity isn’t always straightforward, Lex writes.
Berry wars A US fruit company brought its blueberries to China in the hopes of winning over a new customer base. But the project backfired when China set up a blueberry industry of its own, the Wall Street Journal reports.
News round-up

rows.title: Iron ore trader Radiant alleges Glencore hid their ties from audited records
rows.content:
Iron ore trader Radiant alleges Glencore hid their ties from audited records
Embattled iron ore trader Radiant World has alleged that Glencore sought to keep the “true nature” of their relationship out of its audited records, in a lawsuit that is seeking more than $2bn in damages from the Swiss commodities group.
Radiant alleged in a lawsuit filed in Singapore on Tuesday that Glencore’s “formal records did not fully reflect the parties’ private arrangements” or the “true nature and extent of the trading relationship”. It claims Glencore instead insisted on communications through in-person meetings and messages sent on WhatsApp.
“Glencore directed those channels so that the true commercial arrangements would not be reflected in its audited records,” according to the lawsuit. Radiant understood Glencore’s approach stemmed from increased regulatory scrutiny following investigations of the Swiss company by the US Department of Justice, the lawsuit added.
Radiant is joined in the Glencore lawsuit by partner companies including Sapphire Minmetals.
In response to questions from the FT, Glencore published a statement on its website saying: “These claims are meritless and we will contest them vigorously.”
Glencore said it had “evidence that these companies sent falsified invoices and contracts as well as fabricated emails, which they fraudulently claimed to have received from Glencore personnel, to a number of financial institutions.”
“We take these issues seriously and are conducting a review of our historic business activities” with the groups that are part of the lawsuit, it added.
The lawsuit marks an escalation in a dispute between Radiant, which has come under pressure in recent months over alleged inconsistencies in the documentation underpinning its trades, and Glencore, one of its biggest trading counterparties and financial backers.
Some banks and trading firms, including Glencore, have cut Radiant off due to concerns over alleged fake documents. Radiant has denied any wrongdoing.
In its lawsuit, Radiant linked the alleged attempts to conceal their relationship to the increased regulatory scrutiny of Glencore following its 2022 guilty pleas to multiple counts of bribery and market manipulation, which included $1.5bn in penalties. The DoJ settlement required the commodities group to retain independent compliance monitors to check its internal controls.
“Glencore preferred oral communications and physical meetings every month including multiple meetings in Singapore,” according to the legal complaint.
“Glencore also directed that documentation recording the transactions entered into with the claimants be routed and prepared in non-standard ways, including the sending of documents to Glencore’s Delhi office,” it states.
Radiant has sought to portray Glencore as the dominant partner in their relationship, which helped fuel its unprecedented rise, and says the withdrawal of its support has substantially contributed to the trader’s current crisis.

rows.title: Carney calls for ‘unique alliance’ with EU in plea for closer trade ties
rows.content:
Carney calls for ‘unique alliance’ with EU in plea for closer trade ties
Good morning. News to start: Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney told the FT that the 10 EU member states that have not yet ratified a nine-year-old trade deal with Canada should do so to make both sides “more resilient, more independent”, ahead of his Europe visit this week.
Today, Carney tells our Canada correspondent that he wants to “deepen co-operation” with Europe, and our technology correspondent reports on a plea from telecom CEOs to match sovereignty rhetoric with supportive policies.
Bringing transatlantic back
From defence to trade to Eurovision, Mark Carney wants Canada to get closer to Europe in as many ways as possible as a way to safeguard “like-minded partners” against global turmoil, he told Ilya Gridneff.
Context: US President Donald Trump’s aggressive foreign and trade policies have upended relations with the EU and Canada and forced them to rethink their geopolitical approaches. Carney has promoted the concept of “middle powers” pooling resources and clout to maintain their global standing.
Carney travels to Europe this week promoting a “unique alliance” between Canada and Brussels as part of a pivot away from the US.
“We see opportunities to deepen our co-operation with Europe,” he told the FT in an interview in Toronto, citing “people-to-people ties, research ties and, of course, the defence industry.”
Carney will travel to Strasbourg tomorrow to attend European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen’s State of the Union address and make his own speech to MEPs on Thursday.
“There’s many areas where, in a form of deeper partnership, a form of alliance, we can drill down and have better outcomes for Europeans and Canadians,” he said.
As the FT reported this week, the two sides hope to agree on how much Canada will contribute to a Brussels-led €90bn loan to Ukraine before an EU summit in Montreal at the end of October.
Last year, Canada launched the ambitious New EU-Canada Strategic Partnership of the Future and the Security and Defence Partnership to deepen co-operation across trade, technology, energy and security.
In February, Canada became the first non-European country to join the EU’s Security Action for Europe (Safe) initiative to access tens of billions of dollars in cheap defence loans.
In May, Carney was the first non-European leader to attend the European Political Community Summit in Armenia.
But despite Carney’s desire to deepen the relationship between Canada and the EU, challenges remain.
Only 17 of the EU’s 27 member states have ratified a trade agreement with Canada that went into provisional effect in September 2017 because of concerns that its agricultural exports might damage European farmers.
EU leaders want to secure more stringent agreements at the Canada-EU Summit at the end of October in Montreal.
Carney used a speech at Davos last year to rally the world’s “middle powers” against a US-dominated world order that he said was undergoing a “rupture, not a transition”.
Chart du jour: Poland’s Venezuelan misadventure
The extraordinary story of how Poland’s state-backed oil company asked a crypto trader to secure shipments of Venezuelan crude — and lost $230mn.
No connection
Europe’s telecom CEOs have warned the EU its planned overhaul of connectivity and cyber security rules risks undermining the investment case for building the continent’s sovereign technology infrastructure, writes Barbara Moens.
Context: Brussels is pushing for more tech sovereignty to decrease its dependency on mostly American suppliers. European telecom companies provide the physical and digital networks needed for that sovereignty push.
But in order to do that, European policymakers need to rethink parts of legislation that are currently on the table, more than a dozen operators wrote in a letter to von der Leyen, European Council president António Costa and European parliament president Roberta Metsola, and seen by the FT.
In the letter, 17 telecom chief executives, including the heads of Orange, Deutsche Telekom, Telefónica and Telenor, argue Europe risks losing control of one of the layers of the technology stack where it still has strong domestic players “due to incoherent policy reforms”.
The companies specifically point to the Digital Networks Act and the Cybersecurity Act, which were proposed by the Commission earlier this year.
The Digital Networks Act “fails to address Europe’s need to materially improve investment and innovation conditions for connectivity”, the executives argue in the letter, while the Cybersecurity Act, which mandates the phaseout of high-risk suppliers from critical infrastructure, will lead to higher costs for the sector, the companies argue.
“We need a proportionate, risk-based approach that takes into account alternative mitigation measures, instead of broad restrictions mandating infrastructure replacement with no regard for investment life cycles or compensation,” the letter states.
What to watch today
- European Council president António Costa meets Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker in Vienna, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni in Rome and French President Emmanuel Macron in Paris.
- European parliament plenary session in Strasbourg.
- EU ministers for cohesion policy meet in Dublin.
Now read these
- Germany’s ‘guerrilla unit’: Inside the secretive defence ministry team buying up arms for Ukraine.
- Shelter-in-place: Vladimir Putin has moved his main foreign policy conference from Sochi to Moscow owing to security fears.
- ‘Made in Europe’: The UK, Japan and Turkey are seeking individual deals to include their car sectors in the EU’s preferential industrial policies.
