rows.title: Is the Bank of Japan right to fear an overshoot in inflation?
rows.content:
Is the Bank of Japan right to fear an overshoot in inflation?
All eyes in Japan will be on manufacturing and services purchasing managers’ indices due for release on Thursday, as investors mull how aggressively the Bank of Japan will press ahead with interest rate rises and whether it will stay ahead of the curve in containing inflation and propping up the yen.
Ambiguous messaging from the central bank over the past week has left some analysts guessing that the next rate rise could come as soon as October; others suspect December is more likely. BoJ governor Kazuo Ueda said that each policy meeting would discuss tightening and that no timetable had been set.
The stakes are high. On Friday, the BoJ lifted its policy rate by a quarter point to 1.25 per cent, its highest in 31 years, arguing that there was a rising risk that inflation could overshoot the central bank’s 2 per cent target.
That risk, said Ueda, was being propelled higher by the US war in Iran, as high oil and commodity prices continued to expose Japan’s vulnerability as a major importer with a weak currency. The PMIs will offer the first post-meeting signal of whether Ueda’s fears of an overshoot are supported by the data.
In August, Japan’s manufacturing PMI was 54.9 points, marking the eighth consecutive month of expansion in factory activity — any reading above 50 marks expansion rather than contraction. The services PMI also rose in August, to 52.5 points.
Japanese companies are winning new export orders and business sentiment is improving. But output prices rose at an annual pace of 7.6 per cent in August, as companies passed on rising import costs. Leo Lewis
How robust is Eurozone growth?
In spite of a 40 per cent surge in oil prices since early July, the Eurozone economy held up better than most analysts expected during the summer.
After the European Central Bank lifted its growth forecasts by 0.1 percentage points to 0.9 per cent in 2026 and by 0.2 points to 1.4 per cent next year, closely watched purchasing managers’ indices from S&P Global on Wednesday are expected to underscore the economy’s resilience.
Economists polled by Reuters expect the manufacturing PMI to repeat the August reading of 52.7 points, well into expansionary territory and the highest level in 51 months. The Services PMI is expected to have fallen slightly by 0.1 points to 51.5 points, still signalling healthy expansion.
Economists at Société Générale argue that growth momentum in the Eurozone is higher than the headline data suggests, as GDP numbers are distorted by frequent and big revisions to Irish data.
“Excluding Ireland provides a clearer view of underlying momentum,” they argued in a recent note, adding that, from that perspective, the region’s economy would grow by 1.2 per cent this year and 1.1 per cent in 2027.
This, they added, suggests “a gradual acceleration and growth above estimated potential”, despite a drought over the summer that disrupted waterborne transport and hit harvests. Olaf Storbeck
Are UK businesses weathering the Iran war?
UK investors will also look to purchasing managers’ indices next week, for any indication that a difficult geopolitical backdrop and the upcoming Budget are weighing on business confidence.
Economists polled by Bloomberg expect S&P Global’s composite purchasing managers’ index, a measure of activity across manufacturing and services, to fall to 52 points in September from 52.5 in August, still above the 50-point mark separating expansion from contraction.
Ellie Henderson, economist at Investec, expects the index to remain above the 50-point threshold, supported by companies working through backlogs of existing orders.
However, she expects business sentiment to have deteriorated in September following the intensification of the Iran war. Oil and natural gas prices have risen sharply over the past two weeks, despite retreating somewhat in recent days.
Higher energy prices and elevated borrowing costs are also complicating the task facing chancellor John Healey as he prepares to present his first Budget on October 28.
The two factors are expected to have eroded the government’s fiscal headroom — the margin by which it is forecast to meet its key rule of balancing the current budget, excluding capital investment, by 2029-30. If so, it raises the prospect of further tax increases.
So far, both business and consumer confidence have improved following the change in prime minister from Sir Keir Starmer to Andy Burnham, who has enjoyed stronger public support.
September’s GfK consumer confidence index, to be published on Friday, will give an indication of whether the new prime minister’s honeymoon is beginning to fade. Bloomberg’s poll of economists suggests that this is the case, with the index seen edging down from August. Valentina Romei

rows.title: World’s best-performing sovereign wealth fund expects equities pullback
rows.content:
World’s best-performing sovereign wealth fund expects equities pullback
The world’s best-performing sovereign wealth fund expects the recent outperformance in global equities to ease after it reported 14 per cent growth in the year to June despite being underweight on high-flying technology stocks.
New Zealand’s superannuation fund gained prominence after it was named the top-performing sovereign wealth fund last year by data provider Global SWF based on its performance over the previous two decades, when its average annual returns exceeded 10 per cent.
The fund, which supports the pensions of New Zealand’s retirees and is about half invested in equities, said on Wednesday that it grew 14.2 per cent to NZ$94.4bn ($54.2bn) in the year to the end of June.
The increase came despite the fund being underweight on US stocks, where the S&P 500 index rose by more than 20 per cent in the same period on the back of investor enthusiasm for AI.
As a result, the New Zealand Superannuation Fund — which is invested in timber, property and private investments alongside equities — slightly lagged behind its own passive reference benchmark, which is 80 per cent invested in global equities.
Jo Townsend, chief executive of the Guardians of New Zealand Superannuation, which manages the fund, said a concentrated portfolio might have captured recent gains in the short term, but a diversified strategy was more suited to its long-term mandate.
“Returns for US equities over the past couple of years are close to double annualised returns for the past 20 years,” she said. “So we would expect there to be some reversion to the mean at some point.”
The fund lowered its 20-year annual return outlook to 7.2 per cent from 7.8 per cent earlier this year, which Townsend said reflected a view that returns on equities would ease after a strong period of outperformance.
New Zealand Superannuation was the country’s largest taxpayer last year, and the government has invested NZ$27.4bn into the fund since it was established in 2001.
Over the past 20 years, it has significantly outperformed its passive reference fund, generating NZ$22bn more than the benchmark in that period.
Neighbouring Australia’s Future Fund, whose board has A$356bn ($254bn) under management, reported a slightly higher return of 14.8 per cent in the year to June.
The Australian fund’s performance has improved after the Labor government overhauled its mandate in 2024 to direct more investment towards “national priority” investments in energy transition and residential housing.

rows.title: Larry Ellison shows even billionaires struggle with liquidity
rows.content:
Larry Ellison shows even billionaires struggle with liquidity
It’s not unusual for an ageing investor to consider reshuffling their nest egg. But when that investor is the 82-year-old Larry Ellison, co-founder of Oracle, things become altogether more complicated.
Oracle disclosed last week that Ellison, who still serves as chief technology officer and executive chair of the board, had put in place a plan to sell 50mn Oracle shares, currently valued at more than $7bn, in transactions between June and October. Days later, it said Ellison had yet to sell a share and that the plan was being cancelled. No reason for the reversal was given.
It isn’t hard to see why Ellison may have wanted the cash. Like many boomers, he is supporting the ambitions of his children — in this case Paramount Skydance boss David Ellison. The Oracle magnate is part of a group putting in more than $40bn of equity to fund a $110bn takeover of Warner Bros Discovery, having previously helped David buy Paramount at a valuation of more than $20bn.
It also seems plausible that Ellison can’t get hold of such huge chunks of money without selling equity. Oracle generates massive dividends for him, but even those only amount to $2bn per year. And Oracle disclosures show nearly a third of Ellison’s shares are already pledged “as collateral for personal indebtedness”.
But the patriarch’s flip-flopping on the sale reflects the fact that for top executives — even those whose shareholding is worth $175bn — generating liquidity from equity in the companies they run is not totally straightforward. Selling shares, even through “programmatic”, or pre-arranged, automated methods, is often interpreted as a bearish signal by outside investors.
And if the sale is big enough, it can itself push down the share price of the company. Elon Musk sold billions of dollars’ worth of Tesla stock in 2022 to fund his purchase of social network Twitter, now called X, at a moment when there were questions about the electric vehicle group’s growth prospects: its stock fell about two-thirds that year.
Oracle can ill-afford a further confidence knock. Its equity has halved in value over the past year as investors fret about its push into AI infrastructure and its debts of more than $150bn, with separate big obligations located off the balance sheet.
In this context, Ellison’s side quests into the media world are not great news for Oracle shareholders. The tie-up between Paramount Skydance and WBD is beset by legal challenges. Assuming the two do eventually combine, the resulting company will also be highly leveraged. Besides competing for Ellison’s time, any snafus raise the possibility that Ellison might have to sell further chunks of his software stock.
Ellison may not exactly treat Oracle shareholders like family, but they are undeniably tied up with the family’s sprawling empire, for better or for worse.

rows.title: China’s AI listings glut drags Hong Kong stocks lower
rows.content:
China’s AI listings glut drags Hong Kong stocks lower
A glut of Chinese AI companies raising equity in Hong Kong is contributing to the stock market’s lacklustre performance, with investors warning that initial public offerings are pulling cash out of established names.
While equity issuance in the Asian financial hub has surpassed last year’s total — helped by a bumper crop of AI listings and follow-on offerings — the benchmark Hang Seng index has declined close to 3 per cent.
The disparity between equity issuance and overall market performance highlights weak global demand for Chinese stocks, even as those companies face growing pressure to raise capital and expand overseas.
Most global fund managers remain neutral or underweight on Chinese equities, meaning any new companies coming to market are competing with existing positions in investors’ portfolios.
“Hong Kong’s market has enough turnover to process a busy IPO calendar, but new deals are competing directly with existing China exposure inside portfolios,” said Sat Duhra, an Asia ex-Japan portfolio manager at Janus Henderson Investors.
For many Chinese companies, issuing equity in Hong Kong is one of their only funding options as credit growth has slowed in the mainland.
“Right now banks are not lending money,” said Hao Hong, chief investment officer at Hong Kong hedge fund Lotus Asset Management. “All the companies need money and the government thinks the market is a better vehicle.”
However, China’s securities regulator has been selective about the types of companies that can list in the mainland to preserve liquidity, said fund managers and analysts.
“Regulators are trying to stabilise [mainland market] sentiment, and large equity issuance onshore can work against that objective,” said Duhra. “Hong Kong allows Chinese companies to raise capital without drawing directly on domestic liquidity.”
There are signs that the listings glut has slowed down the market. In the first half of the year, shares of newly listed Chinese AI start-ups such as Z.AI and MiniMax rallied sharply.
But more than half of the companies that listed in Hong Kong in the third quarter have seen their share prices fall, tracking a global tech sell-off in July as investors soured on AI.
“The IPO market became a bit of a momentum trade,” said Nicholas Chui, a portfolio manager at Franklin Templeton. “Anything that came into the market in the first quarter or the second quarter, people just said it was free money . . . That has largely evaporated.”
Global tech stocks took a further hit on Monday after the biggest AI companies called for a slowdown in the technology’s development in response to warnings over its safety. China’s spy agency also warned of the risks AI could pose to the country’s political and social stability.
Tilly Zhang, a technology and industrial policy analyst at Gavekal Dragonomics in Beijing, was sceptical that the recent uptick in warnings would signal an end to Hong Kong’s fundraising frenzy.
“Both for the US and for China they are stuck in this competition,” said Zhang. “Nobody wants to take the cost of losing in this critical tech competition. More people can talk about it and make more rules about it, but they will definitely not slow down on AI advancement.”
Many of the newly public companies are not profitable and work in areas such as biotech and semiconductors. The number of lossmaking groups, based on trailing 12-month net profit, has been rising this year.
“If you are listing with negative free cash flow with a muddled path to profitability you’re going to struggle to perform post-listing,” said Aadil Ebrahim, head of equities at Klay Capital in Singapore.
Hong Kong’s woes have been compounded by mainland China having more listed hardware companies that are supplying the AI infrastructure build-out.
After surging to a record last year, mainland Chinese investment in Hong Kong has “really fallen away”, said John Woods, chief investment officer for Asia at Lombard Odier. “On a relative attraction level, Hong Kong is losing out to more AI-oriented thematics on the mainland.”
Some of the main Hang Seng benchmark’s largest constituents are legacy consumer tech companies that have sold off heavily this year. Tencent, Alibaba, Xiaomi and Meituan account for more than 20 per cent of the index and are among the most exposed to a slowdown in Chinese consumer sentiment.
Meanwhile, some of Hong Kong’s top-performing stocks this year are from the AI industry but were not in the Hang Seng Tech index for most of the year. The index provider added Z.AI and MiniMax to the tech composite in June, but some investors said the moves were too late.
“Whenever they do this it tends to be the peak of that specific industry,” said Hong of Lotus Asset Management.
“In 2021, they worked overtime to push out the Hang Seng Tech index to include all the internet names, and that was precisely the peak of the Chinese internet companies,” he added. “Whoever is presiding over this construction of the Hang Seng Tech index is seriously lagging.”
Hang Seng Indexes Company said: “The Hang Seng index closely tracks the Hong Kong stock market and reflects its overall performance and market composition.”
It added: “While AI-related companies have become increasingly prominent globally, their impact on the overall Hong Kong stock market is limited due to their relatively small share of total market capitalisation.”
Data visualisation by Haohsiang Ko in Hong Kong

rows.title: Predictability but at a price: tidal power’s struggle to scale up
rows.content:
Predictability but at a price: tidal power’s struggle to scale up
Simply sign up to the Renewable energy myFT Digest -- delivered directly to your inbox.
In the seventh century, Irish monks found a way to use the cyclical rise and fall of ocean tides to help them mill grain.
This ancient technology has come a long way since then, and now offers a clean and predictable source of energy. The first modern tidal energy plant was built at La Rance, northwestern France, in the 1960s, and meets the power needs of 225,000 people.
Coastal regions across the world are now looking to tidal energy to help even out the fluctuations of other forms of renewable energy.
But while the technology is proven, there are relatively few instances of it because the construction costs are often prohibitively high. Marine energy companies are trying to bring these down by scaling up their supply chains and developing cheaper options such as modular floating turbines.
Since it depends on the gravitational pull of the sun and moon, tidal power is very predictable. But scaling up this energy source will require investment in infrastructure such as underwater energy cables, as well as careful planning to minimise the harm that tidal dams and lagoons can cause to marine ecosystems.
How does it work?
When tides rise, water moves in on the land and fills coastal streams and lagoons. When they fall, that water rushes back to the ocean. Tidal technologies capture the energy created by this flow and turn it into electricity in two ways: tidal range, and tidal stream.
Tidal range uses the difference between high and low tide, and uses similar technology to conventional hydropower stations, often by building a dam-like structure called a barrage across a bay or estuary. Water collects on one side of the barrier with the tides, and then flows through turbines, generating electricity. These are large-scale construction projects that can take a long time to build, but last for decades and can provide significant amounts of energy.
Streams, on the other hand, capture the kinetic energy of moving tidal currents. In places such as archipelagos or fjords, water is pushed through narrow channels, which makes it flow faster. That is used to turn underwater turbines, generating power. This kind of tidal power avoids the massive construction work required for barrages and is generally deployed in smaller, more modular projects.
What are the pros and cons?
Tidal energy’s predictability makes it a powerful complement to wind or solar power, which are easier and cheaper to build but also depend on the weather.
But the technology hasn’t reached commercial scale yet, which is why it still has very high upfront costs and relies on government funding and other subsidies in most places, said Elisa Obermann, the chief executive of Marine Renewables Canada.
Experts expect the price to go down as the technology evolves and the supply chains needed for its implementation scale up, similar to what has happened with solar energy over the past decade or so.
Another drawback is the environmental impact of the facilities, especially for tidal-range facilities which involve building a barrage. Harvesting power from tides can interrupt the flow of migratory species such as eel or salmon, and also disrupt intertidal habitats such as mudflats and salt marshes. That impact can be mitigated by spatial and marine planning, which can help find contingency plans and potentially build alternative ecosystems for those species, says Afryea Charles, the founder of ocean-technology consulting company Ecolexica.
Will it save the planet?
Tidal has the potential to become one part of a diverse mix of renewable energies that stabilises the electricity grid by helping to balance supply and demand.
It is unlikely to become a predominant part of any energy mix, and can only be deployed in coastal areas where tidal currents are strong — but it could serve as a backbone in a hybrid energy system, helping to keep critical services such as hospital or food refrigeration running during storms or other events that disrupt conventional energy supplies, says Soufiane Haddout, a researcher and fluid mechanics expert at Ibn Tofaïl University in Morocco.
At the moment, operational facilities are largely concentrated in the Northern hemisphere. As construction costs come down, it could meaningfully strengthen energy resilience in archipelagic or island nations such as the Philippines and Indonesia where communities are particularly vulnerable to climate change, Haddout says.
Has it arrived yet?
Tidal energy has passed the demonstration stage, but has not yet reached large-scale commercialisation, says Obermann. Some projects have been operating for decades, proving the technology’s viability. However, more investment in the supply chains needed to build these facilities will be necessary to bring down its installation cost and make it more widely available, she says.
A key factor to bring down the cost of building tidal facilities will be the development of modular, floating turbine systems that would be easier to install and could make it possible to deploy the technology in a wider range of locations, says Haddout.
Who are the winners and losers?
Tidal energy has the potential to make some coastal and island nations less dependent on energy imports, including diesel and other fossil-fuel supplies, says Charles. “The price of oil is going up, and a lot of countries really want that independence,” she adds.
In some locations, it is possible that areas suitable for tidal power, such as lagoons, are also popular holiday destinations, such as beaches, potentially affecting the tourism industry.
However, tidal energy can also present opportunities for tourism: the La Rance station in France has become a popular tourist destination with a visitor centre. Sihwa Lake Tidal Power Station in South Korea, the world’s biggest tidal lagoon, has become a hotspot for birdwatching and its observatory has attracted more than 1mn visitors since 2014.
Who is investing in it?
Tidal energy has received significant funding from private investors, and because it is not yet fully commercial, government support is still critical to its development.
Governments in Europe and Asia have been particularly active in funding research and implementation for tidal projects, says Charles. That support comes in grants for research and projects as well as systems such as government-backed revenue guarantees. In the UK, for instance, the Contracts for Difference scheme protects companies and consumers from volatile energy prices by striking deals with energy developers that guarantee a “strike price” for energy from low-carbon technology. If the electricity sells for less than the contractually-agreed strike price, the government then pays the difference.
“The focus now needs to shift from demonstrating that the technology works to enabling commercial investment at scale,” says Obermann. “The goal isn’t for government to fund the industry indefinitely. It’s to help get tidal to the point where private capital can invest confidently and the industry can become self-sustaining.”

rows.title: UK contends with rise in workplace disputes about disability discrimination
rows.content:
UK contends with rise in workplace disputes about disability discrimination
A rising tide of disputes over disability discrimination is an “enormous challenge” to the tribunal system and is adding to the multibillion-pound cost of workplace conflict to employers, the chair of the UK’s conciliation body has warned.
Baroness Maggie Jones of Acas said disability-related cases had driven a surge in demand for the organisation’s individual dispute resolution service of 26 per cent in the past year, as employers faced pressure to meet the needs of neurodiverse staff and those with mental or physical health conditions.
“Employers are struggling to understand what reasonable adjustments they really have to make — they understand the concept of [their legal obligation] but they don’t understand the practicality,” she said.
“The numbers of individual disputes are just going up,” she said, noting the rising share of cases relating to disability reflected rising numbers diagnosed as neurodivergent. Stress and anxiety are also “a real issue”, Jones added.
Another factor driving the increases is AI, which many workers are using to put together claims — often of greater length and complexity.
The Acas chair said the rise in disability-related disputes was not just a UK issue, noting colleagues in Australia and New Zealand had also seen a surge.
In the UK, however, workers who make a claim against their employer are facing longer waits for their case to be heard, as tribunal backlogs threaten to undermine the Labour government’s reforms of workers’ rights.
Jones spoke to the FT following the release of new figures showing the number of open cases in the employment tribunal system had reached a new high of 70,000 in the three months to June — more than 50 per cent higher than a year ago and up almost 10 per cent from the previous quarter.
This is even before full implementation of the Employment Rights Act, a sweeping upgrade of workers’ rights that includes new protections against unfair dismissal and doubles the length of time employees will have to lodge a tribunal claim in most cases.
A notification to Acas, which triggers an offer of “early conciliation”, is a precursor to a tribunal claim. The rise in demand for this service has put Acas under pressure and led to delays in appointing conciliators, forcing the government to extend the maximum period allowed for this intervention.
Jones is leading a push to promote informal dispute resolution and head off cases before they arrive on Acas’s doorstep. A new code of practice is out for consultation that encourages employees and their bosses to talk problems through face to face.
At present, both employees and line managers are too quick to put concerns into writing so that “it all becomes formal very, very quickly”, Jones said.
“Once that happens, people’s views become entrenched . . . they don’t know how to compromise,” she added. “We are trying to encourage people to talk to each other . . . it requires, on both sides, the employee and the employer, to take some risks.”
Acas argues employers will gain from efforts to prevent formal disputes: it has previously estimated the cost to UK employers of managing and resolving disputes totals some £28.5bn a year.
Lawyers and campaign groups, however, say a push for informal dispute resolution requires caution and will not resolve tribunal backlogs unless the government better resources the courts, Acas and advice services.
“There is a risk that a conversation with a line manager is not recorded, nothing improves and no one knows the conversation happened,” said Emer Sheehy, policy manager at Citizens Advice.
Backlogs mean “bad faith employers might drag out claims and hope that workers drop their cases in the two years it can take to reach a hearing”, Sheehy noted, adding that the charity was aware of many cases where employers blatantly failed to pay the awards ordered by tribunals.
Acas is also grappling with the rise of AI-assisted claims, as workers turn to the new technology to help them research their rights, draft documents and argue their case.
Jones acknowledged AI was “a huge issue” fuelling both the number of cases and their complexity, with chatbots generating “reams of argumentation” that were “clogging up” the system.
Yet Acas is turning to AI itself to make its online advice more accessible, help its advisers understand cases faster and explore the potential to offer advice on simple cases through chatbots in future.
“In the longer term, we will have to embrace AI to make sense of cases written by AI,” Jones said, adding that the technology would also help it do more with limited resources.
“It does concern us that the people who get their cases heard are the most persistent and those who know how to use the technology,” she said. “We need to make sure the people in greatest need of help are those we reach out to.”

rows.title: Drill, baby, drill: geothermal energy developers borrow techniques from oil and gas
rows.content:
Drill, baby, drill: geothermal energy developers borrow techniques from oil and gas
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
Rapidly rising electricity demand — driven by data centres, manufacturing and electrification — is pushing companies, politicians and investors to look at niche technologies.
One of them is next-generation geothermal, which uses high-tech drilling techniques borrowed from the oil and gas industry to harness heat deep in the earth’s crust.
While conventional geothermal energy has been around for decades, and harnesses naturally occurring reservoirs underground, next-generation technologies tap hot rock underground in places that lack the naturally occurring water and permeable fractures that would have been needed in the past.
Next-gen geothermal is promoted as a Goldilocks power source: unlike wind and solar, it can run around the clock; unlike fossil fuels, it’s relatively clean; and unlike advanced nuclear, it’s less of a technological moonshot.
Its cheerleaders say it could be a low-emitting source of reliable power just as the grid needs more of it — but costs will have to come down.
How does it work?
Conventional geothermal finds naturally occurring reservoirs, while next-generation technologies create them.
The conventional method is constrained by geology: developers must find places where heat, water and permeable rock naturally coincide. Next-generation geothermal can create or mimic those conditions instead.
The two main ways this is achieved are enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) and closed-loop geothermal.
EGS borrows methods from oil and gas by creating fractures in rock, so water can circulate through and pick up the heat. When it returns to the surface, it helps create a vapour which is used to spin a turbine and create electricity. It uses the large rotary drilling rigs and cementing techniques found in the industry.
The closed-loop method drills kilometres-deep wells and adds sealed, fluid-filled pipes that absorb heat from the surrounding rock, which it returns to the surface, where it is used to heat another fluid that generates electricity. EGS projects are best suited to places where developers can safely fracture hot rock, while closed-loop is better in places where water and geological conditions are more uncertain.
What are the pros and cons?
Next-gen geothermal could make it possible for vast swaths of land to produce electricity. The US has 40 gigawatts of potential conventional geothermal sources, according to the Department of Energy. Next-gen methods could unlock 5,500GW in the US alone, according to the energy department. Even if only 90GW is developed by 2050, as the US government estimates, that would be enough to power 68mn homes.
Geothermal has a rare advantage in the US of benefiting from bipartisan political support. Democrats support it because of its potential to supply bountiful clean energy while Republicans like how it is a reliable and continuous source of power. Unlike solar and wind, the Trump administration did not cut tax credits supporting geothermal and, in February, it announced $171.5mn to fund full-scale tests and drilling.
But costs are high and will need to come down for the technology to prove economic — conventional geothermal plants can cost between $4,800 and $6,300 per kilowatt while next-generation plants come in at $15,000 per kilowatt. These costs may come down by making drilling faster, cheaper and more resource-efficient, but that is a long way away.
And since next-gen geothermal plants lack the decades-long operating record of conventional plants, it is far more uncertain how their wells and reservoirs will perform over time.
Will it save the planet?
Next-gen geothermal is not exactly zero-emission, since it requires huge amounts of steel, cement, diesel and electricity to build the plants. Its median lifecycle emissions are 32g of carbon dioxide per kilowatt hour of electricity generated, according to the National Renewable Energy Laboratory. However, the equivalent figures for fossil-fuel production are far larger — natural gas produces 490g and coal 820g.
If next-gen geothermal does expand to 90GW by 2050 and this displaces the same amount of natural gas electricity-generating capacity, roughly 325mn tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions could be avoided, according to the US energy department and the World Resources Institute.
These predictions are uncertain because geothermal would displace a mixture of fossil fuels and renewable energy, especially as solar and wind continue to advance. The key advantage it has over other renewables is that it is not limited to when the sun shines or the wind blows. But unlocking these benefits would require the technology to scale rapidly by bringing costs down.
Has it arrived yet?
Next-gen geothermal has moved out of the laboratory but is still a nascent commercial technology. Only a handful of projects are operating worldwide, and the first utility-scale fleet is yet to arrive.
Fervo Energy, a developer headquartered in Houston, has a Project Red in Nevada that has been up and running since late 2023, supplying to the grid and proving that an artificial geothermal reservoir can deliver. But the plant is small, generating on average up to 3 megawatts. The company’s Cape Station plant in Utah has 500MW under construction, with its first 33MW set to come online at the end of this year, scaling to 100MW in 2027. The site has potential capacity of 4.3GW.
Outside the US, Canadian clean-energy company Eavor started supplying electricity from its closed-loop project in Germany in December 2025. It provides roughly 8MW of electricity.
The tech is therefore somewhere between demonstration and commercial deployment: proven in small projects but not in large plants or a wide range of geographies.
Who are the winners and losers?
If next-gen geothermal scales, some of the biggest winners could be the oil and gas industry since developers need its drilling rigs, steel casings, wellheads and workers. Fervo signed an $800mn agreement in April with pipe manufacturer Vallourec as it builds out its projects. In the US, these benefits could be felt most keenly in Republican states, which tend to have bigger oil industries, while Democrats get to advance their clean energy agenda.
Utilities and data centres could gain another source of round-the-clock power that could potentially lower costs.
The biggest potential losers are natural gas companies due to the risk of displacement if geothermal scales.
Communities could gain jobs and tax revenue, but NIMBYist concerns over drilling and water use could create issues for developers. Construction can cause months of drilling noise, bright lights and heavy truck traffic, as well as concerns over earthquakes as developers fracture rock underground.
Who is investing in it?
The money flowing into geothermal is starting to widen beyond venture capital, although developers commonly bemoan the “missing middle” stage between the development and construction phases in which drilling and subsurface activities take place and where it is harder to secure finance.
In March, Fervo raised $421mn of non-recourse project debt for its Cape Station project. The facility was overseen by a group including Barclays, HSBC, and the Royal Bank of Canada, with Bank of America and JPMorgan also participating. Fervo then raised $2.2bn through its May IPO.
As Milo McBride, a fellow in the sustainability, climate and geopolitics programme at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, puts it, investors are moving “away from just VC funding towards more institutional capital” as lenders become more comfortable with the technology.
Earlier-stage companies are more tied to raising money through equity. Utah-based geothermal developer Zanskar raised a $115mn series C round in January, led by US private equity firm Spring Lane Capital. The US next-gen geothermal company Sage Geosystems raised $97mn the same month. Public money is still a key player, as shown by the US energy department’s $171mn funding. In Europe, Eavor has drawn debt from the European Investment Bank and an EU grant.
Large buyers make projects more creditworthy. Google in early September pledged to buy 396MW from Fervo’s Cape Station, with the option for another 600MW — offering long-term revenues and giving lenders confidence they will be repaid.

rows.title: UK and Japan seek to fully benefit from ‘Made in Europe’ car sector rules
rows.content:
UK and Japan seek to fully benefit from ‘Made in Europe’ car sector rules
The UK, Japan and Turkey are seeking deals to include their carmaking sectors in the EU’s “Made in Europe” rules, amid concerns the bloc’s flagship new industrial policy will damage jobs and production.
The EU is proposing to focus the bloc’s public contracts and subsidies for technologies such as electric vehicles and clean energy on European-based manufacturing, in a radical shift from free-trade orthodoxy to counter China’s dominance in these industries and others.
Although countries that have trade agreements with the EU are included in parts of the Made in Europe scheme, clauses requiring vehicles to be assembled in the bloc to receive support — and excluding trade partners from some EV subsidies and fleet schemes — could damage non-EU carmakers’ businesses.
Carmakers with manufacturing operations in the UK, Japan and Turkey are therefore seeking to fully benefit from the proposed EU Industrial Accelerator Act that lays out the rules.
Japanese business representatives said Tokyo was seeking a bilateral deal with Brussels to include its industry in the EU scheme.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has raised concerns with French President Emmanuel Macron, saying the British car industry should not be caught in the crossfire of a policy aimed at tackling Chinese competition. The UK is seeking to link the issue to talks with the EU about a reset in relations that are expected in November.
Turkey, which is in a customs union with the EU, has sought to convince the European Commission not to cut the country’s car industry out of the Made in Europe rules.
EU-Turkey automotive trade is worth about €54bn annually including parts, with the EU having a €2bn export surplus. Ömer Bolat, Turkish trade minister, told the FT its exclusion would “hit the EU’s own industrial base”.
Canada was also seeking talks to gain access to the EU scheme, by keeping its industrial plans “aligned”, industry minister Mélanie Joly said this year.
Officials in Brussels said they were open to discussions with countries about individual deals to include their car sectors in the Made in Europe rules. “It’s about using our single market to open new business for our companies,” said one official.
Several people said the Japanese government has made it a top priority to negotiate Japan’s status in a “bilateral agreement” that would guarantee the country’s businesses were included from the beginning of the EU scheme’s implementation, likely by early 2027.
EU officials believe that aspects of Japanese public contracts — such as a clean-energy vehicle subsidy scheme — are not sufficiently favourable to the bloc’s companies. “We have no lessons to take from the Japanese on open markets,” said another official.
There are also concerns that Chinese carmakers could choose to set up shop in countries such as Turkey rather than the EU if the nation was included in the EU scheme.
However, Kemal Yazıcı, president of OIB, the Turkish car exporters association, said: “Turkey should not be treated as a ‘back door’ for Chinese automotive production.” He noted that it accounted for just 0.1 per cent of China’s total outward investment, while Chinese investment in Europe was about 38 times larger.
EU member states and the European parliament are currently negotiating legislation to underpin the Made in Europe rules, and trade partners want their status protected in those discussions, as any separate deals could prolong uncertainty for businesses.
Members of the European parliament are proposing the EU rules apply to manufacturing in the bloc but the European Commission would have discretion to include European trade partners like the UK.
Christophe Grudler, who is helping to draft the lawmakers’ position, said the legislation should stay true to its European ambitions, with exceptions only for neighbouring countries to the EU such as the UK.
“If we say it’s ‘Made in Europe’ and it’s manufactured on the other end of the world, voters are going to say these European legislators are mad,” he said.

rows.title: Sullivan & Cromwell hires team of Kirkland partners in private equity push
rows.content:
Sullivan & Cromwell hires team of Kirkland partners in private equity push
Sullivan & Cromwell has hired a team of lawyers from rival Kirkland & Ellis in a push to build a US private equity practice, a marked shift for an elite firm that has largely avoided acting for buyout groups.
The US corporate law firm has historically focused on Fortune 500 clients rather than private capital dealmakers. Hiring the four Kirkland partners, which will mark the first time S&C has had a team of US partners solely working on private equity deals, is an acknowledgment that the previous approach is no longer tenable.
“Private equity is now, in the US, a third of M&A activity,” Scott Miller, co-chair of S&C, told the FT. “We simply have to participate in that part of the market.”
The white-shoe firm has hired Los Angeles-based Hamed Meshki to lead its global private equity practice. It hired two other LA-based Kirkland partners, Luke Guerra and Guirgis Nasief, and New York-based Y Michael Chung.
The group specialises in private equity-led acquisitions and counts Oaktree Capital and Clearlake Capital as clients.
Miller said that in the past, acting for buyout groups was seen as inconsistent with representing large companies on M&A deals.
“The image you might have had from the turn of the century of private equity, slash-and-burn, cut costs, lever companies up, and pick at the bones of the carcass, that’s not the way these firms operate . . . I don’t think they ever really did operate that way, but that was certainly the perception,” Miller said. He said that was seen as “inconsistent with how a firm like ours . . . would practise”.
Law firms such as Kirkland and Latham & Watkins have grown rapidly as a result of private equity’s boom in recent decades. Buyout groups can be lucrative clients for law firms because they generate far more regular dealmaking business than companies.
The hires from Kirkland come amid a talent war among Wall Street law firms, which have historically relied on homegrown talent and shied away from lifting groups from rivals. Miller said that even seven or eight years ago it would have been difficult for S&C to bring in a group of partners from a rival firm.
“We would have viewed it as a very big change to our culture,” he said. “We made a decision a couple of years ago that we could do that, and bring in people and integrate them into our way of thinking, without having to do it one partner at a time.”
For decades, S&C and other elite law firms such as Cravath, Swaine & Moore and Wachtell, Lipton dominated dealmaking advisory work, acting strictly for big companies. S&C’s clients over the years have included AB InBev, Nike and Goldman Sachs.
Miller told the FT that the firm’s private equity effort would for now focus on transactional work rather than broader assignments for financial sponsors such as drafting limited-partner agreements or designing fund structures.
“We want to focus on the M&A piece,” he said. “We may do more funds formation work . . . but that wasn’t the strategic imperative here. The funds formation work is probably ripe for some disruption through AI and we don’t really see the M&A work being disrupted in the same way.”
S&C, which itself has suffered a handful of partner defections in recent years, has been expanding its London private equity operation. Last year it hired London-based Kon Asimacopoulos, Michael Francies and Barney Reynolds as it sought to expand its presence in restructuring, private equity and financial services in the city. Francies joined after retiring from rival Weil, where he spent 26 years.
Last week it also hired LA-based Viet Dinh, a well-known figure in conservative legal circles who worked in the George W Bush administration and was most recently the top lawyer at Rupert Murdoch’s Fox Corporation.
The firm has separately taken on President Donald Trump as a client, acting for him as he challenges his conviction in the Stormy Daniels hush-money case among other matters.
Miller said he expected his firm to increase its US private equity effort from the equivalent of about 10 full-time partners, including the new group, to about 20 within a year.
“I don’t think we’ll be Latham or Kirkland in terms of volume, I think we’ll focus on more selective transactions,” he said. “What we offer to lawyers who join us . . . is the highest quality work, the most intellectually challenging work, and we have to continue that.”

rows.title: The Extended Farageverse is coming together
rows.content:
The Extended Farageverse is coming together
The Nigel-Farage-benefiting-from-crypto-sphere grew vastly bigger this month, after Reform UK received record-breaking donations from two crypto billionaires. More on that here and here. But a smaller, lesser-noticed Farage-linked crypto group is also planning to grow.
Stack BTC — the bitcoin treasury company in which Farage has a 5.6 per cent stake — said on Tuesday that it plans to buy Direct Bullion, the gold dealer that has paid the Reform leader hefty sums in return for dubiously useful promotional content, for a cool £12mn.
To Alphaville’s repeated delight, Stack is chaired by Kwasi Kwarteng, the UK’s former chancellor of 2022 mini-budget disaster fame, who was chuffed at the deal.
I am thrilled. We are achieving exactly the strategy we set out at the very beginning. 
Buying BTC directly from capital raising and also buying businesses to generate fiat to buy BTC. This is the twin pillar strategy in action. We are achieving what we set out to do. https://t.co/tUcPqLRglh
The deal both highlights the entangled nature of the Extended Farageverse, and represents the Reform UK leader’s two main interests — touting gold and touting crypto — being subsumed into one business.
Stack is buying Direct Bullion from its founder Paul Withers. Withers is also the biggest shareholder in the bitcoin company, holding 23 per cent. Withers is a friend of Farage, who was paid a total of £405,000 by Direct Bullion over the past year, for 24 hours’ worth of work.
However, Direct Bullion had a turnover of £52mn last year and made a post-tax profit of $2.15mn. Stack’s market cap is just £5.2mn, and it lost money in the six months to January, so how will it get £12mn to do this deal?
The deal will technically be considered a reverse takeover and a related-party transaction, even though Stack said in a statement that “Paul Withers has not participated, and will continue to refrain from participating, in any Board discussions or decisions relating to the Proposed Acquisition”.
Stack said £3mn will be paid in cash from its own balance sheet, having raised £4.27mn so far this year. A small portion (just £94,700 of it) came from retail investors which the bitcoin company tapped to little success in March.
A further £4mn will be given in Stack shares and £5mn will be paid as an earnout subject to the gold dealer making at least £2.5mn in the first year after the acquisition, and if it hits the same figures in years three to five, getting roughly £1.33mn for each year that it hits the mark.
As Kwarteng suggested, the plan is to sell gold bars and coins to retail investors and plough the proceeds into buying more bitcoin. And Stack said it wants to do more deals like this to secure “ongoing source[s] of liquidity” to stack more sats. As David Galan, chief executive of Stack, told Alphaville:
This is intended to be deal number one. We would like to be able to buy other precious metals dealers and another area that’s quite interesting to us is [gold] custody.
To Alphaville’s enormous surprise and regret, bitcoin treasury companies have faced a bruising year as the hype has died down and investors question the model of constantly raising money to spend on buying digital coins.
Billions of dollars have been wiped off the value of these companies since the height of the fundraising frenzy last summer, and many are dumping their tokens and pivoting back to their original businesses. Even Michael Saylor’s Strategy — the OG “bitcoin treasury company” — is now forced to sell bitcoin to stay alive.
Shares in thinly traded Stack were flat on Tuesday and have plunged 64 per cent since Farage first invested in the business in March. The Midas touch.

rows.title: Ørsted boss says Europe must act on ‘unfair’ Chinese wind turbine makers
rows.content:
Ørsted boss says Europe must act on ‘unfair’ Chinese wind turbine makers
Europe must act against Chinese wind turbine makers that benefit from “unfair” state support, but cannot afford to close itself off from global supply chains, the boss of Danish wind farm developer Ørsted said.
Rasmus Errboe hailed the wind power sector as a “European industrial success story” as he backed efforts by the EU to clamp down on Chinese manufacturers with access to large government subsidies.
“Competition needs to happen on fair and equal terms,” he told the FT. “We’ve in recent years seen the European Commission being much more active in addressing unfair trading practices. I see this as a necessary and also natural development.”
EU officials are keen to protect the European wind industry and prevent it from replicating the fate of the continent’s solar industry, which has been decimated by competition from cheaper rivals from China. The OECD found Chinese solar companies received the most subsidies of any manufacturers in the sector by a “significant margin”.
The Commission is currently investigating Goldwind, the world’s largest turbine manufacturer, over whether it benefited from unfair subsidies to outcompete European rivals. The chief executive of German turbine maker Nordex, José Luis Blanco, has called for “non-western” companies to be banned from selling turbines to the EU under cyber security rules.
The EU is concerned about developing an over-reliance on high-value Chinese technology that would leave it dependent on the trade partner. In the wind sector, this includes key components such as gearboxes and blades, but there are fewer worries about lower-value parts used in these components.
Saying his priority was a “thriving” European wind sector, Errboe said: “If you look at the entire value chain for wind, this obviously does not mean closing ourselves off to the outside world. Developers and equipment manufacturers benefit from access to a global supply chain.”
China’s presence in Europe’s wind turbine industry is small, accounting for less than 3 per cent of new turbine capacity last year, according to the Global Wind Energy Council. Chinese turbine manufacturers’ attempts to break into the sector have been restricted, with leading company Ming Yang shut out from the UK’s offshore market on national security grounds.
European wind is on track for a record year, with 24GW of capacity set to be installed in 2026. Wind provides about a fifth of Europe’s electricity. Wind Europe, the trade body, says total offshore and onshore wind installations will grow to 436GW by 2030
The record installation marks a turnaround for a sector that was heavily disrupted by Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which drove up borrowing costs.
But it is still short of the EU aim to install 500GW of wind production as part of an aim for 42.5 per cent of Europe’s energy needs to come from renewables by 2030.
The Commission is under pressure from member states including France to replace a later 2040 renewables target with a “clean energy” version that would include nuclear deployment.
Errboe, who on Wednesday takes over the rotating chair of Wind Europe, said he was not against a target that included nuclear but called on Europe to set specific goals for wind deployment at an EU and member-state level.
“You’re going to need many different technologies,” he said.
The European Court of Auditors has recently criticised Europe for failing to invest sufficiently in renewables deployment. Fossil fuel imports are costing about €500mn extra per day compared with before the outbreak of the war in Iran in February, according to Commission president Ursula von der Leyen.
Additional reporting by Rachel Millard in London

rows.title: The great British (and American) fork in the road
rows.content:
Good morning. Markets’ first take on the possibility that AI might end humanity is that this is bad for tech stocks, but not all that bad. A wobble here and there — a decent one for OpenAI backer SoftBank — but nothing dramatic. I guess the calculation is that, sure, annihilating everyone is sub-optimal, and could trigger class action lawsuits, but on the plus side, a safety timeout for frontier model development might allow the hyperscalers to get back to generating free cash? What a time to be alive. For now.
Strikingly, even the possible end of civilisation is not enough to put a bid under US Treasuries. The 10-year yield yesterday touched 5 per cent, a big scary round number. Send your thoughts on how to trade an extinction event to [email protected]. Do not cheat with ChatGPT.
We are in a state of flux
If you are struggling to shake the feeling that we’re living in the part of the movie where the boffins are fretting about an approaching disaster and the politicians and general population are not listening (hello, AI-pocalypse), then you are not alone and you may be on to something.
I am simplifying crudely for effect, but nonetheless, a new working paper from the National Bureau of Economic Research makes for interesting/slightly alarming reading, coming to the conclusion that “today . . . institutional uncertainty in the US and UK is as elevated as it was in the early 1940s — a signal missed by other leading measures of risk”.
The paper’s authors — Michael Callen, Saipremnath Muthukumaran and Noam Yuchtman (London School of Economics), Gregory Levy (University of Oxford) and Jonathan Weigel (University of California) — scrutinised the widely accepted argument that institutional change often comes about at critical junctures, “moments where multiple institutional futures are possible, including a return to the status quo”. They scrape through nearly 12mn articles from the Times of London, from 1800 to 2019, to see if they can identify these critical junctures before and while they unfold, rather than only in retrospect, as we generally do.
Obviously, this throws off big moments that do not fundamentally rewrite institutions, such as the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre, the 2011 Arab Spring and the 2014 Umbrella Revolution in Hong Kong. But it still recognises that these were critical junctures, or CJs for short. Newspaper text, the researchers say, provides a useful window into these moments when the rules of the road are in question.
Thanks in no small part to the Scottish independence referendum of 2014 and the Brexit vote of 2016, the CJ index for the UK looks like this:
Now, the gradual increase in sensationalisation in the news over recent decades, driven first by rolling television news and then by the web, may be playing a role here, as the authors suggest. But if they’re right that these measures have some kind of predictive function and provide warnings of incipient ruptures, then that feels like something investors should take seriously.
On that note, see if this line from the paper sounds familiar to you (with our highlight):
When the rules of executive succession, electoral competition, civil liberties or judicial authority are thrown into question — when no one is quite sure who will rule, by what means, or under what constraints — we argue a polity is at a critical juncture.
Hmmm. And right now:
We remain agnostic on exact thresholds that define a critical juncture, [but] the index surfaces moments when core political and economic rules were deeply contested, offering both expected and unexpected insights into Britain’s turbulent 20th century. We reproduce similar analyses for the US, France and India — which have the next four largest shares of articles in the Times. Strikingly, in most of these countries, the CJ index estimates a current level of institutional uncertainty comparable to that in the early 1940s, during World War II.
We are, the authors conclude, “well into an era of substantial uncertainty”, and it’s worth noting that this is looking at a dataset that ended in 2019, before Trump 2.0 and Covid-19, and well before the masters of the AI universe realised that — oopsie — they may accidentally have created the Torment Nexus. If this is an early warning system, then maybe we’re already living through the subsequent turmoil.
The other obvious question here is whether this is as scary as it sounds. I’m minded to think it is, because I lean more into the idea that institutions matter than some of my colleagues do (hi Rob), but one thing that has stuck out from the past few years is the impressive ability of markets, particularly of risk assets, to shrug off a series of pretty big shocks.
The genuinely, admirably, permanently optimistic multi-asset team at HSBC pointed out recently that markets have weathered a “breathtaking” series of blows in the past five years, and they see no reason to think that will change. Reasons to be cheerful include vibrant earnings, even outside of tech and AI, enhanced firefighting skills at central banks since the crash of ‘08, much lower sensitivity to oil prices than in the ‘70s/‘80s, relatively low corporate leverage and so on.
There’s an element of cynicism, even moral hazard, here. As the team points out:
Particularly in the US, equities, wealth effects and financial conditions have become so intertwined that it’s hard to imagine that central banks wouldn’t intervene if equities were indeed to drop sharply and sustainably. We’ve seen this time and again in the last 16 years.
Maybe the new normal is an era of critical junctures in institutions and rock-solid resilience in markets. Funny old world, although I have my doubts that central banks can QE their way out of a robot apocalypse.

rows.title: Bessent to meet He Lifeng in New York ahead of Trump-Xi summit
rows.content:
Scott Bessent to meet He Lifeng in New York ahead of Trump-Xi summit
US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent will meet his Chinese counterpart He Lifeng in New York on Sunday as the two sides try to bridge differences ahead of next week’s summit between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in Washington.
Bessent and US trade representative Jamieson Greer will host the Chinese vice-premier and his delegation for a final round of negotiations before Trump welcomes the Chinese president to the White House on September 24, according to a US official.
The meeting comes as the two sides remain at odds over several issues, including AI competition and rare earths, and ahead of the expiry in November of the trade war truce that the US president and Xi, his Chinese counterpart, agreed in South Korea last October.
Trump will host Xi for meetings and a state dinner, just four months after he met him in China. Xi has not visited Washington since 2016. He met then-president Joe Biden in San Francisco in 2023 and Trump at Mar-a-Lago in 2017.
Bessent and He are expected to discuss AI in New York. China in May said Trump and Xi had agreed to set up an AI dialogue, while the US president said the leaders had discussed “guardrails” in Beijing. But the two sides have not held any senior-level meetings on the topic since May.
Trump and Xi reached a ceasefire in their trade and technology war last October when they met in Busan, South Korea, following months of tit-for-tat measures, including tariffs and export controls.
In Busan, Trump agreed to postpone the imposition of export controls that would have affected thousands of Chinese companies. Beijing held back draconian restrictions on exports of rare earths and critical minerals.
Ahead of the summit in Washington, China has pushed to extend the Busan truce for the rest of Trump’s term. But several people familiar with the talks said the US was insisting on a six-month extension, partly because it believes China is not fully living up to the commitments on rare earths reached in Busan.
The US has also been pushing China to ease restrictions on rare earth exports to Japan, in pressure partly designed to help an ally but also because the restrictions are having a knock-on impact on US supply chains.
Washington and Tokyo are particularly concerned about China slowing exports of yttrium, a hard-to-substitute metal used in an array of products including lasers, aircraft engines and semiconductors.
The two sides have also been hammering out details for a Board of Trade that Trump and Xi agreed to create in Beijing. The mechanism would identify products in non-sensitive areas for tariff reduction.

rows.title: The perils of productivity numbers
rows.content:
Britain has finally uncovered how to boost its lacklustre productivity growth: get better data.
Using a new methodology, the Office for National Statistics now reckons the UK’s output per hour worked grew by 1.3 per cent per year on average between 2009 and 2019. That is almost double the previous annual figure of 0.7 per cent. (An earlier estimate of the country’s post-2008 productivity was awarded “UK statistic of the decade” by the Royal Statistical Society.)
The drop in the nation’s productivity following the global financial crisis remains. But Britain now looks like less of an outlier among advanced economies.
Even if it is difficult to measure, productivity growth rightly remains a focus of policymakers across the world. An economy will struggle to raise living standards and maintain political stability without becoming better at creating more output from existing, or fewer, resources.
But the latest ONS revision highlights that higher official productivity numbers are not an end in themselves. The fixation over the data point brings to mind the McNamara fallacy, named after former US defence secretary Robert McNamara. The ex-Ford Motor Company executive was criticised for focusing too much on quantifiable measures, such as enemy body count, to monitor progress in the Vietnam war. This approach gave a narrow perspective on the conflict and was open to misinterpretation. For instance, some operations may have generated striking numbers, but not necessarily strategic gains.
In a similar way, productivity is only a proxy for prosperity. After all, it is not as if Britons woke up on Friday morning, following the release of the revised figures, feeling better about their economic fortunes.
Indeed, economic productivity — whether it is defined as output per worker or hour worked — is a flawed measure. For one, the numerator, GDP, is imperfect. It includes many items that aren’t necessarily productive or reflective of higher living standards. For instance, the healthcare sector contributes just under one-fifth of US annual output, but a significant proportion of this activity is driven by administrative bloating and a cycle of poor treatment, overtreatment and sickness. Many statistical agencies also struggle to capture a lot of output, particularly the value of intangibles such as digital products and software.
The recent ONS revision, however, pertains to the denominator. By using alternative data sources that reflect standard practice at many other national data bodies, it was able to better calculate employees’ annual leave, sickness and absences. This updated methodology showed that people had been working fewer hours than previously thought. GDP estimates were unchanged. In other words, Britain had not suddenly produced more; it had simply produced the same amount with less labour.
This underscores another consideration: the drivers of productivity growth matter and bring different economic effects depending on whether workers are reallocated, complemented or replaced. For instance, reducing labour inputs can be a sign of progress: displaced work hours can be shifted to leisure or, in time, towards more productive sectors. But it is also possible, up to a point, to have higher headline numbers alongside rising automation, surging joblessness and a greater concentration of the gains. Belgian AI video start-up AiCandy takes this idea to its extreme in a hyperbolic mockumentary that imagines today’s tech leaders using laid-off humans to do high-intensity cycle workouts to generate electricity for AI data centres.
The ONS revision should come then with three timely lessons for Britain and beyond. First, accurate statistics matter. Estimates of productivity feed into the fiscal arithmetic, influencing policy and politics while also shaping the national narrative. That said, though output per hour is an important baseline metric, understanding the dynamics behind productivity matters more than the decimal-point estimate itself. We mustn’t forget why we’re measuring it in the first place.
And finally, there are no statistical shortcuts to prosperity. Whatever the number is, the ongoing task for policymakers seeking tangible productivity gains remains the same: put land, labour, energy and capital to better combined use.
