rows.title: UK employers cut jobs as labour market remains weak over summer
rows.content:
UK employers cut jobs as labour market remains weak over summer
UK employers cut jobs, vacancies declined and private sector wage growth remained subdued over the summer, according to official data that could ease Bank of England policymakers’ concerns over high inflation becoming entrenched in the economy.
Payroll employment in the three months to July fell by 39,000, or 0.1 per cent, from the previous quarter, the Office for National Statistics said on Tuesday. The drop left payroll employment down 84,000, or 0.3 per cent, from the same period in 2025.
Early figures for August — although likely to be revised — showed a further 0.1 per cent or 26,000 decline, the ONS said, adding that many small businesses had warned that high labour costs were stopping them from hiring.
The number of vacancies edged lower to 702,000 in the three months to August, down by 1.1 per cent from the previous three months and the lowest since 2014, excluding the pandemic period. The ONS’s estimate of unemployment, based on its labour force survey, was stable at 4.9 per cent.
Private sector wage growth remained relatively subdued, with average weekly earnings, excluding bonuses, 2.9 per cent higher than a year earlier in the three months to July — slightly above the 2.8 per cent figure analysts had expected.
Economists said the tepid wage pressures would allow rate-setters on the BoE’s Monetary Policy Committee to keep rates at 3.75 per cent when they give their latest decision on Thursday, despite the inflationary threat posed by the renewed surge in oil prices.
Andrew Wishart, economist at Berenberg, said that “much looser labour market conditions than during the last major energy price shock in 2022” made a new price-wage spiral “highly unlikely”.
He added that the BoE was still likely to use this week’s meeting to signal it could raise interest rates in November unless energy prices fall back.
Following the release of Tuesday’s data, traders kept the chance of the MPC raising borrowing costs this week at roughly 35 per cent, but a quarter-point move is fully expected at its November meeting. The pound edged lower against the dollar, falling 0.2 per cent to $1.347.
The latest evidence of a lacklustre labour market comes despite a pick-up in economic activity over the summer, with GDP expanding 0.4 per cent in July.
July’s unexpectedly robust start to the third quarter, alongside the sharp recent rise in energy prices, is likely to have intensified debate on the MPC over how long it can keep rates unchanged.
James Smith, economist at ING, said that the signs of labour market weakness gave the MPC some room on borrowing costs.
“The UK jobs market is far, far cooler than it was when the Ukraine shock hit four years ago,” he said, adding that this reduced the risk of “severe second-round effects on inflation from higher energy prices” and meant that a “wholesale hawkish pivot” from rate setters looked unlikely this week.
Public sector workers have seen much bigger pay awards over the past year, with wage growth, excluding bonuses, rising 6.3 per cent in the three months to July.
This underpinned growth of 3.9 per cent in total wage growth, including bonuses, across the economy in the three months to July.
This figure will be used to uprate the state pension next year under the “triple lock” policy that ensures it rises at the highest of inflation, average wages and 2.5 per cent.
The Institute for Fiscal Studies said this implied the full new state pension would increase from the current £241.30 per week (or about £12,500 per year) to £250.70 per week (about £13,000 per year) next April.
“The big winners from today’s ONS data are pensioners,” said Julia Diniz, economist at the Resolution Foundation think-tank, noting that private sector workers, in contrast, had seen their pay fall in real terms over the past year.
Additional reporting by Ian Smith. Data visualisation by Amy Borrett

rows.title: Iran uses spyware disguised as MRI scan results to hack critics, say western officials
rows.content:
Iran uses spyware disguised as MRI scan results to hack critics, say western officials
Iran has used spyware disguised as MRI scan results to collect information on dissidents, activists and journalists around the world, western intelligence agencies have warned.
The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre, America’s FBI and the Dutch intelligence and security service on Tuesday said they had uncovered a tool, dubbed Chosen Brick, being used by Iran to hack electronic devices including computers.
The malware allows attackers to collect a target’s contacts, emails and social media messages, while also providing access to the device’s microphone, the agencies said in a joint statement.
Personal details of victims targeted with Chosen Brick had already appeared on pro-Iranian leak websites, the agencies added, noting that Iran’s intelligence services had a record of plotting to kidnap or kill perceived enemies of the Islamic regime abroad.
“The details of this cyber campaign reveal how Iran ruthlessly uses digital surveillance in pursuit of its aim to repress critics of the regime, stealing emails and messages and accessing devices,” said Paul Chichester, director of operations at the NCSC, part of the UK’s signals intelligence agency GCHQ.
Iran’s embassy in London did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The western intelligence agencies said they were publicising details of the alleged Iranian campaign in order to warn potential targets.
The attackers tended to first engage with a target on social messaging platforms, such as WhatsApp and Telegram, having previously conducted extensive research on the person in order to present themselves as a “trusted” entity, the joint statement said.
Having built a rapport, the attackers then convinced the target to unknowingly download the spyware by clicking on a web link or downloading a file. In at least one case, the file appeared to be a set of MRI scan results, the statement added.
The FBI said the spyware had been deployed on behalf of Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security since at least 2023.
“MOIS cyber actors likely use this malware to collect intelligence, conduct data leaks and inflict reputational harm,” it added.
Both the NCSC and FBI said the spyware exclusively targeted Microsoft Windows operating systems and remained on infected devices even after rebooting.
“The malware may change and the actors may change, but the approach is remarkably consistent: exploit trust, gain access, steal information,” said Gary Barlet at US cyber security company Illumio.
“The real takeaway from the NCSC is that organisations and individuals still underestimate how often they’re being targeted,” he added.
Additional reporting by Andrew England

rows.title: Landmark US crypto bill fails as Senate splits over Trump ethics concerns
rows.content:
Landmark US crypto bill fails as Senate splits over Trump ethics concerns
A landmark crypto regulation bill backed by the digital currency industry failed to advance in the US Senate on Tuesday, as Democrats insisted on stronger limits on Donald Trump’s ability to profit from the industry.
Democrats rebelled against the so-called Clarity Act in the absence of stricter controls on Trump, who reported earning more than $1bn from his crypto businesses last year. Another critical fight was over yields offered on stablecoins, which the banking industry opposed as a threat to deposits and lending. 
The vote tally was 49 in favour and 50 against, largely along party lines and well short of the 60 required to move the bill forward. The bill was a first-of-its-kind regulatory framework for digital assets that the industry hoped would head off the types of crackdowns launched during the Biden administration.
The failure is a massive setback to the crypto industry, which spent more than a year negotiating and record sums of lobbying dollars for a favourable market structure from the Republican-controlled US Congress. It is also a blow to Trump, who took office vowing to make the country the “crypto capital of the world”.
“This legislation failed squarely because Republicans refuse to say no to the president,” said Ruben Gallego, a Democrat from Arizona who was involved in the discussions.
Crypto has entered a bear market as retail investors turn their attention to volatility in AI stocks and equity markets. The price of bitcoin fell 3 per cent after the vote failed and the cryptocurrency is down 35 per cent over the past year.
With Democrats expected to gain more political power in November’s midterm elections, crypto companies and their leaders now face the prospect of a changing political environment in Washington that could bring more resistance to their agenda.
For now, the industry will look to regulatory clarity from agencies overseeing securities and derivatives, which can use rulemaking powers to set policy for cryptocurrencies. Pro-crypto groups would also push for the Senate to reconsider the bill, said Kristin Smith, president of the Solana Policy Institute.
Crypto interests such as Andreessen Horowitz, Ripple Labs and Coinbase have backed a Super Pac called Fairshake to elect pro-crypto candidates, amassing more than $260mn for the 2024 elections. The group had a war chest of more than $100mn at the end of July, according to the latest federal filing.
Still, the industry’s deep pockets could not clinch necessary bipartisan support for the legislation. In the final weeks leading up to the vote, Senate Democrats demanded stronger guardrails on Trump’s business dealings in the crypto industry.
The White House ultimately conceded some but not all of the Democrats’ demands.
“We knew it would always come down to ethics,” said Rebecca Rettig, chief legal officer at Jito Labs, which develops blockchain software. “The political environment is too charged for certain policymakers to vote on a bill that is anything but a 100 per cent win on ethics.”
The Clarity Act also became an issue in a high-profile battle between the nascent crypto industry and some of the country’s largest and oldest banks.
Banks won concessions from the crypto sector after they argued that allowing stablecoin issuers to reward customers with yield could lead to massive outflows of deposits away from the banking industry.
The fight led to a dramatic public fallout between JPMorgan chief executive Jamie Dimon and Coinbase head Brian Armstrong, who at times took to social media platform X to mock his Wall Street rival.
But the threat was most acute for smaller community banks that may not be able to compete by launching their own stablecoins. They have argued that a strained deposit base would in turn affect their ability to lend to the real economy in the areas they serve. The US counts more than 4,000 banks, of which the vast majority are community banks.
A group of multiple trade bodies representing banks of all sizes said in a statement that lawmakers should be able to “support creating a strong, durable regulatory framework for digital assets that will set the course for US global leadership for decades to come” while also protecting “the bank lending that drives economic growth”.
Pro-crypto forces dismissed the bank lobby’s argument.
“There’s no sense in sugarcoating it: today’s vote was a major disappointment — and, I believe, a failure of American leadership,” Patrick Witt, executive director of Trump’s council of advisers for digital assets, posted on X.
“This much is clear: it increases the risk that the standards that global financial markets adhere to in the future will be those of Brussels or Beijing, rather than Washington and New York.”

rows.title: Beijing launches drone buyback in crackdown after Citic Tower crash
rows.content:
Beijing launches drone buyback in crackdown after Citic Tower crash
Beijing has launched a drone buyback programme in a bid to eliminate the vehicles as authorities in the Chinese capital crack down after a plane crashed into the city’s tallest tower in June.
The government will buy back drones from owners who have preregistered their devices. Other owners will have until November 15, when the rules come into effect, to remove all drones and components from a restricted area around the city.
“The public security organs will conduct patrols and inspections . . . and crack down on overdue transfers out of Beijing,” the state-run Beijing Daily said.
In June, a light aircraft struck Citic Tower in one of the city’s busiest business districts, killing the pilot and injuring 13 others and shocking residents accustomed to ultra-tight security in the Chinese capital.
The plane took off from a flying school on Beijing’s outskirts and flew to within about 7km of the closely guarded Zhongnanhai leadership compound, where President Xi Jinping works and occasionally hosts foreign leaders.
Police later suggested the pilot’s mental condition was to blame for the incident, saying the man, whom they identified as a 66-year-old divorcee, had multiple references to suicide in his diary.
China has already been cracking down on drone use. The country is the world’s biggest producer of commercial drones, with Shenzhen-based DJI accounting for 70 to 80 per cent of the global market for non-military, non-governmental devices, according to Drone Industry Insights.
But authorities both in China and elsewhere have become more cautious about their expansion as the war in Ukraine has demonstrated the effectiveness of drones — including modified commercial models — as weapons.
Recreational drones are now banned in multiple cities around the world including New York, but the restrictions in Beijing are expected to be more severe.
As part of an amnesty while the new restrictions come into effect, Beijing drone owners can either cash in their aircraft for a maximum of Rmb3,000 ($447), dispose of them or restrict their use beyond the no-fly zone limits, which were not outlined.
Neil Liu, a 30-year-old amateur photographer in Beijing, said he felt “sad” and “deceived” by the ban in a country that has previously championed the “low-altitude economy”.
“First I was told after registration that I would be able to enter and exit Beijing [with the drone],” he said.
“I am still weighing my options: whether to sell it or deposit it at a friend’s house outside Beijing for my travels overseas,” Liu said.
For some drone owners, the inconvenience of owning one might outweigh the benefits.
Luo, a Beijing-based office worker in her forties who asked to be identified only by her surname, bought a small DJI drone for her boyfriend several years ago.
She complained that she received calls from police every year demanding that they refrain from flying it ahead of landmark political events.
“I was forced to sign a document at a police station once,” she said. “I might use the buyback scheme to sell it.”

rows.title: Von der Leyen backs Canada’s ‘associate membership’ bid
rows.content:
Ursula von der Leyen backs Canada’s ‘associate membership’ bid
Ursula von der Leyen has endorsed Mark Carney’s pitch for Canada to become an “associate member” of the EU, in a bold proposal from the European Commission president to deepen ties with Ottawa as a way for Brussels to withstand pressure from the US and China.
“I said we must urgently reimagine our partnerships. So, I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to being the first associate member of the European Union,” von der Leyen said on Wednesday.
Speaking to the European parliament, with Carney in the audience, von der Leyen’s proposal sparked a standing ovation from lawmakers.
“In short, we want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible,” she said.
Donald Trump’s trade war against the EU and Canada and his belligerent attitude to Nato have spurred efforts by western liberal democracies to work more closely together. Carney has called for so-called middle powers to coalesce in defence of multilateral global governance — though several EU governments remain sceptical, partly because they are wary of alienating the US president.
“This is not a partnership against anyone else, but for our common strength,” von der Leyen said. “We see the world with the same eyes.”
The EU has no framework for “associate membership”, meaning von der Leyen’s proposal would need the unanimous approval of the bloc’s 27 member states. In addition to concerns about Trump’s reaction, several capitals are wary of granting Ottawa preferential treatment beyond existing trade and investment partnerships.
Canadian and EU officials had initially floated the concept of associate membership in the weeks leading up to Carney’s visit to Strasbourg. But in the face of scepticism from EU capitals and Carney’s domestic political opponents, the Canadian prime minister this week said he was instead seeking a “unique alliance” with the bloc.
An EU-Canada free trade deal, known as Ceta, is still not ratified by 10 EU member states, including France, Italy and Poland, nine years after being signed. Several EU member states have suggested ratification should first be completed before embarking on new steps.
Ceta is in force provisionally, meaning tariff cuts, customs rules and market access for goods and services already apply. But with elections due next year in France, Italy and Poland, the prospects for ratification in those member states are dimming.
Von der Leyen on Wednesday said that the two sides “will move from Ceta to an Alliance for the Future, to create a common prosperity and economic security space”.
That would include elements such as “intelligent manufacturing”, “a tech alliance” and “mak[ing] the Arctic a flagship joint project”, von der Leyen said. “We will integrate defence industrial bases . . . We will work on energy, critical minerals and batteries. On AI, quantum, cyber and economic security.”

rows.title: Jon Ossoff’s Georgia race stirs talk of 2028 US presidential audition
rows.content:
Jon Ossoff’s Georgia race stirs talk of 2028 US presidential audition
Sleeves rolled up, standing tall in the middle of the Georgia Theatre in downtown Athens, Georgia, last Sunday, Jon Ossoff delivered a brutal political message about Donald Trump, his family and his allies.
They “made you pay more for everything” and “lied us into war”, said the 39-year-old senator running for a second term to represent the southern US battleground state.
“All while the crook president and his crook family raked in billions from all over the world.”
As Democrats attempt to wrench control of the US Senate from Republicans in November’s midterm elections, Ossoff has emerged with a message his party hopes will carry them to victory this year and even set a model for the 2028 election.
Derided by Trump as “Pee-wee Herman”, the eccentric 1980s comedian who also sported short dark hair, Ossoff has placed the administration’s alleged grift and conflicts of interest at the heart of his campaign, tying them to the cost of living crisis, the war in Iran and the spread of AI, all political weaknesses for Trump and congressional Republicans.
“Democrats need to run on corruption the way Ossoff is. He talks about corruption as a function of the cost of living,” said Paul Begala, the veteran Democratic strategist. He compared Ossoff’s message with the 1982 country song “She Got the Goldmine (I Got the Shaft)”.
At the same time, Ossoff, the first Jewish senator from Georgia, has appeared to overcome the divisions between the socialist left and moderate Democrats that have torn the party apart elsewhere.
A former documentary film-maker known for taking great care with his words, Ossoff has delivered his message through well-choreographed viral moments from rallies that have attracted national attention.
In April, he attacked Trump as the “faithless president” who “depicts himself as Christ”. In May, he blasted the president for “building a monument to himself”.
A furore erupted last month when Ossoff made a passing, if deliberate, reference to Trump’s loyal aide Natalie Harp, saying the president would rather “build his ballroom and travel with Natalie” than govern, eliciting a vitriolic backlash from the White House.
In Athens, Ossoff blasted what he called the “Mar-a-Lago mafia” and warned that Trump “dismantles precautions and calls us fools for worrying” about AI regulation because of his inner circle’s ties to Big Tech.
While Ossoff was considered one of the most vulnerable sitting Democrats heading into the 2026 midterms, he now leads his Trump-backed Republican rival Mike Collins by just under 8 percentage points. If he wins with a solid margin in a crucial swing state, which Trump won in 2016 and 2024 but lost in 2020, Ossoff would be positioned for a presidential run in 2028.
“His desire isn’t just to win this election, it’s to win it in such a blowout that he could change his mind in 2028 or after,” said one senior Georgia Democrat.
On the campaign trail, Ossoff has denied any plans for a presidential run.
As Ossoff’s political profile has risen, with echoes of Barack Obama’s youth and oratory skills, Republicans have portrayed him as feeble, effeminate and beholden to the far left.
“He’s a man too weak and too vain to stand up for what’s right,” Collins said at the Republican midterms convention in Dallas, Texas, earlier this month.
An anti-Ossoff ad released by a spending group backing Senate Republicans attacked Ossoff for being a “pretty boy” who spends lavishly on “hair and make-up . . . even more than the ladies”. After Ossoff’s comments about Trump and Harp, White House communications director Steven Cheung took to X to label the Georgia senator “Jon Jackoff” and “the biggest cuck loser”.
This week, Brian Kemp, Georgia’s two-term governor who backed a different candidate in the Republican Senate primary this year, belatedly endorsed Collins and will be fundraising for him later this month, which could help boost support for Ossoff’s rival.
After the Athens rally, outside the theatre, Vin Rainwater, a 42-year-old man who works in the construction business who had just listened to Ossoff, was sceptical of his appeal.
“I don’t think adhering to anti-Trump rhetoric is going to serve us moving forward, Trump’s going to be gone in a couple of years,” he said. “Low common denominator ‘booting Trump around’ stuff — it’s cool but it doesn’t do anything for us.”
But others were far more enthusiastic. “He seems to have integrity,” said Isabel Reuter, a 29-year-old woman who works at the University of Georgia. “He’s the best chance we have at moving back up out of the trenches,” she added.
“Jon probably needs to get some more experience . . .[but] his message is pointing out all the contradictions that the Republican Party and Trump have put forward,” says Pamela Luiz, a 73-year-old retired nurse who attended the rally.
Sirak Yilma, 23, a law school student from Roswell, in the Atlanta suburbs, who had volunteered in phone banks for Ossoff in high school, said the Democrat had a “very similar ideology [to me] he’s not too far left, he’s not too far to the centre . . . I like what he stands for”.
“He has had a lot of viral moments, [but] I don’t think he’s doing it just for attention purposes,” Yilma added.
As for a possible 2028 run, Begala said Ossoff’s statements denying any interest should be taken with a grain of salt, and that for now the senator seemed to have struck the right chord for the party.
“I’m old enough to remember Bill Clinton promising in 1990 he wasn’t going to run in 1992 and Barack Obama promising in 2006 he wasn’t going to run in 2008,” said Begala.

rows.title: Odey judgment is lesson for firms over ethical failings, warns FCA
rows.content:
Crispin Odey judgment is lesson for firms over ethical failings, warns FCA
Financial services companies taking a “slapdash” approach to ethics will be punished under new rules designed to stop the type of “horrific” behaviour that led to hedge fund boss Crispin Odey being fined and banned, the financial watchdog has warned.
Therese Chambers, co-head of enforcement at the Financial Conduct Authority, told the FT its stricter rules against harassment and other bad behaviour that came into force this month would ensure “people can speak up” and be protected against misconduct.
Her comments came hours after Odey lost his legal challenge against a lifetime ban and fine imposed by the FCA for frustrating attempts to discipline him over his alleged sexual harassment of female employees of his now-defunct hedge fund.
Chambers said the regulator did not have enough data to know if Odey’s case was symptomatic of “a genuinely widespread problem” of sexual harassment in the City of London. But she added: “We’ve all heard of specific incidents like this, which are pretty horrific.”
Since it banned and fined Odey last year, the FCA has given itself more power to tackle such behaviour by expanding its rules on non-financial misconduct beyond banks to the 37,000 other financial services groups it regulates from the start of this month.
“It’s the firms that are perhaps a bit more slapdash about the way they operate where there may well be gaps in the way that they treat their staff and the way in which they report and oversee incidents in the workplace,” said Chambers. “Those are the firms that need to be very mindful of these new requirements.”
During the court hearing, Odey was confronted with more than 46 sexual harassment allegations by former staff of the hedge fund he founded, as well as accusations of falsifying company minutes, misleading investors, bullying colleagues, trying to silence victims and threatening the regulator.
Chambers said the tribunal’s decision was “very gratifying” and she hoped it would encourage more victims of harassment and bullying in the workplace to speak up.
“This is very much an instance of the system being there to protect people who are being mistreated who might otherwise feel that they can only operate in a culture of silence where they’re not able to call bad behaviour out,” she said.
London’s Upper Tribunal on Monday published scathing findings against Odey, concluding that he had “a warped set of values”. But it said the case had not hinged on whether or not there had been “sexualised misconduct in the workplace”.
Instead, the judges upheld the FCA’s findings that Odey “lacked integrity” and acted with “reckless disregard” for his company’s corporate governance and breached the regulator’s rules by twice firing executives who were trying to investigate his alleged misconduct.
Chambers said a vital lesson for the City of London from the Odey case was that “ethical behaviour is of absolutely paramount importance when you’re managing other people’s money” and “there are consequences for them if they choose not to do that”.
Although the FCA was “not in the business of pursuing technical breaches of rules through enforcement cases”, Chambers said “if we see something that is serious we will act” to enforce the new rules on non-financial misconduct.
Odey, who did not respond to a request for comment, has two weeks to appeal against the judgment.

rows.title: FirstFT: US mega-donors overwhelmingly back Republicans, FT analysis shows
rows.content:
FirstFT: US mega-donors overwhelmingly back Republicans, FT analysis shows
This article is an on-site version of our FirstFT newsletter. Subscribers can sign up to our Asia, Europe/Africa or Americas edition to get the newsletter delivered every weekday morning. Explore all of our newsletters here
Good morning and welcome to FirstFT. In today’s newsletter:
- US billionaires line up to bankroll Republicans’ election push
- European Commission president endorses Canada’s pitch to become an “associate member”
- The Federal Reserve should defy Trump and raise borrowing costs today, say economists
- The world’s best-performing sovereign wealth fund gives its verdict on equities
You can listen to today’s top news stories in the FT News Briefing podcast.
US mega-donors are overwhelmingly backing the Republicans in this year’s midterms race, according to FT analysis, as billionaires from Silicon Valley to Wall Street bankroll President Donald Trump’s party ahead of November’s crunch ballot.
Sixteen of the country’s 20 largest donors have ploughed money into the GOP’s campaign, with billionaires such as SpaceX chief Elon Musk, Blackstone boss Stephen Schwarzman and hedge fund manager Paul Singer giving tens of millions of dollars, even as the party trails the US Democrats in opinion polls.
Investor George Soros is the standout Democratic donor, giving a total of $102mn in the 2025-26 election cycle. Other mega-donors have channelled cash to candidates pushing deregulation of cryptocurrency, with some building huge war chests around the digital assets. Candidates promoting AI have also benefited from the huge cash injections, as have those pushing for gambling industry deregulation.
“What you’re seeing is a mild break from expectations,” said Stanford political scientist Adam Bonica, who has studied donations from America’s wealthy since 1980. It is not unusual for top donors to lean Republican, but the balance in this election is “especially skewed”. Read more here.
Here’s what else we’re keeping tabs on today:
- Nato: Mark Rutte, the alliance’s secretary-general, meets UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham in London.
- US monetary policy: The Federal Reserve concludes its two-day rate-setting meeting, in which it is widely expected to raise borrowing costs by a quarter point.
Join us tomorrow for a live Ask an Expert Q&A with John Gapper, the FT’s chief UK business columnist, who will be answering your questions on the UK Budget and the outlook for British business. Submit your questions here.
Five more top stories
1. US and Chinese determination to dominate AI makes it harder for the two countries to find common ground on safety, think-tanks and technology companies say. Analysts will closely watch the summit meeting next week between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping for signs their governments can co-operate on AI risks.
- ‘We don’t need new regulations’: Nvidia chief Jensen Huang and Meta boss Mark Zuckerberg have pushed back against efforts to co-ordinate a slowdown in research in the name of safety, saying companies should address risks individually instead.
- Opinion: The main Trump-Xi summit achievement will be it happening at all, writes senior trade writer Alan Beattie.
2. European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen has endorsed Prime Minister Mark Carney’s pitch for Canada to become an “associate member” of the EU, in a bold proposal from Brussels to deepen ties with Ottawa amid pressures from the US and China.
- The EU is poised to ban the use of social media, certain gaming platforms and AI chatbots by children under 15 without parental supervision.
3. Exclusive: OpenAI has held early conversations with investors about raising another private funding round at a $1.2tn valuation before its planned initial public offering, according to people familiar with the matter. The investment would follow a March round in which the ChatGPT maker raised $122bn at an $852bn valuation.
4. The US has charged five individuals in connection with what it called a “global assassination network” controlled by Russia in a sweeping indictment that includes claims of a murder-for-hire plot on American soil. The Department of Justice said the group was paid to conduct surveillance and plotted to kill dissidents in the US and Lithuania.
5. The so-called Clarity Act, a landmark crypto regulation bill backed by the digital currency industry, failed to advance in the US Senate yesterday, as Democrats insisted on stronger limits on Trump’s ability to profit from the industry. The US president reported earning more than $1bn from his crypto businesses last year.
Nuclear fusion’s moment of truth
Private nuclear fusion companies are attracting billions of dollars from Silicon Valley investors and energy majors, all lured by the promise of abundant, cheap and clean energy. But insiders warn that as competition for funding intensifies, fusion companies are making overly optimistic claims about the cheapness of the electricity they hope to produce, writes Ryohtaroh Satoh.
We’re also reading . . .
- Iran’s hidden leader: Mojtaba Khamenei’s absence from public view has been a source of speculation.
- Tax competition: Switzerland’s 26 cantons compete fiercely for companies, wealthy residents and the revenues they bring, writes Mercedes Ruehl.
- Stocks slump: New Zealand’s sovereign wealth fund, which is the world’s best performing, expects the recent outperformance in global equities to ease after it reported 14 per cent growth in the year to June.
Chart of the day
The US Federal Reserve should defy Trump and raise borrowing costs today, according to the majority of economists polled by the University of Chicago’s Booth School of Business on behalf of the FT, with most expecting a quarter-point increase.
Take a break from the news . . .
The art market has long followed new wealth, from Italian Renaissance-era merchants to the 20th century’s investment bankers. Today’s cohort of wealthy tech bosses is gradually making its presence in the collector community felt.
Thank you for reading and remember you can add FirstFT to myFT. You can also elect to receive a FirstFT push notification every morning on the app. Send your recommendations and feedback to [email protected]

rows.title: Hackers say they breached Italian state email to target Revolut ‘crypto whales’
rows.content:
Hackers say they breached Italian state email to target Revolut ‘crypto whales’
Hackers who claim they were behind a data breach at Revolut say they obtained confidential customer information by compromising an Italian government email system and exchanging messages with the online bank over several months while posing as law enforcement.
The claims, made in a series of messages sent to the FT, suggest the hack affecting almost 700 Revolut customer accounts was more extensive than the data breach first acknowledged by the payments group on Friday.
In messages sent via Telegram, a hacker or hackers using the pseudonym iamnotavillain said they had first contacted Revolut a “couple of months ago, posing as a law enforcement entity” from Italy. 
Over the following weeks the hackers said they had repeatedly asked Revolut to share confidential account details for specific customers, including addresses, phone numbers and transaction histories, claiming the information was needed for ongoing law enforcement activities. 
“Revolut was complying like a ‘good boy’,” the purported hackers said.
The FT contacted the hackers via Telegram after they set up a website late on Monday displaying redacted screenshots of some of the information allegedly obtained from the bank.
The group then shared further screenshots with the FT, including images of some of the emails they claimed to have exchanged with Revolut while posing as Italian law enforcement.
Those messages appeared to show Revolut sharing customer account information with an arm of Italy’s interior ministry via the government’s La Posta Elettronica Certificata email system.
A person familiar with the matter confirmed that the requests Revolut received had come via Italy’s PEC system and the email exchanges had continued for several months.
PEC is a secure network overseen by a government agency that is used by Italian authorities, companies and private citizens to send official or legal correspondence — the digital equivalent of registered post.
Italy’s postal police, state police, interior ministry and cyber security agency declined to comment on the matter, although officials confirmed that investigations were under way.
The hacker’s requests for customer information do not appear to have been random. The group told the FT they selected the 680 targets by using blockchain analysis to identify Revolut accounts with significant crypto holdings.
“I rather not disclose my exact way of getting it, but it was via onchain analysis,” iamnotavillain said, describing the targets as “crypto whales”.
Most of the 680 customers came from Switzerland and France but Revolut also handed over data on residents in 31 other mainly European countries, including the UK, Germany and Spain, the hackers added.
The identity and motivation of the perpetrators remain unclear. Hackers often demand a ransom in exchange for the return or destruction of the stolen data.
A person familiar with the situation said Revolut had not been contacted by the perpetrators and was yet to receive a ransom demand.
Giulia Pastorella, a lawmaker from Italy’s opposition Azione party, has demanded immediate clarification from the interior ministry, calling the reported security breach of a ministry PEC email account “alarming at an unimaginable level” and pledging to raise the issue in parliament.
“We could be facing the tip of the iceberg,” Pastorella said in a social media post. “How many other emails have been sent from that governmental PEC? How many other companies have fallen victim to this scam?”
Revolut said its own systems and databases remained fully secure and had not been breached.
“This incident involved the fraudulent misuse of an official, state-regulated legal communication channel to impersonate legitimate authority requests,” it said.
Additional reporting by Giuliana Ricozzi in Rome

rows.title: A hotter planet meets dearer money
rows.content:
A hotter planet meets dearer money
The writer is the chief economist at German bank LBBW and former chief sovereign ratings officer at S&P
After heatwave after heatwave moved across Europe and North America through the summer, the costs of global warming and drought have become ever more evident. They have been visible in parched fields, strained electricity grids, lower labour productivity and rising insurance losses. Meanwhile, some scientists warn that the planet is warming faster than previously feared. Adapting to a hotter world is becoming more urgent. The bill for delay is rising.
Nowhere is the financing challenge greater than in emerging markets and developing economies. These countries are home to most of the world’s people, and all of global population growth. They are also poorer, which means domestic savings are typically insufficient to finance the investment needed to curb emissions and adapt to climate change. Yet they are among the places likely to suffer most from a warming planet. Failed harvests, water stress and mass migration are no longer distant possibilities.
Poorer countries must not follow the fossil-fuel-heavy development path of today’s rich economies. On current trends, the share of greenhouse-gas emissions coming from emerging and developing economies would rise from about 42 per cent today to 53 per cent by mid-century. That would make the world’s climate goals near impossible to meet.
As domestic savings fall short of mitigation and adaptation needs, the focus has shifted towards foreign finance. The Baku-to-Belém roadmap agreed as part of the UN Climate Change conferences estimated that emerging and developing economies would need about $1.3tn a year in external funding by 2035 even after taking into account what they can raise domestically. Even before recent interest rate moves, that target looked daunting. Now it looks even harder to reach.
Long-term interest rates in bond markets have risen sharply over recent weeks, reflecting several forces. Most importantly, investors are becoming more worried about the long-term sustainability of rich countries’ public finances. Almost everywhere, rich countries are on a borrowing binge. Their public debt has climbed to close to 110 per cent of GDP, up from less than 70 per cent at the start of the century.
An uncomfortable truth is that significant fiscal pressures still lie ahead. Ageing populations will weigh on budgets. Artificial intelligence will erode tax bases that remain heavily dependent on labour income. Fiscal challenges are most visible in America. On current policies, the Congressional Budget Office estimates that the federal debt ratio would reach 190 per cent of GDP by the mid-2050s. That looks like a train wreck in waiting.
As debt-servicing costs rise, the fiscal positions of countries deteriorate. It is a daunting problem for rich countries and for poorer ones it is even more challenging.
Higher rates make it harder for emerging economies to attract the capital needed for climate investment. A study by the Bank for International Settlements found that a 1 percentage point increase in the US Treasury term premium has historically been associated with a 1.5 point rise in local-currency yields in emerging markets, a 6 per cent depreciation of their currencies and bond and equity fund outflows of about 8 per cent of net total assets at the onset of the shock. In plain English: just as climate investment in poorer countries becomes more critical, it is becoming less affordable. The reason? Fiscal indiscipline in the rich world.
So the next UN climate summit, COP31 in Antalya, needs to make tangible progress on climate finance. Multilateral development banks and bilateral aid will fall short. Their balance sheets are too constrained to raise the required sums.
Several options deserve serious consideration. Carbon taxes could raise revenue while discouraging emissions. New and targeted allocations of IMF special drawing rights — funds that can be used to pay debt or be exchanged for dollars, euros and other currencies — could channel liquidity towards climate investment. Some have made the case for so-called “solidarity levies” on activities that benefit from globalisation, such as shipping, aviation or financial transactions. Another option could be to securitise future official development assistance to raise resources for urgent mitigation projects. None of these instruments is a silver bullet in itself but they could form part of a plausible financing package.
The $1.3tn target for the amount of money that emerging and developing economies will need by 2035 is no doubt highly ambitious. The great risk is that climate finance becomes another victim of short-term politics.
Still, this summer’s punishing heat should remind leaders what is at stake. Stabilising the climate will not come for free and failing to act now would be more expensive still. The choice is not between paying or not paying. It is between paying earlier for mitigation and adaptation, or paying more later for disaster relief, reconstruction, food insecurity and displaced populations.
World leaders will need to think beyond the usual menu of ambiguous pledges and vague communiqués. Innovative financing instruments are no longer a technocratic luxury. They have become a necessity.

rows.title: Billionaire Tata scion faces battle of his life to avert listing
rows.content:
Billionaire Tata scion faces battle of his life to avert listing
As Noel Tata entered the boardroom, the 69-year-old scion of one of India’s most famous business families knew he had a fight on his hands.
Lined up against him were two senior executives of Tata Sons, the private holding company which controls the $280bn Tata Group’s 26 listed companies, the board’s two independent directors and a fellow nominee for Tata Trusts, the company’s largest shareholder.
Top of Thursday’s agenda was how to respond to a ruling from India’s central bank, the Reserve Bank of India, that Tata Sons needed to list on the stock exchange — something Noel had long resisted because he felt it would irrevocably change the character of the group.
He told people before the meeting that he expected board members to make a fresh push to keep the chair, N Chandrasekaran, universally known as Chandra. Chandra supports a listing, as part of a push for more transparency, but said last month he would quit after failing to win Noel’s support.
Noel, who chairs the charitable trusts, was confident as he walked past a mural depicting what was at stake: the vast spread of Tata’s business empire, from energy and IT services to steel and car manufacturing. He had prepared written statements and an opinion from a former chief justice of India backing his stand that Chandra should not get an extension.
“A decision upon the chairmanship taken now . . . would be open to serious legal challenge by any shareholder who chose to bring it,” Noel told the board meeting. This company, he added, “should not expose itself to a challenge of that kind at any time. It should certainly not do so at a moment when it has matters of far greater consequence pending before its regulator.”
The board ignored him. The meeting ended with a statement saying that Chandra had been reappointed for five years and Tata Sons would begin steps to comply with the central bank’s listing directive. Tata Trusts denounced the board’s decision as a “legal nullity” because the Tata Trusts’ two nominees to the board were split.
“It’s the first time I’ve seen the executive, in a sense, go against the larger shareholders. That’s clearly a first,” said Amit Tandon, founder and managing director of Mumbai-based Institutional Investor Advisory Services, questioning if the board would secure shareholder support. Shareholders are set to vote at an AGM, in theory due to take place by the end of the year.
At stake is the future of India’s biggest conglomerate and some of its choicest assets, which could become targets for corporate raiders if cross-shareholdings between Tata Trusts and some of the companies it controls are unwound. A listed Tata Sons could be worth over $120bn, analysts say, making it India’s biggest IPO.
The more than 150-year-old Tata Group has long relied on special treatment from Indian authorities to retain control via the charitable trusts over its web of companies, which include Air India, Jaguar Land Rover, Tata Steel and IT giant Tata Consultancy Services.
In the past 30 years, amendments to laws have allowed the company to buy back shares to strengthen its control over group companies, and in 2002 the government exempted Tata from the need to have a government-appointed nominee for its trusts.
A decade ago, Noel’s predecessor and half-brother Ratan removed Cyrus Mistry, one of the heirs of the minority shareholder Shapoorji Pallonji Group, as chair of Tata Sons. The Supreme Court ultimately ruled in Ratan’s favour.
Even as Noel campaigned against a listing, people close to the discussions say that two powerful blocs were lobbying officials in favour: Chandra and his allies, who are well connected in New Delhi, and heavily indebted minority shareholders, SP Group, which wants to monetise its 18 per cent stake.
When the board met on Thursday, it asked Chandra to step out of the room while it discussed his extension. With Noel opposing and trust vice-chair Venu Srinivasan in favour of the resolution, Saurabh Agrawal, the company’s chief financial officer, backed Chandra. The two independent directors, Anita George and Harish Manwani, also backed Chandra as they felt an experienced hand was needed to comply with the listing directive. Chandra and Srinivasan did not respond to requests for comment.
Tata’s outsized national importance means that decisions about its future — such as the central bank ruling — need prior approval from the top of the Indian government, several people say.
“Delhi definitely had a role to play,” in the central bank’s latest decision, a person close to Tata said. “The offices which will eventually prevail in cases like these,” he added, are heading the country’s government.
The finance ministry and the central bank did not respond to requests for comment.
Noel, who took over as chair in 2024, now faces the battle of his life to avoid a listing and keep Tata under the control of the charitable trusts.
He argues that the conglomerate’s unique structure allows it to take a long-term view of its businesses and points out that the dividends which flow to the trusts fund millions of dollars of charity projects.
His rivals argue that he is trying to maintain family control over a vast conglomerate, which needs the greater transparency and market discipline that would come with a listing.
Chandra, 63, is a formidable adversary. A Tata lifer, he rose through the company’s ranks to lead India’s largest IT services firm, Tata Consultancy Services, before Ratan Tata picked him to head the holding company.
Many big decisions taken under Chandra’s leadership, including investing in semiconductors, have been “very closely associated with what the government wants to do,” said one person who had worked with him.
At the heart of the bitter feud is the holding company’s governance.
According to the articles of association of Tata Sons, a majority of the trusts’ nominee directors have to agree on any key decision. But the board’s two current trust nominees — Noel and Chandra’s ally Srinivasan — do not see eye to eye on almost anything. This could be the basis of a legal challenge to the decision to extend Chandra’s term.
Before the Thursday meeting, Sir Dorabji Tata Trust, one of the two main trusts, asked Srinivasan not to attend given his public support for a listing. Srinivasan refused, saying he had a duty as the board member to vote for what he felt was best for the company.
While Noel hopes shareholders will vote down Chandra’s replacement at an AGM later this year, that meeting could be delayed.
Sir Ratan Tata Trust, the second main trust, has been unable to hold key meetings to nominate trust attendees to the AGM ahead of a Charity Commission ruling on Srinivasan’s complaints about the number of lifetime trustees.
While no legal challenge is yet under way, Noel believes that the courts will ultimately strike down Thursday’s board decision and that once the Charity Commission issue is settled, the trusts will align at an AGM, forcing Chandra out.
In the meantime, Chandra can quickly start work on the listing, a person close to him said.
Still the trusts’ opposition to Chandra will make things tricky, said Tandon. “Chandra can turn around and say he got the majority. But at the end of the day, he will have to work with the largest shareholder.”

rows.title: US says Chinese groups used Binance to launder $61mn from Iranian oil deals
rows.content:
US prosecutors say Chinese groups used Binance to launder $61mn from Iranian oil deals
Two Chinese companies used Binance accounts to launder $61mn in payments for black-market Iranian oil and attempted to funnel the funds back to the Iranian government, US prosecutors have alleged.
The justice department filed a forfeiture complaint seeking to seize the funds, which were sent through a network of digital wallets that received and distributed more than $1.5bn in proceeds from the illicit sale of Iranian oil, according to the US government. At least some of the funds were used to finance terrorism, prosecutors said.
The $61mn in transactions subject to the US forfeiture effort occurred in May and June last year and were frozen in the ensuing months, prosecutors said. 
“Individuals and entities have used cryptocurrency trading accounts at Binance to conduct cryptocurrency transactions representing the proceeds of black-market sales of Iranian oil to buyers in China that were funnelled to the Government of Iran, its agents, and its proxies to finance terrorist activities,” prosecutors said in the seizure complaint. 
In a prepared statement, a Binance spokesperson said: “This case was not filed against Binance and does not allege wrongdoing by Binance. Binance has zero tolerance for sanctions violations or illicit activity, and Binance did not permit any transactions with sanctioned individuals. We will continue to co-operate with law enforcement on this matter.” 
The case was filed against currency in a series of digital wallets, not against Binance or the two Chinese companies, Hexa Whale Trading and Blessed Trust. The DoJ also did not specify the terrorist activity that the funds were used to finance. 
Binance pleaded guilty to US criminal charges in 2023 related to breach of anti-money laundering laws and paid a $4.3bn fine. The group’s founder Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty to failing to protect against money laundering and was sentenced to four months in federal prison. 
US President Donald Trump pardoned Zhao in October last year, as he has embraced cryptocurrencies during his second White House term and overhauled US regulatory oversight of the industry. 
An Abu Dhabi fund purchased a $2bn Binance equity stake from Zhao last year and paid entirely using USD1, a stablecoin issued by World Liberty Financial, a crypto company controlled by Trump’s family. 
Binance.com does not operate in the US. US customers are served by a separate entity, Binance.US. The company remains subject to a monitorship until 2028 under a plea agreement it entered with the US Treasury and justice departments.

rows.title: Germany’s Merz stands his ground but for how long?
rows.content:
Friedrich Merz did not mince his words. Sunday’s regional election in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern was a “disaster” for his Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the German chancellor said.
Early results suggested the CDU might scrape its way into the north-eastern state’s parliament with 5 per cent of the vote, by far its worst regional result since the Federal Republic was founded in 1949. If the party failed to secure parliamentary representation, it would turn disaster into catastrophe.
It also says a lot about the dire straits the CDU is in that Merz described the estimated 19 per cent the party won in the regional election in Berlin as “respectable”. The CDU’s vote share in the German capital fell by nearly a third and it is almost certain to be ejected from the government it has led there since 2023, supplanted by the far-left.
The two regional elections confirm the relentless advance of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), after its stunning victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt two weeks ago.
In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the AfD notched up another win with a projected 38 per cent, more than doubling its vote share, although it has no way of forming a parliamentary majority, unlike in Saxony-Anhalt. In Berlin, where its appeal is more limited, the AfD won an estimated 16 per cent, up seven percentage points compared with elections in 2023.
Merz’s instant assessment, delivered moments after exit polls landed on Sunday evening, looked like an attempt to pre-empt a threat of CDU rebellion against him. He insisted he would stay on and pursue his planned welfare and economic reforms, which would require “backbone, steadfastness and patience”.
The most unpopular German chancellor of the modern era is digging in. But how much patience will his party and the German public grant him? And what can a badly weakened chancellor, leading a fractious coalition with the centre-left Social Democrats, still achieve?
The CDU’s crushing defeat against a triumphant far right in Saxony-Anhalt brought rumblings of revolt from the party’s grassroots, its youth wing and from some MPs. It sparked fevered speculation about a possible Kanzlertausch, or chancellor swap.
In recent days, the party barons have circled the wagons. The CDU’s regional premiers pledged their support. Merz’s two most likely rivals are Hendrik Wüst and Markus Söder, the popular regional premiers of North Rhine-Westphalia and Bavaria respectively.
The lack of consensus over who should take over might be Merz’s biggest saving grace. Wüst, a moderate, faces his own regional election in April 2027. Söder, a boisterous conservative, could take the fight to the AfD, but some Christian Democrats would be reluctant to hand the chancellorship to their smaller Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union that he leads. In any case, any Merz successor would face the same economic problems and political constraints.
By vowing to concentrate on reforms, Merz is trying to buy some time from his party. Ditching him now could distract and destabilise the coalition and potentially derail a moderately ambitious set of changes to pensions, out-of-work benefits and employment rules due to be adopted in the coming months. The chancellor hopes these measures will boost business confidence and help raise growth after years of economic stagnation. Whether they are enough to transform his political fortunes is another matter.
The government has only a slender majority in the Bundestag. CDU parliamentarians are in restive mood. Some accuse Merz of making too many concessions to their Social Democrat coalition partners, and the chancellor cannot count on their support.
The plunge in Merz’s popularity, after only 16 months in office, has been unusually steep especially for a leader who has taken some bold and decisive steps on infrastructure investment, defence spending and support for Ukraine. An emergency (and ill-targeted) cut in fuel taxes, rushed out by the government on Friday evening, is a reminder that Germany still has some fiscal room for manoeuvre that neighbouring governments lack.
But the lesson from elsewhere in Europe is that in today’s politics once you become deeply unpopular — like French President Emmanuel Macron or Britain’s former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer — it is near impossible to recover. All the more so when the public disaffection is linked to perceived character: arrogance in Macron’s case, dithering in Starmer’s. Merz is haughty and clumsy. He will need better political skills to survive long.
Europe was already facing a tumultuous 12 months with elections in France, Italy, Spain, Poland and Greece. Now upheaval in Germany’s political leadership will be added to the mix.

rows.content:

rows.title: A top London lawyer wants to create ‘the California of Europe’ in the Algarve
rows.content:
A top London lawyer wants to create ‘the California of Europe’ in the Algarve
“Welcome to Portugal!” says Neel Sachdev, stepping out of his red open-top 1977 Mercedes 450 SL in a matching red outfit, sunglasses and trademark beaded bracelets on both wrists.
The car is on brand for the British-Indian lawyer, who had already texted five photos of the vehicle to me that morning, including one with his Gucci tennis racket holder in the back. Sachdev tells me he bought the car, which arrived from the Netherlands that week, as a throwback to his childhood watching high-glamour American TV series such as Hart to Hart and Dallas.
As we edge towards Sachdev’s holiday house in the hills of Santa Bárbara de Nexe, amid Europe’s fourth heatwave of the summer, I feel like I am entering another orbit. Sachdev’s orbit.
Sachdev has become a well-known figure in London’s Big Law scene. In 2023, he staged a coup, defecting from Kirkland & Ellis, the world’s largest law firm, to join rival Paul Weiss, where he is now global vice-chair and head of the London office.
Since then, he has grown the UK arm of the elite Wall Street firm from a satellite office of about 15 lawyers to 275, and taken a wrecking ball to the capital’s legal market. Sachdev’s build-out acted as a catalyst for a new wave of investment by US law firms, as American lawyers sought to service their lucrative private equity clients in Europe. The influx of firms has led to lawyers switching employers at an unprecedented rate in London, and top partners now earning upwards of $20mn a year.
“There’s definitely more of a star culture,” Sachdev, a private equity specialist, says. “I’ve helped clients with finding divorce lawyers; drafting wills. The model is the consigliere model. You’re the go-to lawyer, point person . . . I play tennis regularly with probably 10,” says Sachdev, whose resident doubles tennis partner in London is the perennially cheery TV chef Ainsley Harriott (not a client).
We are in Portugal to visit Sachdev’s side hustle. In 2022, a real estate investor neighbour and now business partner went to the Algarve and found a plot of land, a former orange grove, ripe for development.
After checking with his astrologer in India — also used by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Sachdev says — Sachdev co-invested in the plot and built a house. (He also called on his astrologer before leaving Kirkland, and says he sometimes takes the same astrological approach to prospective Paul Weiss hires.)
Today, 10 more houses are under various stages of construction to rent or sell on the land, named Laranjeiras — “orange trees”. The total plot cost €1.5mn and the houses, which all range in size between 5,000 and 6,000 square feet and have pools, were valued at more than €3mn apiece this year, Sachdev says. They are expected to be finished by 2028.
While many high-earning lawyers own multiple holiday homes and some passively invest in real estate, few have rolled up their sleeves for something as ambitious.
As I step inside the completed four-storey property, I catch a glimpse of the 25-metre pool in the garden, a non-negotiable for Sachdev, a keen swimmer. A bowl of goggles sits in the middle of the outside table. The kitchen side is filled with electric appliances designed by Dolce & Gabbana. Classical music hums through the network of slick speakers.
The interior is minimalist, all wooden furniture and white walls. In the basement there is a gym. Sachdev’s Portuguese personal trainer also works with English football players Jadon Sancho and Rio Ferdinand, he says.
On a tour, he tells me to touch the trunk of one of his garden statues of the elephant-headed Hindu god Ganesh, a nod to his heritage, for luck. “I have a great antiquities dealer,” says Sachdev, as if I might have doubted it.
Within 30 minutes of the photographer arriving, Sachdev, 51, has invited him to snap his birthday party the following week. Champagne from the year of his birth will be served. “Everything is an opportunity, it’s never a burden,” says Sachdev. “My kids say I’m toxically positive.”
Sachdev is channelling that positivity into a bet that the opportunity in Santa Bárbara de Nexe will pay off. He believes the region has the potential to become the “California of Europe”. United Airlines started a seasonal direct flight from New York to Faro airport, 15 minutes from the plot, last spring in response to an influx of Americans to the region. Indeed, it has the same sunny climate as the Golden State.
Sachdev’s venture here is an extension of what he has quietly been doing in London for 20 years. He lived in Hackney before it was cool, where he met his neighbour and business partner, and the pair co-invested in real estate in the burgeoning area. “I found it fascinating from an entrepreneurial perspective,” says Sachdev. “The whole thesis of my career is no different to property investing . . . you have to be entrepreneurial, you have to be thoughtful about risk, and you have to hustle.”
His business partner, who has also built his own house on the plot and lives there, manages the development day-to-day. The pair have hired local builders, architects and interior designers. Portugal is “very open to external investment. There’s a lot of local talent here,” says Sachdev.
While real estate is always a bet, the country has gained a reputation for its friendly attitude towards wealthy individuals over the past 14 years. More than 12,700 golden visas — residency in exchange for investment — have been granted, not including family members, since the Portuguese programme started in 2012, according to government statistics.
Covid-19 spurred Portugal’s popularity further as people rethought their lifestyle set-ups. The most sought-after schools in Lisbon, two and a half hours north of Santa Bárbara, have waiting lists as demand outpaces supply, the International School Advisor, a schools search engine, said in April.
Houses in the Algarve have increased from an average asking price of €2,367 per square metre in December 2020 to more than €4,000 this year, according to online real estate platform Idealista.
Sachdev says that he saw the main risk as being whether the bottom dropped out of the Algarve market while they were building. However, the project was partly personal — driven by the advice of a client to create a place that appealed to his kids to spend time with him as they got older. Sachdev says, “We will be very, very exclusive about who we sell to.”
Jack Harris, a partner at Knight Frank, said that supply still hasn’t caught up with demand for real estate in Portugal post-financial crisis. He also notes a lot of national interest in the Algarve; Santa Bárbara is a more peripheral neighbourhood that is expected to appreciate. “The standalone detached villas . . . are the most attractive product.”
Unlike some of the neighbouring towns that are populated with celebrities, business people and athletes — retired footballer Luís Figo’s house is visible on a far hilltop from Sachdev’s house — Santa Bárbara feels less polished and has more local life.
“I don’t want to sit in Nobu here. I want to sit in the local beach shack and eat the best octopus in the world,” says Sachdev. “Also, it doesn’t shut down. A lot of the islands in Europe, they sort of shut down for winter. We like coming here for Christmas and going for walks on the beach.”
The town, a five-minute walk away, has a clutch of restaurants, cafés, a mechanic and even a vet, with an old church in the centre. There is little glamour but lots of old-style charm. A plaque on the wall of one restaurant dates it to 1895. Sachdev has been trying to purchase the entire row. The local owners aren’t willing to sell.
We bypass the town and drive in Sachdev’s Range Rover to lunch at a popular place, 2 Passos, near the beach. It’s fully booked this time of year, but a quick call to local fixer — Simon, the “sheriff of Santa Bárbara” — and we’re eating octopus salad and king prawns.
Life was not always this way. Sachdev’s Indian parents emigrated from Kenya to the UK in the 1970s when Idi Amin, the “butcher of Uganda”, was expelling South Asians from his country. His father had worked in an oil refinery and his mother was a teacher, but without equivalent UK qualifications they started a corner shop in London’s Clerkenwell, an inner-city suburb on the cusp of regeneration.
Every day at 5am, the shop would deliver newspapers to Alexander McQueen and other local fashion houses. Sachdev would help out in school holidays. “What I learnt from my parents, including working in the shop . . . was just service . . . just be responsive, be helpful,” he says.
Sachdev’s parents prioritised education, spending most of their income on their children’s private school fees. His background was never highlighted at the prestigious City of London School, he says, but became more of a differentiator when he started at UK “magic circle” law firm Freshfields. “Nobody looked like me,” says Sachdev. “All the partners were: white man, grey suit. So I felt more left out there.”
I ask Sachdev between sips of Aperol Spritz what he’s going to do when he retires from the law. UK lawyers tend to leave the profession by 60. “I’ve always wanted to run for London mayor”.
Sachdev thinks he could make the city more attractive to the ultra-wealthy again, while also ensuring money is fed back into the state.
I’m tempted to view the conversation as a flight of fancy, but the morning after I arrive back in London I see he’s sent me a text: “Epic day with the FT!! Thinking about London mayor too . . . ”
Suzi Ring is the FT’s legal correspondent in London
