rows.title: Have Hong Kong’s eateries gone to the dogs?
rows.content:
Dogs join diners as Hong Kong bets on the pet economy
On a rainy and humid Saturday morning in central Hong Kong, Ollie, a nearly ten-month-old dachshund wearing a nappy and a dashing pink coat, is on the way to meet her brother at a nearby café. Thanks to new rules introduced this summer, that meeting can now take place indoors.
Across the Chinese territory, around 990 dining establishments have a licence that allows pets inside, marking the end of a decades-old prohibition.
For Ollie’s owners, 30-something Andy and Pinky, the liberalisation is a blessing in a city with multiple rules governing dogs on public transport, on beaches and in parks. “We need to eat,” says Andy. “Now we don’t need to leave her at home.”
The impetus for Hong Kong’s rule change is partly economic — a boost for a hospitality sector that has been hard hit by the rise in people heading north for cheaper meals out. Unveiling the overhaul, the territory’s chief executive John Lee said that the government wanted to support businesses offering “pet-friendly spaces” and noted that the island’s 400,000 pet cats and dogs generated “an enormous consumption market”.
Yet the rules — which require a leash no longer than 1.5 metres — have prompted some disquiet from diners. There have been complaints about pets being fed with restaurant utensils and standing on tables.
The Food and Environmental Hygiene Department tells me that the introduction of indoor pet licences in July has been “generally smooth”. But, it adds, it did initially receive feedback about “the control of dogs, dogs coming into contact with dining tables, and the cooking or heating of food on dining tables”.
The FEHD has instituted two prosecutions against people who failed to keep their dogs under control, 17 against food business operators for allowing dogs to enter and five against dog owners for patronising non-permitted restaurants. Sixty-two restaurants have withdrawn from the scheme.
“It seems society is quite divided,” said Stephanie, a 30-something bank employee and the owner of Muimui (Cantonese for little sister), a two-year-old Shetland sheepdog. “Some people don’t like dogs. They launch online attacks on the restaurant owners to try to get them to change their mind.”
For the most part, Hongkongers seem to love dogs — impeccably groomed lapdogs are everywhere, sometimes nestled under their owners’ arms, sometimes in backpacks or dog strollers.
In Elephant Grounds, a hipster café in central Hong Kong, half a dozen small dogs rest and sip water inside the entrance while their owners chat over coffee. The dogs are well behaved — though I notice one snuffling into his owner’s food.
Many of the dog owners I chat with connect Hongkongers’ love of dogs to the prohibitively high cost of having children. Hong Kong, an expensive city known for its compact apartments, has one of the world’s lowest fertility rates.
Claudia, a retired beauty industry professional who regularly visits Elephant Grounds with her three-year-old Bichon Olee, says children are too expensive. “That’s my reason.”
“It is just the practicalities of it,” explains Professor Stuart Gietel-Basten at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology. “It all compounds each other. [A person has] been through high-intensity education, got a job, still cannot afford a house and the single worst thing [they] can do is have children . . . Having a pet is not an unreasonable compromise.”
Still, allowing dogs inside restaurants is not popular with everyone.
As a couple wheel a mongrel called Mut into a café on the west Kowloon waterfront promenade, manager Thierry Perreau says dogs are welcome — but he reserves judgment as to how successful the scheme will be.
“There can be barking. Some people don’t like dogs next to them,” he says, recalling a time he was bitten in a different restaurant while trying to negotiate service outdoors for a party with two pets. “In a small place like this, having a pet on a leash when you are carrying plates is not comfortable,” he adds. “All customers say it is a cute dog until it isn’t.”

rows.title: Dangote IPO is a test for African capitalism
rows.content:
It is the biggest industrial project in Africa in a generation, but Nigerians can now have a small piece of the Dangote Refinery for the price of a soft drink. Aliko Dangote, Africa’s richest man, hopes that up to 10mn people will participate by purchasing at least 10 shares at ₦525 ($0.40) each. That should be within reach of all but the poorest Nigerians. The initial public offering will raise $1.6bn, valuing close to a generous-looking $50bn the massive refinery that took a decade to build on swampland outside Lagos.
Both the IPO, the biggest ever in Africa, and the project itself — at 700,000 barrels a day, the world’s largest so-called single-train refinery — are important milestones for Nigeria and the continent. The refinery has ended six decades in which Nigeria, frequently Africa’s biggest oil producer, exported large volumes of crude only to import petrol, diesel and jet fuel. That not only squandered vast amounts of foreign exchange, it also engendered a rentier economy where arbitrage trumped production. The refinery and Dangote’s broader industrial complex also theoretically make Nigeria self-sufficient in fertiliser and polypropylene.
It was a stroke of luck that the refinery was reaching full capacity just as war was starting in Iran. Nigeria has had few petrol shortages and Dangote has supplied other countries with diesel and jet fuel to such an extent that his refinery is credited with playing a material role in keeping European carriers airborne. As margins spread, the refinery has made windfall profits.
The IPO is not without risk, however. A valuation of nearly $50bn for an asset that cost $20bn to build looks steep. It is a premium of nearly 10 per cent over the price of July’s $2.5bn private placement, which implies investors on the street will be paying more than the club of insiders who got first dibs on the listing. The small free float of just 3.3 per cent means liquidity will be tight. Dangote argues that investors are buying a ride on expansion plans that should see it double capacity to 1.4mn b/d by 2028-29.
If this is to be Nigeria’s “Tell Sid” moment — on the lines of the 1986 ad campaign for a privatisation that turbocharged popular capitalism in Britain — ordinary investors need to benefit. It would be unfortunate if they bought an asset priced against current windfalls only to see its value subsequently fall.
Still, Dangote’s stated reasoning that African capital should fund African infrastructure is right. There is as much as $4tn in financial assets in Africa, but little of it is deployed as risk capital for productive investments, with much recycled through high-yielding government debt. Deepening capital markets is an important step towards funnelling some of this money to better uses. Nigeria should push to make Lagos a meaningful financial centre.
More is at stake. Throughout Africa, there is grandiose talk about ending the export of raw materials, from cobalt to cocoa, by processing them domestically. Mostly it is just talk. When action is taken, too often it ignores the realities of shoddy roads and ports and expensive or non-existent power.
Dangote’s success in completing a project that many thought impossible is as much a cautionary tale as a tribute to his bloody-mindedness. He literally had to build the supporting infrastructure around him to make the project viable. Even after it was completed, vested interests, including state companies, ensured he initially struggled to secure the crude oil required to keep it running.
Africa needs more private businesses to succeed. But government policies across the continent — from wanton neglect of public infrastructure to tax shakedowns of successful entrepreneurs — make it all but impossible for them to reach scale. If people are crowing today that Dangote proves it’s possible to make money by investing in Africa, the reverse could also be true. His refinery may be the exception that proves the rule.

rows.title: How the shipping industry could make itself greener
rows.content:
How the shipping industry could make itself greener
Simply sign up to the Renewable energy myFT Digest -- delivered directly to your inbox.
The global container shipping industry has grown beyond recognition from its roots 80 years ago when a few wartime vessels were repurposed, to become one of the key enablers of globalisation.
There are now 7,000 vessels — the largest of which sail the equivalent of ten return trips to the Moon in their lifetimes — moving three-quarters of global trade.
Yet the ships are virtually all powered by fossil fuels, and shipping is on average responsible for about 3 per cent of the world’s annual greenhouse gas emissions. Container ships often use a particularly dirty fuel called bunker fuel.
Cleaning up the industry is a mammoth undertaking. Unlike roads, rail or factories, these vessels operating at sea cannot simply be plugged into a cleaner electricity grid.
Cleaner fuels are required for decarbonisation. Two of the key alternative fuel sources for shipping are ammonia and methanol.
How does it work?
Ammonia and methanol are two fuels that could power ships. They can be made using renewable electricity sources, making them carbon-free fuels. The process for both starts with producing hydrogen through water electrolysis, which is when an electric current is sent through water. The hydrogen can then be turned into ammonia or methanol using further chemical processes.
These sustainable synthetic fuels have energy densities similar to fossil fuels and therefore can be used in existing engines with “little or no” modification, then transported using mostly existing infrastructure, according to the Royal Society, a UK science academy.
What are the pros and cons?
There is little debate about whether clean fuels could replace oil or gas in global shipping from a technology standpoint.
But it all comes down to costs. Energy companies have not wanted — or been sufficiently incentivised — to make the necessary investments. And without sufficient scale, the green energy industry has been unable to compete against petrochemicals.
In recent years, and prior to the oil market turbulence linked to the Iran war, green ammonia had been priced around $600 to $1,050 per tonne, compared to $500 to $600 a tonne for heavy fuel oil. Green ammonia prices for longer-term offtake agreements — in which a specific output is agreed beforehand — could be significantly lower, analysts say, although the exact prices are not public
The big question is whether the costs of clean fuel production can come down far enough to compete with oil. Given that most ship owners have long been reluctant to give up fuels, regulation and incentives are needed to help kick-start the industry. On the other side of the coin, growth and scale would be helped by penalties and minimum carbon prices imposed on ship owners for fossil fuel use.
David Fishman, a Shanghai-based energy analyst at the Lantau Group, said that while it was still possible to make technical improvements to existing processes — such as more efficient electrolysers — gaining greater scale and experience is the most likely way to lower costs. “We’re not innovating a new chemical process here,” he says. “We’re debating whether we can extract, synthesise, and isolate those valuable molecules in a way that is cost competitive with the current way we do it, which incurs a lot of carbon emissions.”
Will it save the planet?
For years, shipowners have been touting improvements in energy efficiency and fuel use as evidence of their commitment to fighting climate change. But emissions continue to rise as the expansion of global trade far outpaces these incremental efficiency improvements inside fossil-fuel-powered engines.
Total “tank-to-wake” greenhouse gas emissions — emissions resulting from fuel use onboard — rose 12 per cent from 2016 to 2023, according to the International Council on Clean Transportation. What’s more, the industry’s emissions of highly polluting soot — so-called “black carbon” — remain a significant concern as they are rising rapidly, according to the group.
A 2025 report commissioned by the UK transport department found that the shipping industry could achieve a staggering 95 per cent reduction in emissions if stronger policies supported the use of sustainable fuels. The lowest-cost pathway to slashing carbon emissions would involve ammonia produced entirely through renewable methods, so-called green ammonia, the report noted.
Has the technology arrived yet?
China is racing ahead of the rest of the world in trying to utilise its abundant and low-cost solar and wind resources to help decarbonise its vast industrial sector.
According to data from Mission Possible Partnership, an international non-profit focused on carbon-intensive sectors, 12 ammonia production sites in China have already received approval for funding and a further 54 have been announced. For methanol, 21 plants in China have passed the final funding-approval stage and a further 88 projects have been announced.
MPP estimates $23.7bn has been invested across the 33 methanol and ammonia projects that have either become operational or reached a final investment decision in China. Comparative figures are not available for Europe or the US. Europe has one clean ammonia project, the US has five.
Who is investing in it?
While this is still very much a nascent industry, agreements between shipping groups and Chinese clean-fuel suppliers are multiplying.
An illustrative example can be found in Jilin, China’s far north-east province bordering North Korea, where state-owned energy conglomerate CEEC claims to have built the world’s largest facility of its kind, producing 45,000 tonnes of green hydrogen alongside 200,000 tonnes of green ammonia and green methanol annually and planning to further increase production in the coming years. CEEC signed an agreement with Belgian shipping group CMB.TECH last year to supply a fleet of new dual-fuelled ships, using clean ammonia and diesel from the site.
Over the past year, a multilateral effort led by the International Maritime Organization to reach a historic climate deal for the global shipping industry — a deal that would potentially encourage other countries to compete with China in clean fuels — has been stalled by US and Saudi Arabian opposition.
Chinese companies’ advance in the sector has been bolstered by the country’s large investments in renewable energy as well as strong state support for emerging industries such as green ammonia and green hydrogen production.
Earlier this year, the Chinese Communist Party released its latest five-year plan outlining the country’s strategic economic, social and technological development goals. The plan called for greater efforts in substituting oil and gas with alternative fuels. It also specifically targeted green hydrogen, ammonia and methanol as core pillars for growing non-electricity renewable energy uses.
As with industries such as computer chips, AI and electric vehicles, the policy support for clean fuels sparked a surge of investment from Chinese companies, both private and state-owned. Listed companies Envision and Towngas, as well as state shipping giant COSCO and the Shanghai International Port Group all launched new initiatives supporting green fuel.

rows.title: Time for a pause on cutting-edge AI
rows.content:
There is a Jekyll-and-Hyde quality to the world’s most powerful AI bosses. The same executives now talking about slowing the pace of work on cutting-edge models given the risks to humanity have been competing hell-for-leather to advance AI, chasing trillion-dollar flotations. But the backing of two AI titans — Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk of SpaceX — for the slowdown call by a third, Dario Amodei of Anthropic, ought to become a watershed moment for the industry.
President Donald Trump dismissed the calls as “negative forces”, insisting the US must beat China in the AI race. But as Trump’s techno-libertarian former AI tsar David Sacks pointed out, since these companies dominate cutting-edge AI they can “pace the frontier” themselves, without waiting for regulation. Such co-operation has seemed unlikely, but the slowdown calls suggest companies realise it is time to act. They should use their power to slow, or better still pause, development of the most advanced frontier models until the risks can be understood and contained.
Such calls are not made lightly. The extraordinary potential benefits of even more powerful AI should not be forgone. Hundreds of billions of dollars are being sunk into AI development that underpins the value of the US stock market. There are indeed risks of the capabilities falling first into the hands of an authoritarian China. But, even setting aside insider warnings that AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade”, some models are clearly starting to escape control.
The hack of Hugging Face during an OpenAI model test showed AI agents working in a swarm to escape guardrails and cover their tracks. Whether or not this meets industry definitions of “artificial general intelligence”, it looks like human-level reasoning abilities. The big labs are also racing towards using AI to help create more advanced AI, known as recursive self-improvement. As Amodei noted, left unchecked, this could “outrun our ability to understand and control these systems”.
Even in a best-case scenario, legislation could not keep up with the current pace of AI’s advance. That makes it incumbent on the top labs to pause sensitive research and model testing. They need to come up with standards and best practices on AI safety, talked about for years with scant progress. Amodei’s promise to embed independent researchers working alongside staff and reporting publicly is a start, but outside audits will quickly need more teeth.
A more responsible US administration than Trump’s would already be using existing regulation to strengthen guardrails. Lina Khan, the former Federal Trade Commission chair, argues that law enforcers already have the powers to charge companies and CEOs for creating and releasing dangerous or defective products. Companies whose agents hack into other businesses could also face civil liabilities, though criminal charges are harder to bring.
Companies will always be tempted to depart from voluntary agreements if they can grab share, making a legislative framework necessary longer-term. A political shift at the US midterm elections might yet ease the path. One law that would concentrate minds would be to make top executives criminally liable for harm caused by their models.
US tech bosses warn that a slowdown in the US alone would be ineffective if China or others push ahead. Chinese companies’ heavy reliance on US research means a US pause would slow the entire industry at least for a time — though, like the US ban on advanced chip exports, it could be a spur and an opportunity for China to catch up. AI safety and security issues are on the agenda when President Xi Jinping visits Washington this month. The Chinese leader sees AI as a crucial tool of economic and military modernisation. Ultimately, however, unconstrained AI escalation is no more in Xi’s interests than it is in Trump’s — or the interests of the rest of us.

rows.title: Supreme Court rejects Trump’s mail-in ballot restrictions for midterms
rows.content:
Supreme Court rejects Donald Trump’s restrictions on mail-in ballots for midterms
The US Supreme Court has rejected Donald Trump’s attempt to restrict mail-in ballots ahead of November’s midterm elections in a major blow to the president.
In a one-paragraph decision that did not explain the court’s reasoning, the justices on Monday left in place a lower court’s ruling that blocked Trump’s executive order requiring the US Postal Service to curtail voting by mail.
“The Government is unlikely to succeed on the merits of its challenge to the District Court’s preliminary injunction,” the justices wrote in the unsigned decision. “And the equitable factors applicable for obtaining emergency relief from this Court do not favor a stay.”
Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented.
Justice Brett Kavanaugh, writing in a concurrence, said applying limits to mail-in ballots ahead of the midterms “would be arbitrary and capricious in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act because state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections”.
The decision thwarts Trump’s attempt to overhaul the electoral system, which he has repeatedly pledged to do while continuing to push unfounded claims of widespread fraud in the 2020 presidential election.
The US president on Tuesday railed against the opinion, writing in a post on Truth Social that “Republicans just got another bad decision” from the Supreme Court, which “has really let our Country down!”
Citing other cases the Trump administration has lost before the top court, including on birthright citizenship and tariffs, the president added: “This Supreme Court is bullied and cajoled by the Radical Left into making decisions that have set America back at least a hundred years. These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves.”
Kavanaugh’s focus on how Trump’s order failed to give election officials enough time to adapt before November leaves open the possibility that curbs on mail-in ballots could still be implemented ahead of the 2028 presidential race.
Kavanaugh said there was “at least a fair prospect” that it would fall within the US Postal Service’s authority to implement new rules on mail-in ballots.
Mail-in ballots have long been in Trump’s crosshairs, as they are more popular among Democratic voters compared with Republicans. Overall, about one-third of voters vote by mail.
The Supreme Court decision follows months of legal wrangling on mail-in voting. The president in March issued an executive order mandating the creation of a federal list of eligible voters and directed the postal service to limit mail ballot deliveries to those people.
Solicitor-general D John Sauer had argued to the top court that the postal service’s final rule required “only modest envelope-design and addressee-information requirements” for ballots sent by mail. It ensures states carry the responsibility for determining voter eligibility but does not dictate ballot content, counting procedures or deadlines, he said.
“The rule thus plainly does not seize control of states’ administration of elections — it simply imposes reasonable preparation requirements for certain election-related mail,” Sauer said.
Attorneys for the 23 states that sued to block the order said there was “nothing ‘modest’, equitable or lawful” about the new restrictions. It would take “Herculean” efforts by state and local election officials to even begin to comply, they said.
“In some states, unrebutted evidence establishes that compliance with USPS’s rule would be impossible ahead of the midterms, meaning that millions of voters would be unable to vote by mail and some would not be able to vote at all,” the states’ attorneys said, noting that areas including North Carolina and Wisconsin had started mailing ballots.
In his dissent, Alito took issue with the states’ argument that they lacked the time to comply with the new rules, saying they “cannot claim the timing of the rule tilts the equities in their favor when they, and the courts hearing their claims, are responsible for so much of the delay”.
Lawyers for voting rights groups that sued said the restrictions were “unprecedented eleventh-hour requirements”, asserting that no federal statute nor the Constitution assigns the executive branch such power.
California senator Alex Padilla, the Democratic ranking member of the committee on rules and administration, celebrated the decision on Monday evening.
“Trump tried to rewrite the rules. He lost. We won. Vote by mail works. California, ballots start going out to every registered voter in October. Go make your voice heard,” he wrote on X.
The Supreme Court previously ruled that an initial legal challenge to Trump’s executive order was premature, allowing it to take temporary effect without pronouncing on its legality.
The ruling followed a federal judge’s decision to indefinitely freeze the postal service plan as challenges to it moved through the courts.
A federal appeals court last week kept that block in place, saying that allowing the rule change would be likely to “result in the disenfranchisement of millions of voters across the country while providing minimal — if any — gains in combating voter fraud”.
Additional reporting by James Politi in Washington

rows.title: Trump’s regulatory rollback puts $400mn in US audit fees at risk
rows.content:
Trump’s regulatory rollback puts $400mn in US audit fees at risk
US accounting firms are fighting to save more than $400mn in fees that could be at risk if a Securities and Exchange Commission proposal to roll back post-Enron audit rules is approved in the coming months.
The SEC has proposed slashing the number of US-listed companies that are required to get an audit opinion on the quality of their internal financial controls, a rule that led to a fee bonanza for accounting firms when it was introduced in 2002.
Companies with a public float below $2bn would be exempted from the rule, up from $700mn now, and those that go public in the future — even giant technology companies with trillion-dollar market valuations — would be spared the requirement for their first five years on the market.
The rollback is part of Paul Atkins’ effort to “make IPOs great again”, alongside axing quarterly reporting and other deregulatory proposals. The SEC chair, appointed by Donald Trump last year, says the need to get an audit opinion on internal controls deters companies from going public by adding complexity and expense to an audit.
The 2002 Sarbanes-Oxley Act required all US-listed companies to certify they have strong internal controls to prevent fraud, and around half must also get their auditor to sign off on the opinion. The SEC proposal, published in May, would exempt a further 27 per cent of public companies from auditor attestation, the agency estimated, about 1,700 companies.
“It’s a significant contributor to fees and to the extent it gets rolled back, the auditors are going to feel it in the pocketbook,” said Bob Conway, a former audit partner and regulator and author of The Truth About Public Accounting.
The US Government Accountability Office last year analysed companies before and after they hit the current threshold requiring auditor attestation and found that the switch of status added 13 per cent to audit fees at the median company. Companies that would be newly exempt paid $3.8bn in audit fees last year, according to data from Ideagen Audit Analytics, implying that the extra fees are worth $430mn to audit firms.
Some company surveys and academic studies, plus an alternative methodology considered by the GAO, suggest the related fees could be significantly higher. Internal controls testing is integrated with the rest of the audit, so accounting firms do not break out the fees separately, and regulators have tweaked the rules on several occasions since they were first introduced.
Audit firms say regulators are likely to be disappointed by the scale of the savings. They will have to recreate at least some of the internal controls tests as part of the regular audit in order to achieve the same level of comfort with a company’s financial statements, they wrote in comment letters to the SEC.
The Big Four — EY, Deloitte, PwC and KPMG — opposed the rollback, along with smaller accounting firms and many investor groups. The long carve-out for new public companies came in for particular criticism, with some commenters saying the likes of SpaceX or Anthropic would be an important part of investors’ portfolios and should have watertight financial controls.
The Center for Audit Quality, which represents big accounting firms, is pushing the SEC to consider the impact of the rollback alongside other proposals such as allowing companies to report twice a year instead of quarterly.
Dennis McGowan, CAQ vice-president, said the SEC should conduct a cost-benefit analysis of its full package of reforms and argued that the cost of an internal controls audit could be reduced instead by new regulatory guidance to audit firms.
“Independent auditor attestation is associated with stronger controls, improved financial reporting and greater investor confidence,” he said. “Those benefits need to be weighed carefully against the potential cost savings.”

rows.title: Russian warship fires flares at Danish helicopter over Baltic Sea
rows.content:
Russian warship fires flares at Danish helicopter over Baltic Sea
A Russian warship fired flares at a Danish helicopter over the Baltic Sea in the latest sign of what Denmark’s government called increasingly risky and reckless behaviour from Moscow.
Denmark called in Russia’s ambassador after a Russian frigate in international waters fired two flares at a Danish helicopter that was taking “routine” photographs of it. Danish military said one of the flares passed the helicopter at close range.
“Reckless action from Russia towards Danish military during a routine overflight yesterday. Russian actions are meant to intimidate and divide. They will not succeed. We will not waver,” said Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.
Jeppe Bruus, Denmark’s defence minister, said: “This is the first time we have seen an incident of this kind to the best of my knowledge, and it demonstrates that the Russians are becoming more willing to take risks. It is therefore a serious incident, and that is also why we are summoning the Russian ambassador for a meeting.”
Russia’s ambassador to Denmark said the helicopter behaved in a provocative manner and that Russian attempts to de-escalate the situation in the Baltic Sea had been rebuffed by Copenhagen.
European governments, particularly along Nato’s eastern flank, have warned in recent weeks that Russia is becoming more confrontational in an attempt to dissuade countries from supporting Ukraine. Russia is also stepping up hybrid attacks, including provocations, arson and the weaponisation of migration into the EU, they added.
Denmark has been one of the most vocal supporters of Ukraine. Last year, the Scandinavian country closed multiple airports after unconfirmed sightings of drones, with suspicion falling on Russia.
The Danish incident came after Nato fighter jets shot down a drone over Lithuania for the first time.
Lithuanian authorities said it was not yet clear whether the drone — which came from Belarus — was Russian or Ukrainian, but that it appeared to be carrying explosives. It was shot down west of the capital Vilnius, and investigators were examining the wreckage.
Similar incidents have taken place in neighbouring Poland, Latvia and Estonia. Many have involved stray Ukrainian drones, which Baltic officials believe were forced off course by Russian jamming, but some have been Russian unmanned devices.
Nato secretary-general Mark Rutte this week said that Russia was becoming “increasingly reckless” after a drone attack at Leipzig airport was attributed by German officials to Moscow.

rows.title: Scientists test new (and old) navigation systems to end GPS dependence
rows.content:
Scientists test new (and old) navigation systems to end GPS dependence
On a UK military test flight over southern England in May 2024, a team of British and American physicists carried a briefcase-sized object containing one of the strangest substances in the universe: a cloud of atoms cooled so close to absolute zero temperature that they merged into a single quantum state.
Known as a Bose-Einstein condensate, it is a new form of matter first created in a laboratory in 1995. The experiment, carried out by BAE Systems, Infleqtion, a Colorado-based tech company, and UK-based defence company QinetiQ, marked the first time such an object is known to have survived intact aboard an aircraft in flight. Defence companies such as BAE believe it could help solve one of modern warfare’s most pressing problems: how to navigate when GPS disappears.
The race to build alternatives to satellite navigation has accelerated as Russia’s war in Ukraine and conflict in the Middle East have demonstrated how vulnerable GPS has become to jamming, spoofing and other disruptions.
Rather than assuming satellite signals will always be available, the world’s militaries are now designing aircraft, drones and missiles that can find their way using entirely different methods. These range from revived cold war radio beacons to quantum sensors that can, as whales and some birds are thought to do, navigate by using the Earth’s magnetic field.
GPS, widely used since the turn of the century, triangulates satellite signals to provide precise location, time and velocity for crucial services such as aviation, shipping, road transport, telecommunications, electricity grids and financial markets.
Alan Woodward — a visiting professor at the University of Surrey who worked for UK government intelligence during the cold war and now specialises in systems security — says the main problem with navigation systems using satellites is that they are controlled either by a particular government or by a “tech bro”.
“You have got to have fallbacks,” he says. “That’s why a lot of this research has been quietly going on in the background.”
The risk posed by GPS interference is “very significant” for critical national infrastructure, the economy and national security, says Malcolm Macdonald, a signal processing and space technology expert at the University of Strathclyde.
“This is what we already see in eastern Europe and the Middle East where jamming is a regular day-to-day occurrence,” Macdonald says. “This then further extends into the battlefield where GPS is typically unavailable.”
Among the most high-tech (and most expensive) potential solutions is the one developed by Infleqtion, a Colorado-based quantum technology company whose experimental technology was aboard the flight over England.
By using lasers to hold atoms almost perfectly motionless — at a temperature of a few billionths of a degree above absolute zero, even though the casing of the device remains at room temperature — the technology creates a quantum sensor.
This is capable of detecting minute movements with far greater precision than conventional inertial navigation systems, such as the laser ring gyroscopes used by advanced aircraft and cruise missiles. (Inertial navigation measures the movement of an object from its starting point using sensors such as accelerometers and gyroscopes and does not rely on outside signals.)
Unlike GPS, which depends on triangulating precisely timed radio signals received from satellites, it cannot be jammed because it is self-contained.
Matthew Kinsella, Infleqtion’s chief executive, said the material is orders of magnitude more precise than the current state of the art in inertial navigation. “Crucially, it does not drift,” he said.
At about $1mn per unit, the likely cost is for the moment prohibitive except for valuable submarines, ships and aircraft. “It’s not something you would put on a single-use drone,” says Kinsella.
The assumption that GPS would always be available has quietly become one of the first casualties of modern electronic warfare. Due to electronic jamming, many previously fearsome GPS-guided weapons, such as Himars rocket artillery and Excalibur guided artillery, have ceased to be accurate in Ukraine.
But the problem is no longer confined to war zones. About 40 per cent of European air traffic is now affected by interference with GPS, according to European aviation authorities, with evidence pointing to Russia’s heavily militarised Kaliningrad exclave and the Kola Peninsula as major sources of disruption.
Commercial airliners — particularly in the eastern Mediterranean near Israel, or in the Black Sea near Ukraine — have reported losing GPS signals or receiving false position data, forcing pilots to revert to traditional inertial navigation sensors.
Another possible high-tech solution comes from Canadian start-up SBQuantum, based in Quebec, which is developing quantum magnetometers that navigate by reading subtle variations in the Earth’s magnetic field. The approach is similar to one of the methods scientists believe is used by whales, sea turtles and migratory birds to navigate across oceans.
“Nature has mastered magnetic navigation to some extent,” said David Roy-Guay, founder and chief technology officer of SBQuantum. “We’re kind of catching up there.”
The company’s “Zero Drift Navigator” is designed to work alongside an aircraft’s inertial navigation system, periodically correcting the gradual errors that accumulate once GPS signals are lost. Unlike GPS, the characteristics and anomalies in Earth’s magnetic field cannot easily be jammed or spoofed.
The trade-off is accuracy. Magnetic navigation generally requires detailed maps of the Earth’s magnetic landscape and currently offers precision measured in tens or hundreds of metres rather than the metres or centimetres provided by GPS.
SBQuantum says its first-generation system is targeting accuracy of about 100 metres throughout an entire flight and is expected to cost about $25,000. That is cheap enough for large drones, aircraft and autonomous underwater vehicles, though not yet for expendable munitions, nor is it accurate enough for missiles or shells.
Other companies are developing vision-based systems that allow drones and missiles to compare live camera images with stored satellite imagery, technology once available only for the most advanced cruise missiles that is now cheap enough to use on drones.
The use of multiple navigation systems that can take over from each other when one of them is blocked is also on the agenda. Rather than betting on a single solution, defence planners are increasingly building redundancy into the next generation of weapons.
“For me, the most resilient system is one that merges multiple techniques rather than relies only on one of them,” Macdonald says.
Modern cruise missiles such as the latest Tomahawk combine GPS with inertial navigation, terrain contour matching and optical scene-matching, ensuring that if one method is denied another can take over.
German-American drone software company Auterion markets technology for battlefield drones that combines satellite signals with inertial sensors and a downward-facing camera that continuously compares live video of the terrain below with digital maps. The company says the entire package adds only “low tens of thousands” of dollars to the cost of a drone, though the mapping does not work well over water or featureless terrain.
Another such combination of sensors was trialled on Sept 9, when Sandbox AQ, a spin off from Alphabet Inc, demonstrated a quantum-sensing magnetic navigation device paired with a visual navigation system on a one-way attack drone made by Northrop Grumman.
The potential disruption to satellite-based navigation has also triggered the re-emergence of pre-GPS techniques — what Woodward calls “the old ways” — that use ground-based infrastructure.
The UK, for example, is building ground-based transmitters and receivers known as enhanced long-range navigation (eLoran), based on the Loran system first deployed during the second world war and later used by shipping until the rise of GPS. In May, the UK government announced it had awarded a £6mn contract to develop eLoran to a partnership led by QinetiQ.
A significant advantage of eLoran is that spoofing or jamming it requires large, high-powered transmitters, meaning potential attacks should be easy to spot and so more preventable.
Another option is to stop relying on GPS signals emitted from satellites in geostationary orbits 20,000km above Earth and use other satellites instead.
Todd Humphreys, director of the Radionavigation Laboratory at the University of Texas at Austin, said different satellite constellations in lower orbits may provide more robust signals that are harder to jam. Companies operating such satellites include telecoms company Iridium and Elon Musk’s internet data company Starlink, both of which offer navigation services.
“There is no silver bullet,” said Humphreys of the search for alternatives to GPS, “but several bronze bullets have emerged.”

rows.title: PwC revenues fall for first time in two decades
rows.content:
PwC revenues fall for first time in two decades
PwC UK’s revenues fell last year for the first time in more than two decades as it was hit by a prolonged slump in its Middle East consulting business.
PwC said on Wednesday that total revenue for the UK group, which includes operations in the Middle East, fell by 3 per cent to £6.2bn in the 12 months to June.
Revenues in the Big Four firm’s Middle East business contracted 15 per cent to £1.7bn, with the fall outweighing a 2 per cent increase in sales by its larger UK-based operations.
Despite the fall in revenues, average pay for the firm’s near-1,000 partners rose to a record £935,000 as it reduced staff numbers and cut costs. PwC UK’s senior partner, Marco Amitrano, was paid £4.8mn, up from £4.3mn a year earlier.
The record payouts came as the firm cut back on hiring, slashing staff numbers across the UK and Middle East by 4,000 or almost 12 per cent.
It is the second year of falling sales in PwC’s Middle East business, which has been hit by a wider slowdown in lucrative Saudi Arabian consulting projects, previously the engine for rapid growth at the firm.
PwC said it had been a “challenging year” for its Middle East business, citing “the impact of regional conflict, wider market disruption and currency movements”.
The firm had last year cut the jobs of about 60 partners and 1,500 staff in the region after being hit with a year-long ban on winning work from Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund.
The firm this year parachuted in its UK managing partner Laura Hinton to run the Middle East business as it sought to navigate the slowdown. 
PwC is the first of the Big Four firms — which also include Deloitte, EY and KPMG — to report its UK results for the most recent financial year. 
The firms are grappling with a sector-wide slowdown and the rapid development of AI, which threatens their business models. Technology is automating routine consulting and audit tasks and raising questions about the industry’s labour-intensive staffing model, while firms are simultaneously shifting more work offshore.
In the year to June 2026, PwC’s consulting unit was the laggard with revenues falling by about one-tenth to £1.8bn. Sales at its risk advisory unit declined by a similar proportion, while revenues in its tax, audit and deal advisory divisions were flat or rose slightly.
Even before the fall in revenues in its most recent financial year, PwC’s revenues had flatlined in 2024-25. Sales growth across the group had hovered between 9 per cent and 16 per cent annually for three financial years between 2022 and 2024 as the firm benefited from a post-pandemic surge in demand for consultants and rapid growth in the Middle East.

rows.title: The Indian business empire being forced to list against its will
rows.content:
The Indian business empire being forced to list against its will
India’s biggest conglomerate is being forced by the central bank into a $120bn listing it does not want, potentially opening some of the country’s most valuable and closely held companies to rivals and raiders.
The Reserve Bank of India at the weekend rejected an appeal by software-to-Range Rover maker Tata for an exemption from rules requiring it to list its holding company.
A listing may value Tata Sons at more than $120bn, according to analyst estimates, which would make it India’s largest-ever initial public offering. It would profoundly transform the ownership and governance of the renowned Mumbai-based business house, which has remained closely held for more than a century.
But it would be a major blow for Noel Tata, chair of the charitable trusts that control the group and a scion of the founding family, who has resisted an IPO.
The “RBI would not make a decision as big as this without getting an implicit informal go-ahead from the government”, said Nirmalya Kumar, visiting professor at the Indian School of Business and a former Tata executive, echoing a sentiment voiced privately by other senior executives familiar with Tata.
Noel has argued a listing would fatally undermine Tata Sons’ ability to exercise long-term stewardship of the vast conglomerate, which assembles Apple iPhones, runs Air India and makes products including Tetley tea, steel and Jaguar Land Rover cars.
Disagreement over whether to list was a crucial factor in a boardroom feud this year, which culminated in long-serving Tata Sons chair N Chandrasekaran announcing last month he would step down at the end of his term next February.
This means Tata faces the prospect of being forced into a complex listing as it is seeking a new leader for the holding company.
Senior executives and foreign investors in India have long complained about what they say is the increasingly arbitrary nature of regulation in the country, citing uncertainty about the rule of law as a deterrent to investment.
“A company which does not want to go public is being forced to by the government,” said a person close to Tata Sons, adding that the regulatory uncertainty surrounding the process “is going to do serious damage to foreign investment”.
Nitin Potdar, a lawyer who has advised several multinationals in India and worked for Tata in the past, said the RBI’s shifting rules on listing requirements suggested it was applying the law in a selective manner.
Most large Indian companies’ ownership is “structured in a way whereby the actual owner is always hidden” and “to avoid transparency”, he said.
“No one asks them to put their ownership into one structure,” said Potdar. “And here is a conglomerate which has transparently said: ‘I am one holding company’ . . . and you want to penalise that company.”
More than two dozen Tata businesses, including IT services provider Tata Consultancy Services and retail chain Trent, are already listed. Tata Sons wields control over them through large stakes.
Listing the holding company could make some of those subsidiaries targets for corporate raiders, especially as some shareholders have already said they would sell in the event of a listing.
Tata Sons’ largest minority shareholder Shapoorji Pallonji — a debt-laden construction and engineering group with longstanding ties to the Tata family — has long pushed for a listing to sell part of its 18 per cent stake.
Rival conglomerates “will have an interest in Tata Sons”, said a person who serves as a director in its subsidiaries.
The regulatory clash stems from the RBI’s move in 2022 to classify Tata Sons as an “upper-layer” non-bank financial company under rules introduced to compel India’s biggest “shadow banks” to go public and face tougher supervision.
The RBI said at the time its push to list shadow banks was aimed at introducing more transparency and reducing systemic risks in the financial sector.
In an attempt to remove itself from the framework that triggered the listing requirement, Tata Sons in March 2024 formally sought to surrender its RBI-imposed registration as a core investment company after repaying its borrowings.
But the RBI changed its policy this year and set Rs1tn ($10.4bn) in assets as the threshold for large shadow banks, long after Tata, which has Rs2tn in assets, applied to deregister. This meant the conglomerate was still caught by the listing rules.
Several people familiar with Tata said the RBI’s listing order would not have come without a nod from the top level in Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government, given the company’s outsized importance to the Indian economy.
The RBI, finance ministry, Tata Trusts and Tata Sons did not respond to requests for comment.
People with knowledge of the company said Chandrasekaran did not oppose a listing, while Noel — who took charge after the death of his half-brother Ratan Tata two years ago — has accused the outgoing chair of ignoring the trusts’ wishes to remain private.
Modi’s government has taken a keen interest in Tata’s stability. Last year, two senior ministers held an extraordinary meeting with Noel and Chandrasekaran as the group was engulfed in a governance crisis. Since then, the two men’s relationship has deteriorated further, according to people close to them.
“It’s a little bit like an Indian soap opera,” said Kumar at the Indian School of Business. “It’s quite a headache for Noel.”
Local media have speculated that Tata Sons’ board could ask Chandrasekaran to reconsider his departure to help steady the ship ahead of an IPO, but a person close to the company said his staying on was “not an option”.
Executives close to Tata said the group’s leadership was considering its options ahead of a board meeting on Thursday, including whether to mount a legal challenge to the RBI decision, which could delay a flotation.
“Litigation through India’s court system . . . has historically run long,” said Sumit Agrawal, managing partner at Mumbai-based Regstreet Law Advisors and a former officer at India’s capital markets regulator. But he cautioned on Tata’s “low probability of success”.
“Indian courts have historically given RBI wide deference on prudential and systemic classification matters,” he said, “generally applying a light-touch reasonableness standard rather than second-guessing the regulator’s technical judgment.”
An executive close to Tata acknowledged a legal challenge would give the company “some time, but I don’t think it will be more than that”.
The ultimate decision on how to respond will depend on the charitable trusts, but that process could prove complicated.
One of the principal bodies, the Sir Ratan Tata Trust, faces regulatory scrutiny and has been blocked from conducting business or board meetings until its conclusion.
A person familiar with the matter said Tata’s management team under Chandrasekaran had already started working quietly on IPO paperwork this year, but a listing could still take two years.
“In the long run, there is no way they can escape this listing,” said Kumar. “It’s like fighting a tide . . . the only thing is they can delay this tide.”

rows.title: Chevron plans drilling spree as it overhauls oil and gas search
rows.content:
Chevron plans drilling spree as it overhauls oil and gas search
Chevron plans to dramatically increase the number of wells it drills next year as part of a surge in spending which aims to overhaul how the US company searches for oil and gas.
Kevin McLachlan, who was recruited from TotalEnergies last year to lead Chevron’s exploration arm, told the FT his budget would jump by more than 50 per cent compared with 2025, as he seeks to turn around a disappointing performance at the unit.
The extra funds are part of a shake-up at Chevron’s exploration arm, which includes greater use of artificial intelligence technologies, enhanced accountability and new hires to bring fresh ideas, he said.
Chevron’s spending on conventional exploration and appraisal activity plunged 36 per cent to $1.82bn between 2021 and 2025 compared to the previous five-year period, according to data from Wood Mackenzie, a research group.
But after a decade in which Chevron concentrated investment on less risky drilling programmes and the US shale patch, the company is expanding exploration activity in frontier locations, including South America, Sub-Saharan Africa and the Eastern Mediterranean in search of blockbuster discoveries.
“Two years ago . . . we drilled 10 wells. Next year we’ve got a programme of 20 exploration wells and probably, I don’t know, five or six appraisal wells on top of that. So, it’s a significant increase,” he said in his first interview since taking the role last November.
“We needed to increase the spend because we just didn’t have the exposure. So we’ve increased our spend on seismic data, which is the enabling piece of how to generate prospects, without which you can’t generate ideas.”
Last year, Chevron boss Mike Wirth told analysts he was “not happy” with the exploration teams’ results after they struggled to find new discoveries in recent years. It followed an announcement in July 2025 that Chevron did not find commercial quantities of oil and gas at a highly anticipated well in Namibia’s Orange Basin.
The company’s reserves — the amount of oil and gas it can potentially extract — had also fallen to a decade low of 9.8bn barrels of oil equivalent by the end of 2024, which is almost half that of its biggest rival ExxonMobil.
Soon after, Chevron poached McLachlan from TotalEnergies, where the geophysicist was credited with turning around performance at the French company’s exploration division after a period of high spending and limited successes. McLachlan prioritised drilling low-cost and low-emissions prospects while at Total and made several high-profile discoveries in Suriname, South Africa and Namibia.
Exploration teams led by McLachlan at TotalEnergies won the coveted “most admired explorer” at Wood Mackenzie’s annual exploration awards in 2020, 2021 and 2023. They also scooped the “Discovery of the Year” award in 2023 for the Venus discovery in offshore Namibia — one of the largest offshore discoveries made in the past decade.
“I wouldn’t be here if the intention wasn’t to have this accolade come to Chevron,” said McLachlan when asked if he could repeat his success at what he calls Chevron’s “exploration factory”.
Chevron’s total exploration spending — which, unlike Wood Mackenzie’s data, includes spending on unconventional projects, including shale — is likely to surpass $1.5bn this year, up from just under $1bn last year.
The company is making more and larger bets to find oil and gas. Last year, it secured exploration blocks in Brazil, Egypt, Guinea-Bissau, the Gulf of Mexico, Namibia, Peru and Suriname. Chevron’s total exploration acreage has doubled since 2024.
Andrew Latham, senior vice-president of energy research at Wood Mackenzie, said Chevron was the “comeback kid” in high-impact exploration, after underperforming many of its peers due to its concentration on growing its shale operation in the Permian Basin, the largest US oilfield.
“As the Permian now starts to mature, international wildcatting is back high on its agenda,” he said.
McLachlan pinpoints several hotspots of activity including Namibia, Guyana, Guinea-Bissau and Egypt but cautions against a tendency to try to “pick winners”.
“We’re looking to build new businesses. This isn’t just about one good opportunity,” he says. “You have to execute a programme. You need statistics on your side. You need to use all the technology and interpretations.”
Chevron is incorporating artificial intelligence into its exploration activities under a programme called “exploration moonshot”, which is designed to drive efficiency and improve outcomes.
The company is testing AI tools on vast amounts of seismic data to perform tasks that human interpreters cannot and then testing the results.
“We’re testing the machine before we let it go. It was 90 per cent accurate in its predictability of the discovery wells against the dry holes. That is pretty good,” he said.
“We’re really on the cusp and I believe this is going to be transformational to our quality and success rate ultimately. We are also generating prospects with it . . . The world is changing fast and we are part of that.”
But human expertise will remain central to the company’s exploration efforts, as it seeks to compete with Exxon, which, together with its partner Hess, made one of the largest oil discoveries in decades in Guyana in 2015. Part of the team that found the 1bn-plus barrel Liza oilfield about 120 miles off the coast of Guyana now works with McLachlan following Chevron’s $53bn takeover of Hess.
“We’ve kept the Guyana-dedicated team in place working with ExxonMobil. But we’ve also integrated into exploration their ideas,” said McLachlan, adding that this has brought new perspectives and talent into Chevron.
McLachlan has made several key hires, including Emmanuelle Garinet, who he worked closely with at Total and is now Chevron’s director of exploration Americas and Sub-Saharan Africa. Last month, Chevron announced it had found oil at a well drilled off the coast of Angola, an encouraging early-stage discovery that could build momentum for its work in Sub-Saharan Africa.
McLachlan says he would not make bets on where the future discoveries are going to come from but he suggests the company has the right building blocks in place for success.
“I’m excited . . . we have things in the pipeline, you’ll see more,” he says.

rows.title: The long shadow of quantitative easing
rows.content:
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
Good morning. As a percentage of nominal GDP, the balance sheets of the Bank of England, the European Central Bank and the Federal Reserve are now at levels not seen since before the era of Covid-19 expansions. But the central banks’ experience of shrinking their balance sheets — a process known as quantitative tightening — suggests they may not be able to go much further, and nor do they really need to.
The Fed was the first to start normalising its balance sheet in 2017. Its first attempt ended in August 2019, only for a repo-market blow-up the next month to reveal that it had gone too far. Its second attempt has been more orderly, but to avoid another “repocalypse” it ended QT late last year.
The BoE’s approach has been the most controversial. Unlike the Fed and ECB, it has shrunk its bond portfolio through maturities and outright gilt sales. As a share of GDP, its balance sheet has fallen by just over half from its 2022 peak. But this may also have pushed up UK borrowing costs, with some estimates putting the effect as high as 0.7 percentage points. The BoE will decide on September 17 how much further to shrink the balance sheet over the coming year.
The ECB was the last to start quantitative easing and has also been the slowest to unwind it. Its balance sheet was shrinking before it began QT, but mainly because banks were repaying crisis-era loans and nominal GDP was rising quickly. Its caution reflects the challenges of maintaining financial stability across a 21-country currency union.
The era of large-scale asset purchases may be over, but large central bank balance sheets are probably here to stay.
Send us your thoughts: [email protected].

rows.title: CATL develops pick-up truck batteries for US despite trade barriers
rows.content:
CATL develops pick-up truck batteries for US despite trade barriers
CATL has developed a new battery technology for American vehicles despite the Chinese group being mostly shut out by US trade barriers amid security concerns and tense relations between Washington and Beijing.
Zhu Lingbo, chief technology officer of CATL’s international business unit, said the world’s biggest battery maker has developed “tall” batteries with the power output needed for American pick-up trucks. He said the batteries for the lucrative market had already been tested by US carmakers, although he did not specify which companies.
The comments came as US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent and his Chinese counterpart He Lifeng are scheduled to meet in New York ahead of a high-stakes summit in Washington between presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping.
The leaders of the world’s two most powerful economies, who last met in Beijing in May, are expected next week to discuss AI, access to the Chinese-dominated supply chain for rare earths and the expiry in November of the trade war truce.
CATL dominates the market for electric vehicle batteries and has been aggressively pivoting to batteries for energy storage and data centres.
The group, alongside large swaths of the Chinese EV and battery industry, has for years been knocking on the door of the American auto and energy sectors with low-cost, high-tech cars and batteries.
However, the Chinese groups face high tariffs, requirements for localisation as well as the threat of bans on national security concerns from Washington. CATL was last year designated by the Pentagon as having alleged military links; the company denies the claim.
Sales of EVs in the US have plummeted after the end of EV tax credits and Trump’s rollback in regulations to cut vehicle emissions. According to research group Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, the penetration of EVs and plug-in hybrids in the US is expected to remain less than 10 per cent this year, compared with 65 per cent in China.
Taken together, the barriers make it almost impossible for Chinese groups to competitively export EVs or their batteries to the US or invest in US factories.
Zhu, speaking on Sunday at the company’s headquarters in Ningde, in the south-east of China, said “even with this kind of very intense geopolitics” the US market holds the potential to be “huge business”.
He said CATL could potentially license the new battery technology for US groups to manufacture on American soil. This would be a similar arrangement the group already has with Ford and Tesla for EV battery production in the US.
Ford has recently widened its relationship with CATL to produce energy storage batteries, which has angered members of Congress and fellow Detroit automakers.
Industry groups representing the US auto industry sent a letter to Trump last week, calling for the government to maintain its policy to keep Chinese carmakers and supply chains out of America. The letter came after Trump recently said he would “be OK” if China wanted to build car plants in the US as long as they hired American workers.
In Europe, CATL is developing new battery factories in Hungary and Spain, alongside its German plant. It is also building battery-swapping stations for electric lorries in Europe.
The company is also actively scouting new European locations for production facilities, Zhu said, without naming which countries. He added that CATL would require Beijing’s sign-off for any further European investment.

rows.title: How Switzerland turned tax competition into a national sport
rows.content:
How Switzerland turned tax competition into a national sport
As countries across Europe compete to lure the world’s wealthy and their money, Switzerland has a peculiar advantage: it has spent decades competing with itself.
European governments are wrestling with how much they can tax highly mobile companies and wealthy individuals without driving them away — or how much they should offer to persuade them to come. Greece and Italy, particularly, are stepping up the competition to draw people and business in Europe.
But Switzerland has been conducting its own version of this experiment for decades. Its 26 cantons compete fiercely for companies, wealthy residents and the taxes they bring. When there is a dispute over where someone really lives, rivals can end up in court, with judges examining everything from water bills and supermarket shopping to toilet paper purchases to decide which canton gets to collect the tax.
Politicians are happy to join in. Heinz Tännler, finance director of low-tax Zug, has suggested that left-run cities such as Zurich drive away the taxpayers his canton attracts. He has described them as some of Zug’s most useful economic promoters.
The latest prize in this cantonal contest is Vontobel. The 102-year-old private bank said last month that it would move its headquarters and more than 1,500 employees from Zurich to a new campus in Baar, in Zug, from 2030. About 300 client-facing staff will remain in central Zurich.
For Zurich, it is unquestionably a loss. A prominent headquarters, jobs and tax revenues will cross the cantonal border. The move has revived debate over whether Switzerland’s largest city is doing enough to compete with its lower-tax neighbours.
The country’s highly decentralised federal system gives cantons wide powers over taxation, while municipalities also set their own rates. The result is something akin to international tax competition compressed into a country of 9mn people.
Lucerne this year narrowly dethroned Zug as the canton with Switzerland’s lowest corporate tax burden (11.66 per cent vs 11.71 per cent), compared with about 19 per cent in Zurich and 14 per cent in Geneva. For wealthy individuals the gaps can be wider still: the top personal income tax rate is about 22 per cent in Zug, compared with more than 40 per cent in Geneva. Schwyz, next to Zurich, has meanwhile become a favourite home for wealthy residents drawn by some of the country’s lowest personal tax rates.
SGS, the testing and inspection group that had long been headquartered in Geneva, completed its move to Baar in Zug this year. The company had said the “value creation” — or financial benefits — of moving to Zug, including incentives, was twice as high as relocating to another office in Geneva.
Geneva is responding to concerns. Its voters approved a corporate tax overhaul in 2019 that sharply reduced rates for many companies and backed cuts to personal income tax in 2024. And now the canton is pursuing another prize. Millennium Management, one of the world’s biggest hedge funds, is in discussions with the canton over a tax deal as it considers expanding its presence there.
Vontobel says tax was not behind its move. The bank needed space to bring together staff spread across seven Zurich buildings. Baar offered a modern campus, good transport links and room to expand. Daniel Leupi, Zurich’s finance chief, has also pushed back against suggestions of an exodus from his canton. Only one other company among the city’s 50 biggest corporate taxpayers has moved to a lower-tax canton over the past decade, he wrote in the Neue Zürcher Zeitung.
There are limits to playing Zug at its own game. Leupi estimates that cutting Zurich’s cantonal profit tax rate from 7 to 6 per cent would cost the city SFr150mn ($183mn). Replacing that revenue would require companies employing about 75,000 people. Zurich, he argues, simply does not have room for them.
That gets to the clever part. A company moving from Zurich to Zug is a defeat for Zurich, but not necessarily for Switzerland. Baar is little more than 20 minutes by train from Zurich. Companies and taxpayers can cross tax borders without leaving the same economic region, let alone the country.
Other governments are trying to decide how much sovereignty they can monetise to attract the global rich. Switzerland has made its cantons compete to do much the same thing.
“It’s good to try to be better than your neighbours,” said a Swiss executive at a business industry association. “That’s the way our federalist system works.”

rows.title: The Gulf cargo trade that vanished
rows.content:
The Gulf cargo trade that vanished
David, a businessman from the UK, set up his healthcare company in Dubai more than five years ago because the city “was perfectly positioned between Europe and Asia”.
But almost seven months into the conflict triggered by the US and Israeli attacks on Iran, conditions for his company — which imports medical examination gloves from China and south-east Asia and sells them in the Gulf and the UK — have changed sharply.
For most of this year, his business has been paying up to $10,000 to ship a 40ft container to the United Arab Emirates from China, up from $1,250 before Iran largely closed off the vital Strait of Hormuz. Marine insurance costs have shot up from $120 per container to $1,000.
Typical transit times from China to the UAE have doubled to 60 days. The businessman, who asked that his full name not be used, said loads were often stuck halfway, awaiting transhipment at India’s Mundra port or Colombo in Sri Lanka.
“Business is good, if only I can get products into port,” David said. “It’s a nightmare to get containers into the UAE just now.”
For more than a month, President Donald Trump has been boasting that the strait is open, its mines cleared, and the US is in “control” of the waterway — despite ongoing tit-for-tat strikes with Iran.
His administration has repeatedly said the US has been escorting tankers loaded with millions of barrels of crude oil through the chokepoint.
Yet while Trump focuses on oil, the strait remains shuttered to other commodities. Businesses have for months been incurring huge costs to circumvent what has become the main battleground in the US’s war with Iran.
As well as supplying much of the world’s oil, the Gulf is also a key supplier of liquefied natural gas, refined fuels, petrochemicals, feedstock for fertilisers and helium. Qatar, the world’s second-largest producer of LNG, has exported negligible amounts of gas since the war began.
While some oil tankers have been shuttling in and out of the strait under US air cover, other shipping traffic has fallen to minimal levels, in part because the rates those vessels can earn — compared with much higher rates for tankers — make it not worth the risk.
Supertankers are in some cases earning record rates for Middle East trades of $1mn per day, while bulk cargo ships are still only earning in the tens of thousands.
Container ships are among the most risk-averse. The number that travelled through to the Gulf between March 1 and September 7 this year was down to 240, some 94 per cent down from 4,198 vessels a year earlier, according to maritime analyst Xeneta.
Before the crisis, 99 container services operated in or transited into the Gulf, amounting to 10 per cent of the global container fleet. Only 11 remain active, 10 of which are shuttling between ports within the Gulf, while one is a dedicated Iran-China service.
Exports of critical commodities have fallen away. In January, 2.93mn tonnes of limestone travelled through the strait, along with 1.45mn tonnes of sulphur, 1.1mn tonnes of nitrogen fertiliser and 1.74mn tonnes of corn, according to commodities platform Kpler.
In August, those numbers fell to zero for limestone, 120,000 tonnes of sulphur, 340,000 tonnes of nitrogen fertiliser and 310,000 tonnes of corn. These include dry-bulk cargo ships travelling to and from Iran.
In the Gulf itself, there have not been serious shortages, but some brands have disappeared from shops’ shelves. A sports shop said it had run out of children’s cycling helmets; car dealers have been unable to bring in new models; bars have run out of specific drinks. And costs for businesses and consumers have risen.
“What the Americans are doing now is not viable long term . . . it’s only focused on getting oil and gas out, it’s not focused on getting cargo and commodities in,” said a Gulf official. “Eventually there’s a limit to this.
“We’re paying three times the price of rice [before the war] because we’re doing it overland. It’s OK for now, but not long term — not for the Gulf and not for the Americans.”
Jason Tuvey, Middle East economist at Capital Economics, said the pressure on supplies would strain Gulf countries’ national budgets. They have “certainly been providing fiscal support to alleviate supply disruptions and most, with the exception of the UAE, have kept local fuel prices steady,” he said.
“That all comes at a fiscal cost, and at a time when the likes of Qatar, Kuwait and Bahrain are suffering a big blow to their revenues.” Saudi Arabia would likely need to keep cutting back spending, he said.
Shipping companies face more disruption after Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels this month tightened their control over the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, another strategic waterway.
A key problem is that Jebel Ali port on Dubai’s northern coast, by far the region’s biggest shipping hub, has in effect been cut off from the sea by the shuttering of the Strait of Hormuz.
Before the war, it handled about 40,000 20-foot equivalent units (TEU) a day, according to Lloyd’s List, making Jebel Ali the ninth-busiest port in the world.
Goods shipped to and from the east and west would dock there. Those destined for the UAE’s neighbours would be transferred on to smaller vessels for their onward journey.
But now the main UAE port for transit cargo outside the Strait of Hormuz is Khor Fakkan, which is far smaller. Khor Fakkan has six berths and 18 quay cranes, compared with Jebel Ali’s 27 berths and 120 cranes.
Khor Fakkan is now struggling with the volumes being thrust its way.
“I’ve had a couple of containers dumped in Mundra and then I have to wait and hope for confirmation that they are going to be put on the next ship,” David said. “It just depends on available capacity.”
Others are trucking in goods over land from Omani ports, from Jeddah or from Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea coast. Gulf governments are flying in items considered a priority.
As a result, Oman has enjoyed a boom at its ports, which lie outside the strait, with cargo volume soaring 69 per cent this year. Transit truck traffic has increased nearly threefold to 116,088 so far in 2026 from a year earlier, according to official Omani data.
Businesses operating in Qatar, Bahrain and Kuwait have little choice but to truck or fly goods in, as those states’ ports lie inside the Gulf on the wrong side of the cul-de-sac that is Hormuz.
“You have countries like Qatar: basically the way that we serve them today is bring the cargo to Jeddah, truck it to Dammam and then take it on the ship to Qatar. That’s the quickest way to get it there,” said Vincent Clerc, chief executive of Danish shipping line Maersk.
Hapag-Lloyd, the German shipping line, said the so-called “land bridge” added around seven to 10 days of extra time and “significant additional infrastructure and co-ordination”. The company said the Gulf crisis had left it incurring additional costs of $50mn per week.
It is a huge challenge for trucks and planes to match the volumes that container vessels can transport.
Tobias Maier, chief executive for the Middle East and Africa at DHL Global Forwarding, said it takes 10,000 trucks to ferry the equivalent of one ship carrying 20,000 20ft containers. A Boeing 777 jet, meanwhile, could typically handle 100 tonnes of cargo, similar to just five 20ft containers, he added.
“So to replace one ship of 20,000 20ft containers you need 4,000 flights,” he said. “It’s just the mathematics.”
The slower journeys also bring problems.
Clients of Europastry, a producer of frozen bakery goods, have been using ships and trucks to transport the company’s products to the UAE from Europe. Dovile Vilkiene, the group’s general manager for the Middle East, said alternative trade routes had become “newly established”. But the lead times can be challenging.
“It takes three or four weeks more than before. We also face issues with the shelf lives of the goods that arrive because of uncontrollable routes and delays at the offloading,” she said. “At the same time, manufacturing and raw material costs are increasing.
“The customers here don’t want to absorb price increases,” she said, as they face rising costs across their businesses as a result of the war.
Scott Livermore, chief economist at Oxford Economics Middle East, said food was at the centre of the inflationary effects of the crisis. Food prices were “particularly sensitive to trade disruption, with producers already reporting higher input costs. This channel is heavily influenced by shipping traffic,” he said.
Dubai’s DP World, which operates Jebel Ali, is planning two new port terminals in Fujairah, one of the UAE’s emirates on the Gulf of Oman coast, in a push by the UAE to reduce economic exposure to the strait. The facilities, with roughly half of Jebel Ali’s general cargo capacity, will take about two years to build.
David, the British businessman, said Dubai remained his preferred hub for business, adding that the planned new Fujairah ports should alleviate the UAE’s shipping bottlenecks.
But until then, and as long as shipping through the strait is throttled, he said: “We will inevitably do less business here.”

rows.title: Scotch producers fume over legal protection for English whisky
rows.content:
Scotch producers fume over legal protection for English whisky
Scotch whisky backers have attacked the UK government’s decision to grant geographical indication status to English whisky, arguing that new rules in England risk hurting the reputation of Scotland’s most valuable goods export.
Last week, UK ministers approved legal protection for English whisky, bringing it in line with Scotch, Welsh and Irish counterparts.
The change, which takes effect next month, means “English Whisky” and “English Whiskey” will be legally protected names under the UK Spirit Drinks Geographical Indications (GI) scheme and officially recognises the product as distinct from neighbouring categories.
Under current rules, single malt Scotch whisky must be mashed, fermented and distilled at a single distillery in Scotland, according to the Scotch Whisky Association (SWA), which speaks for the sector. Some processes involved in producing English single malt whisky can take place outside the primary distillery, it said.
Wendy Chamberlain, Liberal Democrat MP for North East Fife, on Tuesday said the UK government’s move risked disadvantaging Scotch producers that had invested to meet traditional production standards, and called for it to be “properly scrutinised”.
The ruling Scottish National Party called for the decision to be reversed, saying it would add to other challenges facing Scotch such as duties and high energy costs.
“Our whisky is our premier product and it is absolutely wrong for the Labour UK government to dilute that status by giving English whisky the same legal protections,” said Laura Mitchell, SNP MSP for Moray, which is home to brands such as Glenfiddich, The Macallan and The Glenlivet.
In 2025, the value of Scotch exports was £5.4bn, representing almost a quarter of Scotland’s international goods exports and 21 per cent of all UK food and drink exports.
The SWA said it was “profoundly concerned” by the decision, saying it undermined the established definition of “single malt” and “jeopardises the category which the Scotch whisky industry established”. It was considering its position and “next steps” following consultation with the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), the trade body added.
Scotch makes up more than 90 per cent of single malt worldwide and more than 95 per cent of single malt in the UK.
Unlike Scotch, English whiskies must be made from 100 per cent UK-grown cereal grain, and will be allowed to mature in wooden casks other than oak.
The English Whisky Guild, a new trade body formed to represent English whisky producers, first applied for GI status in 2022.
Tagore Ramoutar, vice-chair of the English Whisky Guild, called the objections “bewildering” because the GI-codified production practices had existed in England for more than two decades.
“Without the English whisky GI, these practices would continue without any regulation,” he said. “I think the debate would be much more interesting if it focused on our groundbreaking rule that English whisky must only use UK grain.”
The number of English whisky distilleries has jumped from 46 in 2023 to 70 today. The sector already exports to 32 different countries, including Canada, Japan and China.
