The Scotch whisky industry has faced several tough years as overproduction over the past decade has combined with a slump in demand triggered by a global cost of living crisis and changing drinking trends.
In the first half of 2026, the value of Scotch exports rose about 3 per cent to £2.5bn, with volumes up more than 6 per cent to 655mn 70cl bottles.
UK whisky was carved out of the US tariff regime by President Donald Trump and has benefited from UK free trade agreements with countries such as India, where demand for Scotch is growing.
Defra said in a statement that the English Whisky application was considered through the statutory GI process and the government remained committed to supporting the success of the Scotch whisky industry and the wider UK sector.
There was no statutory UK-wide definition of “single malt” and each whisky had its own traditions and practices, the department added.

rows.title: Trump rejects calls from tech bosses for AI slowdown
rows.content:
Donald Trump rejects calls from tech bosses for AI slowdown
Donald Trump has rejected calls for an AI slowdown after tech bosses and Democrats urged tighter regulation of the industry over rising fears that the technology poses an existential threat.
The heads of some of the leading US AI groups — Dario Amodei of Anthropic, Sam Altman of OpenAI and SpaceX’s Elon Musk — this weekend called for a more cautious pace of development following dramatic safety warnings over rapidly advancing model capabilities.
But the president said on Sunday that while some “guardrails” were possible, it was imperative for the US to retain its international leadership in the area.
“Look, we’re leading China in AI . . . and, frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins,” Trump told reporters during a trip to his Doonbeg golf course in Ireland.
“We can put guardrails, we can do this and that, but I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn’t be bringing it up and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen,” he added.
The comments come two weeks before China’s President Xi Jinping is expected to visit Washington for a summit with Trump following their meeting in Beijing in May.
After the May summit, Trump said the two leaders had discussed AI guardrails. Chinese state media said the presidents had agreed to set up an AI dialogue.
Advocates for AI safety are hoping that Trump and Xi will have further discussions on AI in Washington, particularly as the bilateral dialogue does not appear to have produced any high-level meetings on the issue so far. In recent months, the US has accused Chinese companies of stealing the intellectual property of American AI labs through a process known as “distillation”.
Safety concerns surrounding the rapid pace of AI advances were thrown into the spotlight over the past week after Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned with a warning that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
Anthropic chief Amodei responded in an essay on Saturday that the industry “must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models” and called for the monitoring of frontier companies by third-party evaluators, the establishment of industry safety standards and global co-ordination of rules.
Altman and Musk voiced support for the proposals.
But the Trump administration and Republican lawmakers pushed back, arguing that the companies can take steps to slow their advance without the need for drastic measures that would hand a competitive edge to China.
The president’s former AI tsar David Sacks said on Saturday night that the companies should “stop pretending you need anyone else’s permission”.
“Go ahead and pace the frontier. You are the ones setting it,” Sacks wrote on X.
“The easiest way not to build superintelligence is for you to agree not to build it. Demanding your preferred regulatory framework as the price of that will look like blackmail of the public and the political system.”
Mike Johnson, Republican Speaker of the House of Representatives, urged people not to “panic” as he echoed Trump’s concerns about China and called for a meeting between tech bosses and lawmakers at the White House.
“We cannot put a moratorium on this, because China will overlap us, and that’s the challenge. It’s national security, balanced with the immediate security of making sure the models are safe,” Johnson told CNN’s State of the Union.
Democrats lashed out at the Republican response and demanded rapid steps towards industry regulation. Arizona senator Ruben Gallego accused both Johnson and Trump of “not meeting the moment” on the threat posed by AI.
“We can’t just use this idea that if we do this we’re somehow going to lose to China, because AI does not care, once it becomes fully dangerous, whether we’re Chinese or American,” he said.
At a campaign rally in Athens, Georgia, Democratic senator Jon Ossoff blasted Trump for his response and accused tech titans of digging “bunkers” while warning of human extinction.
“A capable president would move swiftly to secure and reassure the American people, rush inspectors into frontier labs, fortify the nation against bioterrorism, demand legislation from Congress and lead the world to an AI treaty,” he said.
“But instead the president and the speaker of the House sit on their hands and hope for the best.”
Hakeem Jeffries, House minority leader and Johnson’s Democratic counterpart, told ABC This Week that Republicans had “abandoned their responsibility” and called for Congress to “take decisive action now”.
Coxon, the former Anthropic researcher, on Sunday welcomed Amodei’s proposal as a “substantial step” towards slowing the unchecked advancement of frontier AI but said there was a need for “more engagement with China”.
“The concept of building a superintelligence . . . it’s been likened to summoning an alien species,” he told ABC. “So I think thinking about it in terms of an alien mind that we don’t fully understand is — is pretty terrifying.”

rows.title: AI bosses’ safety push sparks rift inside OpenAI and Anthropic
rows.content:
AI bosses’ safety push sparks rift inside OpenAI and Anthropic
Bold promises by the bosses of Anthropic and OpenAI to constrain AI’s development are sparking tensions inside the two companies over security and other concerns, highlighting the practical challenges of turning rhetoric into reality.
Staff at the makers of Claude and ChatGPT are rushing to implement recommendations from their respective chief executives, Dario Amodei and Sam Altman, to slow AI’s rate of progress to avert disastrous consequences, following a series of dire warnings from researchers.
The two chiefs have become increasingly vocal in recent months about the need to “pace the frontier” of AI model development, culminating in a rare show of unity between the two rivals last weekend. Despite their public comments, little is in place internally to implement the new proposals, according to several people close to the companies.
Amodei published a detailed essay on Saturday calling for slower AI development, independent model evaluations and increased co-ordination between labs and governments globally. He has also called for legal protection from US competition rules that could inhibit such collaboration, which other AI labs are also anxious to secure.
Staff inside OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as the safety researchers they would rely on to conduct this work, were blindsided by the weekend’s announcements. Though many employees agree about the need to slow down, they also fear that putting it into practice could jeopardise their work.
A particular issue inside both companies is the plan to embed outside evaluators within the labs to oversee model development. Some fear this could compromise the security of their prized technology, according to people familiar with internal discussions, with one describing it as a source of “conflict”.
Amodei, who left OpenAI to found Anthropic in 2021 over safety concerns, on Saturday proposed that external testers should have “employee-like access” to the leading labs, including badges, laptops, entry to offices and access to internal tools.
Leading AI companies already engage third parties to test their models for performance and safety, but Amodei’s proposal would substantially increase their role.
Altman said it was a “great idea” and that OpenAI would follow suit.
However, their consensus is far from complete. OpenAI said it wanted to work with other labs but that its approach to the issues was more pragmatic than that of Anthropic.
OpenAI also said it had “already taken concrete steps, including pausing certain frontier training, to pace development”, while Anthropic has not put its research on hold.
Implementing the chief executives’ commitments to increase access for third-party experts while balancing security and data protection will also pose big practical challenges, according to people close to both companies.
Some staff members are concerned about granting outsiders too much access to systems that are both extremely powerful and the focus of intense competition in the tech industry.
AI labs already have strict security measures for employees, including only granting access to certain systems or restricting training data.
In recent months, OpenAI has tried to further restrict access to protect intellectual property and sensitive information and to prevent rogue employees from tampering with systems. The company said providing meaningful access while protecting sensitive systems requires careful design.
“Right now, most third-party organisations have much, much less access than even the lowest-access full-time employee. So probably there will need to be some kind of binding requirement to establish this across the industry,” said Miles Brundage, a former OpenAI researcher who is now executive director at the AI Verification and Evaluation Research Institute.
Anthropic said it has long worked with third-party assessors and intends to embed an evaluator within the company in the near future.
The independent organisations that act as evaluators have gained prominence this year after security breaches by AI agents during testing and development at OpenAI and Anthropic.
Two non-profits, METR and Redwood Research, led an investigation into OpenAI agents’ July attack on AI developer site Hugging Face, reviewing tens of thousands of logs from more than 1,200 agents.
OpenAI said the collaboration set an important precedent for the industry and can inform future investigations. They received laptops from OpenAI with evidence, and were able to work from the company’s San Francisco headquarters and interview staff. The two research groups did not receive payment for the investigation, published last month.
However, the investigation attracted criticism for its extremely limited scope, with specific dates that confined it to the Hugging Face incident.
Other critics have accused the safety organisations of being too cosy with the AI labs to provide effective oversight. “Stop pretending METR is independent when it is intertwined with Anthropic’s investors and staff,” White House AI adviser David Sacks said in a post on X on Sunday.
METR said it does not accept donations from AI companies or their staff and that its employees have to declare conflicts. “Our goal is to get information from inside these companies into the public domain,” it added.
David Krueger, who used to work at the UK’s AI Security Institute, the government agency that tests models, said governments rather than AI labs should determine access.
“All of these organisations only have the access that the AI companies grant them, and that is just completely inadequate,” said Krueger, a professor of responsible AI at the University of Montreal.
“[The focus on evaluations] gets the burden of proof fundamentally backwards; it creates a precedent of acting like AI systems are safe until proven dangerous,” he added.
Amodei has advocated for federal legislation requiring permanent embedded evaluators and third-party audits, while also proposing a narrow antitrust exemption so companies can collaborate on voluntary rules in the meantime.
Other labs are also seeking an antitrust waiver, worried that without one, they could be targeted by future administrations for illegally collaborating.
Big Tech lobbyists have been visiting lawmakers this week in Washington, pushing for an antitrust carve-out to be tacked on to the National Defense Authorization Act, an annual must-pass defence budget bill.
Attorney-general Todd Blanche on Tuesday declined to say if companies would need an antitrust waiver. “To the extent that those companies are looking to regulate themselves or fix problems that they have, that they should do that, but working with us if necessary,” he said, adding that the Department of Justice was “not going to try to regulate AI”.
The push for guardrails faces opposition from President Donald Trump, who on Monday called AI safety concerns a “hoax” and said a slowdown in American research would harm the US and let Chinese technology catch up.
“Traditional auditors and risk assessors have been thinking about the trust problem for centuries,” said Rajiv Dattani, co-founder of the Artificial Intelligence Underwriting Company, a start-up building auditing for insurance of AI. “The AI industry can draw on successes and failures from electricity, cars, financial audits and nuclear energy.”
Additional reporting by Joe Miller in Washington and George Hammond in San Francisco

rows.title: The British right’s patriotism problem
rows.content:
Sadiq Khan says it is time to defend London against hostile propaganda from the American right. No. Just brush it off. It is beneath the dignity of the best city on Earth to rebut hate videos that someone called RedPill3000 or whatever posts from a ghastly Sun Belt condo. (Or from Moscow.) Also, the hatred is a perverse compliment. Which other city, century after century, unhinges people like this? Which has got inside the heads of tsars and French officials and now Maga? I don’t know but the interest is not reciprocated.
It is at least nice to see whose side Khan is on. Others in British politics, further to the right, leave some doubt. Nigel Farage is tongue-tied whenever Americans smear his nation. Perhaps the Reform UK leader doesn’t want to contradict his friends. Perhaps he agrees with them.
This month, two of Farage’s colleagues stepped down after a television sting. In the footage, each seems to propose ways around British electoral law in order to receive a donation from an American. Soon after, Reform UK accepted a total of £72mn from two entrepreneurs who had until recently been living in Hong Kong and Thailand. As with Farage’s silence about Maga’s anglophobia, these gifts seem odd for a British nativist movement. This blessed plot, this earth, this realm, this Koh Samui.
The British right has a patriotism problem. Or would, if Andy Burnham chooses to make an issue of it. Whatever else is wrong with the Labour prime minister — a certain glibness, for example — he seems at ease in his own country.
So do most of his compatriots. Some 57 per cent of Britons are “fairly satisfied” with life. You have to add up those who are “not at all satisfied” and “not very satisfied” just to reach 31 per cent. That share could be enough to elect Farage, of course, given the fragmentation of politics, but he would need to mobilise quite a lot of it and hope the more-or-less content majority doesn’t consolidate behind a cheerier party.
British voters, like American ones, are glum about their country in the abstract but not about their own lives. And so an opposition politician has to proceed with care. Bashing a vague “status quo” is fine. Cross into all-purpose negativity, however, and people start to ask questions. For example, if things are so irredeemable, what would be the point of a new government? Also, do I want to spend five years with this person?
If the right becomes what the left has stereotypically been — a drag to be around — it will lose. Ask yourself who was the last incoming elected prime minister who was a downer. Sir Keir Starmer became one in office and never recovered. The correct answer is perhaps Ted Heath in 1970, and even he just had a lugubrious personal manner rather than an apocalyptic view of Britain.
“Life is crap, vote for us” is a losing message. The first half is not true and, even if it were, the second does not follow. Farage, who built his career on studied bonhomie, used to know all this. Two things have changed since then. One is that he has grown morose with age. The other is that a movement of even bleaker people has grown around him: not just billionaires of a millenarian cast of mind but a voter base that likes very little about modern Britain. More Labour, Liberal Democrat and Green voters approve of King Charles than do Reform UK voters, whose view of other national institutions, and of their fellow citizens, is no sunnier.
lf a socialist is someone who loves The People more than actual persons — the unsmiling Lenin being the classic case — a nationalist is not so different. An abstraction called Britain is dear to them, just not many currently existing three-dimensional elements of it. Even Kemi Badenoch can seem uncomfortable with the country as it is. According to the Conservative leader, Britain must never become “multicultural”. First of all, too late. Second, if the alternative is “assimilation”, as she suggests, where has it worked? France? She should state which of the following she regards as more harmonious, and less of a powder keg: London or Paris, Manchester or Marseille.
Years ago, some western conservatives got it into their heads that Russia, which has a lower fertility rate than Britain, was a fortress of Christian tradition. The constant need to believe that somewhere else has got things right is rather suspect. Oikophobia, the fear or rejection of one’s own, is seen as a disease of the liberal left. Looking at Khan stick up for London, that seems unfair. Last year, Ed Miliband told Elon Musk to “butt out of our politics” while British conservatives stared at their shoes.
To run on patriotism from the left is audacious, but there are successful precedents. Mark Carney in Canada and Anthony Albanese in Australia did it, with some unwitting help from Donald Trump. Burnham is a more natural demagogue than either. He could stigmatise Reform as the plaything of Trump-smitten exiles and bitcoin bros whose first loyalty is to their purses. It is crude stuff and might arouse primal emotions among voters, but he is not going to win the next election with a flutter of those eyelashes alone. “Love it or leave it,” jingoes used to say to critics of their country. We love it, you left it, Burnham can say to at least a few Reform donors.

rows.title: Oil, yen and egonomics
rows.content:
Oil, yen and egonomics
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent cowed currency traders this week by claiming anyone shorting the yen was betting against “the house”. But he has failed to will US government borrowing costs lower, while his boss has failed to will the Strait of Hormuz open again. As Brent crude smashes through $100 a barrel, hosts Rob Armstrong and Katie Martin ask what Bessent can actually do to keep yields from continuing to surge. Also, Rob shorts a lunch-disrupting coffee company, and Katie shorts AI headbangers.
For a free 30-day trial to the Unhedged newsletter go to: https://www.ft.com/unhedgedoffer.
You can email Robert Armstrong and Katie Martin at [email protected].

rows.title: German chancellor Merz vows to stay on despite ‘disaster’ in regional elections
rows.content:
German chancellor Merz vows to stay on despite ‘disaster’ in regional elections
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Sunday vowed to stay in office to press ahead with reforms despite heavy losses for his Christian Democratic Union party and surges in support for the far right and far left in regional elections.
Merz’s conservatives were on the brink of failing to win parliamentary representation in the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, where estimates based on partial results put their vote share at just below 5 per cent, the threshold for entering the Landtag. The CDU secured 13 per cent in previous elections in 2021.
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) was expected to become the largest party in the former East German state, the partial results showed.
The results are set to be the CDU’s lowest in any state election in Germany’s postwar history.
Speaking minutes after polls closed on Sunday, Merz, who is grappling with record unpopularity, sought to quash speculation that the setbacks would trigger an immediate leadership crisis following weeks of mounting unrest within his party.
“This is a disaster,” Merz said of the result in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the former home state of ex-CDU chancellor Angela Merkel.
The result, he added, was a reaction to his government’s necessary economic reforms, which he would seek to pursue in order to achieve “prosperity”.
“The reforms must come,” Merz said, adding: “What needs to be done requires backbone, steadfastness and patience. I will demonstrate this as the CDU’s party leader and, especially, as our country’s chancellor.”
The losses for Merz’s party come two weeks after the AfD’s shock victory in elections in Saxony-Anhalt, where the far-right party is now trying to form its first regional government.
The latest results risk emboldening CDU critics who blame Merz’s low personal ratings and seek a change at the top of the party.
Some CDU insiders told the FT last week that falling below the 5 per cent threshold for representation in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern’s parliament could be a catalyst for a new party leader and even chancellor.
Merz convened a meeting with party heavyweights in Berlin on Sunday evening to consider lessons from the elections and to try to cement their loyalty.
In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, a state of 1.5mn inhabitants, the governing Social Democrats were on course to come second with a vote share of 35.5 per cent, compared with 39.6 per cent in 2021, according to early estimates.
The AfD was expected to more than double its tally to 38.1 per cent, up from 17 per cent.
In the city-state of Berlin, the CDU was projected to be relegated to second place with 19 per cent, down from 28.2 per cent in the previous 2023 elections.
The hard-left Die Linke party, which has vowed to expropriate property from corporate landlords in the German capital, is expected to surge to first place with an estimated 25.1 per cent.
The party, which has also harnessed alarm about the surge of the far right, was set to more than double its result from the 12 per cent it secured in 2023.
The AfD was forecast to come third in Berlin with 15.8 per cent, up from 9 per cent previously.

rows.title: China’s economy shows signs of weakness as investment slumps
rows.content:
China’s economy shows signs of weakness as investment slumps
China’s domestic economic indicators weakened further last month, piling pressure on policymakers to take more forceful measures to reinvigorate growth in the world’s second-largest economy.
Retail sales grew 0.4 per cent year on year in August, data from the National Bureau of Statistics showed on Tuesday, down from 0.6 per cent growth in July and falling short of a median forecast of 0.8 per cent growth from analysts polled by Bloomberg.
Fixed-asset investment declined 7.2 per cent over the first eight months of the year on a year earlier, deepening from a fall of 6.7 per cent in the year to July and slightly weaker than median analyst expectations of minus 7.1 per cent.
Industrial production strengthened, meanwhile, rising 5.2 per cent year on year. That exceeded growth of 4.5 per cent in July and median analysts’ expectations of 4.8 per cent, as China’s export machine has roared ahead in recent months.
“The divergence within China’s economy continued to widen in August, with consumption and investment both underperforming market forecasts, but exports and industrial production both stronger than expected,” said Lynn Song, chief economist for greater China at ING.
China has relied in recent years on industrial output and exports — which rose 25 per cent in August — to drive economic activity, as a five-year property sector slowdown has weighed on household confidence and damped domestic consumption.
The latest data suggested that “strategic manufacturing remains capable of generating strong output growth but the domestic demand base needed to absorb that expanding productive capacity remains weak”, said Yuhan Zhang, principal economist at the Conference Board’s China Center.
“The economy is becoming more dependent on productivity gains, technology upgrading and external demand to monetise new industrial capacity.”
China’s export growth has also swelled its trade surpluses, particularly with the EU. That has stoked tensions, as foreign governments worry that competition from high-quality, lower-cost Chinese goods will lead to deindustrialisation in their own countries.
Zhang said the domestic slowdown and the “globalisation of Chinese industrial capacity” were “two sides of the same story”, with implications for China’s outbound investment, trade relations and manufacturing competition globally.
The slowdown in China’s domestic economic indicators has forced Beijing to signal it will speed up public spending this year. Second-quarter economic growth was reported at 4.3 per cent, one of its lowest readings in decades, as weak consumer demand and falling investment weighed on sentiment.
ING’s Song said the government’s rollout of economic policy support measures has been limited, meaning that “downward growth pressures persist”.
Unless the economy showed “unexpectedly strong” growth in September, he added, third-quarter GDP growth will be close to or below the bottom of the government’s full-year 2026 growth target of 4.5-5 per cent.
The property sector, meanwhile, showed further signs of weakness. Data from the NBS on Tuesday showed that new home prices in 70 cities fell 0.17 per cent from July, when they fell 0.18 per cent. Resale home prices fell 0.31 per cent from 0.29 per cent a month earlier.
Fu Linghui, NBS spokesperson and chief economist, said China’s economy was growing positively and was “expected to maintain stable operation, with the quality of development steadily improving”.
But he added: “Of course, we must also recognise that there are still many risks and challenges on the road ahead. The external environment is complex and severe, and the pressure from domestic structural adjustment remains.”
In an apparent acknowledgment of foreign concerns over China’s trade surpluses, Fu also said that “in the next stage, we must . . . promote balanced trade development”.

rows.title: Lula, Costa, Ruto and Carney: Multilateralism is not idealism, it is a necessity
rows.content:
Multilateralism is not idealism, it is a necessity
The writers are president of Brazil, president of the European Council, president of Kenya and prime minister of Canada
As world leaders head to the UN General Assembly in New York this week, we confront a paradox. The global community is more interdependent than ever, even as it becomes more fragmented and polarised.
Our economies are deeply intertwined. Technology links billions of people across borders, while capital, goods, data and ideas move at speeds that would have been unimaginable when the UN was founded in 1945. Global trade reached a record $35tn last year and 6bn people — almost three quarters of humanity — are connected to the internet.
However, geopolitics is moving the other way. 2025 saw 65 state-based armed conflicts across 35 countries, the highest number recorded since 1946, while global military spending rose to a record $2.9tn. International law is under strain. The language of spheres of influence and power politics is back. Economic ties are increasingly used as instruments of pressure and coercion while inequality is on the rise, both within and among countries.
Some may conclude, therefore, the multilateral system has failed. In part, that criticism is understandable. A multilateral system that fails to reflect the realities of today will not survive the test of time. But the need for multilateral co-operation is very much alive. The postwar world is long gone, but the underlying logic that justified multilateral co-operation is more evident than ever.
The climate emergency is going beyond even the most alarming predictions. AI is advancing faster than our capacity to control it. Pandemics can spread across continents in weeks, while financial shocks can disrupt markets in hours. Armed conflicts can destabilise entire regions and force millions to flee from their homes. Global maritime chokepoints, such as the Strait of Hormuz, constrained by conflicts, can paralyse supply chains around the world. No country, however powerful, can manage these challenges alone. Cooperation is therefore not an act of idealism, it is a practical necessity. The question is not whether multilateralism can survive, but how it must evolve to meet the realities of our time.
In this context, we are coming together with a new initiative: ‘Partners for Multilateralism’. P4M is not about creating another exclusive bloc or another international bureaucracy. Its purpose is the opposite: to create a flexible, open framework for countries from different regions and political traditions that are willing to work across divides, to build coalitions for reform and to translate shared principles into practical action. P4M will support the reform of the UN and other multilateral institutions, to make them more representative, legitimate, effective and trusted. It aims to strengthen co-operation between regional organisations, contribute to peace and security, improve global economic governance and develop common approaches to emerging challenges, from AI and climate change to health security and digital transformation.
P4M will seek to renew and strengthen the multilateral system, not replace it; build bridges and bring together countries that may disagree on many issues but share a commitment to the basic principles enshrined in the UN Charter. Principles that are not negotiable, like sovereign equality, territorial integrity, the peaceful settlement of disputes, the prohibition of the threat or use of force, international humanitarian law, sustainable development, human rights and fundamental freedoms.
UN secretary-general António Guterres recently said that “superpowers are discovering their limits”. We believe that the international community must rediscover the extraordinary potential of collective action.
Competition does not have to become confrontation, if we create channels of dialogue and co-operation. Sovereignty is strengthened, not diminished, when countries work together to address shared challenges. National interests are often best advanced through collective action on such challenges.
The real choice is not between preserving the international order established after the second world war or abandoning it. It is between renewing multilateral co-operation in a changing world, or allowing polarisation and power politics to define the next era.
As we contend with a world order that is transforming fast, we call on other international leaders to join us in choosing co-operation over fragmentation, law over power and shared responsibility over division.

rows.title: Japanese utility halts nuclear reactor restart after data manipulation scandal
rows.content:
Japanese utility halts nuclear reactor restart after data manipulation scandal
A Japanese utility has withdrawn applications to restart a nuclear power plant after an independent committee found that pressure from senior management led workers to manipulate earthquake data submitted to the regulator.
Chubu Electric Power said on Monday it would scrap regulatory reviews to reopen two reactors at its Hamaoka plant, pausing an effort that has been ongoing for more than a decade.
The chief executive and chair also resigned after an independent committee found that workers had deliberately manipulated data to pass regulatory reviews.
The decision marks a significant setback in Japan’s pivot back to nuclear power 15 years after the Fukushima disaster.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi views the restart as critical to bringing down energy costs for residents and providing competitive power for Japan’s AI data centres and traditional manufacturing industries, but the move has been plagued with setbacks.
“Given the serious doubts that have arisen regarding the reliability of the application documents and the company’s subsequent handling of matters in the review process, it would not be appropriate to maintain the existing applications,” said Chubu Electric.
The independent review found Japan’s third-largest utility committed “what could be called an act of concealment” by trying to manufacture data sets that justified the choice of seismic waves used in a safety review to reopen the Hamaoka nuclear power station.
The data sets were estimates of how strongly the site would shake during a range of earthquake scenarios, which regulators used to determine whether a plant’s design could withstand them in quake-prone Japan.
The committee identified an “extremely unusual” culture of Chubu Electric engineers operating “under their own logic” and “their own sense of justice” that sidelined compliance with rules governing nuclear safety.
“Those involved appeared not to recognise that there was anything problematic about what they had done,” the report said.
A whistleblower at the company raised the alarm on data manipulation in 2021, sending an email from three years earlier that showed weaker seismic waves were being selected.
Chubu Electric put the department accused of misconduct in charge of a fact-finding investigation, and the whistleblower hotline eventually responded that no compliance violations had been found.
The independent committee, which was formed after the data manipulation became known in January, said pressure from senior management was one of the factors that led to the misconduct, but it did not find evidence of direct orders from top executives to reverse-engineer the data for the regulator.
Japan’s nuclear industry was rocked by reactor meltdowns at Fukushima Daiichi in 2011, leading to the shutdown of the nation’s fleet of 54 reactors.
The incident exposed what critics called a cosy “nuclear village” of utilities, politicians and regulators that prevented a proper safety regime and enabled complacency over the risks.
The country has restarted 15 reactors since the disaster, and the government is aiming to lift nuclear’s share of power generation from 8.5 per cent to about 20 per cent by 2040. That is down from about 30 per cent pre-Fukushima.
The two reactors at Chubu Electric’s Hamaoka had been one of the big hopes for Japan to extend the revival, but their scheduled restart is likely to be pushed back by at least three years to 2032 and 2035 respectively, according to analysts’ estimates.

rows.title: US manufacturers hit by fresh burst of supply chain cost inflation
rows.content:
US manufacturers hit by fresh burst of supply chain cost inflation
Industrial America is contending with a fresh wave of supply chain inflation as Donald Trump’s Iran war pushes up energy costs, tariffs raise import prices and the AI boom strains supplies of crucial electronics.
Manufacturers are paying sharply more for raw materials, energy and freight, with some input costs rising by double-digit rates, according to executives and industry data, forcing some to raise prices and threatening further pressure on consumer inflation.
“We just need to spend more and more money for the same stuff,” said Julie Robbins, chief executive of EarthQuaker Devices, an Ohio-based manufacturer of guitar pedals.
“It feels like we have to try twice as hard to get the same results,” added Robbins, whose company has had to raise prices twice this year.
The mounting price pressures in the American factory sector are the latest sign of the inflation that is sweeping the US, driven by sharply higher fuel prices, levies on imports and the rush to procure electronics used in AI data centres.
The bout of inflation has become a growing political liability for Trump ahead of the midterm elections, contrasting with his claim at the Republican National Convention meeting in Dallas last week that he was “bringing the prices way down, way, way down”.
The price growth has contributed to a rout in the bond market that on Tuesday pushed the US 10-year yield to its highest level since 2007. Elevated inflation has also prompted bets on Wall Street that the Federal Reserve will lift interest rates on Wednesday.
More than a dozen industries within the factory sector reported rising raw material prices in the Institute for Supply Management’s closely watched August survey of executives, with none reporting declines.
ISM’s overall index of prices has also jumped since the start of 2026 and has shown costs rising for 23 consecutive months. Production managers have reported increases in prices of petroleum-based products and steel and aluminium costs.
“Supply chains are paying more for less inventory,” said Zac Rogers, professor of supply chain management at Colorado State University. “The bang for the buck in the supply chain keeps getting worse and worse.”
Inflation data also points to mounting pressure further up supply chains.
While prices charged by producers for finished goods rose 6.6 per cent year on year in August, the cost of goods used in production increased at a much quicker pace.
The price index for intermediate processed goods jumped 11.5 per cent year on year in August, driven by a surge in diesel costs, while the measure for unprocessed goods, such as scrap metal, rose 12.8 per cent, Bureau of Labor Statistics data shows.
Fuel costs have continued rising sharply since the end of August, with pump prices for diesel reaching a record $6.27 a gallon on Tuesday, according to AAA, the motoring group. Wholesale prices for US diesel also rose sharply on Tuesday, suggesting costs for drivers will soon rise further, analysts said.
The cost of transporting goods has also increased markedly, with the average cost per freight shipment rising 16 per cent in August from a year earlier, according to FT calculations based on Cass Information Systems data.
Some manufacturers say it is also getting harder to find the inputs they need.
Traci Tapani, co-president of Wyoming Machine, a metal fabrication company outside Minneapolis, said the group had experienced “disruption” in its ability to secure raw materials. Steel in particular was posing “noticeable supply issues”.
Most executives distinguished the current supply chain squeeze from the disruptions caused by the Covid-19 pandemic, when goods could not be sourced. For the majority of sectors, they remain available but at notably higher prices.
“We’ve gone from scarcity to cost as the primary concern around supply chains,” said Kip Eideberg, senior vice-president for government and industry relations at the Association of Equipment Manufacturers, whose members make machines from tractors to trucks.
But for the electronics industry, the AI boom has made simply securing goods increasingly challenging. The rapid build-out of data centres has driven a frenzy of demand for specialised parts from memory chips to processors that suppliers are struggling to keep pace with.
The electronics sector’s supply chain was “going through another crisis even bigger and more complicated than during and post-Covid-19”, said an industry respondent to the ISM survey in August.
“The demand is kind of everywhere all at once,” said Shawn DuBravac at the Global Electronics Association. “It is, without doubt, driven by a colossal AI infrastructure investment.”
“Depending on the component you’re looking at, you’ve got multiyear lead times,” he added. “The only way that this strain gets resolved is production increases everywhere across the supply chain, or demand, primarily AI infrastructure demand, slows.”
The shortage is being felt globally. In a GEA survey last month, nearly two-thirds of electronics manufacturers worldwide reported limited component availability or extended lead times.
Despite the price rises, in many industries there is little appetite for making splashy investments in additional capacity, as companies contend with uncertainty over everything from the Iran war to tariffs.
“No company is going to put down a big capital expenditure without some certainty that the market will be the same a year from now,” said Rogers.
Robbins at EarthQuaker said the “constant changes make it so you can’t really develop a long-term plan”.
“As a business owner, you really rely on having stability and clarity on what’s going on, and that is not happening right now,” she said.

rows.title: New fertiliser exporters blunt food crisis fears
rows.content:
New fertiliser exporters blunt food crisis fears
Fears that war in the Middle East would trigger a global food crisis by choking off fertiliser supplies failed to materialise because countries outside the Gulf rushed to fill the gap, trade data shows. 
Urea imports from economies shipping via the Strait of Hormuz have dropped 85 per cent from prewar levels, as the US-Israeli war on Iran all but halted traffic through the waterway. But total import volumes fell only 6 per cent, as alternative suppliers boosted shipments by more than a quarter. 
Egypt and Nigeria increased their urea exports by 98 and 81 per cent respectively over that period, according to the International Trade Centre, a joint agency of the UN and World Trade Organization. The US and Russia grew their share in key markets, the data shows, while China also increased its exports.
Analysts warned that fertiliser prices were rising to unsustainable levels for some of the world’s poorest countries.
“New suppliers emerged and supply chains adjusted to a certain degree. But there has been a cost. For many developing countries, the challenge has shifted from finding supplies to being able to afford them,” Pamela Coke-Hamilton, executive director of the ITC, told the FT.
Before the conflict, about a third of globally traded nitrogen fertilisers such as urea and ammonia passed through the Strait of Hormuz, along with almost half of globally traded sulphur, which is needed to turn phosphorus rock into fertiliser.
Nitrogen, phosphate and potassium are the three main macronutrients needed by commercial crops.
“The quickest and most sure way to a food crisis is to not have nitrogen . . . it’s the most important nutrient that we put on crops,” said Willis Thomas, head of fertilisers at consultancy CRU.
ITC data found that average import costs for urea in the second quarter of 2026 rose by 70 per cent compared with a year earlier, while ammonia and sulphur prices also soared. 
Benchmark urea prices in India peaked at nearly $950 per tonne in May. They have since fallen by more than 50 per cent to about $400, according to CRU. 
In Egypt, producers including Abu Qir Fertilizers, MOPCO, Egyptian Basic Industries Corporation and Egyptian Fertilizers Company increased exports. In Nigeria, Dangote Fertiliser was also able to increase exports, with its 3mn-tonne-a-year urea plant becoming an increasingly important source of supply.
Thomas said China had seen “a lot of growth” in export capacity as well as Egypt and Nigeria — though Chinese exports are not included in the ITC data. 
The ITC analysis found that the effects were highly uneven, warning that higher prices could still lead to pressure on international food markets.
For example, Brazil, a major global exporter of soyabeans, cane sugar and maize, saw the cost of importing urea and sulphur increase by 56 per cent and 176 per cent respectively, with import volumes falling by more than one-third.
African countries are particularly exposed to the crisis, with South Africa, Kenya and Mozambique all sourcing more than 70 per cent of their urea imports from Hormuz suppliers before the conflict.
The ITC analysis warned that the concentration of supply left those economies particularly at risk of disruption to established suppliers and the resultant increase in costs.
Thomas said that while global trade had helped “avert a huge food crisis in the near term, in the longer term, higher fertiliser costs will continue to be an issue.
“Phosphate prices remain stubbornly high,” he added. “You can under-apply phosphate for a year or a couple of years but eventually it starts to hurt yields.”
Data visualisation by Maxine Kelly

rows.title: Brussels rebuffs calls for EU-wide digital services tax
rows.content:
Brussels rebuffs calls for EU-wide digital services tax
Europe’s top tax official has ruled out an EU-wide levy on tech giants such as Amazon, Google and Meta until “all possibilities” at a global level to tax digital services are exhausted, despite a renewed push by France for Brussels to take action.
European Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra told the FT the EU should wait until “we exhaust all the possibilities we have in terms of a global solution”, although international efforts to tax digital services companies have been opposed by the US.
“Otherwise, if you don’t do that, you can always wonder whether you should have been given more of a chance,” he said.
France this month called for an EU-wide digital levy, arguing that it could raise substantial revenue for the bloc’s future budget and reduce the burden on European taxpayers.
Paris has the backing of the European parliament but introducing an EU-wide policy would risk a further deterioration of economic relations with the US.
France, Italy, Spain and Austria already have a digital services levy and have been targeted by the US with Section 301 investigations, potentially leading to retaliatory tariffs.
The US-EU relationship already risks entering a new phase of hostility after European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen backed Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s proposal for Ottawa to become an associate member of the EU on Wednesday. US President Donald Trump said in response that he might consider it a “hostile act” and threatened to impose “very serious tariffs” on the EU.
Paris argues an EU-wide digital services tax would shelter individual countries from bilateral retaliation. It would also be a “major revenue generator” for the future EU budget, which is currently under negotiation, France’s EU affairs minister Benjamin Haddad said.
The Commission’s own research into a digital tax estimates it could raise about €5bn a year depending on its design, according to people briefed on the analysis.
But Hoekstra insisted that “by far the best” solution would be a global approach.
The EU shelved plans to unilaterally tax tech giants following a 2021 multilateral agreement among more than 130 countries to tax large multinationals’ profits where they make sales, known as Pillar 1 of a two-pronged deal brokered by the OECD.
“Our logic has always been, by far the best [solution] is to stick to the universal logic of Pillar 1. But if that unfortunately or for whatever reason doesn’t work, then we move towards [the] second best [solution] and that is doing that at the European level,” Hoekstra said.
G7 finance ministers in May tasked the Paris-based OECD with reporting on progress towards a common approach to taxing the digital economy by the end of December.
But hopes for a breakthrough are low as the US remains opposed to a levy it considers discriminatory against its multinational companies, one official said.
Hoekstra said a decision on whether to proceed with a digital tax at an EU level would need to be made “somewhere in the next few months, roughly around the year’s end”.
The OECD’s tax director Manal Corwin said “constructive conversations” were “ongoing” between countries involved in its process to “address the tax challenges arising from the digitalisation of the economy”.
“Members have a strong interest in addressing these challenges in a multilateral setting, to avoid fragmentation and harmful unilateral approaches, and to ensure a stable and certain international tax environment,” Corwin added.

rows.title: Trump’s Iran war has cost US $38bn and caused munitions ‘shortfall’
rows.content:
Trump’s Iran war has cost US $38bn and caused munitions ‘shortfall’
Donald Trump’s war in Iran has cost the US $38bn and left the military with a shortfall of munitions, according to new reports that provide the most detailed accounting to date on the fiscal toll of the conflict.
New assessments from the defence department’s Inspector General and Congressional Budget Office show that the seven-month conflict is inflicting a significant cost on US taxpayers and the military’s ordnance stockpile.
The “munitions expenditure” during the war “has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply”, said the office of Michael Duffy, the under-secretary of defence for acquisition and sustainment, according to the IG report.
While the Pentagon has moved to expand production capacity for munitions, Duffy’s office said the American defence industrial base needed “significant lead times” to do so. The biggest bottlenecks were the production of solid rocket motors, the availability of high-grade explosives and propellants, and recruiting skilled labour, the report said.
The report also noted that the Pentagon’s munitions expenditures “illustrate the magnitude and complexity of the target set posed by Iran”.
The Pentagon IG’s report, released late on Monday, was the first official acknowledgment from a government entity of the munition shortfall since the beginning of the conflict, which has tipped the global energy market into crisis, sent borrowing costs soaring and set off a new wave of inflation across global economies.
The report also contrasted with the insistence of Trump and defence secretary Pete Hegseth that there is no shortage.
A separate estimate from the CBO, lawmakers’ independent fiscal watchdog, put the cost of the conflict at $38bn, with $21.7bn needed to replace munitions — including $13.1bn for missile defence interceptors. The CBO estimated an additional month of war would cost $2-$3bn, depending on the level of intensity.
The CBO also anticipated that the conflict would raise US inflation by 0.5 percentage points to 3.2 per cent this year. The estimates include the cost of repairing damaged facilities and infrastructure.
The White House has asked Congress for more than $67bn in supplemental funding for the Pentagon due to the war, including $21bn for munitions.
General Kenneth Wilsbach, the US Air Force’s top officer, said on Monday that “it wasn’t easy” to “decimate” the Iranian air force and traditional navy.
“Iran’s not a pushover,” he added.
The IG’s report catalogued the damage inflicted on US bases and military aircraft by Iran, with 22 aeroplanes and helicopters damaged or destroyed, including fighter jets and refuelling tankers. Up to 30 MQ-9 Reaper drones were also damaged or destroyed.
US Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, said Iran’s attacks struck hundreds of buildings and structures on US bases in Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar and Saudi Arabia, according to the report, though it did not estimate the cost of that damage. American diplomatic facilities in Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates suffered approximately $184mn in damage from Iranian strikes.
After the US Navy’s Mideast headquarters in Bahrain was hit by Iranian drones and cruise missiles, the service had trouble establishing adequate alternate ports and naval bases, the report said. The navy was forced to use hubs further away, including at the joint US-UK base at Diego Garcia, creating long logistics cycles of 14 to 18 days.
“They blew the hell out of Bahrain,” acting Navy secretary Hung Cao said last week.

rows.title: Freewheeling Hong Kong takes cue from China with first five-year plan
rows.content:
Freewheeling Hong Kong takes cue from China with first five-year plan
Hong Kong has unveiled its first-ever five-year plan, a sweeping economic blueprint that is seen as bringing policymaking in the once freewheeling entrepôt more in line with China’s state-planning model.
The plan, which covers the period to 2030 and was released alongside city leader John Lee’s annual policy address, marked a significant departure for a financial hub that until the 1960s resisted gathering GDP data for fear of encouraging state intervention.
“The five-year plan is Hong Kong’s economic and societal blueprint for the next five years. It is a forward-looking, strategic and directional guiding document,” Lee told the city’s legislature on Wednesday.
The five-year plan, which coincides with mainland China’s own 15th five-year plan, touches on areas including a future mega-metropolis under construction in Hong Kong’s northern reaches and efforts to strengthen technology and industry, as well as the promotion of traditional Chinese medicine and food processing.
In an op-ed published in local media earlier in the week, Lee also offered reassurances that the plan did not herald the demise of capitalism. “I have also been asked whether formulating a five-year plan would change Hong Kong’s original system. The answer is no,” Lee wrote. “The plan will uphold Hong Kong’s rule of law and capitalist system.”
Five-year plans are often seen as a relic of communist command economies. Russia quietly abandoned its five-year plans after the fall of the Soviet Union.
But five-year plans continue to play an important role in China, where the Chinese Communist Party uses them to lend official imprimatur to top priorities and direct industrial policy across the vast state-owned sector.
The first five-year plan under Mao Zedong in 1953 set out ambitious industrialisation targets and paved the way for the collectivisation of most of the nation’s farms. Beijing’s most recent five-year plan, unveiled this year, targets high-end industries such as semiconductors and biotechnology.
Authorities in Hong Kong, meanwhile, hope the city’s plan will rejuvenate an economy that has been battered by pro-democracy protests in 2019 and the Covid-19 pandemic, which hit business confidence and triggered a population outflow.
Officials in the city have come under pressure from Beijing to deliver tangible gains on housing and new developments after cracking down on political dissent and civil society and overhauling the electoral system to ensure a “patriotic” legislature and, in effect, bar the opposition.
They also hope the plan will help diversify the economy beyond its traditional pillars of finance and trade and bind it closer to the Chinese mainland. Chinese companies have driven a listings boom on Hong Kong’s stock exchange, and more of its new graduates have settled in the city under preferential immigration schemes.
The plan’s real significance was in how it demonstrated a new, more active mode of policymaking, said Gary Ng, senior economist at French investment bank Natixis
“We can talk about many of the . . . details, but it is really about the change in the way of policymaking,” he said.
One major focus is the Northern Metropolis mega-project, a plan to redevelop a swath of territory into industrial, technology and logistics hubs to take advantage of the tech and manufacturing booms that powered neighbouring Guangdong province and the megacity of Shenzhen. Planners hope the project area will eventually house a third of Hong Kong’s population and create 650,000 jobs.
It will also include the construction of 70,000 homes over the next five years, which officials say will help ease a decades-long housing crisis in the city that Beijing views as having fuelled the 2019 protests.
Other parts of the plan focus on boosting sectors including finance, technology and tourism.
But experts said official intervention could threaten the vigorous free markets that characterised Hong Kong in the past. Economist Milton Friedman described Hong Kong as the best example of a free-market economy in action, while the Heritage Foundation, a rightwing US think-tank, ranked the city’s economy as the freest in the world for 21 consecutive years until 2015.
In the 1960s, colonial financial secretary John Cowperthwaite even refused to collect GDP data for fear that doing so would spur officials to meddle in the economy.
“The dynamism and vitality that is the hallmark of [Hong Kong’s] economy was historically based on the entrepreneurial spirit of its people and non-interference from the government,” said Steve Tsang, director of the China Institute at Soas.
A five-year plan represented “a reversal” of that legacy, Tsang added. “I doubt that it will make the economy more vibrant and able to adapt to changing market conditions. But it brings [Hong Kong] in line with the practice on the Chinese mainland.”

rows.title: Labour MPs warn against mansion tax change in Budget
rows.content:
Labour MPs warn against mansion tax change in Budget
Labour MPs have warned against any Budget move to cut a planned “mansion tax” threshold to £1.5mn, with one claiming it would amount to “electoral suicide” for the party in its central London strongholds.
Former chancellor Rachel Reeves last year announced a new council tax surcharge on properties worth more than £2mn and some Labour MPs are anxious that new chancellor John Healey might lower that threshold.
Cutting the threshold to £1.5mn would affect about 160,000 extra properties mainly in London and the South East, according to Tax Policy Associates, a think-tank.
One Labour MP said: “This would be electoral suicide in inner London.”
TPA, founded by Dan Neidle, said cutting the threshold of the “high-value council tax surcharge” to £1.5mn would affect 1,536 properties in the Holborn and St Pancras constituency, where Labour is fighting a by-election next month.
The Treasury is declining to comment on any tax “speculation” ahead of Healey’s first Budget on October 28, including a report in the Times which said the option was being considered.
Most tax rates are reviewed ahead of a Budget, especially when a chancellor needs to raise revenues to fill a fiscal hole. Healey’s Budget has been hit by higher government borrowing costs and the economic fallout of the Iran war.
But widening the scope of a mansion tax before it has even been introduced would be highly controversial and opposed by many Labour MPs, confirming the problems associated with imposing wealth taxes.
Reeves considered setting the threshold at £1.5mn last year but decided to set it at £2mn after representations from Labour MPs in London who said it would hit many people living in regular homes rather than “mansions”.
The Labour MP said that if Healey lowered the threshold to £1.5mn there would be legitimate fears that it might soon be cut further to £1mn.
“Anyone in the £1mn to £1.5mn bracket would immediately feel at risk,” the MP said. “Then you are talking about pretty much every non-flat home in Zones 1 to 3.”
TPA’s Neidle said Prime Minister Andy Burnham “may regard this option as tempting but there is, in our view, a serious downside”.
“Tax systems need stability. Expanding a tax before it’s even been introduced is, in our view, the opposite of stability,” he said.
Another Labour MP said Number 10 had a map showing how many constituencies would be affected by such a change, prepared for Reeves’ last Budget in 2025. “I assume they’ll be sharing it with MPs,” they added.
However, Dame Emily Thornberry, Labour MP for Islington South and Finsbury, said she would be prepared to accept a cut in the mansion tax threshold if it were “the first step” to making the tax system fairer.
“I think that council tax valuations really need updating across the board,” she said. “They are clearly not fair.”
The government first announced the extra annual levy on homes worth more than £2mn last November, starting at £2,500 and rising to £7,500 for homes valued at more than £5mn. It is due to take effect in April 2028.
“As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals,” said a Treasury spokesperson.
Homeowners were expected to be informed about six months before the tax comes into force if their property is liable, giving them the opportunity to challenge the valuation.
The Office for Budget Responsibility estimated that about 165,000 homes would be hit by the tax at a £2mn threshold, or less than 1 per cent of UK properties. It is expected to raise a relatively modest £400mn a year by 2029-30.

rows.title: Burnham hopes to build bridges with Trump at first meeting
rows.content:
Andy Burnham hopes to build bridges with Donald Trump at first meeting
Andy Burnham’s once-fervent criticisms of US President Donald Trump have been dismissed by a UK cabinet member as just “politics” as the two leaders prepare to meet for the first time in New York this week.
As mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham said in 2021 in the wake of the Capitol riots that “any UK politician who gave Trump the time of day should be ashamed right now”, and has also previously described US politics as “poisonous”.
The UK prime minister is expected to meet Trump and other world leaders on the margins of the UN General Assembly on Tuesday amid hopes that common transatlantic interests and personal chemistry will overcome past differences.
Bridget Phillipson, women and equalities minister, referring to Burnham’s previous comments, said: “What you’ve just described there is politics. The president knows that. This is far from unique: people will express views at different points on different topics.”
She told Sky News that this was no bar to having “a strong relationship”, which was crucial when it came to issues such as intelligence sharing, defence and supporting Ukraine in its war against Russia.
Lord Kim Darroch, a former UK ambassador to the US, predicted Burnham could strike a good relationship with Trump, who has fallen out with other European leaders including Italy’s Giorgia Meloni and Germany’s Friedrich Merz.
“Trump will want to take the measure of Andy Burnham,” he told the FT. “For Trump, personal chemistry is much more important than ideology.”
The British side is anxious to ensure the meeting goes smoothly. In 2009, attempts to secure a meeting at the UN between former Labour prime minister Gordon Brown and US president Barack Obama led to a hurried 15-minute conversation in the UN kitchens.
Burnham has said he wants to press the case for the US to help Ukraine with air-defence systems, while the war in Iran and bilateral trade relations are expected to be raised with Trump by the prime minister.
In an attempt to prepare the ground for his meeting with Trump, Burnham hailed a deal between the US and Denmark to resolve their dispute over Greenland.
Burnham and his Danish counterpart Mette Frederiksen spoke on Sunday and “welcomed the US’s commitment to the region”, Downing Street said.
Darroch said that Trump was likely to raise issues with Burnham that he felt strongly about, such as immigration and whether the prime minister was going to approve new North Sea drilling for oil and gas.
Burnham is expected to delay any decision on whether to approve the Jackdaw and Rosebank projects until after next month’s Holborn and St Pancras by-election, where Labour is in a fight with Green Party leader Zack Polanski.
Darroch noted that if Burnham indicated he was minded to approve the projects, Trump might tell the US media, posing a potential diplomatic problem.
Other flashpoints could arise over Trump’s recent comments about UK sovereignty over the Falkland Islands, tensions over the joint US-UK air base at Diego Garcia and UK concerns over the war in the Middle East.
Burnham is also due to meet European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen in New York on Tuesday, a spokesperson for the EU executive arm said. They are preparing for an EU-UK summit this year.
Downing Street, which had explored the possibility of Burnham meeting Trump at the White House during his visit to the US, has yet to confirm the meeting in New York or what other bilateral meetings the prime minister might have during his brief visit to the General Assembly.
Trade relations between the UK and US have stabilised after Trump’s initial tariff onslaught against its partners, according to Duncan Edwards, chief executive of the BritishAmerican Business lobby group.
“Services trade between the US and UK continues to grow and physical trade has been remarkably resilient,” said Edwards. “Companies would prefer the tariffs weren’t there but they have been absorbed into business models and the impact is generally modest.”
But on US investment into the UK, he added, “the natural advantages that the UK has historically had over its regional rivals are narrowing . . . the warning lights are flashing and the government should take note”.
Additional reporting by Andy Bounds in Brussels

rows.title: Fed should defy Trump with rate rise, top economists say
rows.content:
Fed should defy Donald Trump with rate rise, top economists say
The Federal Reserve should face down Donald Trump and raise rates for the first time in more than three years, leading economists said, as they backed chair Kevin Warsh’s view that the central bank must focus on taming inflation.
Wall Street is widely expecting Fed officials to resist Trump’s calls for low borrowing costs and hoist the benchmark federal funds rate by a quarter point at the conclusion of its two-day meeting on Wednesday.
Top academic economists polled by the University of Chicago’s Booth School of Business on behalf of the FT concurred with the market’s outlook, with 50 of 51 respondents saying that borrowing costs should be raised from the current 3.5-3.75 per cent range.
While most economists backed a quarter-point rise, 14 per cent called for a jumbo half-point increase amid fears that a surge in fuel prices triggered by Trump’s war with Tehran will morph into a broader inflation crisis.
“The Fed is significantly behind the curve in terms of raising rates. Inflation has been well above target for years,” said Olivier Coibion, professor at the University of Texas at Austin.
“Inflation is not trending back to the target; if anything, it’s moving in the wrong direction, so policy should be reacting strongly.”
US rate-setters cut borrowing costs three times last year as inflation eased sharply after reaching multi-decade highs following the Covid-19 pandemic. But the Iran war, Trump’s tariffs and the AI boom have dented progress ever since.
The Fed’s preferred headline PCE price index is running at 3.7 per cent, nearly double the central bank’s 2 per cent target. Costs further up supply chains are increasing at an even more rapid rate.
Almost 90 per cent of respondents to the poll do not expect the Fed to hit its 2 per cent goal until at least 2028 despite expectations of higher interest rates.
Stronger price pressures have not deterred Trump’s calls for aggressive rate cuts, with the president calling current borrowing costs “ridiculous”. While Trump is unlikely to cheer a rise in interest rates, National Economic Council director Kevin Hassett has said in recent days that the White House respects the independence of the Fed chair.
Warsh, who was picked by Trump to lead the Fed earlier this year, paved the way for an increase in a late-August address in Jackson Hole, when he said the central bank would have “work to do” unless inflation swiftly showed signs of slowing down to levels consistent with its target.
“The Fed has a dual mandate for low unemployment and low inflation. It’s getting an A — or in the least an A-minus — on low unemployment, and it’s getting a poor grade on inflation,” said Alan Blinder, a former Fed official, now at Princeton. “The Fed hasn’t hit its inflation target in years — it’s pretty clear where the work needs to be done.”
The Fed last hit its 2 per cent inflation goal in early 2021.
Odds on a rate rise rose dramatically after data published last week showed consumer prices jumped 0.4 per cent between July and August, leaving the annual rate of inflation unchanged at 3.4 per cent.
Traders are now pricing in a 95 per cent chance of a quarter-point rise in US borrowing costs — a move that would mark the first increase in US interest rates since July 2023.
Still, Sebnem Kalemli-Ozcan, of Brown University, said she viewed Wednesday’s decision as a 50-50 call. “Warsh could still say that we should wait to see how the data turn out with so much uncertainty. So in that sense, it is also possible that they are not going to hike and keep having the family fight.”
Despite the extent of their concerns over inflation, economists were more sceptical than markets that the Fed will raise rates again over the course of 2026, with a slim majority anticipating one — or fewer — rises.
More than 90 per cent of respondents said they agreed with Warsh’s remarks in August that progress on PCE inflation — which has fallen from its peak of more than 4 per cent in May — has done little to address concerns that underlying inflation remains stubbornly high.
The Jackson Hole speech came after Warsh sparked concern on Wall Street after the US central bank’s July decision, when the Fed chair failed to set out how he intended to bring inflation back under control.
“He needs to prove himself. He needs to prove that he’s willing to do what it takes,” said Jón Steinsson, of the University of California, Berkeley. “If he tries to not raise rates yet again, markets are going to start turning against him.”

rows.title: Bad decisions, difficult incentives and excitable markets
rows.content:
Bad decisions, difficult incentives and excitable markets
It is fair to say that the past week has not been a stellar one in central banking. Some of the errors are self-inflicted and some are the result of unfortunate circumstances, but all complicate life for officials at every level. Performing graceful exits from the following troubles will take some skill.
Bad decisions
Kevin Warsh’s original sin was to refuse to say anything substantive about the US economy after the past two Federal Reserve meetings in June and late July. As other members of the Federal Open Market Committee filled the chasm, that made the Fed chair something of a lame duck. Warsh repaired much of the damage with his Jackson Hole speech but, in doing so, gave more concrete guidance than was sensible: “We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do,” he said.
Since there was only one inflation data point between the Jackson Hole speech and Wednesday’s FOMC meeting, the August consumer price index (CPI) figure developed a prominence it should never have had. Ahead of the CPI data release, many brokers’ notes I received said something along the lines of “if after the CPI data our prediction of US core PCE inflation in the month of August is 0.24 per cent, the Fed will hold, but if it is 0.25 per cent it will have to raise”.
The precision was absurd.
As it turns out, most analysts’ estimates of the August core monthly personal consumption expenditures (PCE) measure of inflation rose after the CPI data release and are now a little over 0.25 per cent. This annualises to something over 3 per cent. For what it is worth, the FT Monetary Policy Radar nowcast of August’s core PCE rate was 0.26 per cent. If you use the longstanding Cleveland Fed nowcasts of 0.27 per cent in August and 0.28 per cent in September, this creates a time series for underlying PCE inflation that is edging gradually higher.
The perfectly rational case for a US rate rise on Wednesday, therefore, is that broad underlying inflation has been too high for too long and is showing few signs of moderating at a time when the federal funds rate of between 3.5 and 3.75 per cent is not obviously restraining the economy.
It would also have been rational to point out that some of the inflation strength in Friday’s CPI figure depended on volatile items such as telecoms services and airfares. That information would have helped the case for a hold.
But the decisions to say nothing in June and July and the subsequent hawkish bravado at Jackson Hole make holding rates a much harder prospect now. Warsh’s choice is pretty clear: raise rates or watch his credibility crumble.
Horrible incentives
September’s FOMC decision is, however, a breeze compared with the bind the Fed would encounter if the Republicans win both houses of Congress and President Donald Trump fulfils his promise to send a $5,000 cheque to every US adult. While opinion polls suggest the administration will not hold on to both houses, the giveaway pledge would represent a fiscal stimulus of roughly 3 per cent of US GDP.
The offer to voters is far larger than the combined three rounds of Covid-19 pandemic stimulus cheques or the projected primary deficit in 2027. It dwarfs the cost of extending Obamacare subsidies.
It should go without saying to this sophisticated audience that the effect of cheques on spending depends on how much liquid savings households have in aggregate and the proportion of households that face immediate financial constraints. Most of the research on the pandemic cheques says that households spent much more of the first cheque than the later instalments because of changed constraint profiles.
But such is the proposed size and irresponsibility of Trump’s offer that the Fed would shred its reputation if it did not respond with higher rates. I am sure if he is asked on Wednesday, Warsh will say this is all far too hypothetical to talk about.
Excitable markets
Across the Atlantic, the European Central Bank ended its run of having its meetings go exactly to plan. There was never any doubt about the result: the main Eurozone interest rate was raised a quarter point to 2.5 per cent; ECB president Christine Lagarde said the central bank was “not pre-committing to a particular path” for interest rates and that decisions would be data dependent.
The forecasts, shown below, reinforced the message. They showed Eurozone inflation broadly coming back to target, conditional on interest rates reaching 3 per cent. The inflation forecast was a little higher than in June, as was the assumed interest rate.
Financial markets, however, decided that the ECB would now be keen to raise interest rates rapidly. They are now expecting another three or four increases by the end of 2027. It is all a bit excitable.
Someone has a book to sell
Finally, Lagarde was asked when she would step down as ECB president and had nothing to add to her previous comments that she would at least serve to the end of this year. She was also asked about her autobiography, which has a publication date of January 28, 2027. She said she would promote the book at the weekend or on days of leave from the ECB.
We should not be too po-faced about this. I don’t think publishing a book is entirely incompatible with remaining ECB president. But it is a terrible look that suggests Lagarde thinks she is more important than the institution she leads. I am sure she has more regard for the ECB than that, so will predict now that she will no longer be in post by January 28. The bartering over all the ECB jobs has already started, the FT reported yesterday.
I would be disappointed to be wrong.
What I’ve been reading and watching
- The FT previews Thursday’s rate decisions at the Bank of Japan and Bank of England.
- What we can learn from a practical central banker. A tribute by Huw van Steenis to Charles Goodhart, who turns 90 next month.
- As US government 10-year borrowing costs hover just below 5 per cent, I spoke to Ruchir Sharma on what to fear if they keep rising.
- I lost my patience with all the memes and armchair philosophers who have not looked at European employment trends.
One last chart
The International Energy Agency published its ever-useful monthly oil market report on Friday. The chart below shows the underlying predicament we face.
The year started with abundant energy inventories. One reason energy prices have risen less than many feared when Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz is that the world has sensibly run down those stocks.
Inventories are now at normal levels. Expect energy prices to be more volatile in the future.
Central Banks is edited by Harvey Nriapia

rows.title: BPRE’s extremely large, very huge, getting-bigger NAV discount
rows.content:
BPRE’s extremely large, very huge, getting-bigger NAV discount
Last December, Alphaville gawped at the stock market debut of the Bluerock Private Real Estate Fund, which was being converted from a so-called “interval fund” to a listed one to let investors exit without forcing a fire sale of its assets.
BPRE promptly puked, ending its first day at $14.7 a share — compared to its estimated net asset value of $24.36. This raised pretty awkward questions about the realism of the marks on the underlying properties, and how private marks in general might be a tad optimistic.
At the time, BPRE’s CEO Ramin Kamfar told us that this sharp discount was “temporary and event-driven as shares exchange hands from pent-up sellers to willing buyers”:
BPRE’s early discount to NAV tracks the same experience that you can see if you research other comparable funds that have listed — ie, that they generally open trading at a discount, but that the discount closes to NAV over a reasonable period of time as the pricing more closely converges with the value of the fund’s underlying assets. That dynamic is because selling demand immediately presents itself upon listing, but buying demand generally plays out over time as sophisticated investors wait out peak selling to try to purchase at the most attractive market bottom price. And then as the fund’s shares trade out of pent-up sellers’ hands to willing buyers, the fund discount closes over time.
. . . We expected — and communicated to the market — that they should expect BPRE will trade at a discount in the early period post-listing, but that the discount should likely close over the next several quarters as willing buyers take over from willing sellers.
Which was fair enough. The first day of trading — when any frustrated investor who wanted to exit could suddenly do so — was too short a time period to make overly confident predictions.
But we now have a few more quarters to judge, and, well, those willing sellers still seem to sharply outnumber the willing buyers.
In fact, the gap between the value that public markets actually ascribe to BPRE and its own estimated valuation is even wider than it was when it listed.
Here’s what that looks like as a plain NAV discount. Even by the standards of investment trusts, closed-end funds and the like, this is pretty remarkable. Investors are basically saying BPRE is worth almost half of what it says it’s worth.
Unsurprisingly, this persistent and widening discount has attracted attention from the types of investors that Bluerock probably doesn’t want on BPRE’s shareholder registry.
Boaz Weinstein’s Saba Capital — appetite apparently whetted by his UK trust adventures — quietly accumulated 6.7mn shares in BPRE over the summer, according to its latest 13-F regulatory filing.
